JavaScript Mastery

JavaScript is the language that makes web pages do things: react to a click, fetch data, update what you see. This course teaches it from the bottom up, starting with how values work, because most of JavaScript's famous surprises come from there. It covers the coercion rules (how JavaScript silently converts one type into another), scope and closures (which variables a function can see, and keep), the five rules that decide what this means, the prototypes hiding underneath the class keyword, text stored as UTF-16 (a way of encoding characters that sometimes uses two slots for one), the event loop with its two queues (the scheduler that decides what code runs next), and the DOM and the rendering path (how a page is represented in memory and drawn on screen). It ends with the rest of the browser platform, modules, and the tools that ship code to users.

How to use this course

  • This course is the third step of the web front end. The HTML course covers the document, and the CSS course covers how it looks. This one covers behaviour: what the page does. Two courses build on this one. TypeScript adds a layer of types on top of the JavaScript taught here, and React adds a way of building pages from components on top of both. Neither makes sense without the language running underneath, which is why this course comes first.
  • It assumes HTML and some programming experience. It does not assume you have written JavaScript seriously before. §1 starts with what the language is, who controls its definition, and the four quite different environments it runs in.
  • Everything here was run. Language examples were executed under Node 24. DOM examples ran under jsdom, a program that imitates a browser window. Every printed result is what the runtime really produced, and each example was run twice and the two results compared. Several of them contradict the answer that is widely published: process.nextTick does not always win, and cloneNode does copy a typed input's value. Those results were kept rather than tidied.
  • The authority is MDN and the running engine. The syllabus was derived from the MDN JavaScript Guide and Reference and from the Web API interface pages, fetched on 2026-08-31. Where browser support matters, the course says whether a feature is Baseline, meaning it works in all the major current browsers, rather than guessing.
  • The course has two halves and a capstone. The capstone is a final project that uses everything.
  • §1–§14 are the language: values and coercion, scope and closures, functions and this, objects and prototypes, collections, text and regular expressions, numbers and dates, iterators, asynchrony (code that waits for something without stopping everything else), errors and modules.
  • §15–§17 are the browser platform: the DOM and the rendering path, events and forms, then network, storage, workers and components.
  • §18 builds a real application and then hardens it.
  • Each section has numbered subsections, runnable examples with their real output, and exercises with worked solutions. Do the exercises before opening the solutions. Several are built so that the obvious answer is the wrong one.

You need Node and a browser with developer tools. Check the Node version before starting, because several sections use features that only recent releases ship:

node --version    # v24 or newer

Versions every example in this course was produced against: Node 24 · jsdom 26.1.0.

What you are actually learning

Not a list of methods. Five mechanisms, each of which explains a large group of behaviour that otherwise looks random:

  1. The value model. JavaScript has eight types and eight falsy values (values that count as false in an if). When types are mixed, it converts them with an algorithm you can follow by hand. That is why [] == false is true after three conversions. 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 because numbers follow IEEE 754, the standard for storing decimals in binary, which cannot hold 0.1 exactly. And an id above 2⁵³ arrives from JSON.parse already corrupted, because that is where whole numbers stop being exact. §2 makes all of these things you can work out instead of things you must memorise.
  2. Bindings and what they keep alive. A binding is a name attached to a value. §3 covers scope, closures and the temporal dead zone (the stretch of code where a let variable exists but cannot be used yet). §5 covers the five this rules, applied in a fixed order. Memory leaks take four common shapes: a listener never removed, a detached node, a cache that is never pruned, and a timer that is never cleared. All four are the same mistake: a reference someone forgot they were holding.
  3. The object model. Every object has one link to another object, its prototype, and there is one rule for looking up a property along those links. class, extends, super and instanceof are all just arrangements of that one link (§6–§7). Seeing through the syntax is what makes the error messages readable.
  4. The event loop. JavaScript runs one task, then every microtask (small follow-up jobs, such as the code after an await), then perhaps draws a frame (§12). Once that order is in your head, several classic bugs stop being surprises: await inside forEach, awaits written one after another that should have been one Promise.all, and cancelling work with AbortController.
  5. The rendering path. What the DOM is, and what it costs to read layout information such as an element's size. Interleaving those reads with writes measured 17.6× slower than batching them (§15). This is the difference between an interface that is correct and one that is correct and fast.

By the end you should be able to predict what a piece of JavaScript will do before running it, and explain the cases where it does something else. You should be able to ship browser code that is correct, that uses the platform's own tools for validating forms and cancelling work, and that is free of the classic leaks, all without looking anything up.

SECTION 1

The Language and Its Runtimes

JavaScript is unusual among programming languages in three ways:

  • Nobody owns it. A committee writes its definition, and several companies build the programs that run it.
  • It runs in at least four quite different environments, from a browser tab to a server.
  • It changes every year, on a fixed schedule.

Those three facts explain most of what is otherwise confusing about the ecosystem. They explain why there is a "specification" (the written definition of the language) separate from any implementation (a program that actually runs it). They explain why a feature works in one place and not another, and why your code is often compiled, meaning converted by a tool, before anyone runs it. And they explain why "is this available yet?" is a question with a real, checkable answer rather than a matter of opinion.

This section is the orientation the rest of the course assumes. It covers:

  • what the language actually is, and who decides what goes into it;
  • how source text becomes running code;
  • the two script modes, strict and sloppy, and why one of them is effectively gone;
  • the environments the language runs in;
  • the tooling that sits between what you write and what executes.

It ends with the practical skill that ties them together: deciding whether a feature is safe to use from data rather than from memory.

None of it is trivia. Every item here changes a decision you will make in the first hour of a project.

1.1 ECMAScript, TC39 and the Yearly Release

The language is defined by the ECMAScript specification, a long document published by Ecma International under the name ECMA-262. "JavaScript" is the everyday name, and ECMAScript is the name of the standard. The two names exist mostly for trademark reasons, but the distinction is useful. ECMAScript defines the language itself and says nothing about the DOM, fetch or the file system. All of those are supplied by a host, the environment the code runs in (§1.7).

TC39 is the committee that maintains the standard. Its members are delegates from browser makers, runtimes, large companies that use the language, and invited experts. It meets several times a year and decides by consensus, meaning a proposal goes forward only when nobody objects. Anyone can follow the process, and the proposals are public on GitHub.

Every new idea passes through numbered stages. A proposal stage tells you how far an idea has travelled, and knowing the scale tells you whether to use something yet:

Stage 0
An idea. No commitment of any kind.
Stage 1
The committee is willing to spend time on the problem. The shape will change.
Stage 2
A draft specification exists. Stage 2.7 adds "and the tests are written and approved".
Stage 3
Candidate. Implementations are expected; the syntax is unlikely to change but still can. This is the earliest stage worth using behind a transpiler.
Stage 4
Finished. Two independent implementations ship it, and it enters the next yearly edition.

Since 2015 there has been one edition a year, named by its year. ES2015, still widely called ES6, was the enormous one: it added let, const, classes, modules, arrow functions, promises, Map, Set and template literals. Every edition since has been small by comparison, and that is deliberate. A feature ships when it is ready and joins whichever yearly edition comes next, rather than holding up a release.

The practical consequence is that "ES6" is not a meaningful compatibility target in 2026. Every environment you are likely to support has all of ES2015 and most of what came after. The real question is whether one particular feature is supported, and §1.11 shows how to answer it.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: the ecmascript specification and a proposal stage.

1.2 Engines

A JavaScript engine is the program that reads your source text and runs it. Three engines matter, and they are independent implementations of the same specification: V8 (used by Chromium, Node, Deno and Edge), SpiderMonkey (Firefox) and JavaScriptCore (Safari and Bun).

An engine is not an interpreter in the simple sense of reading one line and doing it. The modern design is a pipeline of stages:

console.log('this engine reports itself as:', typeof process !== 'undefined' ? 'a Node-like runtime' : 'a browser');
console.log('and the language version is not something you query — features are:',
  typeof structuredClone === 'function' ? 'structuredClone exists' : 'it does not');

this engine reports itself as: a Node-like runtime
and the language version is not something you query — features are: structuredClone exists

Here is what happens, step by step:

  1. The source is parsed into an abstract syntax tree, a tree-shaped representation of the code's structure.
  2. The tree is compiled to bytecode, a compact list of simple instructions, and the bytecode is interpreted (run step by step).
  3. Code that runs often is compiled again by an optimising compiler, this time into machine code the processor runs directly. That compiler relies on assumptions about the values it has actually seen so far.

That is just-in-time compilation: compiling while the program runs rather than ahead of time. One consequence is worth carrying into everyday work: the optimiser assumes stability. A function that is always called with numbers gets fast code. If the same function is later called with strings, it is deoptimised, sent back to slower bytecode. In the same way, objects created with the same properties in the same order share an internal shape and are fast to access, while objects built up in different ways are not.

That is honestly as far as the practical advice goes. Fine-tuning your code for one specific engine is a losing game, because the engine's internal rules change between releases. Writing consistent, monomorphic code, where each function sees one kind of value, costs nothing and helps every engine.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: a javascript engine, v8 and just-in-time compilation.

1.3 From Text to Tokens

The lexical grammar is the first stage of reading code: the rules for how characters are grouped into tokens, the smallest meaningful pieces, such as a name, a number or a +. Three of its rules produce behaviour you can see.

The parser turns those tokens into a sequence of statements. The commonest kind is an expression statement: an expression evaluated for its effect, such as a function call or an assignment. An expression statement may not begin with { or function, because those would start a block and a declaration instead. That is why an IIFE (a function expression that is called immediately) needs parentheses around it (§3.6).

Source is Unicode, so identifiers (the names you give variables and functions) may contain far more than English letters. Identifier syntax allows letters from any writing system, $, _, and digits anywhere after the first character:

const $ = 'dollar', _private = 'underscore', café = 'accented', 日本語 = 'any script';
console.log([$, _private, café, 日本語].join(' | '));
console.log('but not a leading digit, and not a hyphen:',
  (() => { try { eval('const 1x = 1'); return 'allowed'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());

dollar | underscore | accented | any script
but not a leading digit, and not a hyphen: SyntaxError

A reserved word is a word the language keeps for itself, so it cannot be used as an identifier. The list is longer than most people think, and part of it depends on the mode:

const results = [];
for (const word of ['class', 'enum', 'await', 'let', 'static', 'implements', 'yield']) {
  try {
    eval(`var ${word} = 1;`);
    results.push(`${word}=ok`);
  } catch (e) {
    results.push(`${word}=${e.constructor.name}`);
  }
}
console.log(results.join(' '));

class=SyntaxError enum=SyntaxError await=ok let=SyntaxError static=SyntaxError implements=SyntaxError yield=SyntaxError

Six of the seven are rejected, and the exception is instructive. class and enum are reserved everywhere. enum is reserved even though the language has never used it; it has been kept in reserve since 1999. let, static, implements and yield are reserved only in strict-mode code, and a module is always strict (§1.5). So in a sloppy script, all four of them are legal variable names.

await came back ok, because it is reserved only at the top level of a module and inside an async function, and the eval above runs in a nested scope. That is the most fine-grained reservation in the language. It is why await can still be a variable name inside a plain function in a module, and why the same file can be valid as a script and invalid as a module.

To have in hand before moving on: the lexical grammar, identifier syntax, a reserved word and an iife.

1.4 Automatic Semicolon Insertion

Automatic semicolon insertion (ASI) means the parser adds a semicolon for you where a statement cannot continue. That does not make semicolons optional. It is a set of rules, and the rules have exceptions.

function returnsUndefined() {
  return
  42;                                   // unreachable — ASI ended the statement above
}
console.log('a newline after return:', returnsUndefined());

const a = 1
const b = 2
console.log('between ordinary statements it is harmless:', a + b);

a newline after return: undefined
between ordinary statements it is harmless: 3

The rule to know is that return, throw, break, continue and yield cannot be followed by a newline before their operand. If they are, the parser inserts a semicolon immediately. So return on a line of its own always returns undefined, silently, with no warning.

The other hazard is the reverse. A line that starts with (, [, `, +, - or / continues the previous line instead of beginning a new statement.

const value = 5
const doubled = value
console.log('two statements, as intended:', doubled)
const list = [1, 2]
console.log('but a line starting with [ would continue the previous one, so this fails:',
  (() => { try { eval('const x = 1\n[1].forEach(() => {})'); return 'ok'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());

two statements, as intended: 5
but a line starting with [ would continue the previous one, so this fails: TypeError

const x = 1\n[1] is parsed as const x = 1[1], which means "index into the number 1". That gives undefined, and calling .forEach on undefined is a TypeError.

The settled advice is to pick a style and let a formatter enforce it (§14.14). Writing semicolons everywhere avoids the second hazard entirely. The no-semicolon style is also fine with Prettier, a formatter that adds a leading semicolon to any line that needs one. What does not work is deciding case by case.

1.5 Strict Mode

Strict mode changes about a dozen behaviours, all in the direction of making mistakes loud instead of silent. Sloppy mode is the original behaviour, kept forever so that old code keeps working.

console.log('in a module, this is undefined rather than globalThis:',
  (function () { return this; })() === undefined);
console.log('assigning to an undeclared name throws:',
  (() => { try { eval('undeclaredName = 1'); return 'created a global'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());
console.log('duplicate parameters are a SyntaxError:',
  (() => { try { eval('(function (a, a) {})'); return 'allowed'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());
console.log('writing to a frozen object throws:',
  (() => { const o = Object.freeze({ a: 1 }); try { o.a = 2; return 'silent'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());
console.log('octal literals like 0755 are rejected:',
  (() => { try { eval('const n = 0755'); return 'allowed'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());

in a module, this is undefined rather than globalThis: true
assigning to an undeclared name throws: ReferenceError
duplicate parameters are a SyntaxError: SyntaxError
writing to a frozen object throws: TypeError
octal literals like 0755 are rejected: SyntaxError

The first two are the most important. Sloppy mode creates a global from a typo: usre = 1 inside a function silently creates globalThis.usre, while strict mode makes it a ReferenceError. And a this of undefined instead of the global object means a method called without its object fails immediately, instead of silently writing to window (§5.11).

You almost never write 'use strict' any more, because a module is always strict, and so is every class body. The directive only matters in a classic script or a CommonJS file. In practice, then, a file's mode is decided by how the file is loaded, not by what is written in it.

1.6 Scripts and Modules

A classic script and a module are two different parse goals: two different sets of rules for reading the same text. The same text can be valid as one and invalid as the other.

a classic script
Sloppy by default. Top-level var becomes a global property. Shares one scope with every other script. Blocks the parser unless deferred.
a module
Always strict. Its own scope. Deferred automatically. Executes once. Can import and use top-level await.

In HTML, <script type="module"> chooses the module rules. For a classic script, two attributes control when it runs:

// <script src="a.js"></script>                  blocks parsing while it downloads and runs
// <script defer src="a.js"></script>            downloads in parallel, runs after parsing, IN ORDER
// <script async src="a.js"></script>            downloads in parallel, runs as soon as it arrives
// <script type="module" src="a.js"></script>    deferred by default
console.log('the ordering guarantee is the difference between defer and async');

the ordering guarantee is the difference between defer and async

The defer attribute keeps document order. Several deferred scripts run in the order they appear in the page, after the HTML has been parsed and before DOMContentLoaded fires. The async script attribute makes no promise about order at all: whichever script finishes downloading first runs first. That suits an independent analytics tag and breaks anything that depends on another script.

A module behaves like defer without being asked, which is one more reason modules are the default for new work.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: the defer attribute, the async script attribute and top-level await.

1.7 Hosts and Runtimes

A host environment is the program that runs JavaScript and supplies everything ECMAScript does not: a global object, an event loop (§12.2), and APIs. The language is the same in every host; the surroundings are not.

const has = (name) => typeof globalThis[name] !== 'undefined';
console.log('language built-ins are always present:', typeof Promise, typeof Map, typeof Intl);
console.log('host APIs are looked up on the global:',
  ['fetch', 'setTimeout', 'queueMicrotask'].map(n => `${n}=${has(n)}`).join(' '));
console.log('a name this host does not provide is simply absent:', has('NoSuchApi'));
console.log('globalThis is the portable spelling of the global object:', typeof globalThis);

language built-ins are always present: function function object
host APIs are looked up on the global: fetch=true setTimeout=true queueMicrotask=true
a name this host does not provide is simply absent: false
globalThis is the portable spelling of the global object: object

Every name in that check is a host API rather than part of the language: none of fetch, setTimeout or queueMicrotask appears in the ECMAScript specification. They are present here because this runtime provides them. A name the runtime does not provide is simply absent, and that absence is the whole mechanism behind feature detection (§1.11).

the browser runtime
The global is the window object. Adds the DOM (§15), events (§16), fetch, storage and workers (§17). Sandboxed: no file system, no arbitrary sockets.
Node.js
Server-side. Adds node:fs, node:http, node:crypto and the rest; no DOM. The global is globalThis, and process carries the environment.
the Deno and Bun runtimes
Deno is permission-based and TypeScript-first; Bun optimises for startup and bundles a package manager and test runner. Both aim at web-standard APIs where Node historically invented its own.
edge and embedded
Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy and similar expose a browser-like subset. No file system, and often no long-lived state.

The hosts have been growing more alike, and you can rely on that. fetch, URL, AbortController, TextEncoder, structuredClone and Web Streams now exist in every one of them, so code written against those runs almost anywhere.

In summary, the vocabulary here is a host environment, the browser runtime, Node.js, the deno and bun runtimes and the window object.

1.8 An Execution Context

An execution context is the internal record the engine keeps for each piece of running code. It notes which variable environment the code uses, what this is, and, for a module, the module's own record. Contexts stack on top of each other as functions call functions, and that stack is the call stack of §12.1.

You never handle an execution context directly. The term is still worth knowing, because the specification and every deep explanation use it. Three practical facts you have already met come from it:

  • Each function call creates a new context, which is why each closure captures its own variables (§3.7).
  • this belongs to the context, which is why it changes depending on how a function is called (§5.11).
  • A module's context is created before its body runs, which is what makes hoisting and the TDZ possible (§3.3).

1.9 The Console and the REPL

console.log() is the first tool everyone learns, and it does more than most people use.

console.log('multiple arguments are joined with a space:', 1, true, null);
console.log('a %s specifier and a %d one are substituted in place:', 'string', 42);
console.log('objects are expandable in devtools, and stringified in a terminal:', { a: [1, 2] });
console.log('console.time("label") … console.timeEnd("label") prints an elapsed span');

multiple arguments are joined with a space: 1 true null
a string specifier and a 42 one are substituted in place:
objects are expandable in devtools, and stringified in a terminal: { a: [ 1, 2 ] }
console.time("label") … console.timeEnd("label") prints an elapsed span

Read the second line carefully. %s and %d are format specifiers: placeholders that are replaced by the arguments, rather than printed alongside them. So the arguments disappear from where they would otherwise appear, and the sentence reads oddly. That is how format specifiers are meant to work, and it is also why they are easy to misuse: an unintended %s silently swallows the next argument.

console.time() starts a timer with a label, and console.time()'s partner timeEnd prints how long has passed. It is deliberately not run here. Its output is a duration, so it is different every time, and that is exactly why a timing call cannot be checked automatically against a fixed expected output (§12.13).

The browser devtools are where most JavaScript is actually debugged. They include a console that runs code inside the page, a sources panel with breakpoints (§13.9), a network panel, and an elements panel showing the live DOM (§15.1). Two shortcuts are worth learning: $0 in the console refers to the element currently selected in the elements panel, and $$('.sel') is short for Array.from(document.querySelectorAll(...)).

The Node REPL (read-eval-print loop: an interactive prompt you get by running node with no arguments) is the fastest way to check a language question. By default it runs in sloppy CommonJS mode. Remember that when a strict-mode behaviour seems not to reproduce; node --input-type=module gets module behaviour instead.

What to carry forward from this subsection: console.log(), the browser devtools and the node repl.

1.10 Transpilation and Polyfills

These are two different problems, solved by two different tools. Mixing them up is a common reason a build ships broken code.

Transpilation converts syntax the target does not understand into syntax it does: optional chaining into a plain conditional, for example, or a class field into an assignment inside the constructor. Babel is the standard tool, and TypeScript, esbuild and SWC can all do it too.

A polyfill supplies a missing API while the program runs, by defining it when it is absent. Syntax cannot be polyfilled, and APIs cannot be transpiled:

// The shape of a correct polyfill: feature-detect, then define.
if (!('groupBy' in Object)) {
  Object.defineProperty(Object, 'groupBy', {
    value(items, keyFn) {
      const out = Object.create(null);
      let i = 0;
      for (const item of items) (out[keyFn(item, i++)] ??= []).push(item);
      return out;
    },
    writable: true, configurable: true, enumerable: false,   // matching a built-in
  });
}
console.log('Object.groupBy is present either way:', typeof Object.groupBy);
console.log(JSON.stringify(Object.groupBy([1, 2, 3, 4], n => (n % 2 ? 'odd' : 'even'))));

Object.groupBy is present either way: function
{"odd":[1,3],"even":[2,4]}

Three details make that a correct polyfill rather than an approximation:

  • It feature-detects before defining, so a native implementation always wins.
  • It uses defineProperty with enumerable: false, so the addition does not show up in a for...in loop over Object (§6.6). Writing Object.groupBy = … instead would make it enumerable, unlike every built-in.
  • It matches the real behaviour, including the result object having no prototype (§6.10).

The usual arrangement is a browserslist entry in package.json that names the browsers you support. Babel and core-js read it and include exactly the transforms and polyfills those browsers need. Setting the list too broadly has a real cost: larger, slower output for browsers nobody uses.

The terms above, gathered: esbuild.

1.11 Feature Detection and Baseline

Feature detection means asking the runtime what it can do, by checking whether a name exists. It replaces user-agent sniffing (reading the browser's name and version string). That was always unreliable and is now actively misleading, because browsers deliberately freeze and fake their strings.

const checks = {
  'a global':        typeof structuredClone === 'function',
  'a static method': typeof Object.groupBy === 'function',
  'an instance method': typeof Array.prototype.toSorted === 'function',
  'a property on an object': 'signal' in AbortSignal,
};
for (const [what, ok] of Object.entries(checks)) console.log(`${what.padEnd(24)} ${ok}`);
console.log('syntax cannot be detected this way — it must be parsed, so:',
  (() => { try { eval('class C { #x; }'); return 'supported'; } catch { return 'unsupported'; } })());

a global                 true
a static method          true
an instance method       true
a property on an object  false
syntax cannot be detected this way — it must be parsed, so: supported

The last line shows the difference that matters. An API is detectable and syntax is not. A file containing syntax the engine does not support fails to parse entirely, before any check inside it can run. That is why new syntax needs a build step, or a separate file loaded only when supported, while a new API needs only an if.

Baseline status is the vocabulary the web platform now uses for "is this safe to use?". It is a published dataset, not an opinion:

Limited
Not in all three engines. Needs a fallback or a polyfill.
Newly available
In Chromium, Firefox and Safari — as of a stated date. Safe for users on current browsers.
Widely available
Newly available plus 30 months. Safe without qualification for almost every audience.

The data is on every MDN page and in the web-features package. That means a lint rule or a CI check (an automatic check on every change) can enforce a Baseline target, instead of relying on someone noticing in review. The habit worth forming: when reaching for something recent, look it up rather than recalling it. This course did exactly that for Temporal in §10.4. It found that Temporal is in Chromium and Firefox and not yet in Safari, which changes the advice from "use it" to "use it behind the official polyfill".

One line each, for reference: baseline status.

1.12 What This Section Established

  1. ECMAScript is the language, and a host supplies everything else — the DOM, fetch and the file system are not in the specification.
  2. TC39 works in five stages, and Stage 3 is the earliest worth using behind a transpiler; Stage 4 means two shipping implementations.
  3. "ES6" is not a useful target in 2026. The question is per-feature, and it has a checkable answer.
  4. JIT compilation optimises on observed stability, so consistent types and consistent object shapes are the only engine-level advice worth following.
  5. Identifiers allow any script, and every one of class, enum, await, let, static, implements and yield is reserved in module code — several of them are not in a sloppy script.
  6. ASI is a set of rules, not optionality. return followed by a newline returns undefined, and a line starting with [ or ( continues the previous one.
  7. A module is always strict, and so is a class body, so 'use strict' is now only for scripts and CommonJS. Strict mode turns a typo'd global into a ReferenceError and a detached this into undefined.
  8. defer preserves document order and async does not; a module is deferred automatically.
  9. globalThis is the portable global, and the same code sees different APIs in a browser, in Node, in Deno or Bun, and at the edge — with fetch, URL and AbortController common to all.
  10. Transpilation is for syntax and a polyfill is for an API, and neither substitutes for the other.
  11. An API is feature-detectable and syntax is not, because unsupported syntax fails the whole parse before any check can run.
  12. A correct polyfill detects first and defines non-enumerably, so a native implementation wins and the addition is indistinguishable from a built-in.
  13. Baseline is data, not opinion — Limited, Newly available, Widely available — and the habit is to look a recent feature up rather than recall it.

Exercises

1. Explain what each does and why.

// a
function f() {
  return
    { ok: true };
}
// b
const x = 1
;[1, 2].forEach(n => n)
// c
'use strict';
undeclared = 1;
// d
if (typeof Array.prototype.groupBy === 'function') { /* … */ }
// e
if (someCondition) { class C { #private = 1; } }
Solution

(a) returns undefined. ASI inserts a semicolon immediately after return, because a newline may not separate return from its operand (§1.4). The object literal below is unreachable, and — worse — it is parsed as a block containing a labelled statement ok: true, so it is not even a syntax error. The fix is to put { on the same line as return.

(b) works, and the leading semicolon is why. Without it, const x = 1 followed by a line starting with [ would parse as const x = 1[1, 2].forEach(...). The defensive leading ; is the convention in semicolon-free codebases, and Prettier inserts it automatically.

(c) throws a ReferenceError. In strict mode an assignment to an undeclared name does not create a global (§1.5). Note the directive must be the first statement in the file or function to take effect — a comment above it is fine, any code above it is not, and in a module it is redundant because modules are always strict.

(d) is always false, and that is the bug. The method is Object.groupBy, a static on Object, not Array.prototype.groupBy (§6.10). A feature detection that names the wrong thing silently disables the feature forever rather than failing loudly — which is the specific hazard of detection code: it always runs, and a wrong check looks exactly like an unsupported environment.

(e) fails to parse in an environment without private fields — the whole file, not just this branch. Syntax is checked at parse time, so guarding it with a condition achieves nothing (§1.11). The workarounds are a build step that transpiles the syntax away, or moving the code to a separate module loaded with dynamic import() (§14.6) so its parse failure is a rejected promise rather than a dead file.

2. You are starting a new project in 2026. Which of var, 'use strict', Babel, a polyfill library and defer do you need, and why?

Solution

var — no. let and const are block-scoped, give a temporal dead zone instead of a silent undefined, and cannot be redeclared (§3.1). There is no situation in new code where var is the better choice; the only reason to know it is to read existing code.

'use strict' — no. Every module and every class body is strict already (§1.5). Writing the directive in a module is harmless and misleading, because it suggests the file might not have been strict otherwise. The one place it is still required is a CommonJS file or a classic script, and a new project should have neither.

Babel — probably not, and this is the answer that has changed. Babel exists to transform syntax for targets that lack it, and current browsers have essentially all of it. What a new project does need is a bundler (§14.13), and Vite or esbuild handles the small amount of down-levelling that remains. The cases where Babel is still the right tool are narrow: a Stage 3 proposal you want early, a custom transform, or a genuine requirement to support a browser several years old.

A polyfill library — measure first, then only what is missing. Importing all of core-js unconditionally adds tens of kilobytes for APIs your users' browsers already have. The right arrangement is browserslist naming the actual targets and letting the toolchain include exactly the polyfills those targets need (§1.10). For a single missing API, the fifteen-line feature-detected polyfill of §1.10 is smaller and clearer than a dependency.

defer — no, because you should be using modules, which are deferred automatically (§1.6). <script type="module" src="app.js"> gives you deferred execution, strict mode, its own scope and import in one attribute. defer remains relevant only for a classic script you cannot convert.

The pattern across all five: each was a necessary workaround for a constraint that no longer applies, and each carries a cost — var costs correctness, 'use strict' costs clarity, Babel and a blanket polyfill cost build time and bytes, defer costs the module system. The right question for any of them is not "is it harmful" but "what would I lose by removing it", and in 2026 the answer for all five is "nothing".

What a new project does need, by contrast: a bundler, a linter, a formatter, a test runner and a CI pipeline (§14.17) — none of which are compatibility workarounds.

3. A feature works in Chrome and fails in Safari. Describe how you would establish what is wrong and what to do.

Solution

First, get the actual error rather than the report. "Fails in Safari" is a symptom. Connect Safari's Web Inspector — from a Mac via Develop ▸ device, or from any machine using a real Safari in a browser-testing service — and read the console. The error type immediately splits the problem in two.

A SyntaxError means the file did not parse, which is a syntax-support problem (§1.11). The whole module failed, so nothing in it ran — which is why the symptom is often "the entire feature is missing" rather than one broken function. The fix is a build target that down-levels that syntax, and the diagnosis is to check the syntax against MDN's baseline data.

A TypeError of the form "undefined is not a function" means a missing API. That is the polyfillable case, and the fix is a feature-detected polyfill or a fallback path (§1.10).

Anything else — a wrong value, a layout difference, an event not firing — is a behavioural difference, not a support gap, and is the hardest of the three because both engines are running your code successfully.

Second, confirm it against data rather than guessing. Look the feature up on MDN and read its baseline record: which engines, from which version, and whether it is Limited, Newly available or Widely available (§1.11). This is the step that turns "Safari is broken" into "this is Baseline Limited; Safari has not shipped it", which is a different and actionable statement. This course did exactly that for Temporal (§10.4) and for Math.sumPrecise (§10.1), and in both cases the published data contradicted what a reasonable person might have assumed.

Third, choose the response deliberately, in order of preference.

Do without it, if there is a well-supported equivalent. This is more often available than people expect and costs nothing afterwards.

Feature-detect and provide a fallback — the enhancement runs where it works and the plain version runs elsewhere. document.startViewTransition in §15.14 is the model: a two-line guard, and the fallback is a page that simply does not animate.

Polyfill it, if it is an API and a faithful polyfill exists. Check the polyfill's own caveats; several common ones are approximations.

Transpile it, if it is syntax. This means a build step and a bundle-size cost, so it is the answer when the feature is load-bearing.

Fourth — and this is the step most often skipped — add it to the test matrix. The bug reached a user because nothing checked Safari. A Playwright project running against WebKit in CI (§14.16) catches the next one before release, and it is the only one of these steps that prevents recurrence rather than fixing an instance.

What I would not do: branch on the user-agent string. It is unreliable by design (§1.11), it breaks when the browser updates, and it fixes the symptom for one browser rather than the class of problem.

SECTION 2

Values, Types and Coercion

JavaScript's reputation for strangeness comes almost entirely from this section. [] + {} is "[object Object]", "0" == false is true, 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3, and typeof null is "object". Each of those is a punchline in some conference talk. Each is also the specified, intended behaviour of a small set of rules that fit on a page.

The rules are worth learning properly rather than avoiding, for a practical reason: the rules that produce funny results also produce serious bugs. For example:

  • a price compared with == against a string;
  • a total that is off by a hundredth of a penny;
  • an id above 2⁵³ that silently becomes impossible to tell apart from the next one;
  • a NaN (the "not a number" value) that passes through six functions before anyone notices.

None of those look funny in production.

This section covers the types a value can have, the conversion rules that move a value from one type to another (called coercion), and how numbers are stored underneath. It ends with the two serialisation formats, JSON and structured clone. Serialisation means turning a value into a form that can be stored or sent and rebuilt later, and these two formats decide what survives that round trip. Every claim was run.

2.1 Eight Types, and typeof

JavaScript has seven primitive types and one object type. A primitive value is a simple value such as a number or a string, and it is not an object. It has no properties of its own, it can never be changed, and it is compared by value: two primitives are equal when they hold the same thing. Objects, by contrast, are compared by identity: two objects are equal only when they are the very same object. Everything else in this section builds on that one distinction. An object reference is what a variable holds when the value is not a primitive: not the object itself, but a pointer to where it lives.

const cases = [['undefined', undefined], ['null', null], ['boolean', true], ['number', 1],
  ['string', 's'], ['symbol', Symbol()], ['bigint', 1n], ['function', () => {}],
  ['object', {}], ['array', []], ['date', new Date(0)]];
for (const [label, value] of cases) console.log(`typeof ${label.padEnd(9)} = ${typeof value}`);

typeof undefined = undefined
typeof null      = object
typeof boolean   = boolean
typeof number    = number
typeof string    = string
typeof symbol    = symbol
typeof bigint    = bigint
typeof function  = function
typeof object    = object
typeof array     = object
typeof date      = object

The typeof operator tells you a value's type as a string, and it has three flaws worth naming:

  • typeof null is "object". That is a bug from 1995 that can never be fixed without breaking existing websites, and it is the reason x === null is the only correct null check.
  • typeof cannot tell apart an array, a Date, a Map or a plain object. Array.isArray() and instanceof cover those.
  • typeof on a function reports "function", even though a function is an object. That one is a convenience rather than a flaw.

The type names themselves are worth being precise about, because each one has a job:

undefined
"No value has been assigned." The default for a declared-but-unset variable, a missing parameter, a missing property, and a function with no return.
the null value
"Deliberately no value." Something a programmer wrote. The distinction is a convention, not enforcement, and it is worth keeping: undefined means nobody set it, null means somebody set it to nothing.
the boolean type
Exactly true and false.
the number type
One type for all numbers: IEEE 754 double precision. There is no integer type, which §2.10 is about.
the string type
Immutable UTF-16 (§9.4).
the symbol type
Unique, non-colliding property keys (§6.11).
the bigint type
Arbitrary-precision integers, written with a trailing n, for when 2⁵³ is not enough.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: a primitive value, an object reference, the typeof operator, the null value, the boolean type, the number type, the string type, the symbol type, the bigint type, ieee 754 and array.isarray().

2.2 A Wrapper Object, and Why You Never Need One

A primitive has no properties, and yet 'abc'.toUpperCase() works. A wrapper object is the reason. When you access a property on a primitive, the engine quietly creates a temporary object around it, reads the property from that object, and throws the object away. That is autoboxing.

console.log('primitives borrow methods:', 'abc'.toUpperCase(), (5).toFixed(1), true.toString());
const wrapped = new String('a');
console.log('typeof new String("a"):', typeof wrapped);
console.log('== "a":', wrapped == 'a', '| === "a":', wrapped === 'a');
console.log('every wrapper object is truthy, even this one:', Boolean(new Boolean(false)));

primitives borrow methods: ABC 5.0 true
typeof new String("a"): object
== "a": true | === "a": false
every wrapper object is truthy, even this one: true

Never call new String, new Number or new Boolean. The result is an object, not a primitive. So typeof gives a misleading answer, === fails against the primitive, and new Boolean(false) is truthy, because every object is. Called without new, the same functions are the conversion functions of §2.4, and those are genuinely useful: Number(), the String() constructor and Boolean() are the explicit way to convert a value.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: autoboxing, the string() constructor and boolean().

2.3 Truthiness

Every value is either truthy or falsy: it counts as true or as false when used in a condition such as an if. There are exactly eight falsy values and everything else is truthy:

const falsy = [false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN];
console.log('all falsy:', falsy.map(Boolean).join(', '));
const surprising = [[], {}, '0', 'false', ' ', new Boolean(false), function () {}];
console.log('all truthy:', surprising.map(Boolean).join(', '));
console.log('so this is a common bug:', '0' ? 'truthy string' : 'never reached');
console.log('and this one:', [] ? 'an empty array is truthy' : 'never reached');

all falsy: false, false, false, false, false, false, false, false
all truthy: true, true, true, true, true, true, true
so this is a common bug: truthy string
and this one: an empty array is truthy

Learn the falsy list and the rest follows: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including '0', 'false', [], {} and ' '. Truthy and falsy depend on the value, not on the type. That is why if (count) is a bug when 0 is a legitimate count: what was meant is if (count != null) or if (count !== undefined).

2.4 Explicit Conversion

Three functions, and their edge cases are where the surprises live:

console.log('Number(""):       ', Number(''), '   | Number(" "):', Number(' '));
console.log('Number(null):     ', Number(null), '   | Number(undefined):', Number(undefined));
console.log('Number([]):       ', Number([]), '   | Number([5]):', Number([5]), '| Number([1,2]):', Number([1, 2]));
console.log('Number("12px"):   ', Number('12px'), ' | parseInt("12px"):', parseInt('12px', 10));
console.log('parseInt("0x1f"): ', parseInt('0x1f'), '  | parseInt("08"):', parseInt('08'));
console.log('String(null):     ', JSON.stringify(String(null)), '| String([1,2]):', JSON.stringify(String([1, 2])));
console.log('String({}):       ', JSON.stringify(String({})));

Number(""):        0    | Number(" "): 0
Number(null):      0    | Number(undefined): NaN
Number([]):        0    | Number([5]): 5 | Number([1,2]): NaN
Number("12px"):    NaN  | parseInt("12px"): 12
parseInt("0x1f"):  31   | parseInt("08"): 8
String(null):      "null" | String([1,2]): "1,2"
String({}):        "[object Object]"

parseFloat() is the decimal version of parseInt(), and it is the one to use for '1.5rem', where parseInt() would give 1. Number() is strict and parseInt() is lenient. Number('12px') is NaN, while parseInt('12px') is 12, because parseInt reads as far as it can and then stops. That makes parseInt right for reading '20px' from a stylesheet, and wrong for validating user input, where trailing garbage should be an error.

Two parseInt details still catch people. It auto-detects hexadecimal: parseInt('0x1f') is 31. And it takes a radix, the number base, as its second argument. Always pass the radix explicitly, both for that reason and because of the .map(parseInt) trap in §8.5.

Number('') and Number(' ') are 0, while Number(undefined) is NaN. That difference is why a form validation can accept an empty field as zero.

To have in hand before moving on: parsefloat().

2.5 Implicit Coercion: + Is Two Operators

+ means addition or joining strings together (concatenation). It decides which only after converting both sides to primitives, and if either side is a string, it concatenates. Every other arithmetic operator converts both sides to numbers.

console.log('1 + "2"     =', JSON.stringify(1 + "2"), '  (string wins)');
console.log('"3" - 1     =', "3" - 1, '    (minus has only one meaning)');
console.log('"3" * "2"   =', "3" * "2");
console.log('1 + null    =', 1 + null, '    | 1 + undefined =', 1 + undefined);
console.log('[] + []     =', JSON.stringify([] + []), '   | [] + {} =', JSON.stringify([] + {}));
console.log('"5" + 3     =', JSON.stringify("5" + 3), '  | "5" - 3 =', "5" - 3);
console.log('true + true =', true + true, '    | "b" + "a" + +"a" + "a" =', "b" + "a" + +"a" + "a");

1 + "2"     = "12"   (string wins)
"3" - 1     = 2     (minus has only one meaning)
"3" * "2"   = 6
1 + null    = 1     | 1 + undefined = NaN
[] + []     = ""    | [] + {} = "[object Object]"
"5" + 3     = "53"   | "5" - 3 = 2
true + true = 2     | "b" + "a" + +"a" + "a" = baNaNa

[] + {} is "[object Object]" because both sides are first converted to primitives: [] becomes '' and {} becomes '[object Object]'. Neither is a number, so + concatenates. 1 + null is 1 because Number(null) is 0, while 1 + undefined is NaN because Number(undefined) is NaN. Nothing here is arbitrary.

The practical rule: never rely on + for conversion. Write Number(x) + y, or `${x}${y}`, and the ambiguity disappears.

2.6 ToPrimitive, and Controlling It

Whenever an object has to be converted to a primitive without you asking, the engine uses the ToPrimitive algorithm. It asks the object for a primitive and passes a hint saying what kind is wanted: "number", "string", or "default". The object may answer through Symbol.toPrimitive. If it does not have one, the engine tries .valueOf() and toString(), in an order set by the hint.

const money = {
  amount: 42,
  valueOf() { return this.amount; },
  toString() { return `$${this.amount}`; },
};
console.log('arithmetic uses the number hint:', money * 2, money - 2);
console.log('a template literal uses the string hint:', `${money}`);
console.log('+ uses the default hint, which prefers valueOf:', money + 1);

const explicit = {
  [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) { return hint === 'string' ? 'as text' : 99; },
};
console.log('hint string: ', `${explicit}`);
console.log('hint number: ', +explicit);
console.log('hint default:', explicit + 0);
console.log('Symbol.toStringTag changes the tag:',
  Object.prototype.toString.call({ [Symbol.toStringTag]: 'Money' }));

arithmetic uses the number hint: 84 40
a template literal uses the string hint: $42
+ uses the default hint, which prefers valueOf: 43
hint string:  as text
hint number:  99
hint default: 99
Symbol.toStringTag changes the tag: [object Money]

That is why new Date() - new Date() gives a number of milliseconds while `${new Date()}` gives a sentence: Date is the one built-in object whose default hint prefers toString. Symbol.toStringTag is a separate mechanism. It controls only what Object.prototype.toString reports, which was the basis of the old [object Array] trick for checking types.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: the toprimitive algorithm, Symbol.toPrimitive and .valueof().

2.7 ==, === and Object.is

Strict equality (===) compares type and value, with no conversion. Loose equality (==) converts the two sides first. Its rules are specified exactly, and they are worth knowing exactly, because you will read code that uses it.

console.log('"5" == 5             :', "5" == 5, '  | "5" === 5:', "5" === 5);
console.log('null == undefined    :', null == undefined, '  | null === undefined:', null === undefined);
console.log('null == 0            :', null == 0, ' | null >= 0:', null >= 0);
console.log('NaN == NaN           :', NaN == NaN, ' | NaN === NaN:', NaN === NaN);
console.log('[] == false          :', [] == false, '  | "0" == false:', "0" == false, '| "" == 0:', "" == 0);
console.log('[] == ""             :', [] == "", '  | [1] == 1:', [1] == 1);
console.log('Object.is(NaN, NaN)  :', Object.is(NaN, NaN), '  | NaN === NaN:', NaN === NaN);
console.log('Object.is(0, -0)     :', Object.is(0, -0), ' | 0 === -0:', 0 === -0);

"5" == 5             : true   | "5" === 5: false
null == undefined    : true   | null === undefined: false
null == 0            : false  | null >= 0: true
NaN == NaN           : false  | NaN === NaN: false
[] == false          : true   | "0" == false: true | "" == 0: true
[] == ""             : true   | [1] == 1: true
Object.is(NaN, NaN)  : true   | NaN === NaN: false
Object.is(0, -0)     : false  | 0 === -0: true

[] == false is true because of three conversions: false becomes 0; [] becomes '' through ToPrimitive; and '' becomes 0. Then 0 == 0. That is three conversions just to compare an array with a boolean.

null == 0 being false while null >= 0 is true is the one genuinely inconsistent corner. == has a special case that makes null equal only to undefined. The comparison operators (<, >= and so on) have no such case, so they convert null to 0.

Use === always, with exactly one exception: x == null is the usual way to test for "null or undefined", and it is clearer than x === null || x === undefined.

Object.is() is a third kind of equality. It differs from === in exactly two places: it says NaN equals itself, and it says 0 and -0 are different. includes, Map and Set use almost the same comparison, called SameValueZero. The only difference is that SameValueZero treats 0 and -0 as equal.

In summary, the vocabulary here is loose equality, strict equality and object.is().

2.8 NaN and the Infinities

The NaN value ("not a number") is the result of a numeric operation that has no numeric answer, and it is the only value that is not equal to itself:

console.log('sources of NaN:', Number('abc'), 0 / 0, Math.sqrt(-1), undefined + 1);
console.log('NaN is contagious:', (NaN + 1) * 2);
console.log('Number.isNaN("abc"):', Number.isNaN('abc'), '| the global isNaN("abc"):', isNaN('abc'));
console.log('Number.isNaN(NaN):  ', Number.isNaN(NaN), '| isNaN(" "):', isNaN(' '));
console.log('Infinity:', 1 / 0, -1 / 0, '| typeof:', typeof Infinity);
console.log('Infinity - Infinity:', Infinity - Infinity, '| 1/-0:', 1 / -0);

sources of NaN: NaN NaN NaN NaN
NaN is contagious: NaN
Number.isNaN("abc"): false | the global isNaN("abc"): true
Number.isNaN(NaN):   true | isNaN(" "): false
Infinity: Infinity -Infinity | typeof: number
Infinity - Infinity: NaN | 1/-0: -Infinity

The global isNaN() coerces its argument first: it converts the argument to a number, then checks. So it answers "is this not a number after conversion?". That is why isNaN('abc') is true and isNaN(' ') is false, since Number(' ') is 0. Number.isNaN() asks the real question: is this value the NaN value? Always use Number.isNaN.

Negative zero is a real, separate value. 0 === -0 is true, so it stays hidden until you divide by it and get -Infinity, or until Object.is tells you the truth. It comes from -1 * 0, from Math.round(-0.4), and from parsing "-0".

What to carry forward from this subsection: number.isnan(), the global isnan() and negative zero.

2.9 Floating-Point Arithmetic

The number type follows IEEE 754 double-precision, the standard format for storing decimal numbers in binary: 64 bits, 53 of them for the digits themselves. Two consequences shape everything numeric in JavaScript.

Most decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly, because the format is binary. That is the first consequence. Just as 1/3 has no exact decimal form, 0.1 has no exact binary form:

console.log('0.1 + 0.2 =', 0.1 + 0.2);
console.log('=== 0.3   :', 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);
console.log('within Number.EPSILON:', Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON);
console.log('0.1 + 0.2 to 17 places:', (0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(17));
console.log('and money goes wrong:', 0.1 + 0.7, '| times 10:', (0.1 + 0.7) * 10);
console.log('integers are exact, so work in cents:', (10 + 70) / 100);

0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004
=== 0.3   : false
within Number.EPSILON: true
0.1 + 0.2 to 17 places: 0.30000000000000004
and money goes wrong: 0.7999999999999999 | times 10: 7.999999999999999
integers are exact, so work in cents: 0.8

That is a floating-point rounding error, not a JavaScript quirk: the same arithmetic in C, Java or Python gives the same answer. Number.EPSILON is the smallest gap between 1 and the next number the format can store, and comparing against it is the standard tolerance test for values near 1. For money, store integer minor units: cents, not dollars, and divide only when displaying.

Above 2⁵³ integers stop being distinct:

console.log('Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER:', Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER);
console.log('+1 === +2 above it:', Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 === Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2);
console.log('isSafeInteger:', Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53 - 1), Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53));
console.log('a 64-bit id from JSON is already wrong:', JSON.parse('{"id":9007199254740993}').id);
console.log('BigInt keeps it:', BigInt('9007199254740993'));

Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER: 9007199254740991
+1 === +2 above it: true
isSafeInteger: true false
a 64-bit id from JSON is already wrong: 9007199254740992
BigInt keeps it: 9007199254740993n

The second consequence is a size limit. A safe integer is one no larger than Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, which is 2⁵³ − 1. Up to there, every whole number has an exact representation. Compare against the Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER constant rather than writing out the number. The JSON.parse line is the one that matters in practice: a 64-bit id from a database arrives already corrupted, silently, before your code even touches it. The fix is for the API to send it as a string.

.toFixed() rounds for display, and it inherits the representation problem:

console.log('(1.005).toFixed(2):', (1.005).toFixed(2), '— not 1.01');
console.log('(2.675).toFixed(2):', (2.675).toFixed(2), '— not 2.68');
console.log('(1.5).toFixed(0):', (1.5).toFixed(0), '| (2.5).toFixed(0):', (2.5).toFixed(0));
console.log('because 1.005 is really:', (1.005).toFixed(20));

(1.005).toFixed(2): 1.00 — not 1.01
(2.675).toFixed(2): 2.67 — not 2.68
(1.5).toFixed(0): 2 | (2.5).toFixed(0): 3
because 1.005 is really: 1.00499999999999989342

The last line shows why: 1.005 is stored as slightly less than 1.005, so rounding it to two places correctly gives 1.00. toFixed is not broken; the input was never exactly 1.005.

The terms above, gathered: double-precision, a safe integer, floating-point rounding error and .tofixed().

2.10 BigInt

The bigint type holds whole numbers of any size, exactly (arbitrary precision). A BigInt literal is written with a trailing n, and BigInt() converts other values:

console.log('exact beyond 2^53:', 2n ** 64n);
console.log('BigInt("9007199254740993"):', BigInt('9007199254740993'));
try { 1n + 1; } catch (e) { console.log('mixing with Number throws:', e.constructor.name); }
console.log('explicit conversion is fine:', 1n + BigInt(1), '|', Number(1n) + 1);
console.log('1n == 1:', 1n == 1, '| 1n === 1:', 1n === 1);
console.log('division truncates:', 7n / 2n);
console.log('no Math methods:', typeof Math.sqrt === 'function' ? 'Math.sqrt(4n) would throw' : '');

exact beyond 2^53: 18446744073709551616n
BigInt("9007199254740993"): 9007199254740993n
mixing with Number throws: TypeError
explicit conversion is fine: 2n | 2
1n == 1: true | 1n === 1: false
division truncates: 3n
no Math methods: Math.sqrt(4n) would throw

Mixing a BigInt and a Number in arithmetic is a TypeError, and that is deliberate. Converting either way could lose information, and the language refuses to guess which loss you want. Comparison is allowed: 1n == 1 is true and 1n === 1 is false, since the types differ. Division rounds toward zero, Math functions do not accept BigInts, and JSON.stringify throws on a BigInt unless you give it a toJSON.

Use it for exact large integers, such as database ids, cryptographic values and high-precision timestamps, and not as a general replacement for Number.

One line each, for reference: bigint() and a bigint literal.

2.11 Numeric Literal Forms

console.log('a numeric separator:', 1_000_000, '| in a BigInt too:', 1_000n);
console.log('binary 0b1010:', 0b1010, '| octal 0o17:', 0o17, '| hex 0xff:', 0xff);
console.log('exponent 1.5e3:', 1.5e3, '| 2e-3:', 2e-3);
console.log('all are the same type:', typeof 0xff === typeof 1.5e3);
console.log('and back out again:', (255).toString(16), (10).toString(2), (255).toString(36));

a numeric separator: 1000000 | in a BigInt too: 1000n
binary 0b1010: 10 | octal 0o17: 15 | hex 0xff: 255
exponent 1.5e3: 1500 | 2e-3: 0.002
all are the same type: true
and back out again: ff 1010 73

Numeric literal forms are only different ways of writing a number in code: every one produces the same number type. A numeric separator _ may appear between digits and is ignored, which makes large constants and bitmasks easier to read. .toString(radix) converts back to text in any base from 2 to 36.

2.12 Pass by Value, Pass by Sharing

Pass by value is what happens for primitives: when you pass one to a function, the value is copied, and the copy is independent. For objects, the reference is copied instead. This is often called pass by sharing, because the caller and the function end up pointing at the same object:

function mutate(primitive, object) {
  primitive = 'changed';
  object.changed = true;
  object = { replaced: true };      // rebinding the local name only
  return { primitive, object };
}
let p = 'original';
const o = { changed: false };
const inside = mutate(p, o);
console.log('the primitive outside is:', p);
console.log('the object outside is:   ', JSON.stringify(o));
console.log('the function saw:        ', JSON.stringify(inside));

the primitive outside is: original
the object outside is:    {"changed":true}
the function saw:         {"primitive":"changed","object":{"replaced":true}}

Both halves matter. Mutating the object is visible to the caller: o.changed became true. Reassigning the parameter is not: the caller still holds the original object. That is why "JavaScript is pass by reference" is wrong. In a true pass-by-reference language, the reassignment would reach the caller too.

2.13 JSON

JSON.stringify() and JSON.parse() are the pair for turning data into JSON text and back. What stringify leaves out is the part to know:

const value = { a: undefined, b: () => 1, c: NaN, d: Infinity,
                e: new Date(0), f: 1, g: new Set([1]), [Symbol('h')]: 2 };
console.log('what survives:', JSON.stringify(value));
console.log('in an array, dropped values become null:', JSON.stringify([undefined, () => 1, NaN]));
console.log('a replacer array picks fields:', JSON.stringify({ x: 1, y: 2 }, ['x']));
console.log('indentation:', JSON.stringify({ x: 1 }, null, 2).replace(/\n/g, '\\n'));
try { const cyclic = {}; cyclic.self = cyclic; JSON.stringify(cyclic); }
catch (e) { console.log('a cycle throws:', e.constructor.name); }

what survives: {"c":null,"d":null,"e":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z","f":1,"g":{}}
in an array, dropped values become null: [null,null,null]
a replacer array picks fields: {"x":1}
indentation: {\n  "x": 1\n}
a cycle throws: TypeError

That one line of output shows six behaviours:

  • undefined, functions and symbol keys are dropped from an object, and become null in an array.
  • NaN and Infinity become null, because JSON has no way to write them.
  • A Date becomes an ISO string through its .toJSON() method, and does not come back as a Date.
  • A Set or Map becomes {}, silently losing everything in it.
  • And a cycle throws: an object that refers back to itself cannot be written out.

The replacer function (passed to stringify) and the reviver function (passed to parse) are the hooks for fixing all of that:

const data = { when: new Date(0), tags: new Set(['a', 'b']) };
const json = JSON.stringify(data, (key, value) =>
  value instanceof Set ? { __set: [...value] } : value);
console.log('with a replacer:', json);
const back = JSON.parse(json, (key, value) =>
  value && value.__set ? new Set(value.__set) : (key === 'when' ? new Date(value) : value));
console.log('revived:', back.when instanceof Date, back.tags instanceof Set, [...back.tags]);

with a replacer: {"when":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z","tags":{"__set":["a","b"]}}
revived: true true [ 'a', 'b' ]

Note that the replacer sees each value after any toJSON has run. That is why when is already a string inside it, and why turning the string back into a Date has to happen on the parse side. .toJSON() on your own class is the cleaner place to define how it is serialised, because it keeps that knowledge with the type.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: json.stringify(), json.parse(), the reviver function and the replacer function.

2.14 Copying: Shallow, Deep, and What Survives

A shallow copy duplicates only the top level, so nested objects are still shared. And a deep copy duplicates everything, all the way down. structuredClone() is the platform's built-in deep copy, and it is strictly better than the JSON round trip:

const source = { d: new Date(0), m: new Map([[1, 'a']]), s: new Set([1]), r: /x/g, u: undefined };
source.self = source;
const cloned = structuredClone(source);
console.log('Date:', cloned.d instanceof Date, '| Map:', cloned.m instanceof Map,
            '| Set:', cloned.s instanceof Set, '| RegExp:', cloned.r instanceof RegExp);
console.log('undefined key kept:', 'u' in cloned, '| cycle preserved:', cloned.self === cloned);

const { self, ...acyclic } = source;
const viaJson = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(acyclic));
console.log('via JSON — Date became a', typeof viaJson.d, '| Map became', JSON.stringify(viaJson.m),
            '| undefined key kept:', 'u' in viaJson);
try { structuredClone({ fn: () => 1 }); }
catch (e) { console.log('but functions cannot be cloned:', e.constructor.name); }

Date: true | Map: true | Set: true | RegExp: true
undefined key kept: true | cycle preserved: true
via JSON — Date became a string | Map became {} | undefined key kept: false
but functions cannot be cloned: DOMException

structuredClone() keeps Date, Map, Set, RegExp, typed arrays, Blob and cycles. It does not carry functions, DOM nodes, or class identity: a cloned class instance comes back as a plain object with the same fields. It is the same algorithm postMessage and IndexedDB use (§17.8), so "will this survive a clone?" and "can I send this to a worker?" are the same question.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: a deep copy.

2.15 What This Section Established

  1. Eight types, and typeof null is "object" — a permanent bug, which is why x === null is the only null check. typeof cannot tell an array from an object.
  2. Never new String/new Number/new Boolean. The result is an object: === 'a' was false, and new Boolean(false) is truthy.
  3. Eight falsy values — false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN — and '0', 'false', [] and {} are all truthy.
  4. Number() is strict and parseInt() is lenient: NaN against 12 for '12px'. parseInt auto-detects hex — '0x1f' gave 31 — so always pass the radix.
  5. + concatenates if either side is a string and every other operator converts to a number. 1 + null is 1 and 1 + undefined is NaN, both from Number().
  6. ToPrimitive takes a hint, which is why money * 2 used valueOf and `${money}` used toString, and why Symbol.toPrimitive can answer all three cases at once.
  7. [] == false is true after three conversions, and null == 0 is false while null >= 0 is true — the one genuinely inconsistent corner.
  8. Object.is differs from === in exactly two places: NaN equals itself, and 0 is not -0.
  9. The global isNaN coerces and Number.isNaN does not — isNaN(' ') was false. Use the latter.
  10. 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, which is IEEE 754 and not a JavaScript defect. Store money in integer minor units.
  11. Above 2⁵³ integers merge. JSON.parse('{"id":9007199254740993}') returned ...992 before any of your code ran.
  12. (1.005).toFixed(2) is 1.00, because 1.005 was never exactly 1.005.
  13. BigInt refuses to mix with Number in arithmetic, though 1n == 1 is true and 1n === 1 is false.
  14. Reassigning a parameter never escapes; mutating the object always does. That is pass by sharing, not pass by reference.
  15. JSON.stringify drops undefined, functions and symbols, turns NaN into null, flattens a Set to {} and throws on a cycle. structuredClone keeps all of it except functions and class identity.

Exercises

1. Predict each line, then explain the rule that produces it.

console.log([] + {}, {} + [], [] == ![]);
console.log(typeof NaN, typeof typeof 1, typeof null);
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3, Math.max() > Math.min());
console.log([1, 2, 3] + [4, 5], "5" - - "2");
console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: [undefined] }));
console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2 === Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 3);
Solution 
[object Object] [object Object] true
number string object
false false
1,2,34,5 7
{"b":[null]}
true

[] + {} and {} + [] both give "[object Object]" here. Both operands become primitives — '' and '[object Object]' — and neither is a number, so + concatenates. The famous claim that {} + [] is 0 is true only when it is typed as a statement at a console prompt, where the leading {} parses as an empty block and the rest is +[], a unary plus on an empty array. Inside console.log(...) it is unambiguously an expression, so both give the same answer.

[] == ![] is true. ![] is false (an array is truthy). Then [] == false runs the chain from §2.7: false → 0, [] → '' → 0, and 0 == 0.

typeof typeof 1 is "string", because typeof 1 is the string "number" and typeof of a string is "string".

Math.max() > Math.min() is false. With no arguments Math.max() returns -Infinity and Math.min() returns Infinity — the identity elements, so that adding arguments always narrows the answer. It looks backwards and is exactly right.

[1,2,3] + [4,5] is "1,2,34,5". Both arrays convert via toString, which is join(','), and the results concatenate. "5" - - "2" is 7: the inner unary minus makes -2, and the binary minus converts "5" to 5, giving 5 - (-2).

JSON.stringify gives {"b":[null]}. undefined as an object property is dropped entirely; undefined inside an array becomes null, because an array's length is part of its meaning and a hole would change it (§2.13).

The last line is true. Both sums exceed MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, where consecutive integers are no longer distinguishable, so +2 and +3 land on the same double.

2. Write deepEqual(a, b) comparing two values structurally. Decide and justify the treatment of NaN, -0, Date, Map, cycles and prototypes.

Solution 
function deepEqual(a, b, seen = new WeakMap()) {
  if (Object.is(a, b)) return true;                       // handles NaN, and -0 !== 0
  if (typeof a !== 'object' || typeof b !== 'object' || a === null || b === null) return false;
  if (Object.getPrototypeOf(a) !== Object.getPrototypeOf(b)) return false;

  if (seen.get(a) === b) return true;                     // already being compared: assume equal
  seen.set(a, b);

  if (a instanceof Date) return a.getTime() === b.getTime();
  if (a instanceof RegExp) return a.source === b.source && a.flags === b.flags;

  if (a instanceof Map) {
    if (a.size !== b.size) return false;
    for (const [k, v] of a) {
      if (!b.has(k) || !deepEqual(v, b.get(k), seen)) return false;   // keys by identity
    }
    return true;
  }
  if (a instanceof Set) {
    if (a.size !== b.size) return false;
    for (const v of a) if (!b.has(v)) return false;
    return true;
  }

  const keysA = Reflect.ownKeys(a), keysB = Reflect.ownKeys(b);
  if (keysA.length !== keysB.length) return false;
  return keysA.every(k => Object.hasOwn(b, k) && deepEqual(a[k], b[k], seen));
}

console.log(deepEqual({ a: [1, { b: 2 }] }, { a: [1, { b: 2 }] }));
console.log('NaN:', deepEqual(NaN, NaN), '| -0 vs 0:', deepEqual(-0, 0));
console.log('Date:', deepEqual(new Date(0), new Date(0)));
console.log('Map:', deepEqual(new Map([['k', 1]]), new Map([['k', 1]])));
console.log('different prototypes:', deepEqual({ a: 1 }, Object.assign(Object.create(null), { a: 1 })));
const x = { n: 1 }; x.self = x;
const y = { n: 1 }; y.self = y;
console.log('cycles:', deepEqual(x, y));

true
NaN: true | -0 vs 0: false
Date: true
Map: true
different prototypes: false
cycles: true

Object.is as the primitive base case decides two questions at once. NaN equals itself — which === denies, and which is right here, because two structures containing NaN in the same place are structurally the same. And -0 is not 0, which is the more debatable choice: it is defensible because 1/x differs between them, so the values are observably distinct. A test-assertion library would reasonably choose the opposite; the important thing is choosing deliberately and documenting it.

Prototypes are compared because {a: 1} and Object.create(null) with the same field behave differently — 'toString' in x differs — and because it makes an instance of class A unequal to a structurally identical instance of class B. Skipping the check is the common shortcut and it makes the function say true for values that are not interchangeable.

Cycles use a WeakMap of pairs already in progress. Recording a → b before recursing means that when the traversal comes back round to the same pair it returns true rather than recursing forever. A WeakMap rather than a Map so nothing is retained after the call (§8.13). Note the subtlety: this assumes equality while proving it, which is the standard co-inductive treatment and is what every real implementation does.

Map compares keys by identity and values structurally. That is forced by the data structure: b.has(k) uses SameValueZero on the key, and there is no way to find "the structurally equal key" without an O(n²) scan. Two maps with structurally-equal-but-distinct object keys therefore compare unequal, which is worth documenting rather than hiding.

Set compares by membership only, for the same reason, which means a Set of objects is compared by identity throughout.

Reflect.ownKeys rather than Object.keys so symbol-keyed and non-enumerable properties are included (§6.9) — otherwise two objects differing only in a symbol property compare equal.

What it deliberately does not handle: typed arrays and ArrayBuffer (which need a byte-wise comparison), getters (which are invoked by a[k], so a getter with side effects runs), and Object.freeze state. Each is a real limitation, and the honest move is to name them rather than let a caller assume total coverage.

3. A cart totals 19.99 + 4.99 + 0.02 and shows 24.999999999999996. Explain precisely why, then give the correct fix and two wrong ones with their failure modes.

Solution

Why. None of 19.99, 4.99 or 0.02 is representable exactly in binary floating point (§2.9) — each is stored as the nearest double, which is slightly off. Adding three approximations accumulates three errors, and the result is the nearest double to a number a hair below 25.

const total = 19.99 + 4.99 + 0.02;
console.log('total:', total, '| === 25:', total === 25);
console.log('the error is about:', Math.abs(total - 25));
console.log('and it changes with the order:', 0.02 + 4.99 + 19.99 === 19.99 + 4.99 + 0.02);

total: 24.999999999999996 | === 25: false
the error is about: 3.552713678800501e-15
and it changes with the order: false

That last line is the part that makes this more than a display problem: floating-point addition is not associative, so summing the same cart in a different order gives a different double. A total computed on the client and the same total computed on the server can disagree in the last bit, and an equality check between them fails.

The correct fix: never store money as a fraction.

const cents = [1999, 499, 2];                        // integers throughout
const totalCents = cents.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
console.log('exact total in cents:', totalCents);
console.log('formatted:', new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' })
  .format(totalCents / 100));

exact total in cents: 2500
formatted: $25.00

Integers below 2⁵³ are exact (§2.9), so the arithmetic is exact, associative and order-independent. The single division happens once, at the edge, for display — and Intl.NumberFormat handles the currency symbol, the separator and the number of minor units per currency, which differs (JPY has none, KWD has three).

Wrong fix 1 — round after every operation.

const round2 = (n) => Math.round(n * 100) / 100;

It hides the symptom and introduces a new error, because n * 100 is itself inexact — Math.round(1.005 * 100) is 100, not 101, for the reason §2.9 measured. Worse, rounding at every step accumulates rounding error in place of representation error, so a long invoice drifts. It also does nothing about the associativity problem.

Wrong fix 2 — compare with an epsilon.

if (Math.abs(total - 25) < Number.EPSILON) { /* treat as equal */ }

This is the right tool for a physics simulation and the wrong one for money, twice over. Number.EPSILON is the gap next to 1.0, so it is far too small for values in the thousands and too large for values near zero — a fixed epsilon is wrong at some scale by construction. And it makes equality approximate, which means a payment of $24.999999 and one of $25.000001 are "equal", which is not a property anyone wants in a ledger.

The general rule: floating point is for measurements, integers are for counts, and money is a count. The same reasoning applies to any quantity where an exact total is part of the requirement — inventory, votes, bytes transferred. Where genuinely fractional exact arithmetic is needed, a decimal library or BigInt scaled by a fixed factor is the answer, not a tolerance.

SECTION 3

Bindings, Scope and Closures

In JavaScript, a variable is a name attached to a value inside an environment: a table the engine keeps of which names exist in a given part of the code. Almost every question of the form "why can this code see that value?" is answered by knowing which environment the name lives in, and when that environment was created.

That sounds abstract, but it decides very practical things:

  • whether a loop counter is shared between iterations or copied for each one;
  • whether a callback created inside a factory function remembers what it was given;
  • why a let throws an error where a var gives undefined;
  • why a component that forgot to remove one event listener keeps a megabyte of page elements in memory for the rest of the session.

This section builds that model in four steps:

  1. The three ways to declare a variable, and what distinguishes them.
  2. Scope, which is where a name is visible.
  3. Closures, which are what happens when a function keeps working after the code that created it has finished, and still remembers that code's variables.
  4. The consequence nobody teaches alongside closures: they are also how memory stays in use. The same mechanism that makes a counter work makes a leak possible.

The section ends with using, the newest declaration form. It exists because closures and garbage collection (the engine freeing memory nobody can reach any more) cannot solve every lifetime problem. Some resources, such as an open file, must be released at a known moment rather than at some unknown later time.

3.1 Three Declaration Forms
