The var keyword, the let keyword and the const keyword all declare a variable, and they differ in three ways: where the name is visible (scope), what happens if you use it before its line (hoisting), and whether it can be given a new value later (reassignment).

scope
before its line
reassignable
var
function
undefined
yes, and redeclarable
let
block
ReferenceError
yes
const
block
ReferenceError
no
function scopes() {
  if (true) {
    var functionScoped = 'var escapes the block';
    let blockScoped = 'let does not';
  }
  const results = [functionScoped];
  try { results.push(blockScoped); } catch (e) { results.push(`blockScoped: ${e.constructor.name}`); }
  return results;
}
console.log(scopes());

const frozen = { a: 1 };
frozen.a = 2;
console.log('const forbids REBINDING, not mutation:', frozen.a);
try { eval('const x = 1; x = 2;'); } catch (e) { console.log('reassigning a const:', e.constructor.name); }

[ 'var escapes the block', 'blockScoped: ReferenceError' ]
const forbids REBINDING, not mutation: 2
reassigning a const: TypeError

The rule for new code is short, and everyone agrees on it: const by default, let when you must reassign, var never. const is not about speed. It is about the reader: a const tells them this name means one thing for the whole block, which is one fewer thing to keep track of.

To have in hand before moving on: the var keyword, the let keyword, the const keyword and function scope.

3.2 What const Actually Constrains

const makes the binding constant, not the value. A binding is the link between a name and a value, and const fixes only that link. This is the most common misreading of the keyword, and it is the same primitive-versus-reference distinction as §2.12. A const holding an object fixes which object the name points to. It says nothing about what is inside that object, which can still change.

const config = { retries: 3, tags: ['a'] };
config.retries = 5;                      // fine — mutating the object
config.tags.push('b');                   // fine — mutating a nested object
console.log('mutation is allowed:', JSON.stringify(config));
try { eval('const c = 1; c = 2;'); } catch (e) { console.log('rebinding is not:', e.constructor.name); }

const frozen = Object.freeze({ a: 1 });
try { frozen.a = 2; } catch (e) { console.log('freeze plus strict mode:', e.constructor.name); }
console.log('const + freeze gives both guarantees:', JSON.stringify(frozen));

mutation is allowed: {"retries":5,"tags":["a","b"]}
rebinding is not: TypeError
freeze plus strict mode: TypeError
const + freeze gives both guarantees: {"a":1}

If you want the contents fixed too, use Object.freeze (§6.8). Note that it is shallow: it freezes only the top level, so Object.freeze(config) would still allow config.tags.push('b').

There is one more thing const gives you that let does not, and it is the practical reason to prefer it: a const cannot be in a partially-initialised state later in the block. When you read a let five lines further down, you have to check whether anything reassigned it in between. With a const you do not. In a long function, that is a real reduction in what the reader has to hold in their head.

3.3 Hoisting and the Temporal Dead Zone

Every declaration is hoisted: the name is created as soon as its scope is entered, before any of the code in that scope runs. What differs is whether the name already has a value at that point, that is, whether it is initialised.

console.log('var before its line:', typeof varName === 'undefined' ? 'undefined' : varName);
var varName = 'assigned later';

try { letName; } catch (e) { console.log('let before its line:', e.constructor.name + ':', e.message); }
let letName = 'assigned later';

console.log('a function declaration is fully hoisted:', declared());
function declared() { return 'callable above its own definition'; }

try { expressed(); } catch (e) { console.log('a function EXPRESSION is not:', e.constructor.name); }
const expressed = () => 'never reached';

var before its line: undefined
let before its line: ReferenceError: Cannot access 'letName' before initialization
a function declaration is fully hoisted: callable above its own definition
a function EXPRESSION is not: ReferenceError

Variable hoisting for var creates the name and sets it to undefined straight away. That is why reading a var before its line gives undefined, silently and uselessly. Function hoisting goes further: the whole function is ready before its line. That is what lets a file define helper functions below the code that uses them.

let and const are hoisted too, so the name exists from the top of the block, but it has no value yet. The stretch between the top of the block and the declaration line is the temporal dead zone (TDZ). Using the name there is a ReferenceError.

The TDZ is a feature, not an inconvenience. It turns a kind of silent bug into a loud error, and it has a property that helps with diagnosis:

console.log('typeof on an UNDECLARED name is safe:', typeof neverDeclaredAnywhere);
try { typeof inTdz; } catch (e) { console.log('typeof on a TDZ binding still throws:', e.constructor.name); }
let inTdz = 1;

typeof on an UNDECLARED name is safe: undefined
typeof on a TDZ binding still throws: ReferenceError

typeof is the one operator that accepts a name that does not exist at all, and it does not accept a name in its TDZ. So if typeof x === 'undefined' throws, you know x is declared later in this very scope. That is a precise diagnosis that is otherwise hard to reach.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: variable hoisting and function hoisting.

3.4 Scope, and the Scope Chain

A lexical environment is the record of the names in one scope, together with a link to the scope that contains it (its parent). The scope chain is that series of links. To find a name, the engine walks the chain outward, scope by scope, until it finds it.

"Lexical" means decided by where the code is written, not by where it is called from. That single fact is what makes closures predictable.

const module_ = 'module scope';
function outer() {
  const outerVar = 'outer';
  function inner() {
    const innerVar = 'inner';
    return [innerVar, outerVar, module_].join(' <- ');
  }
  return inner();
}
console.log(outer());

const shadowed = 'outer value';
{
  const shadowed = 'inner value';
  console.log('inside the block:', shadowed);
}
console.log('outside again:', shadowed);

inner <- outer <- module scope
inside the block: inner value
outside again: outer value

Function scope is what var and function declarations get: the name is visible in the whole function. And block scope is what let, const, class and function declarations inside blocks get: the name is visible only between the nearest { and }. Variable shadowing means an inner name with the same spelling hides an outer one. It is legal and occasionally useful, but a warning sign when it happens by accident.

In summary, the vocabulary here is block scope, a lexical environment and variable shadowing.

3.5 Module Scope, the Global Object, and Pollution

Module scope is the outermost scope of a module (§14.1), and it is not the global scope. A top-level const in a module is private to that module. That is the single biggest practical difference between a module and a classic script.

const moduleLevel = 'private to this module';
globalThis.deliberatelyGlobal = 'set on purpose';
console.log('a module top-level binding is NOT on globalThis:', globalThis.moduleLevel);
console.log('but an explicit assignment is:', globalThis.deliberatelyGlobal);
console.log('and it is readable as a bare name:', deliberatelyGlobal);
console.log('globalThis works in every environment:', typeof globalThis);
delete globalThis.deliberatelyGlobal;
console.log('after deleting it:', typeof globalThis.deliberatelyGlobal);

a module top-level binding is NOT on globalThis: undefined
but an explicit assignment is: set on purpose
and it is readable as a bare name: set on purpose
globalThis works in every environment: object
after deleting it: undefined

That difference ended global scope pollution as a daily worry. In a classic script, a top-level var becomes a property of the global object. So if two scripts each declare config, one silently overwrites the other: the last one loaded wins, and there is no error anywhere. Modules give every file its own scope, so that collision cannot happen. Anything that really is shared has to be exported and imported, which makes the dependency visible.

globalThis is the name for the global object that works everywhere: it is window in a page, self in a worker, and global in older Node. Writing to it is occasionally legitimate, for a polyfill or a debugging hook, and is otherwise exactly what modules exist to avoid.

What to carry forward from this subsection: global scope pollution.

3.6 The IIFE, and Why You No Longer Need One

An IIFE, an immediately invoked function expression, is a function that is defined and called in the same breath. It was the workaround for that exact problem before modules existed:

const api = (function () {
  let privateCount = 0;                      // invisible outside
  return { bump: () => ++privateCount };
})();
api.bump();
console.log('the IIFE module pattern:', api.bump(), '| privateCount is unreachable:', typeof privateCount);

the IIFE module pattern: 2 | privateCount is unreachable: undefined

The mechanism is this whole section in miniature. A function creates a scope; the returned object keeps a reference to that scope (it closes over it); and nothing else can reach in. The parentheses around the function are needed because a statement that begins with function is read as a declaration, and a declaration cannot be called on the spot. Any position where an expression is expected will do, which is why minified code also contains !function(){}() and void function(){}().

You will meet IIFEs all the time in older code and in bundler output, where a bundler wraps each module in one to give it a scope. In new code, a module gives you the same privacy for free. Only two narrow uses remain: creating a scope inside a function that is already too long, and using await somewhere that is not async. Top-level await (§12.9) has largely removed that second one too.

3.7 Closures

A closure is a function together with the environment (the set of variables) it was created in. Every JavaScript function is a closure. The idea becomes interesting when the function keeps living after the call that created it has finished.

function makeCounter(start = 0) {
  let count = start;                          // lives as long as the returned functions do
  return {
    increment: () => ++count,
    reset: () => { count = start; return count; },
    get value() { return count; },
  };
}
const a = makeCounter(), b = makeCounter(10);
a.increment(); a.increment(); b.increment();
console.log('two independent closures:', a.value, b.value);
console.log('after reset:', a.reset(), '| b is untouched:', b.value);
console.log('count is unreachable from outside:', typeof count);

two independent closures: 2 11
after reset: 0 | b is untouched: 11
count is unreachable from outside: undefined

Each call to makeCounter creates a new environment, so a and b share nothing. The three functions returned by one call share a single environment with each other, and that is what makes them behave like one object rather than three unrelated functions.

A huge amount of practical JavaScript rests on this: private state without classes, function factories (functions that build other functions), partial application (§5.9), memoisation (§5.11), and every callback that needs to remember something.

3.8 Closure Over a Loop Variable

Closure over a loop variable is the classic puzzle. It is really a question about scope rather than about closures:

const withVar = [], withLet = [];
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) withVar.push(() => i);
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) withLet.push(() => j);
console.log('var:', withVar.map(f => f()));
console.log('let:', withLet.map(f => f()));

var: [ 3, 3, 3 ]
let: [ 0, 1, 2 ]

With var there is one i for the whole loop, so all three closures see the same variable, and by the time they run it is 3. let in a for header creates a fresh binding per iteration: a new variable for each pass, with the previous value copied forward. That rule exists in the specification purely to make this case work. Before let, the fix was an IIFE inside each iteration, and you will still see that in older code.

Two related cases are worth having straight. for...of and for...in with let also create a binding per iteration, so they never have the problem. And a closure inside a .forEach never had it either, because each callback call is a separate function call with its own parameters. That is one reason the array methods caught on so quickly.

3.9 What Closures Are Actually For

Beyond the puzzle, four patterns account for most closure use in real code. It is worth recognising each one as the same mechanism:

// 1. Private state without a class.
const makeToggle = (on = false) => ({ flip: () => (on = !on), get on() { return on; } });

// 2. A configured function — partial application (§5.9).
const prefixer = (prefix) => (message) => `${prefix}: ${message}`;
const warn = prefixer('WARN');

// 3. A callback that remembers its context.
const handlersFor = (id) => ({ onSave: () => `saving ${id}`, onDelete: () => `deleting ${id}` });

// 4. Caching, where the cache outlives the call that created it (§3.11).
const memoLength = (() => { const seen = new Map();
  return (s) => seen.get(s) ?? (seen.set(s, s.length), s.length); })();

const t = makeToggle();
t.flip();
console.log(t.on, '|', warn('disk almost full'), '|', handlersFor(7).onSave(), '|', memoLength('abcd'));

true | WARN: disk almost full | saving 7 | 4

In every case the returned function is small, and the interesting part is what it captured. That gives a test for whether a closure is the right tool: if the captured state is what makes the function useful, a closure is right; if you are capturing merely to avoid passing an argument, pass the argument.

3.10 Garbage Collection, and How Closures Retain Memory

JavaScript manages memory for you. Garbage collection frees objects that are unreachable. Here, reachability means "can be found by following references from a root", where the roots are the global object, the call stack, and the closures still in use.

Mark and sweep is the algorithm. Start at the roots, mark everything that can be reached from them, and free everything else. One important consequence: reference counting is not used (counting how many references point at each object). So two objects that refer to each other, but that nothing else can reach, are still collected correctly.

let big = { payload: new Array(1000).fill('x') };
const weak = new WeakRef(big);
console.log('reachable through weak:', weak.deref() !== undefined);
big = null;                                  // the only strong reference is gone
console.log('the WeakRef itself does not keep it alive:', typeof weak.deref);
const registry = new FinalizationRegistry((label) => { /* may run, may not */ });
registry.register({}, 'a label');
console.log('FinalizationRegistry accepts a registration:', registry instanceof FinalizationRegistry);

reachable through weak: true
the WeakRef itself does not keep it alive: function
FinalizationRegistry accepts a registration: true

WeakRef holds a reference that does not stop the object from being collected. FinalizationRegistry asks for a callback after an object has been collected. Both are deliberately unreliable: the callback may never run, and deref() may return undefined at any moment. So they are for caches and diagnostics, never for releasing a resource. Releasing resources is what §3.8 is for.

The terms above, gathered: mark and sweep and reachability.

3.11 The Four Leak Shapes

A memory leak in JavaScript is not a failure to free memory. It is a reference you forgot you were holding, which keeps an object reachable. Four shapes cover nearly all of them:

a listener never removed
The listener holds its closure, the closure holds the component, and the event target holds the listener. One AbortController (§16.2) removes all of it.
a detached DOM node
A node removed from the document but still referenced by a variable or a cache. It is out of the page and still in memory, along with every descendant.
a growing cache
A Map keyed by objects that is never pruned. A WeakMap (§8.13) fixes it structurally.
a timer never cleared
A setInterval keeps its callback — and everything the callback closes over — alive forever.

A detached DOM node is the one to recognise on sight:

document.body.innerHTML = '<div id="panel"><p>a thousand rows would go here</p></div>';
const cache = new Map();
const panel = document.getElementById('panel');
cache.set('panel', panel);                   // the leak
panel.remove();
console.log('removed from the document:', !panel.isConnected);
console.log('but still reachable through the cache:', cache.get('panel').textContent);
cache.delete('panel');
console.log('cleared:', cache.size);

removed from the document: true
but still reachable through the cache: a thousand rows would go here
cleared: 0

One line each, for reference: a memory leak.

3.12 Finding a Leak

A heap snapshot in devtools, a picture of every object in memory at one moment, is how you find these. The procedure is mechanical rather than clever.

1
Load the page and take a snapshot. This is the baseline.
2
Do the suspect thing several times — open and close the dialog twenty times, navigate back and forth. Repetition is what turns a one-off allocation into an obvious slope.
3
Take a second snapshot and compare it to the first. Twenty of your component in the diff is the answer.
4
Select one and read the retainers panel, which shows the chain of references keeping it alive, from a root down to the object.

Two columns matter, and they answer different questions. Shallow size is the size of the object itself. Retained size is everything that would be freed if this object went away. Retained size is the number that tells you whether a leak is worth fixing: a 40-byte closure holding on to a 4MB array has a tiny shallow size and a retained size that matters.

The "Detached" filter lists the second shape above directly, and it is usually the fastest first look. Every detached node in that list is an element the page has removed while something in your code still holds on to it.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: a heap snapshot.

3.13 The Resource Problem, and using

Garbage collection handles memory and nothing else. A file handle, a database connection, a lock, a subscription: these must be released at a known point, and until recently try/finally was the only tool for that.

The using declaration gives a name to a resource and disposes of it (releases it) when the surrounding block ends, however it ends:

class Handle {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; console.log(`  opened ${name}`); }
  [Symbol.dispose]() { console.log(`  disposed ${this.name}`); }
}
{
  using first = new Handle('first');
  using second = new Handle('second');
  console.log('  the block body runs');
}
console.log('after the block');

  opened first
  opened second
  the block body runs
  disposed second
  disposed first
after the block

Disposal is in reverse order of acquisition, exactly like nested try/finally blocks, and for the same reason: the second resource may depend on the first. It happens on any way out of the block: reaching the end, return, break, or a thrown exception.

An object becomes usable with using by having a method under a special built-in symbol, a well-known symbol. Symbol.dispose is the synchronous one. Symbol.asyncDispose is the asynchronous one, used with await using:

class Connection {
  async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() { console.log('  connection closed'); }
}
async function work() {
  await using conn = new Connection();
  console.log('  using the connection');
}
await work();
console.log('done');

  using the connection
  connection closed
done

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: the using declaration, Symbol.dispose, Symbol.asyncDispose and a well-known symbol.

3.14 DisposableStack

The DisposableStack object and AsyncDisposableStack cover the case where you cannot list the resources in advance, such as resources opened in a loop or only under some condition:

class Handle {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; console.log(`  opened ${name}`); }
  [Symbol.dispose]() { console.log(`  disposed ${this.name}`); }
}
function openAll(names) {
  using stack = new DisposableStack();
  for (const name of names) stack.use(new Handle(name));
  stack.defer(() => console.log('  a deferred callback also runs'));
  console.log('  all open');
}
openAll(['a', 'b']);

  opened a
  opened b
  all open
  a deferred callback also runs
  disposed b
  disposed a

stack.use() registers a disposable resource, stack.defer() registers a plain cleanup callback, and stack.move() hands everything over to a new owner. That last one is how a constructor passes the resources it opened to the object it is building, without disposing them on the way out.

To have in hand before moving on: the disposablestack object and asyncdisposablestack.

3.15 What This Section Established

  1. const by default, let when reassigning, var never. const forbids rebinding, not mutation — frozen.a went from 1 to 2 without complaint.
  2. var is function-scoped and escapes a block; let and const are block-scoped, which the ReferenceError from outside the if demonstrated.
  3. All declarations hoist; only var and function declarations are initialised. var read as undefined, let threw Cannot access 'letName' before initialization, and a function declaration was callable above its own line.
  4. typeof tolerates an undeclared name and not a TDZ one, which makes a ReferenceError from typeof x a precise diagnosis: x is declared later in this scope.
  5. Scope is lexical — decided by where code is written — so the chain from inner to outer to module scope is fixed at parse time.
  6. Module scope is not global scope. A top-level const in a module is private to it, which is what removed global scope pollution as a daily concern and made the IIFE pattern unnecessary.
  7. Each call creates a new environment, so two counters from one factory shared nothing, while the three functions from one call shared everything.
  8. var in a loop gives one binding and let gives one per iteration — [3, 3, 3] against [0, 1, 2].
  9. Garbage collection is mark-and-sweep over reachability, so cycles are collected and a leak is always a reference someone is still holding.
  10. The four leak shapes: an unremoved listener, a detached DOM node, an unpruned cache, an uncleared timer. The cached node was out of the document and fully alive.
  11. WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry are deliberately unreliable and are for caches and diagnostics, never for releasing a resource.
  12. using disposes in reverse order on every exit path, await using does it asynchronously through Symbol.asyncDispose, and DisposableStack covers the dynamic case.

Exercises

1. Predict the output and explain every line.

var x = 1;
function f() {
  console.log(x);
  var x = 2;
}
f();

function g() {
  console.log(y);
  let y = 2;
}
try { g(); } catch (e) { console.log(e.constructor.name); }

const fns = [];
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { fns.push(() => i); }
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { fns.push(() => i); }
console.log(fns.map(f => f()).join(','));
Solution 
undefined
ReferenceError
3,3,3,0,1,2

f() logs undefined, not 1. The var x inside f is hoisted to the top of the function, creating a local x initialised to undefined that shadows the outer x for the whole function body. The log therefore reads the local one before its assignment. This is the single most confusing consequence of var hoisting: the outer x is not merely unused, it is unreachable from inside f.

g() throws a ReferenceError. let y is hoisted as a binding but not initialised, so the log is in the temporal dead zone (§3.2). The difference in outcome between f and g — a plausible-looking undefined against an immediate error — is the whole argument for let.

The array is 3,3,3,0,1,2. The var loop has one i, shared by all three closures, and it is 3 when they run (the loop exits when the condition fails, so the final value is the one past the end). The let loop creates a fresh binding per iteration, so each closure captured a different i (§3.4).

A detail worth noticing: the two loops both use the name i, and there is no conflict, because the let i is block-scoped to its own loop while the var i is function-scoped — here, module-scoped. If the second loop had also used var, it would have been a redeclaration of the same binding, which var permits silently and let makes a SyntaxError.

2. This component leaks. Identify every retained reference and rewrite it.

class Chart {
  constructor(container, data) {
    this.container = container;
    this.data = data;                                // a large array
    this.cache = new Map();
    window.addEventListener('resize', () => this.redraw());
    this.timer = setInterval(() => this.poll(), 5000);
    container.querySelectorAll('.point').forEach(el => this.cache.set(el, {}));
  }
  redraw() {}
  poll() {}
  destroy() { this.container.innerHTML = ''; }
}
Solution

Four independent leaks, and destroy() fixes none of them.

The resize listener. window holds the arrow function, the arrow closes over this, and this holds data and cache. Since window outlives every component, the whole chart is immortal — and because the handler was never stored, it cannot even be removed by hand: removeEventListener needs the same function object (§16.2).

The interval. setInterval keeps its callback alive forever, and the callback closes over this. It also keeps running, so a page that creates and "destroys" ten charts is polling ten times as often as intended — a performance bug on top of the memory one.

The Map keyed by DOM elements. destroy() sets innerHTML = '', which detaches every .point node — but the Map still holds each one as a key, so every detached node and its subtree stay in memory (§3.5). This is the classic detached-node leak, and it is invisible in the DOM inspector.

The container and data references themselves. destroy() clears the container's contents but leaves this.container, this.data and this.cache intact, so anything still holding the Chart holds all of it.

class Chart {
  #controller = new AbortController();

  constructor(container, data) {
    this.container = container;
    this.data = data;
    this.cache = new WeakMap();                      // does not retain its keys

    const { signal } = this.#controller;
    window.addEventListener('resize', () => this.redraw(), { signal });

    this.timer = setInterval(() => this.poll(), 5000);
    signal.addEventListener('abort', () => clearInterval(this.timer), { once: true });

    for (const el of container.querySelectorAll('.point')) this.cache.set(el, {});
  }

  redraw() {}
  poll() {}

  destroy() {
    this.#controller.abort();                        // listener and timer, in one call
    this.container.replaceChildren();
    this.container = null;
    this.data = null;
    this.cache = null;
  }
}

Why each change. One AbortController owns every subscription, so destroy is a single abort() and it is impossible to add a listener that teardown forgets — including the interval, which is cleared by an abort listener rather than by a separate line someone can delete. WeakMap instead of Map means detached nodes are collectable the moment nothing else references them, and it is the correct structure for "data attached to a node I do not own" (§8.13). Nulling the fields releases data even if a stale reference to the Chart survives — which is the realistic case, since the thing that held it is usually what forgot to drop it.

How you would have found it. Take a heap snapshot, create and destroy the chart twenty times, take another, and compare (§3.5). Twenty retained Chart objects with a growing retained size, and the retainer path in devtools names the culprit directly: window → resize listener → closure → Chart.

The idempotence point: destroy() can now be called twice safely — abort() on an already-aborted controller is a no-op — which matters because teardown gets called from both an explicit call and an unmount path more often than anyone plans for.

3. Implement once(fn) returning a function that runs fn at most once and returns the first result thereafter, and memoize(fn) caching by argument. Explain what each closes over and the lifetime consequences.

Solution 
function once(fn) {
  let called = false;
  let result;
  return function (...args) {
    if (called) return result;
    called = true;
    result = fn.apply(this, args);
    fn = null;                                       // release the original
    return result;
  };
}

function memoize(fn, { keyFn = (...a) => JSON.stringify(a), max = Infinity } = {}) {
  const cache = new Map();
  return function (...args) {
    const key = keyFn(...args);
    if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key);       // has(), not get() — undefined is a valid result
    const value = fn.apply(this, args);
    cache.set(key, value);
    if (cache.size > max) cache.delete(cache.keys().next().value);   // evict the oldest
    return value;
  };
}

let calls = 0;
const init = once(() => { calls++; return { id: 1 }; });
const first = init(), second = init();
console.log('called once:', calls, '| same object returned:', first === second);

let work = 0;
const slow = memoize((n) => { work++; return n * 2; });
console.log(slow(5), slow(5), slow(6), '| underlying calls:', work);

called once: 1 | same object returned: true
10 10 12 | underlying calls: 2

Three invocations, two underlying calls: the second slow(5) came from the cache.

What once closes over: called, result and fn. The fn = null line is the part usually omitted and it matters — without it, the returned function keeps the original alive forever, along with everything it closed over. For a one-shot initialiser that captured a large configuration object, that is a permanent retention of something never needed again (§3.5).

fn.apply(this, args) rather than fn(...args) so the wrapper is transparent when used as a method: obj.method = once(obj.method) keeps working. An arrow function here would break that, because an arrow has no this of its own (§5.14).

What memoize closes over: cache, fn and keyFn, and the cache lives as long as the returned function does. That is the lifetime consequence to state plainly: an unbounded memoise is an unbounded leak. Memoising a function called with a few dozen distinct arguments is free; memoising one called with a user-supplied string grows without limit, which is why max is there and why the eviction takes cache.keys().next().value — a Map iterates in insertion order (§8.11), so that is the oldest entry.

cache.has(key) rather than cache.get(key) ?? compute() because undefined and null are legitimate results, and the ?? form would recompute them every time — a bug that only shows up as a mysterious performance problem.

The keyFn default is JSON.stringify and it is a compromise. It is wrong for object arguments whose key order differs, for functions, for undefined (which stringifies away), and for anything cyclic (which throws). For a single object argument, a WeakMap keyed by the object is strictly better — constant time, no serialisation, and no retention. The honest interface is to make keyFn explicit for anything but primitives.

SECTION 4

Expressions, Operators and Control Flow

This is the section people skim, and it is the one whose gaps show up most often in code review. Operators are not hard. The trouble is elsewhere:

  • JavaScript has around fifty of them, arranged in nineteen precedence levels (the rules for which operator applies first when several appear together).
  • Several were added recently enough that half of working developers have never used them.
  • Three of the newest ones (?., ??, &&=) replace an older defensive habit that is almost right, and fails on exactly the values you would expect to be safe.

The organising idea is that an expression produces a value and a statement does something. JavaScript blurs that line in useful ways. Assignment is an expression, so a = b = 0 works. A ternary (cond ? a : b) is an expression, so it can appear where if cannot. Knowing which construct is which tells you where each may be used.

Destructuring, the syntax for pulling values out of an object or array into variables, gets a full treatment. It changed how JavaScript is written more than any other syntax since 2015, and its interaction with default values has a rule people get wrong, in a way that produces a null-shaped bug.

4.1 Precedence and Associativity

When one expression contains several operators, two rules decide how it is grouped. Operator precedence decides which operator binds tighter, the way * comes before + in arithmetic. And associativity decides the order among operators of equal precedence: left to right, or right to left.

console.log('* before +:', 2 + 3 * 4);
console.log('** is right-associative:', 2 ** 3 ** 2, '— that is 2 ** 9, not 8 ** 2');
console.log('- is left-associative:  ', 10 - 3 - 2);
console.log('assignment is right-associative:', (() => { let a, b; a = b = 5; return [a, b]; })());
console.log('comparison before logical:', true || false && false, '— && binds tighter than ||');
console.log('typeof binds tighter than ===:', typeof 'x' === 'string');

* before +: 14
** is right-associative: 512 — that is 2 ** 9, not 8 ** 2
- is left-associative:   5
assignment is right-associative: [ 5, 5 ]
comparison before logical: true — && binds tighter than ||
typeof binds tighter than ===: true

The nineteen levels are not worth memorising. Four facts are:

** is right-associative, and every other binary operator (one with two operands) is left-associative. && binds tighter than ||, so a || b && c means a || (b && c). Assignment is right-associative, which is what makes chained assignment work. And ?? may not be mixed with && or || without parentheses. That is a SyntaxError, on purpose, because the grouping you meant is genuinely ambiguous:

console.log('mixing ?? with || needs parentheses:',
  (() => { try { eval('null ?? false || true'); return 'allowed'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());
console.log('with them it is fine:', null ?? (false || true));

mixing ?? with || needs parentheses: SyntaxError
with them it is fine: true

For everything else: when in doubt, parenthesise. Nobody has ever been confused by an unnecessary bracket.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: operator precedence.

4.2 Assignment, and the Logical Assignment Operators

The assignment operator gives back the value it assigned, which is what lets you use an assignment inside a larger expression. The compound forms (+=, -=, *=, /=, %=, **= and the bitwise ones) are shorthand for reading a value, applying the operator, and writing the result back.

Logical assignment operators are the three newest and the most misunderstood:

const settings = { retries: 0, name: '', timeout: null };

const a = { ...settings };
a.retries ||= 3;                    // assigns when the current value is FALSY
const b = { ...settings };
b.retries ??= 3;                    // assigns only when null or undefined
console.log('||= overwrote a legitimate 0:', a.retries, '| ??= left it alone:', b.retries);

const c = { ...settings };
c.name ||= 'anonymous';
const d = { ...settings };
d.name ??= 'anonymous';
console.log('the same for an empty string:', JSON.stringify(c.name), JSON.stringify(d.name));

const e = { ...settings, verbose: true };
e.verbose &&= 'enabled';            // assigns only when the current value is TRUTHY
console.log('&&= :', e.verbose, '| on a falsy value it does nothing:', (() => { const f = { v: 0 }; f.v &&= 9; return f.v; })());

||= overwrote a legitimate 0: 3 | ??= left it alone: 0
the same for an empty string: "anonymous" ""
&&= : enabled | on a falsy value it does nothing: 0

That is the whole argument for ??=. ||= fires on any falsy value, so a legitimate 0, '' or false is silently replaced by the default. That is the single most common defaulting bug in JavaScript, and before 2020 it was the only option.

All three short-circuit the assignment itself, not just the value. obj.x ??= expensive() does not call expensive() when x already has a value. More subtly, it does not write to obj.x at all, so a setter is not called and a proxy trap does not fire.

In summary, the vocabulary here is the assignment operator and a proxy trap.

4.3 Short-Circuit Evaluation

Short-circuit evaluation means && and || stop as soon as the answer is known. And, the part that matters, they return one of their operands, not a boolean:

console.log('|| returns the first truthy operand:', 0 || '' || 'fallback' || 'never reached');
console.log('&& returns the first falsy one:     ', 1 && 'two' && 0 && 'never reached');
console.log('so the type is not boolean:', typeof (0 || 'x'), typeof (1 && 2));

let called = 0;
const track = () => { called++; return true; };
false && track();
true || track();
console.log('neither side effect ran:', called);

const user = { profile: null };
console.log('the guard idiom:', user.profile && user.profile.name);
console.log('but || for defaults is the §4.2 trap:', 0 || 'default');

|| returns the first truthy operand: fallback
&& returns the first falsy one:      0
so the type is not boolean: string number
neither side effect ran: 0
the guard idiom: null
but || for defaults is the §4.2 trap: default

Logical AND (&&) returns its first falsy operand, or the last one if none is falsy. And logical OR (||) returns its first truthy operand, or the last one. Nullish coalescing, ??, is the third: it returns the right side only when the left side is null or undefined (together called nullish).

The short-circuit is why isReady && render() works as an if, and why condition && <Component/> is the standard way to show something conditionally in JSX. It is also why that pattern has a famous bug: items.length && <List/> shows a literal 0 when the array is empty, because && returned the number.

What to carry forward from this subsection: logical and, logical or and nullish coalescing.

4.4 Optional Chaining

Optional chaining (?.) stops the whole chain and gives undefined when the value before it is null or undefined, instead of throwing:

const data = { user: { profile: null, tags: ['a'], greet: () => 'hi' } };
console.log('a present path:      ', data.user?.tags?.[0]);
console.log('a null in the middle:', data.user?.profile?.name);
console.log('a missing path:      ', data.missing?.deep?.deeper);
console.log('without it, this throws:',
  (() => { try { return data.user.profile.name; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());
console.log('an optional call:', data.user.greet?.(), '| on a missing method:', data.user.absent?.());
console.log('it stops at null/undefined ONLY — 0 and "" continue:',
  (() => { const o = { count: 0 }; return o.count?.toFixed(1); })());
console.log('the whole chain short-circuits, not just one link:',
  (() => { let calls = 0; const f = () => { calls++; return 1; }; const o = null; o?.a[f()]; return calls; })());

a present path:       a
a null in the middle: undefined
a missing path:       undefined
without it, this throws: TypeError
an optional call: hi | on a missing method: undefined
it stops at null/undefined ONLY — 0 and "" continue: 0.0
the whole chain short-circuits, not just one link: 0

An optional call, fn?.(), is the same idea for calling a function. It is the clean way to call a callback that may not have been passed in. arr?.[i] is the square-bracket form.

Two things to know. The short-circuit covers the rest of the chain, so o?.a[f()] does not call f at all when o is nullish, as the last measurement shows. And it is not a general error suppressor: data.user?.tags[5].name still throws, because only the step right after ?. is protected. Writing ?. at every level is over-defensive and hides real bugs. Put it exactly where a value is legitimately allowed to be missing.

4.5 The Conditional and Comma Operators

The exponentiation operator ** (raising to a power) deserves a note here too. It is the only right-associative binary operator (§4.1). And (-2) ** 2 needs its parentheses: writing -2 ** 2 is a deliberate SyntaxError, because the language refuses to guess whether the minus applies before or after the power.

The conditional operator, cond ? a : b, is the only ternary operator (an operator with three operands), and the only conditional that is an expression:

const count = 3;
console.log('as an expression:', `${count} item${count === 1 ? '' : 's'}`);
const level = count > 10 ? 'high' : count > 5 ? 'medium' : 'low';
console.log('chained, right-associative:', level);
console.log('in a const initialiser, where if cannot go:', (() => { const x = count ? 'set' : 'unset'; return x; })());

as an expression: 3 items
chained, right-associative: low
in a const initialiser, where if cannot go: set

Chained ternaries group from the right, and read like an else if ladder. Two or three are fine when formatted one branch per line. More than that should be a switch or a lookup object.

The comma operator evaluates both sides and gives back the right one. You mostly meet it in for headers and in minified code:

console.log('returns the last:', (1, 2, 3));
for (let i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i++, j--) if (i === 4) console.log('two counters in one header:', i, j);

returns the last: 3
two counters in one header: 4 6

The terms above, gathered: the conditional operator, the comma operator and the exponentiation operator.

4.6 delete, void and in

const obj = { a: 1, b: 2 };
console.log('delete returns a boolean:', delete obj.a, '| now:', JSON.stringify(obj));
console.log('and it is true even for a missing key:', delete obj.nope);
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
delete arr[1];
console.log('on an array it leaves a HOLE, not a shift:', arr.length, JSON.stringify(arr), 1 in arr);

console.log('void always evaluates to undefined:', void 0, void 'anything');
console.log('the in operator checks the whole chain:', 'a' in obj, 'toString' in obj);
console.log('for arrays it asks about indices:', 0 in [7], 5 in [7]);

delete returns a boolean: true | now: {"b":2}
and it is true even for a missing key: true
on an array it leaves a HOLE, not a shift: 3 [1,null,3] false
void always evaluates to undefined: undefined undefined
the in operator checks the whole chain: false true
for arrays it asks about indices: true false

The delete operator removes a property and returns whether the object is now free of it. So it returns true for a key that never existed, and false only for a property that cannot be deleted (a non-configurable one, §6.6). Never delete an array element: it leaves a hole (§8.1) and does not change length. splice is what you want.

The void operator evaluates its operand and returns undefined. It has two real uses: void 0 in minified code, as a shorter undefined that nothing can shadow, and void promise, to say on purpose that a promise is not being awaited (§12.11).

The in operator checks the prototype chain too, which is why 'toString' in obj is true. Object.hasOwn asks only about the object's own properties (§6.9).

One line each, for reference: the delete operator, the void operator and the prototype chain.

4.7 Bitwise Operators

Numbers are doubles (§2.9), but the bitwise operators, which work on the individual binary digits (bits) of a number, convert to 32-bit signed integers first. There are seven:

  • bitwise AND (&) keeps the bits that are set in both operands;
  • bitwise OR (|) keeps the bits set in either;
  • bitwise XOR (^) keeps the bits set in exactly one;
  • bitwise NOT (~) flips every bit;
  • and three shifts, of which the << operator moves bits left, filling with zeros:
console.log('bitwise AND:', 0b1100 & 0b1010, '| bitwise OR:', 0b1100 | 0b1010);
console.log('bitwise XOR:', 0b1100 ^ 0b1010, '| bitwise NOT:', ~5, '— which is -(n+1)');
console.log('the << operator:', 1 << 8, '| the >> operator:', -16 >> 2, '| the >>> operator:', -16 >>> 28);
console.log('32-bit truncation bites:', 2 ** 31 | 0, '| and beyond 32 bits:', 2 ** 32 | 0);

const READ = 1, WRITE = 2, EXECUTE = 4;
let permissions = READ | WRITE;
console.log('a bitmask — has WRITE:', (permissions & WRITE) !== 0, '| has EXECUTE:', (permissions & EXECUTE) !== 0);
permissions |= EXECUTE;
permissions &= ~READ;
console.log('after adding EXECUTE and removing READ:', permissions.toString(2).padStart(3, '0'));

bitwise AND: 8 | bitwise OR: 14
bitwise XOR: 6 | bitwise NOT: -6 — which is -(n+1)
the << operator: 256 | the >> operator: -4 | the >>> operator: 15
32-bit truncation bites: -2147483648 | and beyond 32 bits: 0
a bitmask — has WRITE: true | has EXECUTE: false
after adding EXECUTE and removing READ: 110

The << operator multiplies by a power of two, so 1 << 8 is 256, and it is the cheapest way to build a single-bit flag. The >> operator keeps the sign and the >>> operator does not. That is the only difference between them, and it is why -16 >>> 28 is a large positive number. A bitmask is the one place these come up in ordinary application code: a set of on/off flags packed into one number, as above. The operations are: test a flag with &, add one with |=, and remove one with &= ~.

The 32-bit conversion is the trap. 2 ** 32 | 0 is 0, so a bitwise operation on a value above 2³¹ silently produces nonsense. Math.floor is the correct way to drop the fraction. | 0 as a "fast floor" is a micro-optimisation that is wrong for large numbers and for negatives.

4.8 Destructuring

Array destructuring unpacks by position; object destructuring unpacks by name:

const [first, second, ...rest] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
console.log('array:', first, second, rest);
const [, , third] = [1, 2, 3];
console.log('holes skip positions:', third);
let a = 1, b = 2;
[a, b] = [b, a];
console.log('swap with no temporary:', a, b);

const { name, tags: renamed, missing } = { name: 'Ada', tags: ['x'] };
console.log('object, with renaming:', name, renamed, missing);
const { length } = 'hello';
console.log('it works on any object, including a string:', length);

array: 1 2 [ 3, 4, 5 ]
holes skip positions: 3
swap with no temporary: 2 1
object, with renaming: Ada [ 'x' ] undefined
it works on any object, including a string: 5

A default value in destructuring is used only when the extracted value is undefined. That is the same rule as a default parameter (§5.2), and it causes a specific bug:

const { retries = 3 } = { retries: null };
console.log('null does NOT trigger the default:', retries);
const { timeout = 5000 } = { timeout: undefined };
console.log('undefined does:', timeout);
const { missing = 'fallback' } = {};
console.log('and so does an absent key:', missing);
console.log('the fix for null is ??:', ({ retries: null }).retries ?? 3);

null does NOT trigger the default: null
undefined does: 5000
and so does an absent key: fallback
the fix for null is ??: 3

So an API that returns null for "no value" defeats every destructuring default in your code. The repair is ??, not a default.

Nested destructuring reaches as deep as the data goes, and combines with renaming and defaults:

const response = { data: { user: { name: 'Ada', address: { city: 'London' } }, items: [{ id: 1 }] } };
const { data: { user: { name, address: { city, country = 'UK' } }, items: [{ id: firstId }] } } = response;
console.log(name, city, country, firstId);

function draw({ size = 'medium', coords: { x = 0, y = 0 } = {}, radius = 25 } = {}) {
  return `${size} at ${x},${y} r${radius}`;
}
console.log(draw());
console.log(draw({ coords: { x: 18 }, radius: 30 }));

Ada London UK 1
medium at 0,0 r25
medium at 18,0 r30

The = {} on coords, and on the whole parameter list, is what makes calling with no argument work. Without it, destructuring undefined throws. Note also that deeply nested destructuring pulls out values but gives you no name for the intermediate objects. If you need user as well as name, you must ask for both.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: array destructuring, object destructuring, a default value in destructuring and a default parameter.

4.9 Spread and Rest

Spread syntax expands an iterable into individual elements, and rest parameters gather up whatever is left over. They use the same three dots in opposite directions, and their position tells you which one you are looking at.

console.log('spread into a call:', Math.max(...[3, 1, 4]));
console.log('copy and concatenate:', [...[1, 2], 0, ...[3]]);
console.log('spread works on any iterable:', [...'abc'], [...new Set([1, 1, 2])]);
console.log('object spread merges, later wins:', JSON.stringify({ ...{ a: 1, b: 2 }, b: 3 }));
const { a, ...others } = { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 };
console.log('object rest collects the remainder:', a, JSON.stringify(others));
console.log('spread is SHALLOW:', (() => {
  const original = { nested: { n: 1 } };
  const copy = { ...original };
  copy.nested.n = 99;
  return original.nested.n;
})());

spread into a call: 4
copy and concatenate: [ 1, 2, 0, 3 ]
spread works on any iterable: [ 'a', 'b', 'c' ] [ 1, 2 ]
object spread merges, later wins: {"a":1,"b":3}
object rest collects the remainder: 1 {"b":2,"c":3}
spread is SHALLOW: 99

Array spread needs an iterable (something for...of can loop over), while object spread needs only an object. That is why [...{a:1}] throws while {...[1,2]} gives {0:1, 1:2}. Object rest is the usual way to remove a key without changing the original: const { password, ...safe } = user.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: spread syntax and rest parameters.

4.10 Conditionals

const value = 'b';
if (value === 'a') console.log('a');
else if (value === 'b') console.log('if...else ladder:', value);
else console.log('neither');

function describe(kind) {
  switch (kind) {
    case 'cat':
    case 'dog':
      return 'a pet';                       // deliberate grouping, no fallthrough hazard
    case 'lion':
      return 'not a pet';
    default:
      return 'unknown';
  }
}
console.log([describe('cat'), describe('dog'), describe('lion'), describe('fish')].join(' | '));

function leaky(n) {
  const out = [];
  switch (n) {
    case 1: out.push('one');                // no break — falls through
    case 2: out.push('two'); break;
    case 3: out.push('three');
  }
  return out;
}
console.log('fallthrough with n=1:', leaky(1), '| n=2:', leaky(2));
console.log('switch compares with ===:', (() => { switch ('1') { case 1: return 'matched a number'; default: return 'no match'; } })());

if...else ladder: b
a pet | a pet | not a pet | unknown
fallthrough with n=1: [ 'one', 'two' ] | n=2: [ 'two' ]
switch compares with ===: no match

if...else accepts any expression and applies truthiness (§2.3). Unlike a ternary it is a statement, so it cannot appear where a value is expected. The switch statement compares using strict equality, so '1' does not match case 1. That is a real trap when the value came from a form or a URL, where everything is a string.

Fallthrough is the design flaw. Without break, execution carries on into the next case, which is why n === 1 produced both 'one' and 'two'. Grouping cases on purpose, as describe does, is the one legitimate use; every other fallthrough is a missing break, and linters flag it for that reason. Returning from each case, as describe also does, avoids the whole issue.

A switch on a value with more than a few branches is often better as a lookup object, such as const handlers = { cat: …, dog: … }. That turns control flow into data, which can be extended without editing a statement.

To have in hand before moving on: the switch statement.

4.11 Loops

const items = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
const out = [];
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) out.push(`${i}:${items[i]}`);
console.log('the for statement:', out.join(' '));

let n = 0;
while (n < 3) n++;
console.log('the while loop ran until the condition failed:', n);

let m = 10;
do { m++; } while (m < 3);
console.log('do...while always runs at least once:', m);

const obj = { x: 1, y: 2 };
console.log('for...in gives KEYS, including inherited ones:', Object.keys(obj), (() => { const k = []; for (const key in obj) k.push(key); return k; })());
console.log('for...of gives VALUES, of any iterable:', (() => { const v = []; for (const value of items) v.push(value); return v; })());
console.log('for...of over an object throws:',
  (() => { try { for (const x of obj) {} return 'ok'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());
console.log('with entries you get both:', [...items.entries()].map(([i, v]) => `${i}${v}`).join(''));

the for statement: 0:a 1:b 2:c
the while loop ran until the condition failed: 3
do...while always runs at least once: 11
for...in gives KEYS, including inherited ones: [ 'x', 'y' ] [ 'x', 'y' ]
for...of gives VALUES, of any iterable: [ 'a', 'b', 'c' ]
for...of over an object throws: TypeError
with entries you get both: 0a1b2c

The for statement is the classic three-part loop: a starting step, a condition, and an update. It is still the right tool when you need the index or a step other than one. The while loop checks its condition before each pass, and fits when you do not know the number of passes in advance. do...while checks after, so its body always runs at least once. That is why the counter above finished at 11 rather than 10.

for...in loops over string keys, including inherited enumerable ones (§6.9), and puts integer-like keys first (§6.2). It is right for a plain object and wrong for an array, where for...of or .entries() is correct.

for...of loops over any iterable (§11.1), and it is the default loop in modern JavaScript. It throws on a plain object, which is the error above; Object.entries(obj) is the fix.

4.12 break, continue and Labels

const found = [];
outer:
for (const row of [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]) {
  for (const cell of row) {
    if (cell === 4) break outer;              // a labeled statement
    if (cell % 2 === 0) continue;
    found.push(cell);
  }
}
console.log('the break statement with a label left both loops:', found);

const evens = [];
for (const n of [1, 2, 3, 4]) {
  if (n % 2) continue;                        // the continue statement
  evens.push(n);
}
console.log('continue skipped the odds:', evens);
console.log('but neither works in forEach:',
  (() => { const r = []; [1, 2, 3].forEach(n => { if (n === 2) return; r.push(n); }); return r; })());

the break statement with a label left both loops: [ 1, 3 ]
continue skipped the odds: [ 2, 4 ]
but neither works in forEach: [ 1, 3 ]

The break statement leaves the innermost loop or switch, and the continue statement skips to the next pass. A labeled statement lets either one target an outer loop. A label is the only clean way out of a nested loop; the alternative is a flag variable checked in both conditions.

Note the last line. Inside .forEach, return acts like continue, and there is no way to break at all (§8.5). That difference is a real reason to prefer for...of when a loop may need to stop early.

4.13 with, and What Not to Use

The with statement adds an object's properties to the scope chain. It is forbidden in strict mode, and so in every module and every class body:

console.log('with is a SyntaxError in a module:',
  (() => { try { eval('with ({}) {}'); return 'allowed'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());

with is a SyntaxError in a module: SyntaxError

It is here only so you recognise it in old code and know why it went away. Inside a with, neither a reader nor the optimiser can tell whether a bare name is a variable or a property of the object. That makes scope impossible to decide by reading the code. Destructuring (§4.8) covers every legitimate use of it.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: the with statement.

4.14 What This Section Established

  1. ** is right-associative (2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512), && binds tighter than ||, assignment is right-associative, and mixing ?? with && or || is a SyntaxError by design.
  2. ||= fires on any falsy value and ??= only on nullish — the measurement replaced a legitimate 0 with 3 and an empty string with 'anonymous'.
  3. All three logical assignments short-circuit the write itself, so no setter runs and no proxy trap fires when the assignment is skipped.
  4. && and || return an operand, not a boolean — typeof (1 && 2) is number, which is why items.length && <List/> renders a 0.
  5. Optional chaining short-circuits the whole rest of the chain — o?.a[f()] never called f — and guards only the link it follows, so it is not a general error suppressor.
  6. delete on an array leaves a hole and does not change length. Use splice.
  7. Bitwise operators truncate to 32 bits, so 2 ** 32 | 0 is 0; >> keeps the sign and >>> does not.
  8. A destructuring default fires only on undefined, so an API returning null defeats every default in your code; ?? is the repair.
  9. = {} on a destructured parameter is what makes a no-argument call legal.
  10. Spread is shallow — the nested object was shared and read 99 — and object rest is the idiomatic key removal.
  11. switch compares with ===, so '1' does not match case 1, and a missing break falls through — n === 1 produced two entries.
  12. for...in gives keys including inherited ones; for...of gives values and throws on a plain object.
  13. A label is the only clean exit from a nested loop, and .forEach supports neither break nor continue.

Exercises

1. Predict each line and name the rule.

console.log(1 + 2 + '3', '1' + 2 + 3);
console.log(0 || 'a', 0 ?? 'a', null || 'a', null ?? 'a');
const o = { a: { b: 0 } };
console.log(o.a?.b ?? 'fallback', o.x?.y ?? 'fallback');
const { p = 1 } = { p: null };
const { q = 1 } = { q: undefined };
console.log(p, q);
console.log([1, 2, 3].length && 'yes', [].length && 'yes');
console.log(typeof (2 ** 3 ** 2), 2 ** 3 ** 2);
Solution 
33 123
a 0 a a
0 fallback
null 1
yes 0
number 512

1 + 2 + '3' is '33' and '1' + 2 + 3 is '123'. + is left-associative, so the first evaluates 1 + 2 to 3 and then concatenates; the second concatenates from the start, and every subsequent + has a string operand (§2.5).

0 || 'a' is 'a' but 0 ?? 'a' is 0. || tests truthiness and 0 is falsy; ?? tests only for null/undefined. Both null cases give 'a' because null is both falsy and nullish (§4.2).

o.a?.b ?? 'fallback' is 0. The optional chain resolves to 0, which is not nullish, so ?? keeps it. o.x?.y is undefined, so the fallback applies. This pair is the reason to prefer ?./?? over &&/|| for defaults.

p is null and q is 1. A destructuring default fires only for undefined (§4.8).

[1,2,3].length && 'yes' is 'yes' and [].length && 'yes' is 0. && returns the first falsy operand, which is the number 0 — not false, and not ''. In a template or JSX that renders as a visible 0, which is the bug §4.3 names.

2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512, a number. ** is right-associative, so it is 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9. Every other binary operator would have grouped left and given 8 ** 2 = 64.

2. Rewrite this defensive code using modern operators and explain what each change fixes.

function getConfig(options) {
  options = options || {};
  var timeout = options.timeout || 5000;
  var retries = options.retries || 3;
  var name = options.meta && options.meta.name ? options.meta.name : 'unnamed';
  var onDone = options.onDone;
  if (onDone) { onDone(); }
  return { timeout: timeout, retries: retries, name: name };
}
Solution 
function getConfig({ timeout = 5000, retries = 3, meta, onDone } = {}) {
  const name = meta?.name ?? 'unnamed';
  onDone?.();
  return { timeout, retries, name };
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(getConfig()));
console.log('a legitimate 0 now survives:', JSON.stringify(getConfig({ retries: 0, timeout: 0 })));
console.log('the old || version would have given:', 0 || 3, 0 || 5000);
console.log('an explicit null still needs ??:', JSON.stringify(getConfig({ meta: { name: null } })));

{"timeout":5000,"retries":3,"name":"unnamed"}
a legitimate 0 now survives: {"timeout":0,"retries":0,"name":"unnamed"}
the old || version would have given: 3 5000
an explicit null still needs ??: {"timeout":5000,"retries":3,"name":"unnamed"}

options = options || {} becomes = {} in the parameter list. Same effect for the no-argument case, declared where the reader looks for it — and it no longer reassigns a parameter, which some styles forbid outright.

options.timeout || 5000 becomes a destructuring default. This is the substantive fix: retries: 0 and timeout: 0 are legitimate values that || silently replaced with the defaults, as the third line measures. A destructuring default fires only for undefined (§4.8), so 0 survives.

options.meta && options.meta.name ? … : … becomes meta?.name ?? 'unnamed'. The original repeats options.meta twice — a bug waiting for someone to rename one of them — and the ternary is redundant because ?? already expresses "or the default". Note the last measurement: meta.name being explicitly null still yields 'unnamed', because ?? catches null as well as undefined, which is what the original did too.

if (onDone) { onDone(); } becomes onDone?.(). Shorter, and it means the same thing with one difference worth naming: onDone?.() throws a TypeError if onDone is a non-callable non-nullish value such as 42, whereas the if silently skipped it. That is an improvement — a truthy non-function is a caller bug, and failing fast (§13.7) is the right response.

var becomes const so nothing can be reassigned later in the function, and the shorthand return removes the repetition (§6.1).

One thing deliberately unchanged: the function still accepts an options object rather than positional parameters. Four positional arguments would be shorter and much worse at the call site, and the destructured signature documents every option with its default in one line.

3. Write pick(obj, keys) and omit(obj, keys) without mutating the input, and explain the operator choices.

Solution 
function pick(obj, keys) {
  const out = {};
  for (const key of keys) {
    if (Object.hasOwn(obj, key)) out[key] = obj[key];      // hasOwn, not `in`
  }
  return out;
}

function omit(obj, keys) {
  const drop = new Set(keys);                              // O(1) membership
  return Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(obj).filter(([key]) => !drop.has(key)));
}

const user = { id: 1, name: 'Ada', password: 'secret', email: 'a@b.co' };
console.log('pick:', JSON.stringify(pick(user, ['id', 'name'])));
console.log('pick ignores absent keys:', JSON.stringify(pick(user, ['id', 'nope'])));
console.log('omit:', JSON.stringify(omit(user, ['password'])));
console.log('the input is untouched:', Object.keys(user).length);
const { password, ...safe } = user;
console.log('for a fixed key, rest destructuring is simpler:', JSON.stringify(safe));

pick: {"id":1,"name":"Ada"}
pick ignores absent keys: {"id":1}
omit: {"id":1,"name":"Ada","email":"a@b.co"}
the input is untouched: 4
for a fixed key, rest destructuring is simpler: {"id":1,"name":"Ada","email":"a@b.co"}

Object.hasOwn rather than in in pick. The in operator walks the prototype chain (§4.6), so pick(user, ['toString']) would copy an inherited function into the result — which is both wrong and, for an object built from user input, a route into prototype-related mischief (§7.12).

Object.hasOwn rather than obj[key] !== undefined for the same test. A key that genuinely holds undefined is present, and the truthiness check would drop it, changing the shape of the result.

A Set for the omit list, not keys.includes(key). includes is O(n) per entry, making omit O(n·m); a Set makes it O(n + m) (§8.12). It costs one line and it is the kind of choice that never has to be revisited.

Object.entries → filter → Object.fromEntries is the idiomatic object transform (§6.3). It reads as a pipeline, and it also settles the mutation question by construction — there is no path by which the original could be touched.

When to use rest destructuring instead: the last line does the same job as omit(user, ['password']) in less code, and it is the better choice whenever the keys are known at authoring time. omit earns its place only when the key list is data — a column selection from a query string, a redaction list from configuration.

What both deliberately do not do: copy deeply, or preserve getters and non-enumerable properties. Both produce plain shallow objects with the values read out (§6.4), which is right for a DTO and wrong for cloning a live object — and stating that is better than a subtly leaky implementation that appears to do more.

SECTION 5

Functions and the this Binding

Functions are the basic building block of everything in JavaScript, for three reasons:

  • They are values, so they can be stored, passed, returned and built while the program runs.
  • They carry the scope they were created in with them (§3.7).
  • They are the only construct in the language whose meaning depends on how they are called, and not only on how they are written.

That last property is this, and it causes more confusion than any other single feature. The rules are not complicated. The problem is that there are five of them, and they are usually taught as one.

This section covers the ways to define a function and what actually differs between them, the features of parameters, and the patterns that become possible once functions are values. Then it covers this properly, as a decision procedure: a fixed list of checks you can apply to any call in about five seconds.

The arrow function gets particular attention. The most useful thing to know about it is not that it is shorter. It is that it has no this of its own, no arguments, and no prototype. Those three absences make it exactly right in some places and unusable in others.

5.1 Four Ways to Define a Function

function declared(a, b) { return a + b; }                 // a function declaration
const expressed = function (a, b) { return a + b; };      // a function expression
const named = function adder(a, b) { return a + b; };     // a named function expression
const arrow = (a, b) => a + b;                            // an arrow function
const obj = { method(a, b) { return a + b; } };           // a method definition

console.log([declared, expressed, named, arrow, obj.method].map(f => f(1, 2)).join(' '));
console.log('names:', [declared.name, expressed.name, named.name, arrow.name, obj.method.name].join(', '));
console.log('which have a .prototype:',
  [declared, expressed, named, arrow, obj.method].map(f => typeof f.prototype).join(', '));

3 3 3 3 3
names: declared, expressed, adder, arrow, method
which have a .prototype: object, object, object, undefined, undefined

A function declaration is hoisted whole (§3.3), so you can call it above its own line. A function expression is not, because it is stored in a variable, and the variable is not ready until its line runs. A named function expression gives the function a name that is visible only inside the function itself. That is how a recursive function expression calls itself, and how it gets a readable name in a stack trace, so it is worth doing for anything non-trivial.

An arrow function and a method definition have no .prototype, which is the concrete way of saying "cannot be called with new". A method definition is also the only form that may use super (§7.11).

function.name is the function's own name, and function.name is what a stack trace, a devtools listing and most logging helpers show. When the function is anonymous, the name is taken from the variable it is assigned to. That is why expressed.name is 'expressed' and arrow.name is 'arrow'. The named function expression is the exception: its own name wins, so named.name is 'adder', which is exactly what you want in a stack trace. This naming follows a rule about how the code is written, and it only applies to a direct assignment: [function () {}][0].name is the empty string.

5.2 Parameters

function withDefaults(a, b = a * 2, { unit = 'px', scale } = {}) {
  return `${a} ${b} ${unit} ${scale ?? 'default'}`;
}
console.log(withDefaults(1));
console.log(withDefaults(1, 5, { unit: 'rem', scale: 2 }));
console.log('undefined triggers a default, null does not:', withDefaults(1, undefined), '|', withDefaults(1, null));

function counted(a, b = 1, ...rest) { return { length: counted.length, got: [a, b, rest] }; }
console.log(JSON.stringify(counted(1, 2, 3, 4)));
console.log('.length stops at the first default or rest:', counted.length);

1 2 px default
1 5 rem 2
undefined triggers a default, null does not: 1 2 px default | 1 null px default
{"length":1,"got":[1,2,[3,4]]}
.length stops at the first default or rest: 1

A default parameter is used only when the argument is undefined. Passing null gives you null: that is the difference between "not supplied" and "supplied as nothing" (§2.1). Defaults are worked out left to right at call time, so a later default can use an earlier parameter, as b = a * 2 does.

Parameter destructuring with = {} on the object is the standard way to accept an options object. The = {} matters: without it, calling the function with no arguments throws, because it tries to destructure undefined.

Rest parameters gather the remaining arguments into a real array, unlike arguments, which only looks like an array (§8.10). function.length counts the parameters before the first default or rest parameter. That is why it reported 1 for a function with three parameters: it is the number the function declares, not the number a call passes.

In summary, the vocabulary here is parameter destructuring and function.length.

5.3 arguments, and Why Not to Use It

The arguments object holds every argument that was passed, in an array-like object, and it exists in every function that is not an arrow function:

function old() { return { count: arguments.length, isArray: Array.isArray(arguments), first: arguments[0] }; }
console.log(JSON.stringify(old('a', 'b')));
function modern(...args) { return { count: args.length, isArray: Array.isArray(args) }; }
console.log(JSON.stringify(modern('a', 'b')));
const noArguments = () => { try { return arguments.length; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } };
console.log('an arrow has no arguments of its own:', noArguments('a'));

{"count":2,"isArray":false,"first":"a"}
{"count":2,"isArray":true}
an arrow has no arguments of its own: ReferenceError

arguments is not an array, so it has no map, filter or reduce. It does not include defaults filled in for missing arguments, and it blocks some engine optimisations. Rest parameters replace it entirely. The one thing to know is that an arrow function does not have its own, so arguments inside an arrow refers to the surrounding function's, or throws, as here.

What to carry forward from this subsection: the arguments object and an array-like object.

5.4 Functions Are Values

A first-class function is a function the language treats like any other value: it can be stored, passed and returned. A higher-order function is one that takes a function or returns one, and that describes most of the standard library:

const operations = { double: (n) => n * 2, square: (n) => n * n };
const apply = (name, value) => operations[name](value);
console.log('stored in an object:', apply('double', 5), apply('square', 5));

const twice = (fn) => (x) => fn(fn(x));
console.log('returned from a function:', twice(operations.double)(3));
console.log('passed as an argument:', [1, 2, 3].map(operations.square).join(','));
console.log('functions have properties too:', Object.assign(function tagged() {}, { version: 2 }).version);

stored in an object: 10 25
returned from a function: 12
passed as an argument: 1,4,9
functions have properties too: 2

A callback function is simply a function passed to another function, to be called later. The word describes a role, not a kind of function. That is worth saying because "callback" is often used to mean "the old asynchronous style" (§12.5), and [1,2,3].map(f) uses a callback too.

The terms above, gathered: a first-class function, a higher-order function and a callback function.

5.5 Pure Functions and Immutable Data

A pure function returns the same output for the same input, and changes nothing outside itself. It is not a language feature, since nothing enforces it. But it is the single most useful property a function can have, because a pure function can be tested without setup, cached (§5.11), run in a different order, and run in a worker.

const impure = (cart) => { cart.total = cart.items.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); return cart.total; };
const pure = (items) => items.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);

const cart = { items: [10, 20] };
impure(cart);
console.log('the impure version changed its argument:', JSON.stringify(cart));
console.log('the pure one only returns:', pure([10, 20]), '| the input is untouched');

const original = { a: 1, nested: { b: 2 } };
const updated = { ...original, a: 99 };
console.log('immutable update:', JSON.stringify(updated), '| original:', JSON.stringify(original));
console.log('but it is shallow — nested is shared:', updated.nested === original.nested);
const deepUpdated = { ...original, nested: { ...original.nested, b: 3 } };
console.log('so nested updates must be spelled out:', JSON.stringify(deepUpdated));

the impure version changed its argument: {"items":[10,20],"total":30}
the pure one only returns: 30 | the input is untouched
immutable update: {"a":99,"nested":{"b":2}} | original: {"a":1,"nested":{"b":2}}
but it is shallow — nested is shared: true
so nested updates must be spelled out: {"a":1,"nested":{"b":3}}

Immutable data means producing new values instead of editing old ones. Then you can detect a change just by checking whether the reference changed, and that check is the foundation of every rendering library's update logic. Spread is shallow (§6.4), so a deep update means spreading at every level. That is why libraries for this exist, and why structuredClone followed by a change is often the practical alternative.

5.6 Recursion

Recursion is a function calling itself. The two things to get right are the base case (where it stops) and the depth (how many calls deep it goes):

function flatten(value) {
  if (!Array.isArray(value)) return [value];              // the base case, first
  return value.flatMap(flatten);
}
console.log(JSON.stringify(flatten([1, [2, [3, [4, [5]]]]])));

function depthOf(n) { return n === 0 ? 0 : 1 + depthOf(n - 1); }
let limit = 0;
try { (function probe() { limit++; probe(); })(); }
catch (e) { console.log('stack overflow after roughly', limit > 5000 ? 'thousands of' : 'few', 'frames:', e.constructor.name); }
console.log('an iterative version has no limit:', (() => { let d = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 1e6; i++) d++; return d; })());

[1,2,3,4,5]
stack overflow after roughly thousands of frames: RangeError
an iterative version has no limit: 1000000

Stack overflow is a RangeError, and it happens at a few thousand to a few tens of thousands of nested calls, depending on the engine and the size of each call. Proper tail calls, an optimisation that would let some recursion run without growing the stack, are in the specification but implemented only in JavaScriptCore. So do not rely on tail-call optimisation. Recursion is right for problems that are genuinely tree-shaped and of limited depth, such as walking the DOM or a nested object. A loop, or an explicit stack, is right for anything without a limit.

5.7 Currying and Partial Application

Currying turns a function of n arguments into n functions of one argument each. Partial application fixes some of the arguments and returns a function that takes the rest. They are related, and not the same:

const add3 = (a) => (b) => (c) => a + b + c;              // curried
console.log('curried:', add3(1)(2)(3));

const partial = (fn, ...fixed) => (...rest) => fn(...fixed, ...rest);
const greet = (greeting, punctuation, name) => `${greeting}, ${name}${punctuation}`;
const hello = partial(greet, 'Hello', '!');
console.log('partially applied:', hello('Ada'), '|', hello('Grace'));

const log = (level) => (message) => `[${level}] ${message}`;
console.log('the practical shape:', ['warn', 'error'].map(l => log(l)('disk full')).join(' '));

curried: 6
partially applied: Hello, Ada! | Hello, Grace!
the practical shape: [warn] disk full [error] disk full

The reason either matters is configuration before data. If a function's rarely-changing arguments come first, it can be specialised once and then called many times. That is what makes log('warn') a reusable value, instead of an argument you repeat on every call.

5.8 Composition

Function composition builds a pipeline out of single-purpose functions:

const pipe = (...fns) => (input) => fns.reduce((value, fn) => fn(value), input);
const compose = (...fns) => (input) => fns.reduceRight((value, fn) => fn(value), input);

const trim = (s) => s.trim();
const lower = (s) => s.toLowerCase();
const dashes = (s) => s.replaceAll(' ', '-');

console.log('pipe reads left to right:   ', pipe(trim, lower, dashes)('  Hello World  '));
console.log('compose reads right to left:', compose(dashes, lower, trim)('  Hello World  '));

pipe reads left to right:    hello-world
compose reads right to left: hello-world

pipe is reduce and compose is reduceRight; that is the entire difference. pipe runs the functions in the order you read them, and that alone makes it almost always the better choice.

One line each, for reference: function composition.

5.9 Memoisation

Memoization stores each result, keyed by its arguments, so a repeated call returns the stored answer. It is only correct for pure functions:

function memoize(fn) {
  const cache = new Map();
  return (...args) => {
    const key = JSON.stringify(args);
    if (!cache.has(key)) cache.set(key, fn(...args));
    return cache.get(key);
  };
}
let calls = 0;
const slowSquare = memoize((n) => { calls++; return n * n; });
console.log(slowSquare(4), slowSquare(4), slowSquare(5), '| underlying calls:', calls);

const fib = memoize((n) => (n < 2 ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)));
console.log('memoised fib(35):', fib(35), '— instant, where the naive version takes seconds');

16 16 25 | underlying calls: 2
memoised fib(35): 9227465 — instant, where the naive version takes seconds

The fib case shows what memoisation is really for. It turns an algorithm whose running time grows exponentially into one that grows in a straight line, because the recursive calls find their answers in the cache. The costs are covered in §3's closure exercise: a cache with no size limit is a leak with no size limit, and JSON.stringify as the key function is a compromise.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: memoization.

5.10 Debounce, Throttle and Once

Three wrappers come up all the time, and the difference between the first two is worth being exact about.

Debounce waits until the calls stop: it runs once, after a quiet period. Throttle runs at most once per time interval, however many calls arrive.

function debounce(fn, ms) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => { clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms); };
}
function throttle(fn, ms) {
  let last = 0;
  return (...args) => {
    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - last < ms) return;
    last = now;
    fn(...args);
  };
}
function once(fn) {                            // a once wrapper
  let done = false, result;
