  return (...args) => (done ? result : (done = true, result = fn(...args)));
}

const debounced = [], throttled = [];
const d = debounce((n) => debounced.push(n), 20);
const t = throttle((n) => throttled.push(n), 20);
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { d(i); t(i); }
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 60));
console.log('debounce ran once, with the LAST value:', debounced);
console.log('throttle ran immediately, with the FIRST:', throttled);
let inits = 0;
const init = once(() => ++inits);
init(); init(); init();
console.log('once ran', inits, 'time(s)');

debounce ran once, with the LAST value: [ 4 ]
throttle ran immediately, with the FIRST: [ 0 ]
once ran 1 time(s)

A once wrapper is the simplest of the three, and has the subtlest requirement. It must return the first result on every later call, not undefined. Otherwise an object that is created on first use quietly becomes undefined for every caller after the first.

Debounce for "the user has stopped": search-as-you-type (§16's search exercise), resizing, autosave. Throttle for "at most this often": a live scroll position, a progress update, an API with a rate limit. Using debounce where throttle was wanted gives an interface that never updates while the user keeps moving. The reverse gives one that fires far more often than intended.

5.11 this: Five Rules, in Order

This binding, the value this gets, is decided where the function is called, by the first of these rules that applies:

lexical this
The function is an arrow. It has no this; the enclosing scope's is used, and nothing can change it.
the new binding
new Fn() — this is the newly created object.
explicit binding
fn.call(o), fn.apply(o) or a function produced by fn.bind(o).
implicit binding
o.fn() — this is whatever is left of the dot, and only at the moment of the call.
default binding
None of the above. undefined in strict mode and in a module; the global object in sloppy mode.
const obj = { name: 'obj', who() { return this?.name ?? 'no this'; } };
console.log('implicit:', obj.who());
const detached = obj.who;
console.log('default (a module is strict):', detached());
console.log('explicit:', obj.who.call({ name: 'called' }), obj.who.apply({ name: 'applied' }));
console.log('bound:', obj.who.bind({ name: 'bound' })());
function Ctor() { this.made = true; }
console.log('new:', new Ctor().made);
const lexical = { name: 'outer', arrow: () => (typeof this === 'undefined' ? 'undefined at module top level' : 'x') };
console.log('lexical:', lexical.arrow());

implicit: obj
default (a module is strict): no this
explicit: called applied
bound: bound
new: true
lexical: undefined at module top level

Implicit binding is about the call, not the definition, and that is the whole story of "losing this". const detached = obj.who copies the function, not its pairing with obj, so when you call it there is no object to the left of a dot.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: explicit binding, default binding, lexical this, losing this and the new binding.

To have in hand before moving on: this binding.

5.12 .call(), .apply() and .bind()

function describe(greeting, punctuation) { return `${greeting}, ${this.name}${punctuation}`; }
const person = { name: 'Ada' };
console.log('.call takes arguments separately:', describe.call(person, 'Hello', '!'));
console.log('.apply takes them as an array: ', describe.apply(person, ['Hi', '?']));

const bound = describe.bind(person, 'Hey');
console.log('.bind returns a new function, and can pre-fill arguments:', bound('.'));
console.log('a bound function CANNOT be rebound:', bound.call({ name: 'someone else' }, '.'));
console.log('every .bind call makes a new object:', describe.bind(person) === describe.bind(person));

.call takes arguments separately: Hello, Ada!
.apply takes them as an array:  Hi, Ada?
.bind returns a new function, and can pre-fill arguments: Hey, Ada.
a bound function CANNOT be rebound: Hey, Ada.
every .bind call makes a new object: false

.call() and .apply() call the function immediately with the this you give, and differ only in how the arguments are passed. Since spread exists, fn.call(o, ...args) covers both cases, so .apply is mostly of historical interest.

.bind() returns a new function permanently attached to the this you give it, and it can also fix arguments (partial application). Two consequences bite. A bound function cannot be rebound: the later .call was ignored. And each .bind() returns a different object, which is why removeEventListener('click', this.onClick.bind(this)) removes nothing (§16.2). Bind once, and keep the reference.

5.13 The Arrow Function's Three Absences

An arrow has no this, no arguments, and no prototype of its own. Each absence decides where it belongs:

class Timer {
  seconds = 0;
  tickArrow = () => { this.seconds++; return this.seconds; };
  tickNormal() { this.seconds++; return this.seconds; }
}
const timer = new Timer();
const arrowRef = timer.tickArrow;
const normalRef = timer.tickNormal;
console.log('an arrow class field survives detachment:', arrowRef());
console.log('a normal method does not:',
  (() => { try { return normalRef(); } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());

const badObject = { name: 'obj', get: () => (typeof this === 'undefined' ? 'undefined, NOT the object' : 'x') };
console.log('an arrow as an object method:', badObject.get());
console.log('an arrow cannot be constructed:',
  (() => { try { new (() => {})(); return 'ok'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());

an arrow class field survives detachment: 1
a normal method does not: TypeError
an arrow as an object method: undefined, NOT the object
an arrow cannot be constructed: TypeError

Use an arrow for a callback that should see the surrounding this: a handler stored in a class field, a .map inside a method, the body of a setTimeout. Do not use one as a method in an object literal (it will not see the object), as a prototype method, as a constructor, or anywhere a caller may want to supply this. That last case includes some library callbacks, and every addEventListener handler that wants the element.

The class-field arrow is the pattern worth making a habit: onClick = () => {…} gives a method that is permanently bound and stays the same object. So it can be passed to addEventListener and removed again later.

5.14 Functions Built at Runtime

The Function constructor turns a string of code into a function. It is the last way of defining a function, and the one to know mainly so you can avoid it:

const add = new Function('a', 'b', 'return a + b');
console.log('it works:', add(2, 3), '| and it is a real function:', typeof add);

const outer = 'visible to a closure';
const probe = new Function('return typeof outer');
console.log('but it does NOT close over the surrounding scope:', probe());
console.log('it compiles in the global scope, so this is what it sees:',
  new Function('return typeof globalThis')());

it works: 5 | and it is a real function: function
but it does NOT close over the surrounding scope: undefined
it compiles in the global scope, so this is what it sees: object

That is the one real difference from eval(): the Function constructor compiles in the global scope. So it cannot read or write the local variables around it, and a minifier is free to rename them. eval() does see the surrounding scope, which defeats minification and most optimisation. That is why the two are not interchangeable, even though both run strings as code.

A reasonable Content Security Policy (§17.16) blocks both. And both turn any string that reaches them into code, so a template built from user input becomes remote code execution: an attacker's code running in your page. The legitimate uses are narrow enough to list: a real template compiler, a sandboxed expression evaluator with a vetted grammar, and a benchmark harness that must stop the engine from inlining code.

What to use instead, case by case: JSON.parse for data, an object of functions for choosing behaviour by name, a real parser for expressions, and a closure or a curried function (§5.7) for "a function configured at runtime", which is what most uses of new Function actually want.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: minification and content security policy.

5.15 What This Section Established

  1. Five definition forms, and the differences are real: a declaration hoists whole, an expression does not, a named expression names itself for recursion and stack traces, and an arrow and a method definition have no .prototype so neither can be newed.
  2. A default applies only for undefined, not null, and defaults evaluate left to right so a later one may use an earlier parameter.
  3. function.length stops at the first default or rest parameter — 1 for a three-parameter function — so it is declared arity, not call arity.
  4. arguments is array-like, not an array, and an arrow has none. Rest parameters replace it completely.
  5. A pure function is testable, cacheable and movable, and immutable updates are shallow — updated.nested === original.nested was true.
  6. Stack overflow is a RangeError at a few thousand frames, and tail-call optimisation is specified but not implemented in most engines, so recursion needs bounded depth.
  7. pipe is reduce and compose is reduceRight; currying and partial application both exist to put configuration before data.
  8. Memoisation turns exponential into linear — fib(35) was instant — and its cache is a lifetime commitment.
  9. Debounce runs once after the calls stop, with the last value ([4]); throttle runs immediately and at most once per interval, with the first ([0]).
  10. Five this rules in order: lexical, new, explicit, implicit, default. Implicit binding depends on the call site, which is why const detached = obj.who loses it.
  11. A bound function cannot be rebound, and every .bind() returns a new object — which is why binding inside removeEventListener removes nothing.
  12. An arrow has no this, no arguments and no prototype. A class-field arrow survived detachment where a normal method threw, and an arrow as an object-literal method never sees the object.

Exercises

1. Predict each line and name the rule.

const o = {
  name: 'o',
  regular() { return this?.name; },
  arrow: () => (typeof this === 'undefined' ? 'undefined' : 'defined'),
  nested() { const inner = () => this?.name; return inner(); },
  broken() { function inner() { return this?.name; } return inner(); },
};
console.log(o.regular(), o.arrow(), o.nested(), o.broken());
const { regular } = o;
console.log(regular());
console.log(o.regular.call({ name: 'x' }), o.regular.bind({ name: 'y' }).call({ name: 'z' }));
Solution 
o undefined o undefined
undefined
x y

o.regular() gives 'o' — implicit binding, the object left of the dot.

o.arrow() gives 'undefined' — lexical binding. The arrow was defined in the module's top-level scope, where this is undefined (a module is always strict, and its top-level this is undefined rather than the global object). Being called as o.arrow() changes nothing; an arrow's this cannot be set by the call site.

o.nested() gives 'o'. The arrow captures this from nested, and nested was called with implicit binding, so this is o. This is the pattern that makes arrows so useful inside methods.

o.broken() gives undefined. inner is a normal function called with no receiver — plain inner(), nothing left of a dot — so default binding applies and gives undefined in strict mode. Before arrows, the fix was const self = this at the top of the method, which is why you see that line all over older code.

regular() after destructuring gives undefined. Destructuring extracts the function value; the association with o was never part of it.

.call({name:'x'}) gives 'x' — explicit binding beats implicit. .bind({name:'y'}).call({name:'z'}) gives 'y' — a bound function ignores a later .call, because bind produces a new function whose this is fixed (§5.12).

2. Write pipeAsync(...fns) composing functions that may be synchronous or return promises, threading a value through in order, with the whole pipeline cancellable.

Solution 
function pipeAsync(...fns) {
  return async function (input, { signal } = {}) {
    let value = input;
    for (const fn of fns) {
      signal?.throwIfAborted();                 // check before each step
      value = await fn.call(this, value, { signal });
    }
    return value;
  };
}

const parse = (s) => Number(s.trim());
const doubleLater = async (n) => { await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 1)); return n * 2; };
const format = (n) => `result: ${n}`;

const run = pipeAsync(parse, doubleLater, format);
console.log(await run('  21 '));

const ac = new AbortController();
ac.abort();
try { await run('1', { signal: ac.signal }); }
catch (e) { console.log('cancelled before the first step:', e.name); }

result: 42
cancelled before the first step: AbortError

Why a for...of loop rather than reduce. The synchronous pipe of §5.8 is a reduce, and the asynchronous version cannot be, because each step must be awaited before the next begins. fns.reduce((p, fn) => p.then(fn), Promise.resolve(input)) does work and is the idiomatic one-liner, but it builds the whole chain up front, which makes the per-step cancellation check awkward and the stack traces worse. A loop with await says what it means.

await fn(...) regardless of whether fn is async. await on a non-promise is fine and costs one microtask tick (§12.9), so the same code path handles both kinds of function. That is what makes the composition uniform.

signal?.throwIfAborted() before each step, not only at the start. A pipeline of five steps taking a second each must not run steps 3, 4 and 5 after the user has navigated away. Checking between steps is the finest granularity available without cooperation from the functions themselves — which is why the signal is also passed down to each one, so a step doing its own fetch can abort mid-flight (§12.12).

fn.call(this, …) rather than fn(…) so the composed function is usable as a method — the same transparency point as once in §3's closure exercise. Note the outer function is a function rather than an arrow precisely so it has a this to forward.

What it deliberately does not do: run anything in parallel. Composition is sequential by definition, and if two steps are independent then they are not a pipeline — they are Promise.all (§12.10), and pretending otherwise inside a compose helper hides a real performance decision.

3. A class passes its methods to addEventListener and to setTimeout, and this is wrong in both. Show three fixes, and say which to use.

Solution 
class Panel {
  name = 'panel';
  // FIX 1 — a class field holding an arrow: bound at construction, stable identity.
  onClickField = () => `${this.name} handled a click`;
  // FIX 2 — a normal method, bound once in the constructor.
  constructor() { this.onClickBound = this.onClickMethod.bind(this); }
  onClickMethod() { return `${this.name} handled a click`; }
  // FIX 3 — a wrapper arrow at the point of use.
  attach(target) { target.addEventListener('click', () => this.onClickMethod()); }
}

document.body.innerHTML = '<button id="b">x</button>';
const panel = new Panel();
const broken = panel.onClickMethod;
console.log('unbound:', (() => { try { return broken(); } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());
console.log('field: ', panel.onClickField());
console.log('bound: ', panel.onClickBound());
console.log('stable identity — field:', panel.onClickField === panel.onClickField);
console.log('stable identity — bound:', panel.onClickBound === panel.onClickBound);
console.log('unstable — a fresh bind:', panel.onClickMethod.bind(panel) === panel.onClickMethod.bind(panel));

unbound: TypeError
field:  panel handled a click
bound:  panel handled a click
stable identity — field: true
stable identity — bound: true
unstable — a fresh bind: false

Fix 1 — the class-field arrow — is the one to use for anything that will be passed as a handler. It is bound at construction, it has a stable identity so removeEventListener works, and the intent is visible at the definition rather than at the call site. Its costs are real and small: the function lives on each instance rather than on the prototype, so a thousand instances mean a thousand function objects, and it cannot be overridden by a subclass through super.

Fix 2 — bind once in the constructor — is equivalent in behaviour and worse in readability, because the binding is far from the method. It is the right choice when the method must stay on the prototype (for subclassing, or for a class instantiated in very large numbers).

Fix 3 — a wrapper arrow at the point of use — is correct for this but has no stable identity, so it cannot be removed later by reference. It is fine when the listener is torn down by an AbortSignal (§16.2), which is the modern default, and it is a bug when someone later tries removeEventListener with a new arrow.

The fix that is not on the list: target.addEventListener('click', panel.onClickMethod). That is the bug. Note the failure mode is not silent — in a module it is a TypeError, because this is undefined and reading .name off it throws. In a classic script it would silently read window.name, which is an empty string, and produce a plausible wrong answer instead — one more reason modules are the better environment.

And for setTimeout specifically, the same three fixes apply, with one addition: setTimeout(() => this.tick(), 1000) is so short that the wrapper arrow is almost always right there, since a timer is cancelled by its id rather than by function identity.

SECTION 6

Objects, Properties and Descriptors

Almost everything in JavaScript is an object, and almost nobody knows what a property actually is. That is not a criticism: you can be productive for years treating obj.name = 'Ada' as putting a value in a box. But the box has four settings, and only one of them is the value. The other three explain a long list of things that otherwise look arbitrary:

  • why Object.keys() skips some properties, and why JSON.stringify skips the same ones;
  • why Object.freeze sometimes throws an error and sometimes does not;
  • why spreading an object turns a getter (a property computed by a function) into a plain value;
  • why a class method is invisible to for...in while an object-literal method is not.

This section is about that layer. It starts with the syntax everyone uses. It moves down to the descriptor, the record of those four settings, that the syntax creates. It finishes with Proxy and Reflect, the two APIs that let you step in and change what reading, writing or deleting a property does.

Along the way it settles what "copy an object" really means, and that is the most consequential thing here. There are three different kinds of copy with three different behaviours, and choosing the wrong one is where a surprising number of state bugs come from.

Every block below runs as an ES module, which means strict mode is always on (§1.9). That matters more here than anywhere else in the course. Several operations that fail silently in sloppy mode (the older, more forgiving mode) throw a TypeError instead, and the difference is visible in the output.

6.1 Object Literals and the Shorthands

An object literal is a list of properties inside braces, separated by commas. Four pieces of syntax do nearly all the work:

const key = 'dynamic';
const name = 'Ada', year = 1815;
const person = {
  name,                                    // a shorthand property: `name: name`
  year,
  ['born_' + year]: true,                  // a computed property name
  greet() { return `Hi, ${this.name}`; },  // method shorthand: `greet: function () {}`
  get age() { return 2026 - this.year; },  // an accessor, not a data property
  [key]: 'value from a variable',
};
console.log(JSON.stringify(person));
console.log(person.greet(), '| age:', person.age);

{"name":"Ada","year":1815,"born_1815":true,"age":211,"dynamic":"value from a variable"}
Hi, Ada | age: 211

A shorthand property writes { name } instead of { name: name }. It is worth using consistently, because then the name and the value cannot get mismatched. A computed property name puts any expression inside square brackets, and it is evaluated once, when the object is created. It is the only way to build a key from a variable inside a literal, and it is how symbol keys are written (§6.11).

Method shorthand is not merely shorter than greet: function () {}. A shorthand method has no prototype property and cannot be called with new. More importantly, it is the only form that can use super. An arrow function as a property is a third thing again, and a trap: greet: () => this.name takes this from the surrounding code, which in a module is undefined, so it never sees the object.

Note in the output that age appears in the JSON as a value. A getter runs whenever the property is read, including when JSON.stringify reads it, and that is where §6.4 begins.

In summary, the vocabulary here is an object literal and a data property.

6.2 Access, and the Order of Keys

Dot notation (obj.name) needs a valid identifier. Bracket notation (obj['name']) accepts any expression. You need it for a key held in a variable, a key with a space or hyphen in it, or a symbol:

const settings = { 'font-size': 14, theme: 'dark' };
const which = 'theme';
console.log(settings['font-size'], settings[which], settings.theme);
console.log('a missing key is undefined, not an error:', settings.nope);
console.log('optional chaining stops the crash one level down:', settings.nope?.deep);

14 dark dark
a missing key is undefined, not an error: undefined
optional chaining stops the crash one level down: undefined

Property order is specified, and it is not insertion order:

const mixed = { b: 1, 2: 'two', a: 3, 10: 'ten', 1: 'one' };
console.log(Object.keys(mixed));
console.log('for...in agrees:', (() => { const out = []; for (const k in mixed) out.push(k); return out; })());

[ '1', '2', '10', 'b', 'a' ]
for...in agrees: [ '1', '2', '10', 'b', 'a' ]

Integer-like keys come first, in ascending numeric order, followed by string keys in the order they were added, followed by symbol keys. That is why an object keyed by numeric ids silently reorders itself, and a Map (§8.11) does not. It is the best single reason to use a Map when the keys are data rather than field names.

Note also that 2 became '2'. Every non-symbol key is a string, so obj[1] and obj['1'] are the same property. An object used as a lookup table turns whatever key you give it into a string, so {} becomes "[object Object]".

What to carry forward from this subsection: bracket notation, dot notation and property order.

6.3 Reading an Object as Data

Four static methods turn an object into arrays and back. Together with the array methods, they replace nearly every hand-written for...in loop:

const scores = { ada: 91, grace: 88, alan: 95 };
console.log('keys:   ', Object.keys(scores));
console.log('values: ', Object.values(scores));
console.log('entries:', JSON.stringify(Object.entries(scores)));

const doubled = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(scores).map(([k, v]) => [k, v * 2]));
console.log('mapped: ', JSON.stringify(doubled));
const passed = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(scores).filter(([, v]) => v >= 90));
console.log('filtered:', JSON.stringify(passed));

keys:    [ 'ada', 'grace', 'alan' ]
values:  [ 91, 88, 95 ]
entries: [["ada",91],["grace",88],["alan",95]]
mapped:  {"ada":182,"grace":176,"alan":190}
filtered: {"ada":91,"alan":95}

Object.values() gives just the values, which is what you want for a sum or an average, and Object.entries() gives [key, value] pairs. Object.entries() → .map/.filter → Object.fromEntries() is the standard way to transform an object, and it is worth memorising as one unit. There is no Object.map, and this pattern is why none is needed. Object.values() also pairs well with .some() and .every() to check a whole record at once. Object.fromEntries accepts any iterable of pairs, so it converts a Map or a URLSearchParams in one call.

All four see only own, enumerable, string-keyed properties. Each of those three words leaves something out, and §6.6 and §6.9 explain what.

The terms above, gathered: object.fromentries(), .some() and .every().

6.4 Copying: Spread, assign, and What They Both Miss

Object spread and Object.assign() both make a shallow copy (only the top level is copied), and both do it by reading values and writing them again:

const source = {
  plain: 1,
  get computed() { return 'evaluated at copy time'; },
};
const spread = { ...source };
const assigned = Object.assign({}, source);
console.log('spread:  ', JSON.stringify(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(spread, 'computed')));
console.log('assigned:', JSON.stringify(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(assigned, 'computed')));

const proto = { inherited: 'from the prototype' };
const child = Object.create(proto);
child.own = 'mine';
console.log('spread takes own enumerable only:', JSON.stringify({ ...child }));

spread:   {"value":"evaluated at copy time","writable":true,"enumerable":true,"configurable":true}
assigned: {"value":"evaluated at copy time","writable":true,"enumerable":true,"configurable":true}
spread takes own enumerable only: {"own":"mine"}

A getter becomes a plain value. Both forms call the getter once and store the result, so the copy no longer recomputes. That is either a useful snapshot or a silent bug, depending on whether you knew. When you need the getter itself to survive, use Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors with Object.create.

Three more differences are worth holding on to. Spread and assign copy only own enumerable properties, so inherited and non-enumerable ones are dropped. The prototype is not copied: { ...instance } of a class instance gives a plain object with the fields and none of the methods, which is why spreading a Date or a Map produces {}. And Object.assign mutates its first argument, while spread always builds a new object. That makes spread the better default.

Shallow means one level:

const original = { name: 'config', nested: { retries: 3 } };
const copy = { ...original };
copy.nested.retries = 99;
console.log('the "copy" shares the nested object:', original.nested.retries);
const deep = structuredClone(original);
deep.nested.retries = 1;
console.log('structuredClone is a real deep copy:', original.nested.retries);

the "copy" shares the nested object: 99
structuredClone is a real deep copy: 99

The last line prints 99 because the shallow copy had already changed it; the point is that structuredClone left it at 99 instead of putting it back to 1. A deep copy is structuredClone() (§17.8). JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) is the old way, and it silently destroys Date, Map, Set, undefined, functions and cycles.

One line each, for reference: object.assign().

6.5 Object.create() and Null-Prototype Objects

Object.create() builds an object with the prototype you choose. That includes null, which is the only way to get an object that inherits nothing at all.

A null-prototype object is the correct data structure for a lookup table whose keys come from untrusted input:

const dict = Object.create(null);
dict.toString = 'a string, and no conflict at all';
console.log('prototype:', Object.getPrototypeOf(dict));
console.log("'toString' in {}:", 'toString' in {});
console.log('Object.hasOwn(dict, "toString"):', Object.hasOwn(dict, 'toString'));
try { dict.hasOwnProperty('x'); } catch (e) { console.log('dict.hasOwnProperty throws:', e.constructor.name); }

prototype: null
'toString' in {}: true
Object.hasOwn(dict, "toString"): true
dict.hasOwnProperty throws: TypeError

An ordinary {} inherits from Object.prototype. So 'toString' in obj is true for a key nobody set, and obj['constructor'] returns a function instead of undefined. For a table keyed by user input that is a real hazard, part of the prototype pollution family of vulnerabilities (§7.12), and Object.create(null) removes it completely. The price is that the object has no methods of its own, so you inspect it with Object.hasOwn() and Object.keys(). A Map is usually the better answer still.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: object.keys(), a null-prototype object and object.hasown().

6.6 What a Property Really Is

Every property is described by a property descriptor, a record with four fields, and a property descriptor is what defineProperty actually writes. For a data property, which holds a value, the fields are value, writable, enumerable and configurable. For an accessor property, which runs functions, the first two are replaced by get and set.

The single most important fact about them is that assignment and Object.defineProperty() produce different defaults:

const o = {};
o.assigned = 1;
Object.defineProperty(o, 'defined', { value: 2 });
console.log('by assignment:      ', JSON.stringify(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(o, 'assigned')));
console.log('by defineProperty:  ', JSON.stringify(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(o, 'defined')));
console.log('Object.keys sees:', Object.keys(o), '| JSON.stringify:', JSON.stringify(o));
try { o.defined = 99; } catch (e) { console.log('writing it throws in strict mode:', e.constructor.name); }
console.log('value unchanged:', o.defined);

by assignment:       {"value":1,"writable":true,"enumerable":true,"configurable":true}
by defineProperty:   {"value":2,"writable":false,"enumerable":false,"configurable":false}
Object.keys sees: [ 'assigned' ] | JSON.stringify: {"assigned":1}
writing it throws in strict mode: TypeError
value unchanged: 2

defineProperty defaults every flag to false. So the property is invisible to Object.keys, to JSON.stringify, to for...in and to spread, which is why the serialised object contains only assigned. It also cannot be written or deleted. Assignment sets every flag the other way. That is why two lines that look as if they do the same thing produce properties with opposite behaviour.

the writable attribute
May the value be reassigned? false means a write is ignored in sloppy mode and throws in strict mode.
the enumerable attribute
Does it show up in Object.keys, for...in, spread and JSON.stringify? This is how built-in methods stay out of your loops.
the configurable attribute
May the descriptor itself be changed, and may the property be deleted? Turning it off is a one-way door.
value / get / set
A property has either value and writable, or get and set. Never both — supplying both is a TypeError.

Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor() reads a descriptor back. It is the tool to reach for whenever a property behaves oddly, and it answers "why is this not in my loop?" in one line.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: the writable attribute, the enumerable attribute, the configurable attribute, object.defineproperty(), object.getownpropertydescriptor() and an accessor property.

6.7 Getters and Setters

A getter runs a function when the property is read, and a setter runs one when it is written, so a computed value can look exactly like a stored one. That is the whole point: you can turn a plain field into a calculation later without changing any of the code that uses it.

const account = {
  transactions: [12, -5, 30],
  get balance() { return this.transactions.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); },
  set deposit(amount) {
    if (!(amount > 0)) throw new RangeError('deposit must be positive');
    this.transactions.push(amount);
  },
};
console.log('balance:', account.balance);
account.deposit = 8;
console.log('after depositing 8:', account.balance);
try { account.deposit = -1; } catch (e) { console.log(`${e.constructor.name}: ${e.message}`); }
const d = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(account, 'balance');
console.log('an accessor descriptor has:', Object.keys(d).join(', '));

balance: 37
after depositing 8: 45
RangeError: deposit must be positive
an accessor descriptor has: get, set, enumerable, configurable

Two cautions. An expensive getter is a trap, because it looks like a field and callers will read it inside loops. And a getter that returns a new object each time breaks equality: obj.items !== obj.items. That quietly defeats every cache and change check that relies on identity.

6.8 Freezing, Sealing and Preventing Extensions

Three levels of immutability, each stricter than the last:

const frozen = Object.freeze({ a: 1, nested: { b: 2 } });
try { frozen.a = 9; } catch (e) { console.log('writing to a frozen object throws:', e.constructor.name); }
frozen.nested.b = 9;
console.log('but freeze is SHALLOW — nested.b is now', frozen.nested.b);
console.log('isFrozen(frozen):', Object.isFrozen(frozen), '| isFrozen(frozen.nested):', Object.isFrozen(frozen.nested));

const sealed = Object.seal({ a: 1 });
sealed.a = 5;
try { sealed.b = 1; } catch (e) { console.log('adding to a sealed object throws:', e.constructor.name); }
try { delete sealed.a; } catch (e) { console.log('deleting from a sealed object throws:', e.constructor.name); }
console.log('sealed:', JSON.stringify(sealed), '| isSealed:', Object.isSealed(sealed), '| isFrozen:', Object.isFrozen(sealed));

writing to a frozen object throws: TypeError
but freeze is SHALLOW — nested.b is now 9
isFrozen(frozen): true | isFrozen(frozen.nested): false
adding to a sealed object throws: TypeError
deleting from a sealed object throws: TypeError
sealed: {"a":5} | isSealed: true | isFrozen: false

Object.preventExtensions() forbids adding properties. Object.seal() adds "and none may be deleted or reconfigured", though existing values may still change. Object.freeze() adds "and none may be written". Object.isFrozen() and Object.isSealed() report the current state.

Object.freeze() is shallow, and that is the part that surprises people. A deep freeze is a recursive walk you write yourself, and it is rarely what you want. Freeze the top level of a configuration object to catch accidental changes, and rely on discipline or a library for the rest.

In sloppy mode, every one of those failures is silent. In a module, they throw. That difference alone is a strong argument for modules: a frozen object that silently ignores writes costs you a debugging session, and one that throws gives you a stack trace.

To have in hand before moving on: object.seal(), object.preventextensions() and object.isfrozen().

6.9 Own Versus Inherited

Object.hasOwn() is the modern check for "does this object itself have this property?", and it should replace every other way of writing it:

class Base { constructor() { this.instanceField = 1; } method() {} }
const b = new Base();
console.log('hasOwn(instanceField):', Object.hasOwn(b, 'instanceField'));
console.log('hasOwn(method):       ', Object.hasOwn(b, 'method'), '— methods live on the prototype');
console.log("'method' in b:        ", 'method' in b, '— `in` walks the chain');
const forIn = []; for (const k in b) forIn.push(k);
console.log('for...in:', forIn, '— class methods are non-enumerable, so they are skipped');

const withHidden = {};
Object.defineProperty(withHidden, 'secret', { value: 1, enumerable: false });
withHidden.visible = 2;
withHidden[Symbol('tag')] = 3;
console.log('Object.keys:              ', Object.keys(withHidden));
console.log('getOwnPropertyNames:      ', Object.getOwnPropertyNames(withHidden));
console.log('getOwnPropertySymbols:    ', Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(withHidden).map(String));
console.log('Reflect.ownKeys (all):    ', Reflect.ownKeys(withHidden).map(String));

hasOwn(instanceField): true
hasOwn(method):        false — methods live on the prototype
'method' in b:         true — `in` walks the chain
for...in: [ 'instanceField' ] — class methods are non-enumerable, so they are skipped
Object.keys:               [ 'visible' ]
getOwnPropertyNames:       [ 'secret', 'visible' ]
getOwnPropertySymbols:     [ 'Symbol(tag)' ]
Reflect.ownKeys (all):     [ 'secret', 'visible', 'Symbol(tag)' ]

Four enumeration methods give four different answers, and the differences are worth learning:

  • Object.keys gives own + enumerable + string keys.
  • Object.getOwnPropertyNames() drops the enumerable requirement.
  • Object.getOwnPropertySymbols() gives the symbol keys.
  • Reflect.ownKeys() returns every own key, and is the only complete answer.

Object.hasOwn(obj, key) replaces .hasOwnProperty(). The old method fails on a null-prototype object (§6.5), and it can be overridden by a property that is literally named hasOwnProperty. Both are real failures when the object came from JSON.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: .hasownproperty(), object.getownpropertynames(), object.getownpropertysymbols() and reflect.ownkeys().

6.10 Grouping

Object.groupBy() sorts the items of an iterable into groups, using a function that returns each item's group key. It replaces the reduce that people hand-write more than any other in JavaScript:

const tasks = [
  { title: 'ship', status: 'done' },
  { title: 'test', status: 'todo' },
  { title: 'plan', status: 'done' },
];
const byStatus = Object.groupBy(tasks, (t) => t.status);
console.log(JSON.stringify(byStatus));
console.log('missing group is undefined, not []:', byStatus.blocked);
console.log('the result has a null prototype:', Object.getPrototypeOf(byStatus));

{"done":[{"title":"ship","status":"done"},{"title":"plan","status":"done"}],"todo":[{"title":"test","status":"todo"}]}
missing group is undefined, not []: undefined
the result has a null prototype: null

The result has a null prototype on purpose: otherwise a group key of "constructor" or "__proto__" would collide with an inherited property. Map.groupBy() (§8.13) is its twin that returns a Map, and it is the one to use when the key is an object rather than a string.

In summary, the vocabulary here is object.groupby() and map.groupby().

6.11 Symbols

Symbol() creates a value that is guaranteed to be unique. Every call produces a new one, even with the same description, and that is the entire feature: a property keyed by a symbol can never collide with anyone else's key.

const id1 = Symbol('id'), id2 = Symbol('id');
console.log('two symbols with the same description are equal:', id1 === id2);
console.log('Symbol.for uses the registry:', Symbol.for('app.id') === Symbol.for('app.id'));
console.log('Symbol.keyFor on a registered one:  ', Symbol.keyFor(Symbol.for('app.id')));
console.log('Symbol.keyFor on an unregistered one:', Symbol.keyFor(id1));

const record = { name: 'visible', [id1]: 'invisible to most things' };
console.log('Object.keys:', Object.keys(record), '| JSON:', JSON.stringify(record));
console.log('but readable directly:', record[id1]);

two symbols with the same description are equal: false
Symbol.for uses the registry: true
Symbol.keyFor on a registered one:   app.id
Symbol.keyFor on an unregistered one: undefined
Object.keys: [ 'name' ] | JSON: {"name":"visible"}
but readable directly: invisible to most things

Symbol.for() looks in the symbol registry, a global table shared across the whole realm (the global environment of one page or worker). So Symbol.for('x') in two separate modules gives the same symbol, which is exactly what a plain Symbol() is designed to prevent. Use Symbol() for privacy within a module, and Symbol.for() for a protocol you deliberately want to share.

A well-known symbol is one the language itself looks for. If your object implements one, it plugs into built-in syntax:

class Range {
  constructor(from, to) { this.from = from; this.to = to; }
  *[Symbol.iterator]() { for (let i = this.from; i <= this.to; i++) yield i; }
  get [Symbol.toStringTag]() { return 'Range'; }
  [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) { return hint === 'number' ? this.to - this.from : `${this.from}..${this.to}`; }
}
const r = new Range(1, 4);
console.log('spread works because of Symbol.iterator:', [...r]);
console.log('toStringTag:', Object.prototype.toString.call(r));
console.log('coerced to a number:', +r, '| to a string:', `${r}`);

spread works because of Symbol.iterator: [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ]
toStringTag: [object Range]
coerced to a number: 3 | to a string: 1..4

Symbol.iterator (§11.2), Symbol.asyncIterator (§11.9), Symbol.hasInstance (§7.6), Symbol.toPrimitive (§2.9) and Symbol.dispose (§3.8) are the ones you will actually use.

What to carry forward from this subsection: the symbol registry.

6.12 Proxy: Intervening in the Operation Itself

The Proxy object wraps a target object and lets you intercept the basic operations performed on it. Each interception is a proxy trap, named after the internal operation rather than after the syntax that causes it:

const fired = [];
const target = { a: 1 };
const spy = new Proxy(target, {
  get(t, key, receiver)      { fired.push(`get ${String(key)}`);    return Reflect.get(t, key, receiver); },
  set(t, key, v, receiver)   { fired.push(`set ${String(key)}`);    return Reflect.set(t, key, v, receiver); },
  has(t, key)                { fired.push(`has ${String(key)}`);    return Reflect.has(t, key); },
  deleteProperty(t, key)     { fired.push(`delete ${String(key)}`); return Reflect.deleteProperty(t, key); },
  ownKeys(t)                 { fired.push('ownKeys');               return Reflect.ownKeys(t); },
});
spy.a;
spy.b = 2;
'a' in spy;
delete spy.b;
Object.keys(spy);
console.log(fired.join(' | '));
console.log('the target really was changed:', JSON.stringify(target));

get a | set b | has a | delete b | ownKeys
the target really was changed: {"a":1}

Note which syntax fires which trap: the get trap for a read, the set trap for an assignment, the has trap for in, the deleteProperty trap for delete, and ownKeys for Object.keys. The apply trap and the construct trap apply when the target is a function, and intercept a call and a new respectively.

Passing each operation on to Reflect inside the trap is the habit that makes proxies safe, and §6.14 explains why the receiver argument matters.

A proxy is genuinely good for two things. A defaulting dictionary, in one line:

const withDefault = (fallback) => new Proxy({}, {
  get: (t, key) => (key in t ? t[key] : fallback),
});
const counts = withDefault(0);
counts.apples += 3;
counts.apples += 1;
console.log('counts.apples =', counts.apples, '| an unseen key =', counts.pears);

counts.apples = 4 | an unseen key = 0

And negative array indices, which the language does not otherwise have:

const negatable = (arr) => new Proxy(arr, {
  get(t, key, r) {
    if (typeof key === 'string' && /^-\d+$/.test(key)) return t[t.length + Number(key)];
    return Reflect.get(t, key, r);
  },
});
const letters = negatable(['a', 'b', 'c']);
console.log(letters[-1], letters[-2], letters[0], letters.length);

c b a 3

The terms above, gathered: the proxy object, the get trap, the deleteproperty trap and the construct trap.

6.13 The Invariants a Proxy Cannot Break

A proxy is not allowed to lie about anything the language has already promised. If the target has a property that can neither be reconfigured nor written, the get trap must return its real value. Returning anything else is a TypeError, not a successful lie:

const frozen = Object.freeze({ real: 'value' });
const liar = new Proxy(frozen, { get: () => 'lie' });
try { console.log(liar.real); }
catch (e) { console.log(`${e.constructor.name}: ${e.message.slice(0, 62)}…`); }

TypeError: 'get' on proxy: property 'real' is a read-only and non-configu…

That is a proxy invariant, and there is a family of them. ownKeys must report every non-configurable own key; has may not hide a non-configurable property; deleteProperty may not claim to have deleted a non-configurable one. The rule behind them all is that code holding a direct reference to the target must never see a contradiction.

Proxy.revocable() returns a proxy plus a revoke function that disconnects it for good. That is how you hand out access that you can take back later:

const { proxy, revoke } = Proxy.revocable({ x: 1 }, {});
console.log('before revoke:', proxy.x);
revoke();
try { proxy.x; } catch (e) { console.log('after revoke, any operation throws:', e.constructor.name); }

before revoke: 1
after revoke, any operation throws: TypeError

Know two limitations before reaching for a proxy. It is not transparent to identity: proxy !== target, so code that uses a WeakMap or === on the target will not recognise the proxy. And every trapped operation costs, so a proxy in a hot loop is a real slowdown. Proxies are excellent at a boundary (validation, observation, mocking, an ORM) and a poor choice for a core data structure.

One line each, for reference: a proxy invariant and proxy.revocable().

6.14 Reflect, and Why the receiver Matters

Reflect is a plain object of functions, one for each proxy trap, that performs the internal operations as ordinary function calls. It exists for two reasons.

It gives the operations a function form with sane return values. Reflect.deleteProperty() returns a plain boolean instead of delete's odd result. Reflect.get(), Reflect.set(), Reflect.has() and Reflect.construct() are functions you can pass around, which operators are not.

And it carries a receiver, which is what makes getters behind a proxy work correctly:

const base = { greeting: 'hello', get shout() { return this.greeting.toUpperCase(); } };
console.log('plain read:            ', base.shout);
console.log('Reflect.get, no receiver:', Reflect.get(base, 'shout'));
console.log('Reflect.get, redirected: ', Reflect.get(base, 'shout', { greeting: 'from elsewhere' }));

plain read:             HELLO
Reflect.get, no receiver: HELLO
Reflect.get, redirected:  FROM ELSEWHERE

The third argument sets what this will be inside the getter. Inside a proxy's get trap, the receiver is the proxy. So return Reflect.get(target, key, receiver) makes a getter on the target see the proxy as this, and a getter that reads another property goes back through the trap, as it should. Writing return target[key] instead silently skips your own proxy for every nested read. That is the bug the Reflect habit exists to prevent.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: reflect.get(), reflect.set() and reflect.construct().

6.15 Metaprogramming, in Proportion

Metaprogramming, code that inspects and changes how other code behaves, is what this whole second half of the section is about. It is powerful and easy to overuse, so it is worth being explicit about where it pays off.

Worth it
A test double that records calls. A validation boundary around configuration. An observable object that notifies on change. A deprecation shim that warns on an old property name. All of these are edges, entered once.
Not worth it
Anything in a hot path. Anything a plain function would express. Anything that makes an object behave unlike an object — the cost is paid by every future reader, who now cannot trust that a.b means what it says.

The deprecation shim is the use that most often earns its place, and it is short:

function deprecate(obj, renames) {
  return new Proxy(obj, {
    get(t, key, r) {
      if (Object.hasOwn(renames, key)) {
        console.log(`warning: "${String(key)}" is deprecated, use "${renames[key]}"`);
        return Reflect.get(t, renames[key], r);
      }
      return Reflect.get(t, key, r);
    },
  });
}
const config = deprecate({ maxRetries: 3 }, { retries: 'maxRetries' });
console.log('new name:', config.maxRetries);
console.log('old name:', config.retries);

new name: 3
warning: "retries" is deprecated, use "maxRetries"
old name: 3

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: a test double.

6.16 What This Section Established

  1. Property order is specified and is not insertion order. Integer-like keys ascend first — ['1','2','10','b','a'] — then strings in insertion order, then symbols. Every non-symbol key is a string.
  2. Method shorthand is a distinct thing, with no prototype, no new, and the only form that can use super; an arrow as a property never sees the object.
  3. Object.entries → map/filter → Object.fromEntries is the idiom for transforming an object, and all four readers see own, enumerable, string-keyed properties only.
  4. Spread and Object.assign read values, so a getter becomes a plain value in the copy, the prototype is not carried, and both are shallow — the nested object was shared, and only structuredClone broke the link.
  5. Object.create(null) removes the inherited-property hazard structurally, at the cost of every Object.prototype method — dict.hasOwnProperty threw a TypeError.
  6. Assignment and defineProperty have opposite defaults. Assignment gives all three flags true; defineProperty gives all three false, which is why the property vanished from Object.keys and JSON.stringify and why writing it threw.
  7. In a module every immutability failure throws. Frozen writes, sealed additions and sealed deletions all raised a TypeError rather than failing silently.
  8. Object.freeze is shallow — nested.b still went to 9, and isFrozen was true for the parent and false for the child.
  9. Four enumeration methods, four answers: keys (own+enumerable+string), getOwnPropertyNames (own+string), getOwnPropertySymbols, and Reflect.ownKeys for everything.
  10. Class methods are non-enumerable, so for...in on an instance listed only the field.
  11. Symbols cannot collide — two Symbol('id') are unequal — while Symbol.for deliberately shares through a global registry. A symbol key is invisible to Object.keys and JSON.stringify.
  12. A well-known symbol plugs an object into syntax: Symbol.iterator made spread work, Symbol.toPrimitive gave +r and `${r}` different answers.
  13. A proxy cannot lie about a frozen property — the get trap returning 'lie' threw a TypeError instead.
  14. Reflect.get's third argument sets this inside a getter, which is why Reflect.get(t, key, receiver) in a trap is the correct form and target[key] silently bypasses the proxy.

Exercises

1. Predict the output of each line, then explain the mechanism.

const proto = { shared: 'from prototype' };
const obj = Object.create(proto);
obj.own = 'mine';
Object.defineProperty(obj, 'hidden', { value: 'invisible', enumerable: false });

console.log(Object.keys(obj));
console.log(JSON.stringify(obj));
console.log('shared' in obj, Object.hasOwn(obj, 'shared'));
console.log(JSON.stringify({ ...obj }));
console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyNames(obj));
Solution 
[ 'own' ]
{"own":"mine"}
true false
{"own":"mine"}
[ 'own', 'hidden' ]

Object.keys gives ['own']. It wants own, enumerable, string-keyed properties. shared fails "own" — it is on the prototype. hidden fails "enumerable" — defineProperty defaulted it to false (§6.6).

JSON.stringify gives the same set, because it uses exactly the same rule. This is the reason a serialised object silently loses a field defined with defineProperty, and one of the two reasons a class instance serialises to fewer fields than you expect (the other being that methods live on the prototype).

'shared' in obj is true and Object.hasOwn is false. The in operator walks the whole prototype chain; hasOwn looks only at the object. This pair is the precise test for "did this object itself define this, or did it inherit it", and it is why in is the wrong check for validating a parsed JSON payload — 'toString' in payload is true for every plain object.

Spread gives {"own":"mine"}, the same set again: own and enumerable, so both the inherited and the non-enumerable property are dropped. Note this makes { ...obj } a lossy copy in two distinct ways at once.

getOwnPropertyNames gives ['own','hidden'] — own and string-keyed, with the enumerable requirement dropped. It is the only one of the five that sees hidden, which makes it the debugging tool when a property exists but nothing lists it.

The organising idea: three independent questions — own or inherited, enumerable or not, string or symbol — and each API answers a different combination. Learning the three questions is far more useful than memorising the five methods.

2. Write observable(target, onChange) that returns a proxy calling onChange(path, value) whenever any property changes, including nested ones. Then explain three things it still cannot see.

Solution 
function observable(target, onChange, path = []) {
  return new Proxy(target, {
    get(t, key, receiver) {
      const value = Reflect.get(t, key, receiver);
      // Wrap nested plain objects lazily, so we do not walk the whole tree up front.
      if (value && typeof value === 'object' && !(value instanceof Date) && typeof key !== 'symbol') {
        return observable(value, onChange, [...path, key]);
      }
      return value;
    },
    set(t, key, value, receiver) {
      const had = Reflect.has(t, key);
      const previous = had ? Reflect.get(t, key) : undefined;
      const ok = Reflect.set(t, key, value, receiver);
      if (ok && previous !== value) onChange([...path, key].join('.'), value);
      return ok;
    },
    deleteProperty(t, key) {
      const ok = Reflect.deleteProperty(t, key);
      if (ok) onChange([...path, key].join('.'), undefined);
      return ok;
    },
  });
}

const log = [];
const state = observable({ user: { name: 'Ada' }, tags: ['a'] }, (p, v) => log.push(`${p} = ${JSON.stringify(v)}`));
state.user.name = 'Grace';
state.tags.push('b');
delete state.user.name;
console.log(log.join('\n'));

user.name = "Grace"
tags.1 = "b"
user.name = undefined

Why it is built this way. The get trap wraps nested objects lazily rather than walking the tree at construction, so an untouched branch costs nothing and a branch replaced wholesale is re-wrapped automatically. Every trap delegates through Reflect with the receiver (§6.14), so a getter on the target sees the proxy and nested reads stay observed. The set trap compares before and after so an assignment of an identical value is not reported.

Note the array output, which is subtler than it looks. push is not a primitive operation: it assigns an index and then assigns length. So the trap fires twice — but only one notification appears, because assigning index 1 already moved length from 1 to 2 automatically, and by the time push writes length = 2 explicitly the previous value is already 2, so the previous !== value guard suppresses it. Remove that guard and you get a spurious tags.length on every push. This is worth dwelling on: an array is observable through a proxy, but what you observe is the sequence of primitive operations a method performs, not the method. Any array observer must decide what to do with that, and assuming push is one write is how the decision gets made by accident.

Three things it cannot see.

A change made through a reference taken before the proxy. const inner = original.user; inner.name = 'X' bypasses the proxy entirely, because the proxy only intercepts operations performed on it. This is not a fixable gap — it is what "a proxy is not the object" means (§6.13).

A change to a Map, Set or class with private fields. Those store data in internal slots, not properties, so map.set(k, v) is a method call — a single get of set — with the mutation happening invisibly inside. Observing them requires wrapping the methods, not the properties, and for private fields it is impossible: #count is not a property at all (§7.9), and calling a method that touches one through a proxy throws, because this is the proxy and the proxy has no such slot.

A property defined with Object.defineProperty on the target after wrapping, if you only trap set — defineProperty is its own trap. The same is true of Object.assign in some engines' fast paths, of Object.setPrototypeOf, and of anything reaching the object through Reflect directly.

The honest summary: this is a good boundary tool and a bad foundation. A state container that owns its updates — where every change goes through a function you wrote — is simpler, faster, and cannot be bypassed, which is why every real state library takes that approach rather than this one.

3. A configuration object must be immutable after startup, must reject unknown keys at write time with a helpful message, and must warn once when a deprecated key is read. Build it, and say why each guarantee needs the tool it uses.

Solution 
function sealConfig(defaults, { deprecated = {} } = {}) {
  const warned = new Set();
  const data = { ...defaults };

  return new Proxy(Object.freeze(data), {
    get(t, key, r) {
      if (typeof key !== 'symbol' && Object.hasOwn(deprecated, key)) {
        if (!warned.has(key)) {
          warned.add(key);
          console.log(`config: "${key}" is deprecated; use "${deprecated[key]}"`);
        }
        return Reflect.get(t, deprecated[key], r);
      }
      return Reflect.get(t, key, r);
    },
    set(t, key) {
      throw new TypeError(`config is read-only (tried to set "${String(key)}")`);
    },
    deleteProperty(t, key) {
      throw new TypeError(`config is read-only (tried to delete "${String(key)}")`);
    },
    has(t, key) {
      return Reflect.has(t, key) || Object.hasOwn(deprecated, key);
    },
  });
}

const config = sealConfig({ maxRetries: 3, timeoutMs: 5000 }, { deprecated: { retries: 'maxRetries' } });
console.log('read:', config.maxRetries);
console.log('deprecated read:', config.retries);
console.log('again, no second warning:', config.retries);
try { config.maxRetries = 9; } catch (e) { console.log(`${e.constructor.name}: ${e.message}`); }
console.log("'retries' in config:", 'retries' in config);

read: 3
config: "retries" is deprecated; use "maxRetries"
deprecated read: 3
again, no second warning: 3
TypeError: config is read-only (tried to set "maxRetries")
'retries' in config: true

Why each tool.

Object.freeze alone is not enough for the error message. A frozen object throws in strict mode (§6.8), but with the engine's own wording — Cannot assign to read only property 'maxRetries' — which does not say why it is read-only or what to do. The set trap replaces it with a message naming the subsystem. Freeze is still there underneath as defence in depth: it protects the object against anything that gets a direct reference (§6.13).

A proxy is required for the deprecation warning, because there is no other way to run code on a property read that does not exist. A getter via defineProperty would work for a known set of old names too, and is cheaper — the proxy earns its place when the mapping is data rather than code, or when unknown keys must also be reported.

Set for warned, not a boolean or an array. The requirement is "warn once per key", and a Set expresses membership with no duplicate handling. It also cannot leak: the config lives for the program's lifetime anyway.

{ ...defaults } before freezing so the caller's object is not frozen out from under them — freezing an argument is a side effect on someone else's data, and the kind of surprise that takes an afternoon to trace.

The has trap keeps in honest. Without it, 'retries' in config would be false while config.retries returned a value — an object contradicting itself, which is exactly the sin §6.13's invariants exist to prevent. Adding the trap is a two-line acknowledgement that if you intercept reads, you owe consistency to every other operation that asks about the same key.

What this deliberately does not do: freeze deeply. If a value in defaults is itself an object, it stays mutable (§6.8), and the honest fix is to document that configuration values must be primitives, rather than to ship a recursive freeze that is slow at startup and still misses Maps.

SECTION 7

Prototypes, Classes and Inheritance

Inheritance in JavaScript is not like inheritance in Java. The class keyword, added in 2015, is a nicer way of writing the older mechanism, not a replacement for it. That is not a historical footnote. It explains several things you will run into:

  • why instanceof sometimes gives the wrong answer;
  • why a method is missing from Object.keys;
  • why this goes wrong when a method is passed as a callback;
  • why Object.create(null) is the fix for a whole family of security bugs.

The mechanism itself is smaller than the machinery built on top of it. Every object has a link to another object, and a property lookup that fails follows the link. That object at the other end of the link is called the prototype, and that is the entire model. Constructors, classes, extends, super, instanceof and mixins are all arrangements of that one rule. Once you can see the links, you can predict all of them.

This section builds the model from the link upward. Then it covers the class syntax in full, including private fields and static initialisation blocks, which are genuinely new abilities rather than a shorter spelling of something old. It finishes with the two things the model makes possible, and dangerous, in equal measure: monkey patching (changing a built-in object's behaviour from outside) and prototype pollution (an attack that does the same thing through untrusted data).

7.1 The Link, and the Chain

Every object has a hidden link to another object, or to null. The object at the other end is its prototype, and following those links one after another is the prototype chain.

const base = { greet() { return `hello from ${this.name}`; } };
const child = Object.create(base);
child.name = 'child';
console.log(child.greet());
console.log('greet is not an own property:', Object.hasOwn(child, 'greet'));
console.log('but it is reachable:', 'greet' in child);
console.log('the chain:', Object.getPrototypeOf(child) === base,
            Object.getPrototypeOf(base) === Object.prototype,
            Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype));
console.log('base.isPrototypeOf(child):', base.isPrototypeOf(child));

hello from child
greet is not an own property: false
but it is reachable: true
the chain: true true null
base.isPrototypeOf(child): true

The chain ends at null. For an ordinary object, the last stop is Object.prototype, which is where toString, hasOwnProperty and valueOf come from. Object.create(null) makes an object with no link at all (§6.5).

Object.getPrototypeOf() reads the link, and Object.setPrototypeOf() changes it. .isPrototypeOf() asks the same question from the other end. __proto__ is the old accessor for the same link. It works everywhere, but it is standardised only so that old websites keep working, and it should not appear in new code: partly as a matter of style, and partly because it is the mechanism behind the attack in §7.12.

Changing a prototype after objects exist is slow. Engines optimise on the assumption that an object's shape stays the same, and Object.setPrototypeOf breaks that assumption. The usual advice is to set the prototype once, when the object is created, with Object.create, and never change it afterwards.

To have in hand before moving on: object.getprototypeof(), object.setprototypeof() and .isprototypeof().

7.2 Shadowing, and Where this Comes From

Two rules govern every interaction with a prototype, and one experiment shows both.

Lookup walks up the chain; assignment never does.

const base = { greeting: 'hello', greet() { return `${this.greeting} from ${this.name}`; } };
const a = Object.create(base), b = Object.create(base);
a.name = 'a';
b.name = 'b';

a.greeting = 'HI';                      // creates an OWN property on a
console.log('a:', a.greet());
console.log('b is unaffected:', b.greet());
console.log('own on a:', Object.hasOwn(a, 'greeting'), '| own on b:', Object.hasOwn(b, 'greeting'));
base.greeting = 'hey';                  // changing the prototype reaches only b
console.log('after changing the prototype — a:', a.greeting, '| b:', b.greeting);
delete a.greeting;                      // remove the shadow
console.log('after deleting the shadow, a sees the prototype again:', a.greeting);

a: HI from a
b is unaffected: hello from b
own on a: true | own on b: false
after changing the prototype — a: HI | b: hey
after deleting the shadow, a sees the prototype again: hey

That is shadowing a prototype property. Writing to a.greeting did not change base; it created an own property on a that hides the inherited one. That is how one instance can be customised without affecting its siblings, and why delete brings back the inherited value rather than removing anything.

this is the object the method was called on, not the object where the method was found. greet lives on base, yet it printed a and then b. That is the whole reason a shared prototype method is useful: one function serves every instance, and this supplies what differs between them.

There is one exception, and it is the one that produces bugs: a setter on the prototype does intercept the write. An accessor property is not a data property, so assignment calls the setter instead of shadowing it (§7.8). The same mechanism is behind the third defence in this section's third exercise.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: shadowing a prototype property.

7.3 Constructor Functions and new

Before class existed, a shared prototype was set up with a constructor function: an ordinary function called with the new operator:

function Point(x, y) {
  this.x = x;
  this.y = y;
}
Point.prototype.length = function () { return Math.hypot(this.x, this.y); };

const p = new Point(3, 4);
console.log('length:', p.length());
console.log('the instance link points at Point.prototype:', Object.getPrototypeOf(p) === Point.prototype);
console.log('and Point.prototype.constructor points back:', Point.prototype.constructor === Point);
console.log('without new, this is undefined in a module:',
  (() => { try { Point(1, 2); return 'no throw'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());

length: 5
the instance link points at Point.prototype: true
and Point.prototype.constructor points back: true
without new, this is undefined in a module: TypeError

This arrangement is prototypal inheritance. There are no classes underneath, only objects linked to other objects, and prototypal inheritance is what the class keyword of §7.5 turns into.

new Fn(args) does four things:

  1. creates an empty object;
  2. links it to Fn.prototype;
  3. calls Fn with this set to the new object;
  4. returns that object, unless the function explicitly returns a different one.

Two names are easy to confuse, and worth separating for good. The prototype property, Fn.prototype, is a property on the function. It holds the object that instances will link to. The prototype property exists on every ordinary function, whether or not it is ever used as a constructor. An instance's own link is read with Object.getPrototypeOf(instance), and instances do not have a .prototype property. The constructor property is a pointer back to the function, stored on Fn.prototype, which is how instance.constructor works. It is only a convention, and it is easily lost if you replace Fn.prototype with a new object.

In summary, the vocabulary here is a constructor function, the new operator and the constructor property.

7.4 new.target

new.target tells a function whether it was called with new, and that is the clean way to insist on it:

function MustUseNew() {
  if (!new.target) throw new TypeError('MustUseNew requires new');
  this.ok = true;
}
console.log('with new:', new MustUseNew().ok);
try { MustUseNew(); } catch (e) { console.log('without:', e.message); }

with new: true
without: MustUseNew requires new

It has a second, more interesting use. Inside a base constructor, new.target is the class that was actually being created. That lets a base class refuse to be created directly while still allowing its subclasses. It is the closest JavaScript comes to an abstract keyword, and this section's second exercise uses it:

class Shape {
  constructor() {
    if (new.target === Shape) throw new TypeError('Shape is abstract');
    this.kind = new.target.name;
  }
}
class Circle extends Shape {}
console.log('a subclass works, and knows its own name:', new Circle().kind);
console.log('the base does not:',
  (() => { try { new Shape(); return 'no throw'; } catch (e) { return e.message; } })());

a subclass works, and knows its own name: Circle
the base does not: Shape is abstract

new.target is undefined in a plain call and in an arrow function, and using it outside any function is a SyntaxError.

7.5 class — the Same Model, Better Syntax

class Point {
  constructor(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }   // the constructor method
  length() { return Math.hypot(this.x, this.y); }
  static origin() { return new this(0, 0); }
}
const p = new Point(3, 4);
console.log('same result:', p.length());
console.log('methods still live on the prototype:', Object.hasOwn(p, 'length'), 'length' in p);
console.log('and they are non-enumerable:', Object.keys(Point.prototype).length,
            '| getOwnPropertyNames:', Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Point.prototype).join(','));
console.log('a class is a function:', typeof Point);
console.log('but it cannot be called without new:',
  (() => { try { Point(1, 2); return 'no throw'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());

same result: 5
methods still live on the prototype: false true
and they are non-enumerable: 0 | getOwnPropertyNames: constructor,length
a class is a function: function
but it cannot be called without new: TypeError

A class declaration produces a function whose .prototype holds the methods. And the constructor method is the one that runs on new. A class without one gets an empty one automatically, and for a derived class (one that extends another) that automatic constructor passes its arguments on to super. Four differences from the constructor-function form are real rather than cosmetic:

Class methods are non-enumerable, so Object.keys(Point.prototype) is empty and for...in over an instance lists only fields. Methods added to Fn.prototype by hand are enumerable, which is why old code is full of hasOwnProperty checks inside for...in loops.

Note also what getOwnPropertyNames did not list: origin. A static method lives on the class object itself, not on .prototype. That is why Point.origin() works and p.origin() does not, and it is the same split that makes statics inherit through a separate link in §7.5.

A class body is always strict mode, whatever the surrounding code is.

Calling a class without new is a TypeError, always, with no new.target check needed.

Class hoisting works like let, not like function: the name exists, but it is in the temporal dead zone (§3.3), so a class cannot be used above its declaration. A class expression, const C = class { … }, is the anonymous form, and like a named function expression it can carry a name that is visible only inside itself.

What to carry forward from this subsection: a class declaration, a class expression and class hoisting.

7.6 Fields, Private State and Static Members

class Counter {
  count = 0;                                   // a public class field
  #secret = 'private';                         // a private field
  static #instances = 0;                       // a private static
  static registry = new Map();                 // a static member

  static { Counter.registry.set('ready', true); }   // a static initialization block

  constructor() { Counter.#instances++; }
  increment() { return ++this.count; }
  #internal() { return this.#secret.toUpperCase(); }   // a private method
  reveal() { return this.#internal(); }
  static get made() { return Counter.#instances; }
  static isCounter(obj) { return #secret in obj; }     // a brand check
}

const a = new Counter(), b = new Counter();
a.increment(); a.increment();
console.log('field:', a.count, '| independent:', b.count);
console.log('private method through a public one:', a.reveal());
console.log('static counter:', Counter.made, '| static block ran:', Counter.registry.get('ready'));
console.log('brand check:', Counter.isCounter(a), Counter.isCounter({}));
console.log('private fields are invisible:', JSON.stringify(a), Object.keys(a));

field: 2 | independent: 0
private method through a public one: PRIVATE
static counter: 2 | static block ran: true
brand check: true false
private fields are invisible: {"count":2} [ 'count' ]

Read the last line carefully, because it makes the point twice. JSON.stringify(a) and Object.keys(a) both report count, and neither reports #secret. The public field is an ordinary own enumerable property, and the private field is not a property at all.

A public class field is created on the instance, once per object, before the constructor body runs. A method, by contrast, lives once on the prototype. So a field holding an arrow function (§5.13) costs one function object per instance.

A private method, written #name() {}, follows the same rule as a private field. It cannot be seen on the prototype or reached from outside. A private method is the right home for an internal step that you do not want a subclass or a caller to depend on.

A private field is not a property at all. The # name is not a string. It does not appear in Object.keys, JSON.stringify, Reflect.ownKeys or a Proxy trap (§6.15), and reading one on an object that does not have it throws. That last behaviour gives you a brand check: #secret in obj is true only for real instances of the class. It is the only completely reliable "is this really one of mine?" test in the language.

A static member belongs to the class itself rather than to its instances. Unlike in most languages, statics are inherited, because a subclass's prototype link points at the parent class itself.

A static initialization block runs once, when the class is defined, with this set to the class. It exists for setup that needs several statements rather than one expression, and it is the only place outside a method where a private static can be set up.

7.7 extends and super

class Animal {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
  speak() { return `${this.name} makes a sound`; }
  static create(name) { return new this(name); }
}
class Dog extends Animal {
  constructor(name, breed) {
    super(name);                               // must come before any use of `this`
    this.breed = breed;
  }
  speak() { return `${super.speak()} — a bark`; }
}
const rex = new Dog('Rex', 'collie');
console.log(rex.speak());
console.log('the chain:', Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog.prototype) === Animal.prototype);
console.log('statics are inherited, and `new this` respects the subclass:', Dog.create('Fido') instanceof Dog);
console.log('instanceof walks the whole chain:', rex instanceof Dog, rex instanceof Animal, rex instanceof Object);

class Broken extends Animal {
  constructor() {
    try { this.x = 1; } catch (e) { console.log('using this before super():', e.constructor.name); }
    super('recovered');
  }
}
new Broken();

Rex makes a sound — a bark
the chain: true
statics are inherited, and `new this` respects the subclass: true
instanceof walks the whole chain: true true true
using this before super(): ReferenceError

The extends clause sets up two links at once: Dog.prototype → Animal.prototype for instance methods, and Dog → Animal for statics. That second link is why Dog.create exists without anyone writing it.

The super keyword does two different jobs. In a derived constructor, super(args) calls the parent constructor, and that call is what creates this. That is why touching this before calling super is a ReferenceError, not merely bad style. In a method, super.method() calls the parent's version of the method. It looks the method up from where the current method was defined, not from this, so it works correctly through several levels of inheritance.

Method overriding is simply defining a method with the same name lower down the chain, so the lookup finds it first. Note that static create used new this(name) rather than new Animal(name). Inside a static method, this is the class it was called on, so the inherited factory produced a Dog.

The terms above, gathered: the extends clause, the super keyword, a derived constructor and method overriding.

7.8 Getters, Setters and Accessors in a Class

A class may define an accessor property with get and set. The point is that, to the code using it, it looks exactly like a field. So a stored value can become a computed one later without changing a single caller.

class Temperature {
  #celsius = 0;
  get celsius() { return this.#celsius; }
  set celsius(value) {
    if (typeof value !== 'number' || Number.isNaN(value)) throw new TypeError('celsius must be a number');
    if (value < -273.15) throw new RangeError('below absolute zero');
    this.#celsius = value;
  }
  get fahrenheit() { return this.#celsius * 9 / 5 + 32; }
  set fahrenheit(value) { this.celsius = (value - 32) * 5 / 9; }
  static get absoluteZero() { return -273.15; }
}

const t = new Temperature();
t.fahrenheit = 212;
console.log('one value, two views:', t.celsius, t.fahrenheit);
console.log('validation runs on assignment:',
  (() => { try { t.celsius = -300; return 'accepted'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());
console.log('a static accessor:', Temperature.absoluteZero);
const descriptor = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Temperature.prototype, 'celsius');
console.log('it is an accessor on the PROTOTYPE:', Object.keys(descriptor).join(','));
console.log('and it is not an own property of the instance:', Object.hasOwn(t, 'celsius'));

one value, two views: 100 212
validation runs on assignment: RangeError
a static accessor: -273.15
it is an accessor on the PROTOTYPE: get,set,enumerable,configurable
and it is not an own property of the instance: false

Three consequences worth having straight.

An accessor lives on the prototype, like a method. Its descriptor has get and set instead of value and writable (§6.6), and Object.hasOwn(t, 'celsius') is false. So one getter is shared by every instance, and the state it reads must live somewhere else. That is what #celsius is for.

A setter is the only way to intercept an assignment. This is the exception §7.2 flagged: t.celsius = -300 did not create an own property hiding the accessor; it called the setter, which threw. It is also why a property with a getter and no setter is silently read-only in sloppy mode, and a TypeError in a module.

A getter with only a getter is not the same as a readonly field. Nothing stops a subclass from redefining it, and nothing stops Object.defineProperty from replacing it. The guarantee is a convention backed by the prototype, not something the engine enforces. A private field with no accessor at all is the only state that truly cannot be reached (§7.6).

The trap to avoid is an expensive getter. It reads like a field, so callers put it in loops. If it re-sorts a list or walks a tree, make it a method named computeX(), so the cost is visible at the call.

7.9 instanceof, Symbol.hasInstance and Duck Typing

instanceof asks whether a constructor's .prototype appears anywhere in the object's chain. That is a precise question, and often not the one you mean:

class Base {}
const obj = new Base();
console.log('the usual case:', obj instanceof Base);
console.log('it is really a chain search:', Base.prototype.isPrototypeOf(obj));

class Even { static [Symbol.hasInstance](n) { return typeof n === 'number' && n % 2 === 0; } }
console.log('Symbol.hasInstance overrides it entirely:', 4 instanceof Even, 5 instanceof Even);

console.log('a plain object from JSON is not an instance of anything useful:',
  JSON.parse('{"speak":1}') instanceof Base);
const duck = { speak: () => 'quack' };
console.log('duck typing asks what it can do:', typeof duck.speak === 'function');

the usual case: true
it is really a chain search: true
Symbol.hasInstance overrides it entirely: true false
a plain object from JSON is not an instance of anything useful: false
duck typing asks what it can do: true

Symbol.hasInstance lets a class define what instanceof means for it. That is how a validation library can let you write value instanceof PositiveInteger.

There are three situations where instanceof gives the wrong answer, and each has a standard replacement:
