  • Across realms, such as an array from an iframe or a worker: the constructor is a different function object, so instanceof Array is false while Array.isArray is true.
  • After a structuredClone or a JSON round trip, class identity is gone (§2.14), so an instanceof check on rebuilt data always fails.
  • And for your own types across a module boundary: if the module is loaded twice, there are two separate classes.

Duck typing, checking whether the value can do what you need rather than what type it is, avoids all three. And a brand check with a private field (§7.4) is the reliable alternative when you really need to know the identity.

7.10 Composition, Mixins and When Not to Inherit

Deep inheritance hierarchies are the classic failure of class-based design, and JavaScript makes the alternative easy.

A mixin is a function that adds behaviour to a class. Because extends accepts any expression, mixins can be stacked:

const Serializable = (Base) => class extends Base {
  toJSON() { return { ...this, type: this.constructor.name }; }
};
const Comparable = (Base) => class extends Base {
  equals(other) { return JSON.stringify(this) === JSON.stringify(other); }
};

class Shape { constructor(sides) { this.sides = sides; } }
class Square extends Serializable(Comparable(Shape)) {
  constructor() { super(4); }
}
const sq = new Square();
console.log('mixed-in toJSON:', JSON.stringify(sq));
console.log('mixed-in equals:', sq.equals(new Square()));
console.log('and it is still a Shape:', sq instanceof Shape);

mixed-in toJSON: {"sides":4,"type":"Square"}
mixed-in equals: true
and it is still a Shape: true

Composition over inheritance is the more general answer, and the rule of thumb is the classic one. Inherit when the subclass really is a kind of the parent, and can be used anywhere the parent can. Compose when it merely has the parent's ability. A Square is a Shape; a Logger is not a FileHandle, it has one.

Two more warnings from experience. Depth is the enemy: three levels is usually already too many, because a method's behaviour is then assembled from four places. And Symbol.species exists for a narrow case: controlling which constructor a method such as .map uses to build its result. Modern additions such as .toSorted deliberately ignore it and always return a plain Array, so treat it as legacy.

One line each, for reference: a mixin, Symbol.species and composition over inheritance.

7.11 Monkey Patching

Because prototypes are ordinary objects, they can be changed while the program runs. Monkey patching is doing that to a built-in object:

const originalJoin = Array.prototype.join;
Array.prototype.join = function (sep) { return `[${originalJoin.call(this, sep)}]`; };
console.log('every array in the realm is now different:', [1, 2].join('-'));
Array.prototype.join = originalJoin;
console.log('restored:', [1, 2].join('-'));

Object.defineProperty(Array.prototype, 'last', {
  get() { return this[this.length - 1]; }, configurable: true,
});
console.log('a non-enumerable addition does not break for...in:', [1, 2, 3].last);
const seen = []; for (const k in [1, 2]) seen.push(k);
console.log('for...in still sees only indices:', seen);
delete Array.prototype.last;

every array in the realm is now different: [1-2]
restored: 1-2
a non-enumerable addition does not break for...in: 3
for...in still sees only indices: [ '0', '1' ]

Patching a built-in affects the whole program, cannot be seen where it is used, and collides with any other code that does the same. That includes future versions of the language: Array.prototype.flatten had to be renamed to flat because a popular library had already defined an incompatible one. Do not do it. If you must, for a polyfill, define the property as non-enumerable, as above, and only if it does not already exist.

7.12 Prototype Pollution

Prototype pollution is the security version of the same mechanism. If an attacker can set a property named __proto__ on any object you build from their input, they change Object.prototype, and every object in the program inherits the change:

function unsafeMerge(target, source) {
  for (const key in source) {
    if (typeof source[key] === 'object' && source[key] !== null) {
      target[key] ??= {};
      unsafeMerge(target[key], source[key]);
    } else target[key] = source[key];
  }
  return target;
}
const hostile = JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}');
unsafeMerge({}, hostile);
console.log('an unrelated, empty object is now an admin:', {}.isAdmin);
delete Object.prototype.isAdmin;
console.log('after cleanup:', {}.isAdmin);

an unrelated, empty object is now an admin: true
after cleanup: undefined

An object that nobody touched gained a property, because it inherits from the polluted prototype. In any code that later checks if (user.isAdmin), that is a privilege-escalation bug: someone gets permissions they should not have.

Four defences, from strongest to weakest:

  • Use a Map for anything keyed by untrusted input (§8.11). A Map does not involve prototypes at all.
  • Use Object.create(null) for a plain-object dictionary (§6.5).
  • Reject the three dangerous keys, __proto__, constructor and prototype, in any recursive merge or property-setting helper.
  • Object.freeze(Object.prototype) at startup. It is blunt and occasionally breaks a dependency, but it stops the whole family of attacks dead.

7.13 What This Section Established

  1. One link, one rule. A failed property lookup follows the prototype link; assignment never does, so writing shadows rather than modifies.
  2. this is the object the method was called on, not the one the method was found on, which is what makes a shared prototype method useful.
  3. Shadowing is measurable: writing a.greeting created an own property, left b and the prototype untouched, and delete restored the inherited value. A setter on the prototype is the exception — assignment calls it instead of shadowing it.
  4. An accessor lives on the prototype, with a get/set descriptor rather than value/writable, so Object.hasOwn(t, 'celsius') was false and the state it reads has to live in a private field.
  5. Fn.prototype is a property on the function, not on instances; an instance's link is Object.getPrototypeOf(instance), and .constructor is a back-pointer that is only a convention.
  6. new does four things and new.target detects it. A class throws without new unconditionally.
  7. Class methods are non-enumerable — Object.keys(Point.prototype) was empty while getOwnPropertyNames listed all three — a class body is always strict, and a class is hoisted like let, not like function.
  8. A field is per-instance and a method is per-prototype, so an arrow-valued field costs one function object per object.
  9. A private field is not a property. It is absent from JSON.stringify and Object.keys, and #field in obj is the only fully reliable brand check.
  10. Statics are inherited, because Dog's own link points at Animal — which is why Dog.create('Fido') existed and returned a Dog.
  11. super() creates this in a derived constructor, so touching this first is a ReferenceError.
  12. instanceof is a chain search and gives the wrong answer across realms, after serialisation, and with a duplicated module. Symbol.hasInstance overrides it; a brand check replaces it.
  13. Mixins are functions returning classes, which composes where single inheritance cannot; prefer composition, and treat Symbol.species as legacy.
  14. Monkey patching is global and invisible, and its security form is prototype pollution: merging {"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}} made an unrelated empty object an admin.

Exercises

1. Predict each line and explain.

class A { constructor() { this.x = 1; } m() { return 'A'; } }
class B extends A { m() { return 'B' + super.m(); } }
const b = new B();

console.log(b.m(), Object.keys(b), Object.hasOwn(b, 'm'));
console.log(b instanceof A, A.prototype.isPrototypeOf(b), Object.getPrototypeOf(B) === A);
B.prototype.m = function () { return 'patched'; };
console.log(b.m());
const plain = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(b));
console.log(plain instanceof A, plain.x, typeof plain.m);
Solution 
BA [ 'x' ] false
true true true
patched
false 1 undefined

b.m() gives 'BA'. The lookup finds B.prototype.m first; super.m() inside it looks on A.prototype and returns 'A'.

Object.keys(b) gives ['x'] — only the own, enumerable, string-keyed property set in the constructor. Object.hasOwn(b, 'm') is false because m is on B.prototype, and class methods are non-enumerable in any case (§7.3).

All three checks on the second line are true. b instanceof A walks the chain past B.prototype to A.prototype. A.prototype.isPrototypeOf(b) is the same question spelled directly. Object.getPrototypeOf(B) === A is the static link — the one that makes B.someStaticOfA() work.

After patching, b.m() gives 'patched'. b holds no copy of anything; it holds a link. Changing the prototype changes every existing instance immediately, which is the power and the danger of §7.8 — and note the patch destroyed the super.m() call along with the original method.

The round trip loses everything but data. plain instanceof A is false because JSON.parse produces a plain object linked to Object.prototype; plain.x survives because it was an own enumerable property; plain.m is undefined because methods were never on the instance and JSON has no notation for a function anyway (§2.13). This is the trap behind every "my class instance came back from the API without its methods" — the fix is a static fromJSON that reconstructs, not a cast.

2. Design a small hierarchy for a payment system with Payment, CardPayment and BankTransfer, then argue whether inheritance is the right tool and show the composition alternative.

Solution 
class Payment {
  #status = 'pending';
  static #nextId = 1;
  id;
  constructor(amountMinorUnits, currency) {
    if (!Number.isSafeInteger(amountMinorUnits) || amountMinorUnits <= 0) {
      throw new RangeError('amount must be a positive integer in minor units');
    }
    if (new.target === Payment) throw new TypeError('Payment is abstract');
    this.id = Payment.#nextId++;
    this.amount = amountMinorUnits;
    this.currency = currency;
  }
  get status() { return this.#status; }
  settle() { this.#status = 'settled'; return this; }
  describe() { return `${this.constructor.name} #${this.id}: ${this.format()} (${this.status})`; }
  format() { return new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US',
    { style: 'currency', currency: this.currency }).format(this.amount / 100); }
  static isPayment(o) { return #status in o; }
}

class CardPayment extends Payment {
  constructor(amount, currency, last4) { super(amount, currency); this.last4 = last4; }
  describe() { return `${super.describe()} ending ${this.last4}`; }
}
class BankTransfer extends Payment {
  constructor(amount, currency, reference) { super(amount, currency); this.reference = reference; }
}

const card = new CardPayment(1999, 'USD', '4242');
console.log(card.settle().describe());
console.log(new BankTransfer(50000, 'EUR', 'INV-7').describe());
console.log('abstract base is enforced:',
  (() => { try { new Payment(1, 'USD'); return 'no throw'; } catch (e) { return e.message; } })());
console.log('brand check:', Payment.isPayment(card), Payment.isPayment({ status: 'settled' }));

CardPayment #1: $19.99 (settled) ending 4242
BankTransfer #2: €500.00 (pending)
abstract base is enforced: Payment is abstract
brand check: true false

Why the details are what they are. new.target === Payment enforces abstractness, which the language has no keyword for (§7.2). #status private with a public getter makes the state machine one-way from outside — nothing can set a payment to settled except settle(). Amount in minor units as an integer for the reason §2's floating-point exercise gives. this.constructor.name in describe means the base class need not know its subclasses. And the brand check cannot be forged by a plain object with a status property, which a duck-typing check would accept.

Is inheritance right here? For this shape, yes, narrowly: CardPayment genuinely is a Payment, it is substitutable anywhere a Payment is expected, and the hierarchy is one level deep. That is the case inheritance was designed for.

It stops being right at the second axis of variation. Add "refundable", "recurring" and "requires 3-D Secure" and the hierarchy has to represent every combination — RecurringRefundableCardPayment — which is the combinatorial explosion that makes deep hierarchies unmaintainable.

The composition alternative puts the varying behaviour in a collaborator:

const cardMethod = {
  kind: 'card',
  describe: (p) => `ending ${p.details.last4}`,
  authorize: async (p) => ({ ok: true, ref: `auth_${p.id}` }),
};
const bankMethod = {
  kind: 'bank',
  describe: (p) => `ref ${p.details.reference}`,
  authorize: async (p) => ({ ok: true, ref: p.details.reference }),
};

class Payment2 {
  constructor(amount, currency, method, details) {
    Object.assign(this, { amount, currency, method, details });
  }
  describe() { return `${this.method.kind}: ${this.method.describe(this)}`; }
  authorize() { return this.method.authorize(this); }
}
console.log(new Payment2(1999, 'USD', cardMethod, { last4: '4242' }).describe());

card: ending 4242

What composition buys: a new payment method is a new object rather than a new class, methods can be swapped at runtime (a test double is just another object), combinations do not multiply classes, and the behaviour is testable in isolation with no instance to construct. What it costs: one more indirection, and the type of method is now a convention rather than something instanceof can check.

The honest conclusion: use inheritance for a genuine, shallow is-a with one axis of variation, and reach for composition the moment a second axis appears — which in a payments system it always does.

3. Write safeMerge(target, source) that deep-merges without prototype pollution, and explain each defence.

Solution 
const FORBIDDEN = new Set(['__proto__', 'constructor', 'prototype']);

function safeMerge(target, source) {
  if (source === null || typeof source !== 'object') return target;
  for (const key of Object.keys(source)) {                 // own enumerable only
    if (FORBIDDEN.has(key)) continue;                      // defence 1
    const value = source[key];
    if (value !== null && typeof value === 'object' && !Array.isArray(value)) {
      if (!Object.hasOwn(target, key) || typeof target[key] !== 'object' || target[key] === null) {
        target[key] = Object.create(null);                 // defence 2
      }
      safeMerge(target[key], value);
    } else {
      Object.defineProperty(target, key, {                 // defence 3
        value, writable: true, enumerable: true, configurable: true,
      });
    }
  }
  return target;
}

const hostile = JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}, "nested": {"constructor": 1, "ok": 2}}');
const merged = safeMerge(Object.create(null), hostile);
console.log('no pollution:', {}.isAdmin);
console.log('dangerous keys dropped, safe ones kept:', JSON.stringify(merged));
console.log('the result has no prototype:', Object.getPrototypeOf(merged));

no pollution: undefined
dangerous keys dropped, safe ones kept: {"nested":{"ok":2}}
the result has no prototype: null

Defence 1 — reject the three keys. __proto__ is the direct route; constructor is the indirect one, since obj.constructor.prototype reaches the same place; prototype closes it off on a function target. Blocking all three is necessary, and blocking only __proto__ — which is what most naive fixes do — leaves the constructor.prototype path wide open.

Defence 2 — create intermediate objects with Object.create(null). A merge that creates target[key] = {} gives the attacker a fresh object that does inherit from Object.prototype, so the next level down can pollute through it. A null-prototype object has nothing to pollute (§6.5).

Defence 3 — Object.defineProperty rather than assignment. Plain target[key] = value invokes a setter if one is inherited, so a polluted prototype with a setter on the key can intercept the write and run attacker-influenced code. defineProperty creates an own data property directly and ignores the chain entirely.

Object.keys(source) rather than for...in so the loop never walks source's prototype chain — otherwise a source object that is itself polluted feeds its inherited properties into the target.

The !Array.isArray(value) guard means arrays are assigned rather than merged key-by-key. That is a deliberate semantic choice, not a security one: merging arrays index-by-index is almost never what a caller wants for configuration, and it is worth documenting rather than leaving to be discovered.

What this still does not do. It shares references — a nested array or a Date from source ends up in target unclonged — so a later mutation of the source is visible in the result. If that matters, structuredClone(value) before assigning (§2.14). And the returned object has a null prototype, so it has no toString, no hasOwnProperty and does not work with code expecting a plain object; that is the right default for a configuration store and must be stated.

The strongest defence is not in this function at all: use a Map for anything keyed by untrusted input, and this whole category disappears rather than being defended against.

SECTION 8

Arrays, Collections and Binary Data

An array is the data structure you will use most. It has more methods than any other object in the language: around forty, of which perhaps fifteen are worth knowing by heart. The rest of this section is about the other collections, which exist because an array or a plain object is sometimes the wrong shape:

  • Map, when the keys are data;
  • Set, when the question is "is this in it?";
  • WeakMap, when an entry should disappear together with its key;
  • typed arrays, when you are holding raw bytes rather than values.

Two distinctions run through everything here, and they are worth stating before any of the detail.

The first is mutating versus copying. Half the array methods change the array in place (they mutate it) and return something. The other half leave it alone and return a new array. The newest additions exist entirely to give the mutating methods non-mutating twins. Confusing the two is the most common array bug, because array.sort() looks like it just produces a result, but it actually changes the array and also returns it.

The second is what counts as the same value. indexOf and includes disagree about NaN. A Map keyed by objects compares keys by identity (is it the very same object?), so two objects with identical contents are two different keys. Every collection here makes a choice about equality, and knowing which choice is most of knowing when to use it.

8.1 Literals, Length and Holes

An array literal is a list of values inside square brackets, separated by commas. Array length is not a count of the elements. It is one more than the highest index, and you can write to it:

const list = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
console.log('length:', list.length);
list.length = 1;
console.log('assigning length truncates:', JSON.stringify(list));
list[5] = 'f';
console.log('assigning past the end grows it:', JSON.stringify(list), 'length', list.length);
console.log('Array.isArray:', Array.isArray(list), '| typeof says:', typeof list);

length: 3
assigning length truncates: ["a"]
assigning past the end grows it: ["a",null,null,null,null,"f"] length 6
Array.isArray: true | typeof says: object

Array.isArray() exists because typeof [] is 'object', which tells you nothing. It is also the only check that works across realms (separate global environments): an array from an iframe or a worker fails instanceof Array but passes Array.isArray.

A sparse array has holes: positions that were never assigned. A hole is not undefined. It is a missing property, and the array methods disagree about what to do with one:

const sparse = [1, , 3];
sparse[9] = 10;
console.log('length', sparse.length, '| JSON', JSON.stringify(sparse));
const visited = [];
sparse.forEach((value, i) => visited.push(i));
console.log('forEach visits only real indices:', visited);
console.log('map preserves the holes:', JSON.stringify(sparse.map(() => 1)));
console.log('1 in sparse:', 1 in sparse, '| sparse[1]:', sparse[1]);
console.log('Array.from fills them in:', JSON.stringify(Array.from(sparse)));

length 10 | JSON [1,null,3,null,null,null,null,null,null,10]
forEach visits only real indices: [ 0, 2, 9 ]
map preserves the holes: [1,null,1,null,null,null,null,null,null,1]
1 in sparse: false | sparse[1]: undefined
Array.from fills them in: [1,null,3,null,null,null,null,null,null,10]

forEach visited only three of the ten positions, and map left holes where the input had holes instead of calling the callback for them. sparse[1] reads as undefined, while 1 in sparse is false: that is the difference between "missing" and "present and undefined". The practical advice is short: do not create sparse arrays. new Array(3) creates three holes, which is why new Array(3).map(fn) does nothing at all. Array.from({ length: 3 }, fn) is the correct way to build a filled array of a given size.

Array.of() exists to fix the constructor's worst quirk. new Array(3) means "length 3", while new Array(3, 4) means "two elements". Array.of(3) always means the single element 3.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: an array literal, a sparse array and array.of().

8.2 The Mutating Methods

Six methods change the array in place. A mutating method returns something other than the array itself, usually the removed element or the new length, and that is a reliable way to recognise one:

const q = ['b', 'c'];
console.log('push returns the new length:', q.push('d'));
console.log('unshift returns it too:     ', q.unshift('a'));
console.log('now:', JSON.stringify(q));
console.log('pop returns the element:    ', q.pop());
console.log('shift returns the element:  ', q.shift());
console.log('now:', JSON.stringify(q));

const items = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'];
const removed = items.splice(1, 2, 'X', 'Y', 'Z');
console.log('splice removed', JSON.stringify(removed), 'leaving', JSON.stringify(items));
console.log('splice(2) with no count removes to the end:', JSON.stringify(items.splice(2)));

push returns the new length: 3
unshift returns it too:      4
now: ["a","b","c","d"]
pop returns the element:     d
shift returns the element:   a
now: ["b","c"]
splice removed ["b","c"] leaving ["a","X","Y","Z","d"]
splice(2) with no count removes to the end: ["Y","Z","d"]

.push() and .pop() work at the end and are cheap. .shift() and .unshift() work at the start and are not, because every remaining element has to move along. So a queue built on shift over a large array gets quadratically slower. .splice() does everything: it removes n elements from index i, inserts any number of new ones in their place, and returns what it removed.

.fill() overwrites a range in place. It is most often seen as new Array(5).fill(0), the standard way to get an array of zeros. That works precisely because fill does not skip holes, the way map does.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: .push(), .pop(), .shift(), .unshift(), .splice(), .fill() and a mutating method.

8.3 Slicing, Joining and Concatenating

Three old methods that do not mutate:

const letters = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'];
console.log('.slice(1, 3):  ', JSON.stringify(letters.slice(1, 3)), '— end is exclusive');
console.log('.slice(-2):    ', JSON.stringify(letters.slice(-2)), '— negative counts from the end');
console.log('.slice():      ', JSON.stringify(letters.slice()), '— a shallow copy of the whole array');
console.log('.concat:       ', JSON.stringify(letters.slice(0, 2).concat(['x'], 'y')));
console.log('.join("-"):    ', letters.join('-'));
console.log('.join() default:', letters.join());
console.log('null and undefined join as empty:', [1, null, undefined, 2].join('-'));

.slice(1, 3):   ["b","c"] — end is exclusive
.slice(-2):     ["d","e"] — negative counts from the end
.slice():       ["a","b","c","d","e"] — a shallow copy of the whole array
.concat:        ["a","b","x","y"]
.join("-"):     a-b-c-d-e
.join() default: a,b,c,d,e
null and undefined join as empty: 1---2

.slice() takes a start and an end (the end is not included), accepts negative indices, and with no arguments makes a shallow copy, though [...arr] is the modern way to write that. .concat() joins arrays and single values, and flattens an array argument by one level only. .join() builds a string, with a comma between items by default. It turns null and undefined into empty strings rather than the text "null", which is worth remembering when a joined list has mysterious double commas.

To have in hand before moving on: .concat().

8.4 Finding Things

Seven search methods, which differ in what they return and how they compare:

const nums = [5, 12, 8, 12, 3];
console.log('.indexOf(12):    ', nums.indexOf(12), '| .lastIndexOf(12):', nums.lastIndexOf(12));
console.log('.includes(8):    ', nums.includes(8), '| missing gives', nums.indexOf(99));
console.log('.find(n => n > 9):     ', nums.find(n => n > 9), '— the value');
console.log('.findIndex(n => n > 9):', nums.findIndex(n => n > 9), '— the index');
console.log('.findLast(n => n > 9): ', nums.findLast(n => n > 9));
console.log('.findLastIndex(n => n > 9):', nums.findLastIndex(n => n > 9));
console.log('[NaN].indexOf(NaN):', [NaN].indexOf(NaN), '| [NaN].includes(NaN):', [NaN].includes(NaN));

.indexOf(12):     1 | .lastIndexOf(12): 3
.includes(8):     true | missing gives -1
.find(n => n > 9):      12 — the value
.findIndex(n => n > 9): 1 — the index
.findLast(n => n > 9):  12
.findLastIndex(n => n > 9): 3
[NaN].indexOf(NaN): -1 | [NaN].includes(NaN): true

The last line is the one that catches people. .indexOf() and .lastIndexOf() use strict equality, and NaN !== NaN (§2.10), so they can never find a NaN. .includes() uses SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to itself, so it can. That is the only difference between arr.indexOf(x) !== -1 and arr.includes(x), and it is why includes was added.

.find() returns the first matching value, and .findIndex() the first matching position. When the array can contain undefined, find returning undefined is ambiguous, and that is when you want findIndex and a check for -1. .findLast() and .findLastIndex() search from the end, which saves the .slice().reverse() routine.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: .indexof(), .lastindexof(), .includes(), .find(), .findindex(), .findlast(), .findlastindex() and .reverse().

8.5 Transforming: map, filter, forEach

.map() builds a new array of the same length by transforming each element. .filter() builds a shorter one, keeping the elements a test function accepts (a predicate). .forEach() returns undefined, and exists for side effects:

const orders = [
  { id: 1, total: 30, paid: true },
  { id: 2, total: 12, paid: false },
  { id: 3, total: 45, paid: true },
];
console.log('.map:   ', JSON.stringify(orders.map(o => o.total)));
console.log('.filter:', JSON.stringify(orders.filter(o => o.paid).map(o => o.id)));
console.log('index and array are the 2nd and 3rd arguments:',
  JSON.stringify(['a', 'b'].map((v, i, all) => `${i}/${all.length}:${v}`)));
console.log('a common bug — parseInt takes a radix:', ['1', '7', '11'].map(parseInt));
console.log('the fix is an explicit arrow:        ', ['1', '7', '11'].map(n => parseInt(n, 10)));
console.log('.forEach returns:', orders.forEach(() => {}));

.map:    [30,12,45]
.filter: [1,3]
index and array are the 2nd and 3rd arguments: ["0/2:a","1/2:b"]
a common bug — parseInt takes a radix: [ 1, NaN, 3 ]
the fix is an explicit arrow:         [ 1, 7, 11 ]
.forEach returns: undefined

['1','7','11'].map(parseInt) giving [1, NaN, 3] is the classic proof that the callback receives three arguments: the element, its index, and the array. So map calls parseInt('7', 1), and radix 1 is invalid, hence NaN. It calls parseInt('11', 2), which is binary, hence 3. Passing a bare function to map is safe only when that function ignores extra arguments.

Use map when you want the result, forEach when you do not, and neither when a for...of loop is clearer. You cannot break out of forEach: break is a syntax error, and return only skips one element. That is a real reason to prefer for...of for anything that may stop early. And an async callback passed to forEach has its promise silently thrown away (§12.10).

In summary, the vocabulary here is .filter(), .map() and .foreach().

8.6 reduce, and When Not to Use It

.reduce() collapses an array into a single value. It carries an accumulator from element to element, updating it each time. It is the most general of the iteration methods, and the most often misused:

const nums = [5, 12, 8];
console.log('sum:', nums.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0));
console.log('building an object:', JSON.stringify(
  ['a', 'b', 'a'].reduce((acc, k) => { acc[k] = (acc[k] ?? 0) + 1; return acc; }, {})));
console.log('.reduceRight builds from the right:',
  ['a', 'b', 'c'].reduceRight((acc, x) => acc + x, ''));
try { [].reduce((a, b) => a + b); }
catch (e) { console.log('empty array with no initial value:', e.constructor.name + ':', e.message); }
console.log('with an initial value it is fine:', [].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0));

sum: 25
building an object: {"a":2,"b":1}
.reduceRight builds from the right: cba
empty array with no initial value: TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value
with an initial value it is fine: 0

Always pass the initial value. Without one, reduce uses the first element as the starting value and begins at index 1. That throws on an empty array, and silently changes the accumulator's type when the array has exactly one element. The initial value also shows at a glance what type the result is.

.reduceRight() does the same from the right. It is really useful only for operations that group from the right, such as composing functions.

When not to use it: a reduce that builds an array should be a map or a filter. A reduce that builds a grouped object should be Object.groupBy (§6.10). A reduce whose callback is longer than three lines is a for...of loop that would be easier to read and to debug. The good uses are sums, products, and folding values into a shape no other method produces.

What to carry forward from this subsection: .reduce() and .reduceright().

8.7 Testing, Flattening

const nums = [5, 12, 8];
console.log('.some(n => n > 10): ', nums.some(n => n > 10));
console.log('.every(n => n > 0): ', nums.every(n => n > 0));
console.log('on an empty array — some:', [].some(() => true), '| every:', [].every(() => false));
console.log('.flat() default depth 1:', JSON.stringify([1, [2, [3, [4]]]].flat()));
console.log('.flat(Infinity):        ', JSON.stringify([1, [2, [3, [4]]]].flat(Infinity)));
console.log('.flat also removes holes:', JSON.stringify([1, , 3].flat()));
console.log('.flatMap = map then flat(1):', JSON.stringify(['a b', 'c'].flatMap(s => s.split(' '))));
console.log('flatMap can drop items by returning []:',
  JSON.stringify([1, 2, 3, 4].flatMap(n => (n % 2 ? [n * 10] : []))));

.some(n => n > 10):  true
.every(n => n > 0):  true
on an empty array — some: false | every: true
.flat() default depth 1: [1,2,[3,[4]]]
.flat(Infinity):         [1,2,3,4]
.flat also removes holes: [1,3]
.flatMap = map then flat(1): ["a","b","c"]
flatMap can drop items by returning []: [10,30]

.flat() flattens nested arrays by one level unless you give it a depth, and .flat() also drops holes along the way, which makes it the cheapest way to compact a sparse array. .some() and .every() stop as soon as the answer is known. On an empty array they give the mathematically correct but sometimes surprising answers: some is false (nothing passes) and every is true (nothing fails). .flatMap() lets the callback return [] to drop an element or [a, b] to turn it into two. That makes it a map and a filter in a single pass, and the neatest way to say "transform some, discard others".

The terms above, gathered: .flatmap().

8.8 Sorting

.sort() has two behaviours that surprise everyone once:

console.log('default sort is lexicographic:', [10, 9, 100, 1].sort());
console.log('a numeric comparator fixes it:', [10, 9, 100, 1].sort((a, b) => a - b));

const people = [{ n: 'a', age: 30 }, { n: 'b', age: 25 }, { n: 'c', age: 30 }, { n: 'd', age: 25 }];
console.log('stable — a still precedes c, b still precedes d:',
  people.sort((x, y) => x.age - y.age).map(p => p.n).join(''));

const original = [3, 1, 2];
const result = original.sort();
console.log('sort mutates and returns the same array:', result === original);
const safe = [3, 1, 2];
console.log('toSorted leaves it alone:', JSON.stringify(safe.toSorted()), JSON.stringify(safe));
console.log('locale-aware:', ['ä', 'z', 'a'].sort(), 'vs', ['ä', 'z', 'a'].sort(new Intl.Collator('de').compare));

default sort is lexicographic: [ 1, 10, 100, 9 ]
a numeric comparator fixes it: [ 1, 9, 10, 100 ]
stable — a still precedes c, b still precedes d: bdac
sort mutates and returns the same array: true
toSorted leaves it alone: [1,2,3] [3,1,2]
locale-aware: [ 'a', 'z', 'ä' ] vs [ 'a', 'ä', 'z' ]

With no comparator, every element is converted to a string and compared by code unit, which is why [10, 9] sorts to [10, 9]: the string '10' comes before '9'. That is not a bug, it is the specified default, and it means a comparator function is effectively mandatory for anything except plain ASCII strings.

The comparator returns a negative number if a should come first, a positive number if b should, and zero if they tie. Use a - b for numbers, and a.localeCompare(b) or an Intl.Collator for text, as the last line shows: the default put ä after z, and the German collator put it after a.

.sort() is a stable sort as of ES2019, guaranteed by the specification. Elements that compare equal keep their original order. That is what makes it work to sort by one key and then by another.

.reverse() also changes the array in place. Because it and sort both return the same array they changed, const sorted = arr.sort() gives you two names for one array. That is why the copying methods were added.

One line each, for reference: a comparator function, a stable sort and Intl.Collator.

8.9 The Copying Methods

Four methods added in ES2023 are each a copying method: the non-mutating twin of an older one. They are the right default in any code that receives an array it does not own.

const base = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
console.log('.at(-1):        ', base.at(-1), '— negative indices, unlike base[-1]:', base[-1]);
console.log('.with(1, "X"):  ', JSON.stringify(base.with(1, 'X')));
console.log('.toReversed():  ', JSON.stringify(base.toReversed()));
console.log('.toSorted():    ', JSON.stringify(base.toSorted((a, b) => b.localeCompare(a))));
console.log('.toSpliced(1,1,"Y","Z"):', JSON.stringify(base.toSpliced(1, 1, 'Y', 'Z')));
console.log('the original is untouched throughout:', JSON.stringify(base));

.at(-1):         c — negative indices, unlike base[-1]: undefined
.with(1, "X"):   ["a","X","c"]
.toReversed():   ["c","b","a"]
.toSorted():     ["c","b","a"]
.toSpliced(1,1,"Y","Z"): ["a","Y","Z","c"]
the original is untouched throughout: ["a","b","c"]

.at() accepts negative indices, which base[-1] cannot: inside brackets the index is a property name, and '-1' is just a key nobody set. .with() returns a copy with one position replaced. It is the array version of spreading an object with one property overridden, and exactly what immutable state updates need.

All four are shallow: the new array holds references to the same elements. And all four return a plain Array, even when called on a subclass, as a deliberate simplification.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: .at(), .with() and a copying method.

8.10 Building Arrays From Other Things

Array.from() turns anything iterable or array-like into a real array, with an optional mapping function:

console.log('from a string:', JSON.stringify(Array.from('héllo')));
console.log('from a Set:   ', JSON.stringify(Array.from(new Set([1, 1, 2]))));
console.log('with a mapper:', JSON.stringify(Array.from({ length: 4 }, (_, i) => i * i)));

const arrayLike = { 0: 'zero', 1: 'one', length: 2 };
console.log('from an array-like:', JSON.stringify(Array.from(arrayLike)));
console.log('spread cannot do that:', (() => { try { return [...arrayLike]; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());

const letters = ['a', 'b'];
console.log('arr.entries():', JSON.stringify([...letters.entries()]));
for (const [i, value] of letters.entries()) console.log(`  index ${i} holds ${value}`);

from a string: ["h","é","l","l","o"]
from a Set:    [1,2]
with a mapper: [0,1,4,9]
from an array-like: ["zero","one"]
spread cannot do that: TypeError
arr.entries(): [[0,"a"],[1,"b"]]
  index 0 holds a
  index 1 holds b

An array-like object has a length and numeric keys but no Symbol.iterator, so it cannot be looped with for...of. Examples are arguments, a NodeList in older browsers, and a jQuery object. Array.from handles both array-likes and iterables, while spread handles iterables only. That is the practical difference between them, and the reason Array.from is still needed.

Array.from({ length: n }, fn) is the usual way to "build an array of n computed values". It works where new Array(n).map(fn) does not, because of the holes described in §8.1.

arr.entries() produces [index, value] pairs, which with destructuring gives a for...of loop the index without a separate counter. Array.fromAsync() is the asynchronous version: it reads an async iterable (§11.9), awaiting each value, so await Array.fromAsync(streamOfRows) collects a stream into an array.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: array.from() and array.fromasync().

8.11 Map

The Map object is a collection of key-value pairs that fixes the three things a plain object gets wrong when used as a dictionary.

const m = new Map([['a', 1]]);
const objectKey = { id: 1 };
m.set(objectKey, 'keyed by object identity').set(NaN, 'NaN works as a key');
console.log('size:', m.size);
console.log('map.get by object identity:', m.get(objectKey));
console.log('a structurally identical key misses:', m.get({ id: 1 }));
console.log('map.has(NaN):', m.has(NaN), '| map.get(NaN):', m.get(NaN));
console.log('insertion order is preserved:',
  [...m.keys()].map(k => (typeof k === 'object' ? '{object}' : String(k))));
console.log('map.delete returns whether it was there:', m.delete('a'), m.delete('a'));
console.log('iterating gives [key, value] pairs:', JSON.stringify([...new Map([['x', 1], ['y', 2]])]));

size: 3
map.get by object identity: keyed by object identity
a structurally identical key misses: undefined
map.has(NaN): true | map.get(NaN): NaN works as a key
insertion order is preserved: [ 'a', '{object}', 'NaN' ]
map.delete returns whether it was there: true false
iterating gives [key, value] pairs: [["x",1],["y",2]]
any key type
Objects, functions, NaN, null — compared by SameValueZero, so identity for objects. An object key stringifies to "[object Object]", collapsing every object into one key.
Map iteration order
Strict insertion order, always. An object reorders integer-like keys (§6.2), which a Map never does.
no prototype keys
A key called toString or __proto__ is just a key. No collision, no prototype pollution (§7.12).
.size, and iterable
An O(1) count rather than Object.keys(o).length, and directly iterable with for...of.

map.set() returns the map, so calls can be chained. map.get() returns undefined for a missing key, so map.has() is the way to tell "missing" apart from "present and undefined". map.delete() returns a boolean saying whether anything was removed, measured above as true and then false.

The rule of thumb: a plain object for a record with known field names, a Map for a dictionary whose keys are data. If the keys come from user input, from a database, or from anywhere other than literally written in the source, use a Map.

To have in hand before moving on: the map object, map.get(), map.set(), map.has(), map.delete() and map iteration order.

8.12 Set and the Set Operations

The Set object holds unique values, compared with SameValueZero. So NaN appears only once, and objects are told apart by identity:

const s = new Set([1, 2, 2, 3, NaN, NaN]);
console.log('deduplicated, and NaN kept once:', [...s]);
console.log('add returns the set, has is O(1):', s.add(4).has(4), '| size', s.size);
console.log('deduplicating an array:', [...new Set(['a', 'b', 'a'])]);

const a = new Set([1, 2, 3]), b = new Set([2, 3, 4]);
console.log('.union:               ', [...a.union(b)]);
console.log('.intersection:        ', [...a.intersection(b)]);
console.log('.difference:          ', [...a.difference(b)]);
console.log('.symmetricDifference: ', [...a.symmetricDifference(b)]);
console.log('.isSubsetOf:', new Set([1, 2]).isSubsetOf(a), '| .isDisjointFrom:', a.isDisjointFrom(new Set([9])));

deduplicated, and NaN kept once: [ 1, 2, 3, NaN ]
add returns the set, has is O(1): true | size 5
deduplicating an array: [ 'a', 'b' ]
.union:                [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ]
.intersection:         [ 2, 3 ]
.difference:           [ 1 ]
.symmetricDifference:  [ 1, 4 ]
.isSubsetOf: true | .isDisjointFrom: true

.union(), .intersection(), .difference() and .symmetricDifference() return new sets, and replace the loops of filter and has everyone used to write. .isSubsetOf(), .isSupersetOf() and .isDisjointFrom() return booleans. They accept any set-like object, meaning anything with size, has and keys, so you can pass a Map directly.

The reason to use a Set instead of an array is how the cost grows with size. set.has(x) takes the same time however big the set is (constant time), and array.includes(x) takes longer the longer the array is (linear time). So a membership test inside a loop over n items costs O(n) in total rather than O(n²). Turning an array into a set before a filtering loop is one of the few optimisations that is always worth it and never makes the code worse.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: the set object, .union(), .intersection(), .difference(), .symmetricdifference() and .issubsetof().

8.13 Map.groupBy, WeakMap and WeakSet

Map.groupBy() is Object.groupBy (§6.10) with a Map as the result, so the group key can be an object, or anything else that is not a string:

const tasks = [{ t: 'a', done: true }, { t: 'b', done: false }, { t: 'c', done: true }];
const grouped = Map.groupBy(tasks, (task) => task.done);
console.log('keys are real booleans, not "true"/"false":', [...grouped.keys()]);
console.log('done group:', JSON.stringify(grouped.get(true).map(t => t.t)));

keys are real booleans, not "true"/"false": [ true, false ]
done group: ["a","c"]

WeakMap and WeakSet hold their keys weakly: an entry does not stop its key from being garbage collected. They accept only objects (and unregistered symbols) as keys, cannot be looped over, and have no size. All three restrictions exist because entries can disappear at any moment, and being able to see the size would reveal when garbage collection happened.

const metadata = new WeakMap();
function tag(node, info) { metadata.set(node, info); }
function readTag(node) { return metadata.get(node); }
const element = { id: 'fake-dom-node' };
tag(element, { rendered: true });
console.log('associated data:', JSON.stringify(readTag(element)));
console.log('WeakMap is not iterable:', typeof metadata[Symbol.iterator]);
console.log('and has no size:', metadata.size);

associated data: {"rendered":true}
WeakMap is not iterable: undefined
and has no size: undefined

That is the standard use: associate data with an object you do not own, such as a DOM node or an instance from another library, without stopping it from being collected. A plain Map doing the same job is a memory leak by design (§3.10), because the map holds the last remaining reference to every node ever passed to it.

8.14 Binary Data

The ArrayBuffer object is a fixed-size block of raw bytes. It has no methods for reading or writing them; for that you need a view.

A typed array is a view that reads the buffer as numbers of one type: Uint8Array, Int32Array, Float64Array and so on. It has most array methods but a fixed length, and no push, pop or splice.

const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(8);
const bytes = new Uint8Array(buffer);
const words = new Uint32Array(buffer);
bytes[0] = 255;
console.log('two views share one buffer — words[0] is now', words[0]);
console.log('byteLength', buffer.byteLength, '| Uint8Array length', bytes.length, '| Uint32Array length', words.length);

const wrapping = new Uint8Array([250]);
wrapping[0] += 10;
console.log('Uint8Array wraps rather than overflowing:', wrapping[0]);
console.log('and truncates a float:', (() => { const t = new Uint8Array(1); t[0] = 3.9; return t[0]; })());

two views share one buffer — words[0] is now 255
byteLength 8 | Uint8Array length 8 | Uint32Array length 2
Uint8Array wraps rather than overflowing: 4
and truncates a float: 3

Two views over one buffer are two windows onto the same memory, which is the whole point, and why taking another view of a typed array copies nothing. Writing 260 into a Uint8Array stores 4, silently, because the value wraps around at 256 (it is taken modulo 256). Assigning 3.9 stores 3.

DataView is the view for mixed formats, or formats defined by someone else, and it is the only one that lets you choose the endianness:

const buf = new ArrayBuffer(4);
const view = new DataView(buf);
const asHex = () => [...new Uint8Array(buf)].map(b => b.toString(16).padStart(2, '0')).join(' ');
view.setUint32(0, 0x12345678);
console.log('big-endian (the DataView default):', asHex());
view.setUint32(0, 0x12345678, true);
console.log('little-endian (littleEndian = true):', asHex());
console.log('read back big-endian:', view.getUint32(0).toString(16), '| little:', view.getUint32(0, true).toString(16));

big-endian (the DataView default): 12 34 56 78
little-endian (littleEndian = true): 78 56 34 12
read back big-endian: 78563412 | little: 12345678

Endianness is the order in which the bytes of a multi-byte number are stored: biggest byte first (big-endian) or smallest first (little-endian). DataView defaults to big-endian, which is the order used on networks. A typed array always uses the machine's order, which on every mainstream processor is little-endian. So parsing a binary file format or a network packet means DataView, with the endianness stated explicitly. A Uint32Array over the same bytes would give the wrong numbers on most machines.

A transferable object is the other reason buffers exist. An ArrayBuffer listed for transfer in a postMessage call (§17.8) is moved rather than copied. Ownership changes, the sender's buffer becomes detached with a byteLength of 0, and the cost is the same whatever the size. That is what makes it practical to hand a 50MB image to a worker.

In summary, the vocabulary here is the arraybuffer object and a transferable object.

8.15 Bytes, Text and Base64

btoa() and atob() convert between binary strings and base64, a way of writing bytes using only safe text characters. Their names are the oldest joke on the platform ("binary to ASCII" and back), and their limitation is the thing to remember:

console.log('ASCII round trip:', atob(btoa('hello')));
console.log('btoa("héllo") gives:', btoa('héllo'), '— no error at all');
try { btoa('日本'); }
catch (e) { console.log('btoa("日本") throws:', e.name); }

const utf8 = new TextEncoder().encode('héllo');
const correct = btoa(String.fromCharCode(...utf8));
console.log('via TextEncoder:    ', correct);
console.log('and back:', new TextDecoder().decode(Uint8Array.from(atob(correct), c => c.charCodeAt(0))));

ASCII round trip: hello
btoa("héllo") gives: aOlsbG8= — no error at all
btoa("日本") throws: InvalidCharacterError
via TextEncoder:     aMOpbGxv
and back: héllo

btoa() operates on bytes, not text, and the two encodings of héllo differ: aOlsbG8= against aMOpbGxv. This is the important half. btoa treats each code unit as one byte, so é (U+00E9) becomes the single byte 0xE9. That is the Latin-1 encoding, not UTF-8, where é is the two bytes 0xC3 0xA9. No error is raised: you get valid base64 of the wrong bytes, and the damage only shows when something else decodes it as UTF-8. Only a character above U+00FF, such as 日, does not fit in one byte, and that throws.

So the correct path for real text is TextEncoder → bytes → base64, and the reverse on the way back. The silent case is far more dangerous than the one that throws, which is why both lines are written out.

For anything larger, Blob and File are the right containers. They hold bytes without keeping them in a JavaScript string, they can be streamed, and URL.createObjectURL(blob) gives you a URL you can put in an <img> or a download link.

What to carry forward from this subsection: atob().

8.16 What This Section Established

  1. length is not a count — it is one past the highest index, it is writable, and assigning it truncates. Array.isArray is the only reliable test, because typeof [] is 'object'.
  2. A hole is not undefined. forEach visited 3 of 10 indices, map preserved the holes, and 1 in sparse was false while sparse[1] read as undefined. new Array(3).map(fn) therefore does nothing; Array.from({length: 3}, fn) is the fix.
  3. A mutating method returns something other than the array — push and unshift the new length, pop and shift the element, splice what it removed.
  4. .indexOf cannot find NaN and .includes can — -1 against true. That is the only difference between them.
  5. The callback takes three arguments, which is why ['1','7','11'].map(parseInt) gives [1, NaN, 3].
  6. reduce without an initial value throws on an empty array, and changes the accumulator's type on a one-element one. Always pass it.
  7. some is false and every is true on an empty array, and flatMap returning [] drops an element.
  8. The default sort is lexicographic — [1, 10, 100, 9] — so a comparator is effectively mandatory. Sorting is stable by specification, and sort and reverse mutate and return the same array.
  9. The copying methods are the safe default: .at(), .with(), .toSorted(), .toReversed() and .toSpliced() all left the original untouched, and .at(-1) works where arr[-1] is undefined.
  10. Array.from handles array-likes and spread does not — [...{0:'a', length:1}] is a TypeError.
  11. A Map keys by identity, preserves insertion order exactly, and cannot collide with a prototype. A structurally identical object key missed; NaN worked as a key; map.delete returned true then false.
  12. set.has is O(1) and array.includes is O(n), and the new set operations replace the filter-and-has loops.
  13. WeakMap is how you attach data to an object you do not own without leaking it. Not iterable, no size — both by design.
  14. Two typed-array views share one buffer, values wrap modulo their type (250 + 10 gave 4) and floats truncate.
  15. DataView is big-endian by default and a typed array follows the platform — 12 34 56 78 against 78 56 34 12 for the same number. Binary formats need DataView.
  16. btoa operates on bytes, so real text must go through TextEncoder first — héllo threw an InvalidCharacterError otherwise.

The terms above, gathered: .tospliced().

Exercises

1. Predict each line, then explain the mechanism.

const a = [1, 2, 3];
const b = a;
b.push(4);
console.log(a.length);

const sorted = [10, 9, 1].sort();
console.log(sorted, [10, 9, 1].toSorted((x, y) => x - y));

console.log([1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2).filter(n => n > 2).reduce((s, n) => s + n, 0));
console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map(Number), ['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt));
console.log([...new Set([1, '1', 1, NaN, NaN])]);
console.log([, , ].length, Object.keys([, , ]).length);
Solution 
4
[ 1, 10, 9 ] [ 1, 9, 10 ]
10
[ 1, 2, 3 ] [ 1, NaN, NaN ]
[ 1, '1', NaN ]
2 0

a.length is 4. b = a copies a reference, not the array, so there is one array with two names (§2.12). This is the single most common source of "why did my other variable change".

[10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9]. The default comparator stringifies, and "10" < "9" because '1' precedes '9' in code-unit order. toSorted((x, y) => x - y) gives the numeric answer and, unlike sort, does not touch the original.

The chain gives 10. map → [2, 4, 6], filter(n > 2) → [4, 6], reduce with seed 0 → 10. Note that 2 is excluded because the filter is strict.

map(Number) works and map(parseInt) does not. Number ignores extra arguments; parseInt treats the second as a radix, so it computes parseInt('1', 0) (radix 0 means "guess", giving 1), parseInt('2', 1) (radix 1 is invalid → NaN) and parseInt('3', 2) (binary has no digit 3 → NaN). The [1, NaN, NaN] differs from §8.5's [1, NaN, 3] only because the digits differ, which makes the point better: the failure depends on the data, so it can pass a test and fail in production.

The Set keeps 1, '1' and one NaN. SameValueZero is strict equality with one amendment — NaN equals itself — so the number and the string are different values, and the two NaNs are one.

[, , ].length is 2 and Object.keys gives 0. A trailing comma in an array literal is ignored, so [, , ] is two holes, not three. length counts the span; Object.keys counts the properties that actually exist, and a hole is not one (§8.1).

2. You are given orders, an array of { id, customerId, total, status }, and customers, an array of { id, name }. Produce, for each customer with at least one paid order, their name and their total spend, sorted by spend descending. Write it twice — once naively, once efficiently — and quantify the difference.

Solution

The naive version, which is what most people write first:

function spendNaive(orders, customers) {
  return customers
    .map(c => ({
      name: c.name,
      spend: orders.filter(o => o.customerId === c.id && o.status === 'paid')
                   .reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.total, 0),
    }))
    .filter(row => row.spend > 0)
    .sort((a, b) => b.spend - a.spend);
}

It is O(customers × orders). The filter inside the map rescans the entire order list once per customer, so 1,000 customers and 10,000 orders is ten million comparisons for work that needs ten thousand. It also cannot distinguish "no paid orders" from "paid orders totalling zero", because both produce a spend of 0 — a correctness bug hiding inside the performance bug.

The efficient version makes one pass over each array:

function spend(orders, customers) {
  const totals = new Map();                                  // customerId -> total
  for (const o of orders) {
    if (o.status !== 'paid') continue;
    totals.set(o.customerId, (totals.get(o.customerId) ?? 0) + o.total);
  }
  const nameOf = new Map(customers.map(c => [c.id, c.name])); // one lookup table
  return [...totals]
    .map(([id, spend]) => ({ name: nameOf.get(id) ?? '(unknown)', spend }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.spend - a.spend);
}

const orders = [
  { id: 1, customerId: 'a', total: 30, status: 'paid' },
  { id: 2, customerId: 'b', total: 12, status: 'pending' },
  { id: 3, customerId: 'a', total: 45, status: 'paid' },
  { id: 4, customerId: 'c', total: 20, status: 'paid' },
];
const customers = [{ id: 'a', name: 'Ada' }, { id: 'b', name: 'Bo' }, { id: 'c', name: 'Cy' }];
console.log(JSON.stringify(spend(orders, customers)));

[{"name":"Ada","spend":75},{"name":"Cy","spend":20}]

Why it is faster and also more correct. It is O(orders + customers): one pass to accumulate, one to build the name index, one sort. Building nameOf as a Map turns each name lookup from a linear customers.find() into a constant-time get — the §8.12 point, and the reason the total drops from ten million operations to about eleven thousand on the sizes above. And because the map only ever gains a key when a paid order is seen, "no paid orders" is absence rather than zero, so Bo is correctly excluded while a genuine zero-value paid order would be kept.

Map rather than a plain object for totals and nameOf because the ids are data (§8.11). With an object, a customer id of constructor or __proto__ would collide with an inherited property, and numeric ids would silently reorder the result before the sort.

Map.groupBy is the alternative when you want the orders themselves rather than a running total:

const paidByCustomer = Map.groupBy(orders.filter(o => o.status === 'paid'), o => o.customerId);

That is clearer when the groups are the goal, and slightly wasteful here because it materialises arrays we would immediately reduce away.

3. Implement chunk(array, size) returning an array of arrays, and unique(array, keyFn) removing duplicates by a derived key while keeping the first occurrence. Explain the equality choice in each.

Solution 
function chunk(array, size) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(size) || size < 1) throw new RangeError('size must be a positive integer');
  return Array.from({ length: Math.ceil(array.length / size) },
                    (_, i) => array.slice(i * size, i * size + size));
}

function unique(array, keyFn = (x) => x) {
  const seen = new Set();
  const out = [];
  for (const item of array) {
    const key = keyFn(item);
    if (seen.has(key)) continue;
    seen.add(key);
    out.push(item);            // the FIRST occurrence is kept
  }
  return out;
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(chunk([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)));
console.log(JSON.stringify(chunk([], 3)), JSON.stringify(chunk([1], 5)));
const people = [{ id: 1, n: 'first' }, { id: 2, n: 'b' }, { id: 1, n: 'duplicate' }];
console.log(JSON.stringify(unique(people, p => p.id)));
console.log(JSON.stringify(unique([1, '1', 1, NaN, NaN])));

[[1,2],[3,4],[5]]
[] [[1]]
[{"id":1,"n":"first"},{"id":2,"n":"b"}]
[1,"1",null]

chunk uses Array.from({length}, fn) rather than a loop with push, because the number of chunks is known up front — Math.ceil(length / size) — so the shape is a computation rather than an accumulation. It also handles the two edge cases for free: an empty input gives [] because the length is 0, and a size larger than the array gives one short chunk because slice clamps. The explicit RangeError is there because size = 0 would otherwise produce Math.ceil(n / 0) = Infinity and hang.

unique uses a Set for seen, which is the whole performance story. The obvious out.some(x => keyFn(x) === key) alternative is O(n²) and recomputes keyFn for every comparison; the Set makes each check constant time (§8.12), so the function is O(n) with one keyFn call per item.

The equality choice, and its one sharp edge. A Set uses SameValueZero, which is what you want almost always: 1 and '1' stay distinct — visible in the output — and two NaN keys collapse to one, which === would not do. Note JSON.stringify printed NaN as null, which is JSON's limitation rather than the function's.

The edge is object keys. If keyFn returns an object, the comparison is by identity, so unique(items, x => ({ id: x.id })) deduplicates nothing at all — every call builds a fresh object. A key function must return a primitive, and if a composite key is needed the honest spellings are a template string (`${a}|${b}`, with a separator that cannot appear in the parts) or a nested Map. Silently returning objects is the failure mode worth guarding in a code review, because it produces a function that runs, returns a plausible array, and removes nothing.

Why not [...new Set(array)] for the no-key case? It is correct and shorter, and worth special-casing if the profile justifies it. The loop is kept here because it handles both cases with one code path, and because "keep the first occurrence" is an explicit guarantee the Set spread happens to provide but does not document.

SECTION 9

Text and Regular Expressions

Text looks like the easy part of a language, and it is not. A JavaScript string is stored as a sequence of UTF-16 code units: 16-bit numbers, where some characters take one and others take two. So a string's units are not the same as its characters. And characters are not the same as what a reader would call a single letter, because an accent or an emoji modifier can be a separate character joined to the one before it.

The three differ often enough that str.length is wrong for any string a user might type. Names with accents, emoji, scripts that combine marks, and flags all break the assumption. They break it silently: the code runs, the number looks plausible, and the truncation cuts a character in half.

The second half of the section is regular expressions (patterns for matching text), which have the opposite problem. They fail loudly, and are hard to write rather than hard to notice. The material is organised around the parts that pay off:

  • what the flags actually change;
  • why lastIndex makes a /g regex stateful (it remembers where it stopped), and therefore dangerous to share;
  • how groups and lookaround (checking what comes before or after a match without including it) fit together;
  • the one performance failure, catastrophic backtracking, that makes a working expression take so long that an attacker can use it to block your program (a denial of service), on an input just two characters longer than the ones you tested.

Everything below was run before it was written down, and three of the measured results contradict what is commonly taught.

9.1 String Literals and Template Literals

A string literal uses single or double quotes; the two mean exactly the same. A template literal uses backticks, and adds three things:

const name = 'Ada', items = 3;
console.log(`interpolation: ${name} has ${items} item${items === 1 ? '' : 's'}`);
console.log(`arbitrary expressions: ${items * 2} and ${[1, 2].map(n => n + 1).join('+')}`);
const multi = `first line
  second line, with the indentation preserved exactly`;
console.log(multi);
console.log('escapes:', 'tab\there', '| unicode:', 'é', '\u{1F44B}', '| a quote: \'ok\'');

interpolation: Ada has 3 items
arbitrary expressions: 6 and 2+3
first line
  second line, with the indentation preserved exactly
escapes: tab	here | unicode: é 👋 | a quote: 'ok'

Interpolation (inserting values with ${}), real newlines, and no need to escape the other two quote characters. The indentation inside a template literal is part of the string. That is the one thing to watch when a template sits inside an indented function: every line after the first keeps its leading spaces in the output.

A ${} substitution converts its value to a string using the normal rules (§2.9). So an object becomes [object Object] unless it has a toString, and an array becomes its join(',').

One line each, for reference: a string literal.

9.2 Tagged Templates

A tagged template puts a function name in front of the backticks. The function receives the fixed text pieces as its first argument and the inserted values as the rest. That means the function decides how they are combined, and can escape, translate or reject the values:

function tag(strings, ...values) {
  return JSON.stringify({ strings: [...strings], raw: [...strings.raw], values });
}
const who = 'world';
console.log(tag`hi\n${who}!`);
console.log('String.raw keeps the backslash:', JSON.stringify(String.raw`a\nb`));
console.log('a normal template does not:  ', JSON.stringify(`a\nb`));

{"strings":["hi\n","!"],"raw":["hi\\n","!"],"values":["world"]}
String.raw keeps the backslash: "a\\nb"
a normal template does not:   "a\nb"

Note the two arrays. strings holds the "cooked" pieces, with escape sequences processed, and strings.raw holds them exactly as written: "hi\n" against "hi\\n". String.raw is the built-in tag that returns the raw form joined with the values. It is the right way to write a Windows path or the source of a regular expression without doubling every backslash.

Tagged templates matter because the tag sees the values separately from the text, so it can treat the values as untrusted. Every safe-HTML and safe-SQL template helper is built on this: the fixed text is yours, the inserted values are data, and the tag escapes only the data.

const escape = (s) => String(s).replace(/[&<>"']/g, (c) =>
  ({ '&': '&amp;', '<': '&lt;', '>': '&gt;', '"': '&quot;', "'": '&#39;' }[c]));
const html = (strings, ...values) =>
  strings.reduce((out, part, i) => out + part + (i < values.length ? escape(values[i]) : ''), '');
const userInput = '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>';
console.log(html`<p>Hello, ${userInput}</p>`);

<p>Hello, &lt;img src=x onerror=alert(1)&gt;</p>

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: a tagged template.

9.3 Strings Are Immutable

String immutability means that no method changes a string; every one returns a new string:

let s = 'hello';
try { s[0] = 'H'; } catch (e) { console.log('index assignment throws in a module:', e.constructor.name); }
console.log('the string is unchanged:', s);
console.log('.toUpperCase returns a new string:', s.toUpperCase(), '| original still', s);
s = s.replace('h', 'H');
console.log('reassigning the variable is the only way:', s);
console.log('.repeat:', 'ab'.repeat(3), '| .startsWith:', 'hello'.startsWith('he'), '| .endsWith:', 'hello'.endsWith('lo'));
console.log('.padStart:', JSON.stringify('7'.padStart(3, '0')), '| .padEnd:', JSON.stringify('ab'.padEnd(5, '.')));
console.log('.trim:', JSON.stringify('  hi  '.trim()),
            '| .trimStart:', JSON.stringify('  hi  '.trimStart()),
            '| .trimEnd:', JSON.stringify('  hi  '.trimEnd()));

index assignment throws in a module: TypeError
the string is unchanged: hello
.toUpperCase returns a new string: HELLO | original still hello
reassigning the variable is the only way: Hello
.repeat: ababab | .startsWith: true | .endsWith: true
.padStart: "007" | .padEnd: "ab..."
.trim: "hi" | .trimStart: "hi  " | .trimEnd: "  hi"

.repeat() builds a repeated string. .startsWith() and .endsWith() are the readable replacements for comparing an indexOf result. .trim() removes whitespace from both ends. None of them touch the original, because no operation could. Note that .trim() strips every kind of Unicode whitespace, not only spaces, which makes it correct on text pasted from a document.

The index assignment threw. In sloppy mode it would have been silently ignored. In a module, where strict mode is always on (§1.9), writing to one position of a string is a TypeError. That is the better outcome, because code that thought it was editing a string finds out at once. .padStart() and .padEnd() are for lining up output. Note that .padStart(3, '0') on a string longer than 3 returns it unchanged rather than cutting it.

.split() turns a string into an array, and it has two behaviours worth knowing:

console.log('with a limit:', JSON.stringify('a,b,c'.split(',', 2)));
console.log('capture groups are KEPT in the result:', JSON.stringify('a1b'.split(/(\d)/)));
console.log('without a group they are dropped:      ', JSON.stringify('a1b'.split(/\d/)));
console.log('splitting on the empty string:', JSON.stringify('abc'.split('')));

with a limit: ["a","b"]
capture groups are KEPT in the result: ["a","1","b"]
without a group they are dropped:       ["a","b"]
splitting on the empty string: ["a","b","c"]

Splitting on a regex with a capture group includes the separators in the output. That is either a neat trick for breaking text into tokens or a confusing surprise, depending on whether you meant it.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: string immutability, .split(), .padstart(), .padend(), .repeat(), .startswith(), .endswith() and a capture group.

9.4 Code Units, Code Points and Grapheme Clusters

This is the part that matters, and the part most often skipped. A JavaScript string is a sequence of code units, and there are three different things you might mean by "a character":

  • A UTF-16 code unit is one 16-bit slot, and .length counts UTF-16 code units and nothing else.
  • A code point is one Unicode character. Anything above U+FFFF, such as most emoji, needs two code units, called a surrogate pair.
  • And a grapheme cluster is what a human calls a single character, which may be made of several code points.
const text = 'café 👋🏽';
console.log('.length (code units): ', text.length);
console.log('[...text] (code points):', [...text].length);
console.log('Intl.Segmenter (graphemes):', [...new Intl.Segmenter().segment(text)].length);

console.log('👋 is one character and two code units:', '👋'.length);
console.log('.charCodeAt(0):  ', '👋'.charCodeAt(0), '— half a surrogate pair');
console.log('.codePointAt(0): ', '👋'.codePointAt(0), '— the real code point');
console.log('String.fromCodePoint round trip:', String.fromCodePoint(128075));
console.log('slicing can split a pair:', JSON.stringify('👋'.slice(0, 1)));
console.log('spreading never does:    ', JSON.stringify([...'👋']));

.length (code units):  9
[...text] (code points): 7
Intl.Segmenter (graphemes): 6
👋 is one character and two code units: 2
.charCodeAt(0):   55357 — half a surrogate pair
.codePointAt(0):  128075 — the real code point
String.fromCodePoint round trip: 👋
slicing can split a pair: "\ud83d"
spreading never does:     ["👋"]

That gives three different counts for one six-character string. 👋🏽 is a waving hand plus a skin-tone modifier: two code points, four code units, one grapheme. That alone explains the whole spread between 9, 7 and 6.

The practical rules follow directly:

  • str.length is a byte-ish count, not a character count: it counts storage slots. So it is wrong for a "max 20 characters" check on a name.
  • Iterating a string with for...of or [...str] iterates code points, and never splits a surrogate pair. That is why [...'👋'] has one element, while '👋'.split('') has two broken halves (lone surrogates).
  • .charCodeAt() returns a code unit and .codePointAt() returns a code point. You want the second, unless you are implementing UTF-16 yourself.
  • Going the other way, String.fromCodePoint() builds a string from code points and handles anything above U+FFFF. The older String.fromCharCode() takes code units, and silently produces a broken lone surrogate for an emoji, so String.fromCodePoint() is the one to use.
  • And truncating text for display requires Intl.Segmenter, because cutting at a code-point boundary can still split a flag or a skin-toned emoji in half.

To have in hand before moving on: a utf-16 code unit, .charcodeat(), .codepointat() and a grapheme cluster.

9.5 Normalization

The same visible character can be stored in more than one way. é is either one code point (U+00E9) or two (e followed by a combining acute accent). JavaScript compares strings code unit by code unit, so the two are not equal:

const composed = '\u00E9';                 // é as one code point
const decomposed = 'e\u0301';              // e followed by a combining acute accent
console.log('they look identical:', composed, decomposed);
console.log('=== says:', composed === decomposed, '| lengths:', composed.length, decomposed.length);
console.log('after .normalize():', composed.normalize() === decomposed.normalize());
console.log('NFD splits, NFC joins:', composed.normalize('NFD').length, decomposed.normalize('NFC').length);

they look identical: é é
=== says: false | lengths: 1 2
after .normalize(): true
NFD splits, NFC joins: 2 1

Unicode normalization converts text to one standard form, so that comparison works. .normalize() defaults to NFC, which combines characters where possible. That is the right default, because most systems produce it and it is shorter. The rule: normalise any text that crosses a boundary (arrives from outside your code) before comparing, storing or hashing it. A username typed on macOS, which tends to produce the other form, NFD, will not match the same username typed on Windows (NFC) without it. And the failure is invisible in every log, because both print identically.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: unicode normalization.

9.6 Comparing and Sorting Text

< and > on strings compare code units, which is not alphabetical order in any language:

const words = ['äpfel', 'zebra', 'apple', 'Banana'];
console.log('code-unit sort:', [...words].sort());
console.log('localeCompare: ', [...words].sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b)));
console.log('German collator:', [...words].sort(new Intl.Collator('de').compare));
console.log('Swedish collator:', [...words].sort(new Intl.Collator('sv').compare));
console.log('case-insensitive:', 'a'.localeCompare('A', undefined, { sensitivity: 'base' }));
console.log('numeric ordering:', ['item10', 'item2'].sort(new Intl.Collator(undefined, { numeric: true }).compare));

code-unit sort: [ 'Banana', 'apple', 'zebra', 'äpfel' ]
localeCompare:  [ 'äpfel', 'apple', 'Banana', 'zebra' ]
German collator: [ 'äpfel', 'apple', 'Banana', 'zebra' ]
Swedish collator: [ 'apple', 'Banana', 'zebra', 'äpfel' ]
case-insensitive: 0
numeric ordering: [ 'item2', 'item10' ]

The code-unit sort put every capital letter before every lowercase one, and ä after z, which is wrong in every human language. .localeCompare() returns a negative number, zero or a positive number, and it is the correct comparator for text that users see.

Case-insensitive comparison belongs here too, rather than in .toLowerCase(). Lowercasing both sides with .toLowerCase() before comparing is the folk remedy, and it is wrong for the Turkish dotted i, for the German ß, and for any writing system without upper and lower case. localeCompare with { sensitivity: 'base' } is the correct way to write it.

Intl.Collator is the same algorithm with the language and options fixed in advance. That makes it much faster in a sort, and lets you say what you mean. German sorts ä together with a (it landed just before apple rather than after z), while Swedish treats it as a separate letter at the end of the alphabet, and both are correct for their language.

The numeric: true option gives natural ordering, item2 before item10, which is otherwise a hand-written comparator that everyone gets subtly wrong.

In summary, the vocabulary here is .localecompare().

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: .tolowercase().

9.7 Building a Regular Expression

There are two ways to create one, and the choice depends on where the pattern comes from:

const literal = /\d{4}-\d{2}/;
const built = new RegExp('\\d{4}-\\d{2}');
console.log('equivalent:', literal.source === built.source, '| test:', literal.test('2026-08'));
const userTerm = 'a.b';
console.log('interpolated unescaped, "." matches anything:', new RegExp(userTerm).test('axb'));
console.log('RegExp.escape gives:', RegExp.escape(userTerm));
console.log('escaped, it matches only the literal:', new RegExp(RegExp.escape(userTerm)).test('a.b'),
            new RegExp(RegExp.escape(userTerm)).test('axb'));

equivalent: true | test: true
interpolated unescaped, "." matches anything: true
RegExp.escape gives: \x61\.b
escaped, it matches only the literal: true false

A regular expression literal is compiled once, when the script is parsed, and it is the normal choice. The RegExp constructor takes a string, so every backslash must be doubled, and it is the only option when the pattern is built while the program runs.

RegExp.escape() makes a string safe to put inside a pattern. Note what it produced: \x61\.b. It escaped the leading a as \x61, even though a has no special meaning. That is deliberate. The specification also encodes a leading ASCII letter or digit, so that the result is safe to join onto other pattern text: pasted directly after a \ or inside \c, an unescaped letter would change meaning. Building a pattern from user input without it is both a correctness bug and a ReDoS risk (§9.14).

What to carry forward from this subsection: a regular expression literal, the regexp constructor and regexp.escape().

9.8 test, exec, match, matchAll — and the lastIndex Trap

const g = /a/g;
console.log('first test:', g.test('aa'), '| lastIndex is now', g.lastIndex);
console.log('second test:', g.test('aa'), '| lastIndex is now', g.lastIndex);
console.log('third test:', g.test('aa'), '| lastIndex is now', g.lastIndex);

first test: true | lastIndex is now 1
second test: true | lastIndex is now 2
third test: false | lastIndex is now 0

A regular expression with the global flag is stateful. The lastIndex property records where the next search starts. So calling .test() repeatedly on the same regex object gives true, true, false, true… alternating forever. This is the most surprising thing about regular expressions in JavaScript, and it bites hardest when a /g regex is stored in a module constant and used inside a loop or a validation function.

The fixes, best first: do not use /g with .test(); it is never needed, since test only asks whether there is a match at all. Otherwise, create the regex where it is used rather than sharing one, or reset re.lastIndex = 0 before each use.

The four search methods divide cleanly. .exec() is the only one that both returns groups and can be called again and again to walk through every match; .exec() in a while loop was the standard pattern before .matchAll() existed:

const text = 'a1 b2 c3';
console.log('.test:   ', /\d/.test(text), '— a boolean, cheapest');
console.log('.match without /g:', JSON.stringify('a1'.match(/(\w)(\d)/)?.slice(0, 3)));
console.log('.match with /g:   ', JSON.stringify(text.match(/\w\d/g)), '— all matches, NO groups');
console.log('.matchAll:        ', JSON.stringify([...text.matchAll(/(\w)(\d)/g)].map(m => [m[0], m[1], m.index])));
const re = /(\w)(\d)/g;
let m, found = [];
while ((m = re.exec(text)) !== null) found.push(`${m[0]}@${m.index}`);
console.log('.exec in a loop:  ', JSON.stringify(found));

.test:    true — a boolean, cheapest
.match without /g: ["a1","a","1"]
.match with /g:    ["a1","b2","c3"] — all matches, NO groups
.matchAll:         [["a1","a",0],["b2","b",3],["c3","c",6]]
.exec in a loop:   ["a1@0","b2@3","c3@6"]

The critical difference: .match() with /g returns only the matched strings and discards every capture group. If you need the groups and every match, use .matchAll(). It returns an iterator of full match objects, each with its groups, index and input, and it requires the /g flag. It also has no lastIndex hazard, because it works on a copy of the regex.

The terms above, gathered: .match(), the lastindex property and the global flag.

9.9 The Flags

console.log('i — ignoreCase:', /abc/i.test('ABC'));
console.log('s — dotAll, . matches a newline:', /a.b/s.test('a\nb'), '| without:', /a.b/.test('a\nb'));
console.log('m — multiline, ^ and $ match at line breaks:', 'a\nb'.match(/^b/m)?.[0], '| without:', 'a\nb'.match(/^b/)?.[0]);
console.log('u — unicode, enables \\p{}:', /\p{Script=Greek}/u.test('Ω'));
console.log('v — unicodeSets, set subtraction:', /[\p{Letter}--[aeiou]]/v.test('b'), /[\p{Letter}--[aeiou]]/v.test('a'));
console.log('d — hasIndices, group positions:', JSON.stringify(/(\d+)/d.exec('ab 42').indices[1]));
const sticky = /foo/y;
console.log('y — sticky, must match AT lastIndex:', sticky.test('xfoo'));
sticky.lastIndex = 1;
console.log('  after lastIndex = 1:', sticky.test('xfoo'));

i — ignoreCase: true
s — dotAll, . matches a newline: true | without: false
m — multiline, ^ and $ match at line breaks: b | without: undefined
u — unicode, enables \p{}: true
v — unicodeSets, set subtraction: true false
d — hasIndices, group positions: [3,5]
y — sticky, must match AT lastIndex: false
  after lastIndex = 1: true

The ignoreCase flag does simple case matching, not language-aware matching, so the Turkish dotted and dotless i are not handled. The dotAll flag makes . match a newline, which it otherwise does not; it is the fix for a pattern that works on one line and fails on a paragraph. The multiline flag changes what a regex anchor means: ^ and $ then match at every line break, rather than only at the start and end of the whole string.
