Every timing claim below was measured on this machine: under Node 24 for the language behaviour, and under headless Chromium (a browser running without a window) for anything the browser owns. That was necessary because published accounts of the event loop disagree with each other, and several of them are wrong. Where the two runtimes differ, both numbers are here.

12.1 One Thread, One Stack

A JavaScript realm (one global environment, such as one page or one worker) has one call stack. Calling a function pushes a frame (a record of that call) onto the call stack, and returning pops it off. While the call stack is not empty, nothing else in that realm runs: no timer, no event handler, no promise callback. This is run-to-completion: once a piece of JavaScript starts, it runs to its end without being interrupted.

Run-to-completion is a guarantee, and it is worth calling it one. In a language with preemptive threads, where the system can pause one thread at any moment to run another, count++ can be interrupted between reading the value and writing the new one. So every shared variable needs a lock. In JavaScript, no function can be interrupted partway through, so count++ is atomic (indivisible) as far as other JavaScript is concerned. The whole category of data race, two threads corrupting the same data, which dominates concurrent programming in Java or C++, simply does not exist. That is what you get in return for having one thread.

The price is blocking the main thread. Whatever occupies the stack occupies it alone:

function blockFor(ms) {
  const end = Date.now() + ms;
  while (Date.now() < end) { /* spin */ }
}

const started = Date.now();
setTimeout(() => console.log(`the 10ms timer waited for the stack: ${Date.now() - started >= 100}`), 10);
blockFor(100);
console.log(`synchronous work held the stack for 100ms: ${Date.now() - started >= 100}`);

synchronous work held the stack for 100ms: true
the 10ms timer waited for the stack: true

The timer was scheduled for 10ms and ran at 100. It was not late because the runtime was slow. It was late because the call stack never emptied, so the runtime never had a chance to run it. setTimeout does not promise to run your callback after 10ms. It promises not to run it before 10ms, and to run it as soon as the stack is empty after that.

In a browser, the same stack also draws the page, so the cost is visible. A 100ms block means a dropped frame, a button that does not respond when pressed, a text field that ignores keystrokes. The rule that follows shapes every design decision in this section: work that takes long enough to notice must not be done in one synchronous run. Split it across turns of the loop (§12.3), hand it to a worker (§17.11), or restructure it so the expensive part happens somewhere other than the main thread.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: blocking the main thread.

12.2 The Event Loop and Its Two Queues

When the stack empties, the event loop takes over. Roughly, it works like this:

1
Take one task from the task queue and run it to completion.
2
Drain the microtask queue completely — including microtasks queued by microtasks.
3
If this is a browser and a frame is due, run requestAnimationFrame callbacks, then style, layout and paint.
4
Go back to 1.

Two queues, emptied by different rules, and the difference in step 2 is the whole point. One task per turn; all microtasks per turn.

A task is a new piece of work that arrives from outside the code currently running: a timer firing, a click arriving, a network response landing, a <script> being run. A microtask is a continuation of work already in progress: a promise reaction, a queueMicrotask() callback, a mutation-observer record. The difference is not about importance. It is about when the runtime is allowed to do anything else. Between two tasks the browser may draw the page; between two microtasks it may not.

queueMicrotask() puts a callback straight onto the microtask queue. It is the direct way to say "after the current code finishes, before anything else":

console.log('1 — synchronous');
setTimeout(() => console.log('4 — task'), 0);
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('3 — microtask'));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3 — microtask (a promise reaction is one too)'));
console.log('2 — still synchronous');

1 — synchronous
2 — still synchronous
3 — microtask
3 — microtask (a promise reaction is one too)
4 — task

The synchronous lines finish first, because they are on the stack. Then the microtask queue is emptied, first in, first out. Only then does the timer's task run, even though it was scheduled first and asked for no delay at all.

Under headless Chromium, the same experiment with a frame callback added shows the full order:

sync -> microtask -> promise -> setTimeout 0 -> rAF

Rendering comes after the timer here, because the timer's task was ready first and step 3 happens only once per frame. The part you can rely on is the relationship: microtasks always run before the next task, and rendering never happens in the middle of one.

The dangerous consequence is that the microtask queue can starve the loop. A microtask that queues another microtask never lets step 2 finish:

let n = 0;
function again() { if (++n < 5) queueMicrotask(again); }
queueMicrotask(again);
setTimeout(() => console.log(`the task finally ran, after ${n} microtasks`), 0);

the task finally ran, after 5 microtasks

Five is harmless. Remove the limit and the page never draws again and never responds to another click, with no error and no warning: the tab simply stops. A recursive setTimeout(fn, 0), by contrast, lets everything else run between iterations, because each one is a separate task.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: the task queue.

12.3 Timers, and the Clamp Nobody Mentions

setTimeout() queues a task after at least ms milliseconds and returns an id. clearTimeout() cancels it while it is still waiting, and calling clearTimeout() with an id that has already fired is harmless, not an error. setInterval() queues the callback again after every run, and clearInterval stops it. Three things about setTimeout() and setInterval() are worth knowing precisely.

A zero-delay timeout is not zero. setTimeout(fn, 0) means "as a new task, as soon as possible". It is the standard way to break a long job into pieces so the browser can draw between them. It is also the way to put work off until the current call stack has finished, including code you did not write.

setInterval does not skip, it stacks. If the callback takes longer than the interval, the runtime does not run two copies at once (there is only one thread), but it keeps queueing. You end up with runs back to back and no idle time in between. A setTimeout that schedules itself again measures the interval from the end of the work instead:

function everySecond(fn) {
  let stopped = false;
  (function tick() {
    if (stopped) return;
    fn();
    setTimeout(tick, 1000);   // measured from when the work finished
  })();
  return () => { stopped = true; };
}
const stop = everySecond(() => {});
stop();
console.log('a self-scheduling timer cannot overlap with itself');

a self-scheduling timer cannot overlap with itself

Nested timers are clamped, and only in browsers. This is timer clamping. The HTML specification requires that once a timer's nesting level (how many timers deep it was scheduled from inside other timers) goes above five, any requested delay under 4ms is raised to 4ms. Here it is measured in headless Chromium, running setTimeout(nest, 0) from inside its own callback and recording the gap after each level:

run 1:  0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 5.5, 4.6
run 2:  4.7, 4.7, 4.8, 8.7, 5.9, 4.5, 4.8, 4.8
run 3:  4.5, 5.0, 4.7, 4.8, 4.8, 5.2, 5.1, 4.9

The first six gaps are under a millisecond, and the seventh jumps to about 5ms and stays there. That is exactly the clamp, at exactly the specified level, with timer clamping doing precisely what it is specified to do. Runs 2 and 3 are clamped from their very first gap, because they were still part of the same nested chain: the nesting level follows the chain of scheduling, not the clock. So a chain of zero-delay timers tops out at around 200 iterations per second. That is why setTimeout(…, 0) is a poor choice for an animation loop, and requestAnimationFrame is the right one.

Node applies no timer clamping at all. The same probe under Node 24 gives gaps of 0,2,1,2,1,1,1,1, which matters the moment you move a timing-sensitive loop from one to the other.

To have in hand before moving on: a zero-delay timeout.

12.4 Frames and Idle Time

requestAnimationFrame() schedules a callback to run at step 3 of the loop, just before the browser works out style and layout for the next frame. Two properties follow, and both matter.

requestAnimationFrame() runs its callback once per frame, whatever the screen's refresh rate. So the loop automatically runs at 60Hz on a 60Hz screen and at 120Hz on a 120Hz one, with no configuration. And it does not run at all in a background tab, so an animation stops using battery when nobody is looking, which a setInterval animation never does.

// The shape of every animation loop worth writing.
function animate(durationMs, onFrame) {
  const start = performance.now();
  return new Promise(done => {
    (function frame(now) {
      const t = Math.min(1, (now - start) / durationMs);
      onFrame(t);
      if (t < 1) requestAnimationFrame(frame); else done();
    })(start);
  });
}
console.log(typeof animate);

function

The parameter now that the browser passes to the callback is a DOMHighResTimeStamp: the frame's timestamp, the same for every callback in that frame. Using it rather than Date.now() is what keeps two animations in one frame exactly in step.

requestIdleCallback() is the opposite end. It runs its callback when the browser has spare time at the end of a frame, and passes a deadline object whose timeRemaining() says how much time is left. Where requestAnimationFrame() asks for the next frame, requestIdleCallback() asks for whatever is left over after one. It is right for work that is truly optional, such as preparing an off-screen list or sending analytics, and wrong for anything the user is waiting on, because a busy page may never be idle. Pass { timeout: 2000 } when the work must happen eventually no matter what.

12.5 Callbacks, and What Actually Went Wrong With Them

Before promises, an asynchronous result was delivered by calling a function you passed in. Node standardised the shape, with the error first and the result second, and it works:

function readConfig(name, cb) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    if (!name) cb(new Error('no name given'));
    else cb(null, { name, retries: 3 });
  }, 1);
}
readConfig('api', (err, cfg) => console.log(err ? `failed: ${err.message}` : `loaded ${cfg.name}`));

loaded api

The problem is not one callback; it is combining several. Three dependent steps nest three levels deep, each with its own error branch. The result is the shape everyone calls callback hell, and it is not merely ugly. It is structurally broken in three specific ways.

try/catch does not reach it. By the time the callback runs, the try block that registered it has long since finished, and its frame is gone. A throw inside the callback travels up an empty stack to the top level, not to the code that started the operation. Errors must be handled at every level, by hand, and one missing if (err) silently loses a failure. And the caller has no value to hold. There is nothing to return, store, pass on or wait for. So there is nothing to build combinations such as "all of these" or "whichever finishes first" out of. A promise is exactly that missing value.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: callback hell.

12.6 A Promise Is a State Machine

A promise is an object that stands for a value that is not available yet. It has three states, and it moves between them only once:

the pending state
The initial state. No value, no reason. Every promise starts here.
the fulfilled state
Succeeded, carrying a value. Reached by calling resolve(v).
the rejected state
Failed, carrying a reason — by convention always an Error. Reached by calling reject(r).

Fulfilled and rejected together are called the settled state. Settling cannot be undone and happens at most once: a second resolve or reject call is silently ignored. That is a guarantee, not a quirk. It means a handler you attach can fire at most once, so you never need to guard against a callback being called twice.

You create one with the promise executor: a function that the Promise constructor runs synchronously, straight away, passing it two functions of its own, the resolve callback and the reject callback:

const later = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  console.log('the executor runs synchronously, right now');
  setTimeout(() => resolve('the value'), 5);
  setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('ignored — already settled')), 10);
});
console.log('constructor returned; promise is', 'pending');
console.log('settled with:', await later);
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 20));
console.log('the later rejection changed nothing');

the executor runs synchronously, right now
constructor returned; promise is pending
settled with: the value
the later rejection changed nothing

The second guarantee is that reactions are always asynchronous. Even on a promise that has already settled, .then() waits for a microtask. So a function that returns a promise never calls back synchronously on some occasions and asynchronously on others. That single decision removes a whole family of bugs (nicknamed "releasing Zalgo") that the callback era was full of, where the order of execution changed depending on whether a cache was warm.

In summary, the vocabulary here is the pending state, the fulfilled state, the rejected state, the settled state, the promise executor, the resolve callback, the reject callback and .then().

12.7 .then, .catch, .finally and the Chain

.then(onFulfilled, onRejected) registers reactions, and, which is what makes chaining work, it returns a new promise that settles with whatever the reaction itself produces. .catch(fn) is the same as .then(undefined, fn). .finally(fn) runs on either outcome and passes the original result through unchanged.

Four rules govern what the returned promise does, and everything else about chaining follows from them:

return a value
The new promise fulfils with it.
return a promise
The new promise adopts it — waits for it and takes its outcome. This is what flattens nesting.
throw
The new promise rejects with what was thrown.
return nothing
The new promise fulfils with undefined — the commonest accidental break in a chain.
const steps = [];
await Promise.resolve(2)
  .then(n => { steps.push(`got ${n}`); return n * 3; })
  .then(n => { steps.push(`tripled to ${n}`); throw new Error('step three failed'); })
  .then(() => steps.push('THIS IS SKIPPED'))
  .catch(e => { steps.push(`caught: ${e.message}`); return 'recovered'; })
  .then(v => steps.push(`chain continues with "${v}"`))
  .finally(() => steps.push('finally always runs'));
console.log(steps.join('\n'));

got 2
tripled to 6
caught: step three failed
chain continues with "recovered"
finally always runs

Note what .catch did: it resumed the chain. A rejection skips forward to the next rejection handler, and from there the chain is fulfilled again. That is the correct model: a .catch in the middle is a recovery point, and a .catch at the end is the handler of last resort. Putting one in the middle when you meant the end is how a failure silently turns into a success carrying undefined.

A promise chain is flat, and that is the point. Returning a promise from .then adopts it (the chain waits for it) instead of nesting it. So three dependent asynchronous steps are three lines at the same indentation, with one error path at the bottom.

A thenable is any object with a .then method. The promise machinery adopts thenables, not only real promises, and that is how promise libraries from different authors work together. It is not free: awaiting a thenable takes measurably longer than awaiting a native promise, because the runtime has to schedule an extra job to call its .then method.

const thenable = { then(res) { res('from a thenable'); } };
const order = [];
(async () => { await thenable;          order.push('thenable'); })();
(async () => { await Promise.resolve(); order.push('native promise'); })();
(async () => { await 1;                 order.push('plain value'); })();
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 5));
console.log(order.join(' -> '));

native promise -> plain value -> thenable

The thenable was awaited first and finished last.

Promise.resolve() wraps a value in a fulfilled promise. Given a promise that already exists, Promise.resolve() passes it straight through unchanged, which makes it the safe way to handle a value that may or may not already be a promise. Promise.reject() is its rejected twin. Promise.reject() is the one to use when a guard clause needs to fail inside promise code rather than throw in ordinary synchronous code.

const p = Promise.resolve(7);
console.log('Promise.resolve passes a promise through:', Promise.resolve(p) === p);
console.log('the constructor always makes a new one:  ', new Promise(r => r(p)) === p);

Promise.resolve passes a promise through: true
the constructor always makes a new one:   false

What to carry forward from this subsection: a promise chain.

The terms above, gathered: .finally().

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: .finally().

To have in hand before moving on: promise.resolve().

12.8 The Combinators

Because a promise is a value, collections of promises can be combined. Six static methods cover the useful cases, and picking the wrong one is a common and expensive mistake.

const ok  = (v, ms) => new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms));
const bad = (m, ms) => new Promise((_, j) => setTimeout(() => j(new Error(m)), ms));

console.log('all:       ', await Promise.all([ok('a', 1), ok('b', 2)]));
const settled = await Promise.allSettled([ok('a', 1), bad('b failed', 2)]);
console.log('allSettled:', settled.map(r => r.status === 'fulfilled' ? r.value : r.reason.message));
console.log('any:       ', await Promise.any([bad('x', 1), ok('y', 2)]));
console.log('race:      ', await Promise.race([ok('fast', 1), bad('slow', 20)]));
try { await Promise.any([bad('p', 1), bad('q', 2)]); }
catch (e) { console.log('any, all rejected:', e.constructor.name, e.errors.map(x => x.message)); }

all:        [ 'a', 'b' ]
allSettled: [ 'a', 'b failed' ]
any:        y
race:       fast
any, all rejected: AggregateError [ 'p', 'q' ]
Promise.all()
All must succeed. Fulfils with an array in input order, not completion order. Rejects as soon as any input rejects — the others keep running, they are simply no longer awaited. Use it when you need every result and a partial answer is useless.
Promise.allSettled()
Never rejects. Fulfils with one {status, value} or {status, reason} per input. Use it for independent work where one failure must not discard the successes — six dashboard widgets, a batch of uploads.
Promise.any()
First success wins; rejections are ignored until every input has rejected, and then it rejects with an AggregateError whose .errors holds them all. Use it for redundant sources — three mirrors of the same file.
Promise.race()
First settlement wins, success or failure. Use it to impose a timeout — and note it does not cancel the loser, which §12.12 fixes.

Two newer members complete the set. Promise.withResolvers() returns { promise, resolve, reject }, so the functions that settle the promise are available outside the executor. That is the clean way to connect an event-based API, without the awkward routine of assigning to an outer let from inside the constructor. Promise.try() runs a function and turns a synchronous throw into a rejection, which closes the last gap where an error escapes the promise path. Without Promise.try(), a function that checks its arguments before doing any asynchronous work throws past every .catch in the chain:

const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers();
setTimeout(() => resolve('settled from outside the executor'), 1);
console.log(await promise);
const boom = () => { throw new Error('thrown synchronously'); };
console.log(await Promise.try(boom).catch(e => `Promise.try caught: ${e.message}`));

settled from outside the executor
Promise.try caught: thrown synchronously

One line each, for reference: promise.all(), promise.allsettled(), promise.any(), promise.race() and promise.withresolvers().

12.9 async and await

An async function always returns a promise: a return fulfils it and a throw rejects it. The await operator is allowed only inside one (or at the top level of a module). It pauses the function until its operand settles, then gives back the fulfilled value, or throws the rejection reason. That throw is what lets an ordinary try/catch work again.

async function loadUser(id) {
  if (!id) throw new Error('id is required');
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 1));
  return { id, name: 'Ada' };
}
console.log('returns a promise:', loadUser(1) instanceof Promise);
try { await loadUser(0); } catch (e) { console.log('await rethrows:', e.message); }
const { name } = await loadUser(1);
console.log('awaited value:', name);

returns a promise: true
await rethrows: id is required
awaited value: Ada

await pauses the function, not the thread. While the function is paused, the stack unwinds, the loop runs everything else, and the function continues later as a microtask. That is why the timing is not quite what "await is just .then" suggests:

const log = [];
(async () => { log.push('a1'); await null; log.push('a2'); await null; log.push('a3'); })();
Promise.resolve().then(() => log.push('t1')).then(() => log.push('t2')).then(() => log.push('t3'));
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 5));
console.log(log.join(' '));

a1 a2 t1 a3 t2 t3

The two sequences take turns, one step per microtask, but not in perfect lockstep: a2 beats t1. An await on a native promise that has already resolved costs one microtask, where the two-microtask .then translation taught for years would have predicted wrongly. a1 runs synchronously, as everything before the first await in an async function does.

Top-level await works in a module (§14.2). It pauses the module's evaluation, so the modules that import it wait too. It is genuinely useful for configuration and setting up connections, and genuinely dangerous in a module imported by many others, where it delays everything that depends on it.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: the await operator.

12.10 Sequential and Parallel, and the forEach Trap

await in a loop is sequential by design. Sometimes that is exactly right: the second request needs the first one's answer, or the server limits how fast you may call it. Very often it is not, and it is the most common performance defect in asynchronous JavaScript:

const UNIT = 50;
const sleep = ms => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms));
const work = async n => { await sleep(UNIT); return n * 2; };

let t = Date.now();
const seq = [];
for (const n of [1, 2, 3]) seq.push(await work(n));
const seqUnits = Math.floor((Date.now() - t) / UNIT);

t = Date.now();
const par = await Promise.all([1, 2, 3].map(work));
const parUnits = Math.floor((Date.now() - t) / UNIT);

console.log(`sequential ${JSON.stringify(seq)} took ${seqUnits} x 50ms`);
console.log(`parallel   ${JSON.stringify(par)} took ${parUnits} x 50ms`);

sequential [2,4,6] took 3 x 50ms
parallel   [2,4,6] took 1 x 50ms

Three pieces of work of 50ms each take three units of real time in a loop, and one through Promise.all. The rule of thumb for parallel await, running them at the same time: start everything, then await. .map the work into promises first, then await Promise.all once. Sequential await is a choice, and so is parallel await. Each should be made on purpose, depending on whether the second request needs the first.

The mirror-image bug is an async callback passed to .forEach():

const done = [];
[1, 2, 3].forEach(async n => { await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 1)); done.push(n); });
console.log('immediately after forEach:', done.length);
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 20));
console.log('after waiting:            ', done.length);

immediately after forEach: 0
after waiting:             3

.forEach ignores what its callback returns, so it throws away three promises and returns while the work is still running. The code reads as if it waits, and it does not. Use for...of with await for work done one at a time, or Promise.all(arr.map(fn)) for work done in parallel; never .forEach with an async callback.

Neither extreme suits a large batch: a thousand parallel requests will run out of network connections or get you banned for exceeding a rate limit. A concurrency limit is the middle ground: keep n requests running, and start a new one each time one finishes.

async function mapLimit(items, limit, fn) {
  const results = new Array(items.length);
  let next = 0;
  const worker = async () => {
    while (next < items.length) {
      const i = next++;                       // claimed before the first await
      results[i] = await fn(items[i], i);
    }
  };
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) }, worker));
  return results;
}
console.log(await mapLimit([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2, async n => n * n));

[ 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 ]

The index is claimed with next++ before the first await, and that is what makes the pool safe: run-to-completion (§12.1) guarantees that no other worker can run between reading next and increasing it.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: sequential await and a concurrency limit.

12.11 Rejections Nobody Handled

A rejected promise with no rejection handler is a silent failure. It is the asynchronous version of an empty catch block, and worse, because you did not even write it. Both runtimes detect it, at the end of the turn in which the rejection became unhandled:

process.on('unhandledRejection', r => console.log('unhandledRejection:', r.message));
const orphan = Promise.reject(new Error('nobody caught me'));
setTimeout(() => orphan.catch(() => console.log('a catch attached one turn later')), 0);
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 10));

unhandledRejection: nobody caught me
a catch attached one turn later

The window is one turn of the loop. Attaching a handler within the same turn is fine, and that is the ordinary case, since .catch() is usually written on the next line. Attaching one a turn later is too late to prevent the report, though the handler still runs; Node also prints a PromiseRejectionHandledWarning to say so.

In a browser, the same condition fires the unhandledrejection event on window, and the unhandledrejection event is the hook every error-reporting service uses:

// In a browser. `event.reason` is the rejection value; preventDefault() silences the console.
addEventListener('unhandledrejection', event => {
  report({ kind: 'promise', message: String(event.reason?.message ?? event.reason) });
  event.preventDefault();
});

Three habits prevent it:

  • End every chain that is not itself returned with a .catch.
  • In an async function, either await the call or handle it. void doThing().catch(report) states "start this and do not wait, but report failures" explicitly.
  • Prefer Promise.allSettled to Promise.all when the inputs are independent, because all leaves the other rejections unobserved once one has failed.

To have in hand before moving on: .catch().

12.12 Cancellation

Promises have no cancel method, and that is on purpose. A promise is a view of a result, and several parts of the code may hold the same view. Cancelling belongs to whoever started the work. The platform's answer is AbortController, and it is now the universal convention.

A controller owns a signal. controller.abort(reason) switches the AbortSignal object to aborted, sets signal.reason, and fires its abort event. Every API that accepts a signal watches for that.

const ac = new AbortController();
const waitFor = signal => new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  const id = setTimeout(() => resolve('finished'), 50);
  signal.addEventListener('abort', () => { clearTimeout(id); reject(signal.reason); }, { once: true });
});
setTimeout(() => ac.abort(new Error('user cancelled')), 5);
try { await waitFor(ac.signal); }
catch (e) { console.log('caught:', e.message, '| aborted:', ac.signal.aborted); }

try { await waitFor(AbortSignal.timeout(5)); }
catch (e) { console.log('timeout signal:', e.name, '—', e.message); }

caught: user cancelled | aborted: true
timeout signal: TimeoutError — The operation was aborted due to timeout

Note what clearTimeout achieved: the underlying work actually stopped. That is the difference between cancellation and Promise.race against a timer, which only stops waiting while the request keeps using a connection.

AbortSignal.timeout(ms) creates a signal that aborts itself with a TimeoutError. AbortSignal.any([...]) combines several signals, so a request can be cancelled by a timeout or by the user navigating away. The same signal is accepted by fetch (§17.1) and by addEventListener (§16.6), where it removes the listener. So one object tears down every kind of pending work a component started.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: the abortsignal object.

12.13 Race Conditions in a Single-Threaded Language

Run-to-completion removes data races, but it does not remove a race condition: a bug where the result depends on which operation finishes first. Anything with an await in the middle has a gap where other code runs. If two overlapping operations write to the same place, the last one to finish wins, which is not necessarily the last one to start.

The standard example of a race condition in a browser is search-as-you-type. The user types ab, then abc. The request for ab is slower, so its stale results arrive last and overwrite the fresh ones:

let latest = null;                      // the guard
async function search(term, ms, into) {
  const token = latest = Symbol(term);  // claim, synchronously
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms));
  if (token !== latest) { into.push(`"${term}" discarded — stale`); return; }
  into.push(`"${term}" rendered`);
}
const out = [];
await Promise.all([search('ab', 20, out), search('abc', 5, out)]);
console.log(out.join('\n'));

"abc" rendered
"ab" discarded — stale

The pattern is: claim a token synchronously, before the first await, and after every resumption check that you are still the current operation. An AbortController per keystroke is the other half: it stops the stale request, rather than merely ignoring its answer.

12.14 Promisifying, Retrying, and Timing Out

Wrapping a callback-based API in a promise, promisification, is a five-line job, and always the same five lines:

function promisify(fn) {
  return (...args) => new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    fn(...args, (err, value) => err ? reject(err) : resolve(value)));
}
const readConfig = (name, cb) => setTimeout(() => name ? cb(null, { name }) : cb(new Error('no name')), 1);
const readConfigAsync = promisify(readConfig);
console.log(await readConfigAsync('api'));
console.log(await readConfigAsync('').catch(e => `rejected: ${e.message}`));

{ name: 'api' }
rejected: no name

Retry with backoff is the other universal wrapper. Retrying immediately is worse than not retrying, because a struggling server then gets hit by every client at once. So each attempt waits longer than the last, with jitter (a small random extra delay) so that clients do not retry in sync:

async function retry(fn, { attempts = 4, baseMs = 10 } = {}) {
  for (let i = 0; ; i++) {
    try { return await fn(i); }
    catch (e) {
      if (i >= attempts - 1) throw e;
      const backoff = baseMs * 2 ** i;             // 10, 20, 40 …
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, backoff));
    }
  }
}
let calls = 0;
const flaky = async () => { if (++calls < 3) throw new Error(`attempt ${calls} failed`); return 'ok'; };
console.log(await retry(flaky), 'after', calls, 'attempts');

ok after 3 attempts

Retry only what is idempotent, meaning safe to do twice with the same effect as once, and only what is worth retrying: a 500 error or a dropped connection, never a 400. And put a ceiling on the total, because four attempts with doubling waits already add up to most of a second of delay the user can see.

In summary, the vocabulary here is promisification and retry with backoff.

12.15 What This Section Established

  1. One thread, one call stack, run-to-completion. No JavaScript function can be interrupted partway, which removes data races and makes blocking the main thread the only real concurrency hazard. A timer scheduled for 10ms fired at 100ms behind a synchronous loop.
  2. Two queues, drained on different rules. The event loop takes one task per turn and drains the whole microtask queue between tasks. Measured ordering in Chromium: sync -> microtask -> promise -> setTimeout 0 -> rAF. A self-replacing microtask starves the loop; a self-replacing task does not.
  3. process.nextTick is not simply "first". It preempts promise microtasks in CommonJS and follows them at the top level of an ES module, because module evaluation is already inside a microtask drain.
  4. Nested timers are clamped in browsers and not in Node. Six sub-millisecond gaps, then ~5ms from the seventh onward, and the clamp follows the scheduling chain rather than the clock.
  5. A promise settles once and its reactions are always asynchronous. The executor runs synchronously; a second resolve is ignored; .then on a settled promise still defers to a microtask.
  6. .then returns a new promise, and returning a promise adopts it. That is what flattens chains. A .catch in the middle resumes the chain; forgetting a return fulfils it with undefined.
  7. Awaiting a thenable is measurably slower than awaiting a native promise — awaited first, finished last — and Promise.resolve(p) === p while new Promise(r => r(p)) is a fresh object.
  8. Four combinators, four different failure policies: all fails fast, allSettled never rejects, any wants the first success and aggregates the failures, race takes the first settlement of either kind. withResolvers and try close the last two gaps.
  9. await on a resolved native promise costs one microtask tick, not two — a1 a2 t1 a3 t2 t3, where the async function's second step beats the first .then callback.
  10. Sequential await is a choice. Three time units against one for the same three units of work. .forEach with an async callback discards its promises and returns early — zero results immediately, three later.
  11. An unhandled rejection is reported at the end of the turn, and a .catch attached a turn later is too late for the report though not for the handling.
  12. Cancellation is AbortController, not Promise.race — the difference is whether the underlying work stops. AbortSignal.timeout() rejects with a TimeoutError, and the same signal cancels a fetch and removes an event listener.
  13. Race conditions survive single-threading. Claim a token synchronously before the first await, re-check it after every resumption; the stale "ab" was discarded and the fresh "abc" rendered.

What to carry forward from this subsection: an unhandled rejection and abortsignal.timeout().

Exercises

1. Without running it, write down the exact output order. Then explain each position.

console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log('C'); queueMicrotask(() => console.log('D')); });
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('E'));
(async () => { console.log('F'); await null; console.log('G'); })();
console.log('H');
Solution 
A
F
H
C
E
G
D

The synchronous pass runs first: A, F, H. F is synchronous because everything before the first await in an async function runs immediately — calling an async function does not defer anything by itself. H follows because the async IIFE suspended at await null and returned control.

Then the microtask queue drains in the order things were queued. Three microtasks were enqueued during the synchronous pass, in source order: the .then reaction (queued when Promise.resolve() was already settled), the queueMicrotask(E) callback, and the async function's resumption at await null. So C, E, G.

D is last because it was queued during the drain, by C's reaction. The microtask queue is drained to exhaustion — including microtasks queued by microtasks (§12.2) — so D still runs in this same turn, but after everything already in the queue.

B is not in the microtask list at all. It is a task, and step 1 of the loop takes one task only after the microtask queue is empty. Zero delay does not change its category.

The general rule that answers every question of this shape: sort by phase first — synchronous, then microtasks in FIFO order including ones queued during the drain, then one task — and only within a phase does source order matter.

2. This function is meant to fetch three resources, tolerate any of them failing, and finish in the time of the slowest rather than the sum. It does none of those things. Find all four defects and rewrite it.

async function loadAll(urls) {
  const results = [];
  urls.forEach(async (url) => {
    const res = await fetch(url);
    results.push(await res.json());
  });
  return results;
}
Solution

Defect 1 — .forEach with an async callback discards its promises. forEach ignores return values, so loadAll returns results while all three fetches are still pending. The caller always gets [] (§12.10).

Defect 2 — it is not parallel, and it is not sequential either. It happens to start all three, but because nothing awaits them the function cannot report when they are done. Replacing forEach with a for...of loop and await would fix correctness and make it sequential — three round trips end to end, the defect §12.10 measured at three time units against one.

Defect 3 — one failure loses everything. With Promise.all a single rejection rejects the whole call, discarding two perfectly good responses. The requirement says tolerate failure, which is Promise.allSettled.

Defect 4 — a non-2xx response is not an error to fetch. fetch only rejects on a network failure; a 404 fulfils with res.ok === false, and res.json() then throws an opaque parse error on the error page's HTML. The status must be checked explicitly (§17.2).

async function loadAll(urls, { signal } = {}) {
  const settled = await Promise.allSettled(urls.map(async (url) => {
    const res = await fetch(url, { signal });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${url} -> HTTP ${res.status}`);
    return res.json();
  }));
  return {
    data:   settled.filter(r => r.status === 'fulfilled').map(r => r.value),
    errors: settled.filter(r => r.status === 'rejected').map(r => r.reason),
  };
}

Why this shape. The .map starts every request before anything is awaited, so the total is the slowest rather than the sum. allSettled never rejects, so partial success is representable — and returning both halves is better than returning only the data, because a caller that silently renders two of three results is a bug of its own. The optional signal threads cancellation through (§12.12), so an unmounting component can abort all three at once.

A note on what did not need fixing. There is no try/catch here, and that is correct: loadAll cannot decide what a failure means, so it reports failures as values and lets the caller decide. Adding a catch that logs and returns [] would be the same defect as .forEach, one layer up.

3. Implement withTimeout(promise, ms), which resolves as promise does but rejects with a TimeoutError if ms elapses first. Then explain why the obvious Promise.race implementation is not good enough for a fetch, and write the version that is.

Solution

The obvious version, which is correct as far as it goes:

function withTimeout(promise, ms) {
  const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject(new DOMException('timed out', 'TimeoutError')), ms));
  return Promise.race([promise, timeout]);
}
console.log(await withTimeout(new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r('quick'), 1)), 50));
console.log(await withTimeout(new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r('slow'), 50)), 5)
  .catch(e => `rejected with ${e.name}`));

quick
rejected with TimeoutError

Two things are wrong with it in production, and both are the same thing.

The work does not stop. Promise.race settles the race, not the losers. The slow promise is still pending, its setTimeout still scheduled, and if it were a fetch the connection would still be open and the response still downloading. On a page that times out and retries, you now have two requests in flight, then three. That is the distinction §12.12 draws: race stops waiting, cancellation stops working.

The timer leaks even on the fast path. When promise wins, the timeout's setTimeout is still scheduled. One is nothing; one per keystroke in a search box is a growing pile of pending timers each holding a closure alive (§3.9).

The version that is actually right passes a signal down rather than racing:

async function fetchWithTimeout(url, ms, { signal } = {}) {
  const timeout = AbortSignal.timeout(ms);
  const combined = signal ? AbortSignal.any([signal, timeout]) : timeout;
  return fetch(url, { signal: combined });
}

AbortSignal.timeout(ms) builds a self-aborting signal that rejects with a real TimeoutError, and AbortSignal.any lets the caller's own cancellation compose with it, so the request is aborted by whichever comes first. There is no timer to clear — the signal owns it — and the socket is released the moment either fires.

When race remains the right answer: when the slow operation genuinely cannot be cancelled — a postMessage round trip to a worker that ignores signals, or a third-party callback API you did not write. Then race it, but clear the timer in a .finally() so the fast path leaks nothing:

function withTimeout(promise, ms) {
  let id;
  const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) => {
    id = setTimeout(() => reject(new DOMException('timed out', 'TimeoutError')), ms);
  });
  return Promise.race([promise, timeout]).finally(() => clearTimeout(id));
}
SECTION 13

Errors, Debugging and Resource Management

Most code is written for the path where everything works, and most incidents happen on the other one. This section is about that other path:

  • how to signal a failure so the caller can act on it;
  • how to catch one without destroying the information it carried;
  • how to find the cause of a failure you did not anticipate.

Two ideas do most of the work.

The first is that an error is a value with structure. It has a name, a message, a stack (the list of function calls that led to it) and, since ES2022, a cause. Throwing a string or a plain object literal throws all of that away, and you will want it at three in the morning.

The second is that catching is a commitment. A catch block says "I know what this means and I can handle it". A catch that merely logs the error and carries on is usually worse than no catch at all, because it turns a loud failure into quietly corrupted state.

The debugging half is deliberately concrete. A breakpoint, a place where the debugger pauses your program so you can inspect it, is a better tool than a console.log in almost every case. People reach for the log anyway because nobody showed them the four things a debugger does that a log cannot.

13.1 throw, try, catch, finally

The throw statement takes any value, and try...catch intercepts it:

function parseAge(input) {
  const n = Number(input);
  if (!Number.isInteger(n)) throw new TypeError(`age must be an integer, got ${JSON.stringify(input)}`);
  if (n < 0 || n > 150) throw new RangeError(`age out of range: ${n}`);
  return n;
}
for (const input of ['42', 'abc', '900']) {
  try {
    console.log('parsed:', parseAge(input));
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(`${error.constructor.name}: ${error.message}`);
  }
}

parsed: 42
TypeError: age must be an integer, got "abc"
RangeError: age out of range: 900

Read the two failure messages side by side. The TypeError quotes its value and the RangeError does not, because the first inserts the raw input through JSON.stringify and the second inserts the converted number n. The difference tells you which check failed without reading the source, which is exactly what a good message is for.

Throw Error objects, never strings. throw 'oops' is legal, but it loses the stack, the name, and everything that helps with debugging. A catch that receives it cannot call .message, and every logging tool displays it uselessly.

An optional catch binding lets you leave out the catch parameter when you do not need the error, and finally runs however the block is left:

try { throw new Error('x'); } catch { console.log('caught, binding omitted'); } finally { console.log('finally'); }

function withReturn() {
  try { return 'from try'; }
  finally { console.log('  finally runs before the return completes'); }
}
console.log(withReturn());

function overriding() {
  try { return 'try'; }
  finally { return 'finally wins'; }        // never write this
}
console.log('a return inside finally overrides:', overriding());

caught, binding omitted
finally
  finally runs before the return completes
from try
a return inside finally overrides: finally wins

finally runs after the return value has been worked out, but before the function actually returns, which is what makes it the right place for cleanup. A return or a throw inside finally discards whatever was in flight, including an exception that was on its way out, silently. It is legal, it is never what you want, and most linters flag it.

The terms above, gathered: the throw statement, try...catch and an optional catch binding.

One line each, for reference: the finally block.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: the finally block.

13.2 The Error Object

The Error object carries four things worth knowing:

const error = new Error('something failed');
console.log('error.name:   ', error.name);
console.log('error.message:', error.message);
console.log('error.stack starts with:', error.stack.split('\n')[0]);
console.log('and has frames below it:', error.stack.split('\n').length > 1);
console.log('String(error) is name: message —', String(error));
console.log('but the message is NOT in the enumerable properties:', JSON.stringify(error));

error.name:    Error
error.message: something failed
error.stack starts with: Error: something failed
and has frames below it: true
String(error) is name: message — Error: something failed
but the message is NOT in the enumerable properties: {}

That last line is the one that bites in production. JSON.stringify(error) gives {}, because name, message and stack are all non-enumerable (§6.6). A logger that does JSON.stringify({ err }) records nothing at all. That is why every logging library handles errors specially, and why you must pull out error.message explicitly.

error.name is used by toString and by the first line of the stack, and setting it on a subclass is what makes a custom error identify itself. error.stack has no standard format, but everywhere it is the first line plus one line per function call. It is captured when the error is created, not at the throw, so creating an error early and throwing it later gives a misleading stack.

13.3 The Built-in Error Types

Six types cover almost everything the runtime throws, and recognising them speeds up diagnosis a great deal:

const cases = [
  ['reading a property of null', () => null.x],
  ['calling an undefined name', () => undefinedFn()],
  ['an argument out of range', () => (1).toFixed(101)],
  ['a malformed URI', () => decodeURIComponent('%')],
  ['invalid JSON', () => JSON.parse('{')],
];
for (const [label, fn] of cases) {
  try { fn(); } catch (err) { console.log(`${label.padEnd(28)} -> ${err.constructor.name}`); }
}

reading a property of null   -> TypeError
calling an undefined name    -> ReferenceError
an argument out of range     -> RangeError
a malformed URI              -> URIError
invalid JSON                 -> SyntaxError
TypeError
A value is the wrong type for the operation. The most common by far — reading a property of null, calling a non-function, mixing BigInt and Number (§2.10).
ReferenceError
A name that does not exist, or a TDZ access (§3.3). Almost always a typo or a missing import.
RangeError
A value of the right type but an unacceptable size — an invalid array length, a bad radix, and stack overflow (§5.6).
SyntaxError
Code or data that does not parse. At runtime it means JSON.parse or new RegExp, since real syntax errors happen before anything runs.

URIError comes from the encodeURI/decodeURI family. EvalError is a leftover that modern engines never throw.

13.4 error.cause — Wrapping Without Losing

error.cause is the cause property you pass in the second argument, and it solves the oldest problem in error handling: adding context without throwing away the original error.

function loadConfig(text) {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(text);
  } catch (low) {
    throw new Error('could not load config', { cause: low });
  }
}
try { loadConfig('{oops'); }
catch (high) {
  console.log('outer: ', high.message);
  console.log('cause: ', high.cause.constructor.name, '-', high.cause.message.slice(0, 32));
  let depth = 0, current = high;
  while (current.cause) { current = current.cause; depth++; }
  console.log('chain depth:', depth, '| root type:', current.constructor.name);
}

outer:  could not load config
cause:  SyntaxError - Expected property name or '}' in
chain depth: 1 | root type: SyntaxError

Before cause, both options were bad. You could rethrow the original and lose the context of which config file failed, or throw a new error and lose the position where parsing failed. cause keeps both, it can nest as deep as you like, and every modern runtime prints the whole chain automatically.

Rethrowing is the other half of the discipline. A catch that cannot handle a case must throw it again:

function readSetting(store, key) {
  try {
    return store.get(key);
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof RangeError) return null;      // a case we understand
    throw error;                                        // everything else is not ours
  }
}
const store = { get(k) { if (k === 'bad') throw new RangeError('out of range'); throw new TypeError('store offline'); } };
console.log('handled:', readSetting(store, 'bad'));
try { readSetting(store, 'other'); } catch (e) { console.log('rethrown:', e.constructor.name, '-', e.message); }

handled: null
rethrown: TypeError - store offline

Catch narrowly. A bare catch that swallows everything will one day swallow a TypeError caused by a typo inside the try block, and the bug will show up as "the feature silently does nothing".

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: rethrowing.

13.5 Custom Error Classes

A custom error class gives callers something to check for, and gives you a place to put structured data:

class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(field, message, options) {
    super(message, options);
    this.name = 'ValidationError';     // without this, the name is 'Error'
    this.field = field;
  }
}
class NotFoundError extends Error {
  constructor(what, options) { super(`${what} not found`, options); this.name = 'NotFoundError'; }
}

const err = new ValidationError('email', 'must contain @');
console.log('name:', err.name, '| field:', err.field);
console.log('instanceof both:', err instanceof ValidationError, err instanceof Error);
console.log('String(err):', String(err));
console.log('the stack shows the custom name:', err.stack.split('\n')[0]);

function handle(error) {
  if (error instanceof ValidationError) return `fix the ${error.field} field`;
  if (error instanceof NotFoundError) return 'show a 404';
  throw error;
}
console.log(handle(err), '|', handle(new NotFoundError('user')));

name: ValidationError | field: email
instanceof both: true true
String(err): ValidationError: must contain @
the stack shows the custom name: ValidationError: must contain @
fix the email field | show a 404

Setting this.name is not optional, because name is inherited from Error.prototype and otherwise stays 'Error', so the stack, toString and every log line would report the wrong type.

Passing options through to super is what keeps cause working in subclasses, and it is the line most hand-written error classes forget.

Error.isError() is the reliable test that works across realms, in the same spirit as Array.isArray (§8.1):

console.log('a real error:', Error.isError(new TypeError('x')));
console.log('an object that merely looks like one:', Error.isError({ name: 'Error', message: 'fake' }));
console.log('instanceof would be fooled by a cross-realm error, isError is not:', Error.isError(new Error('x')));

a real error: true
an object that merely looks like one: false
instanceof would be fooled by a cross-realm error, isError is not: true

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: a custom error class and error.iserror().

13.6 AggregateError and SuppressedError

Two error types exist for situations where more than one thing went wrong.

AggregateError carries a list of errors in .errors, and Promise.any throws it when every input rejects (§12.8):

try { await Promise.any([Promise.reject(new Error('mirror A')), Promise.reject(new Error('mirror B'))]); }
catch (aggregate) {
  console.log(aggregate.constructor.name, 'with', aggregate.errors.length, 'errors');
  console.log('messages:', aggregate.errors.map(e => e.message).join(', '));
}

AggregateError with 2 errors
messages: mirror A, mirror B

SuppressedError covers the case where cleanup fails while an exception is already on its way out, such as a disposal (§3.13) that throws while the stack is unwinding. Without it, one of the two errors would be lost:

class BadHandle {
  [Symbol.dispose]() { throw new Error('dispose failed'); }
}
try {
  { using handle = new BadHandle(); throw new Error('body failed'); }
} catch (error) {
  console.log(error.constructor.name);
  console.log('  .error     (from the disposal):', error.error.message);
  console.log('  .suppressed (the original):     ', error.suppressed.message);
}

SuppressedError
  .error     (from the disposal): dispose failed
  .suppressed (the original):      body failed

Both errors survive, which is the whole design. Read the names carefully: .error is the newer failure, and .suppressed is the one it pushed aside.

13.7 Failing Fast, and Validating Input

Failing fast means detecting a broken state as early as possible and stopping, rather than carrying on with a value you know is wrong. The alternative, a default, a ?? 0, a silent return, moves the failure somewhere far away from its cause.

function createUser({ name, email, age }) {
  if (typeof name !== 'string' || !name.trim()) throw new TypeError('name is required');
  if (!email?.includes('@')) throw new TypeError(`email is invalid: ${JSON.stringify(email)}`);
  if (age !== undefined && !Number.isInteger(age)) throw new TypeError('age must be an integer');
  return { name: name.trim(), email, age: age ?? null };
}
console.log(JSON.stringify(createUser({ name: ' Ada ', email: 'a@b.co' })));
for (const bad of [{ name: '', email: 'a@b.co' }, { name: 'x', email: 'nope' }]) {
  try { createUser(bad); } catch (e) { console.log('rejected:', e.message); }
}

{"name":"Ada","email":"a@b.co","age":null}
rejected: name is required
rejected: email is invalid: "nope"

Input validation at the boundary is the practical form of this, and the boundary is the specific thing to get right. Validate where untrusted data comes in (a network response, a form, a URL parameter, a file) and trust it inside your code. Validating the same value at every layer is noise; validating it nowhere is how undefined reaches a database.

Note that the message includes the bad value. An error message should say what was expected, what was received, and where. A message saying "invalid input" costs an hour that "email is invalid: nope" does not.

To have in hand before moving on: input validation.

13.8 The console Beyond log

console.error('goes to stderr, and devtools styles it as an error');
console.warn('a warning');
console.assert(1 === 2, 'printed only when the condition is FALSE');
console.assert(1 === 1, 'never printed');
console.log('console.table(rows) renders an array of objects as a real table');
console.log('console.trace() prints a stack without throwing');
console.log('console.time / timeEnd measure a span');
console.log('console.group / groupEnd nest output');

console.table(rows) renders an array of objects as a real table
console.trace() prints a stack without throwing
console.time / timeEnd measure a span
console.group / groupEnd nest output

Look at what is missing from that output. The error and warn calls and the failing assert produced nothing at all, because console.error(), console.warn() and console.assert() write to stderr (the error output stream), while console.log and console.table write to stdout (the normal output), and the transcript above captures stdout only. That is not a curiosity. A Node process whose stdout is saved to a file loses every warning and error unless stderr is redirected too, which is a real way to lose the only evidence of a production failure.

console.assert() prints only when the condition is false, which feels backwards to most people the first time; the call with a true condition above printed nothing on either stream. console.trace() prints the current stack without throwing, and is the fastest way to answer "who called this?".

console.table() shows an array of objects as a bordered table in a terminal, and as a sortable grid in devtools. It is the fastest way to read a list of records. Its output is the one thing in this section not reproduced here, because the box-drawing characters it prints are banned from this collection's prose. console.time/timeEnd measure how long something took without any arithmetic. All of these are for development: a console.log left in production is unstructured, unfiltered and unsearchable, which is what §13.11 is about.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: console.error().

13.9 The Debugger

The debugger statement pauses the program wherever it appears, if a debugger is attached, and does nothing otherwise:

function suspicious(items) {
  const total = items.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  // debugger;                      // uncomment and open devtools to pause here
  return total / items.length;
}
console.log('the average:', suspicious([2, 4, 6]));

the average: 4

A breakpoint set in the sources panel does the same without editing the file, and it offers four things that make it better than a console.log:

the whole scope
Every variable in every enclosing scope, not the three you thought to log — including the closure scopes (§3.7), which is where the answer usually is.
stepping through code
Step over, into and out of calls, so you watch the state change rather than inferring it from a sequence of logs.
a conditional breakpoint
Pause only when item.id === 4173. This is the one that replaces if (x) console.log(...) in a loop of ten thousand — with no edit, no rebuild and no reload.
pause on exception
Stop at the throw, with the stack still live — including caught exceptions, which is how you find the error a catch is swallowing.

The Node inspector brings the same tools to server code. node --inspect-brk app.js starts the program paused and prints a URL, which Chromium devtools and every major editor can attach to. Use --inspect-brk rather than --inspect when the bug happens during startup.

Source-map debugging is what makes any of this usable on built code. A bundler writes a .map file that links the minified output back to your source, so the debugger shows the file you wrote. Two failures are worth recognising: no map at all, where you are stepping through one long line of minified code; and an out-of-date map, where the line numbers are off by a few and the debugger seems to be lying.

In summary, the vocabulary here is a breakpoint, a conditional breakpoint, stepping through code, the debugger statement, the node inspector and source-map debugging.

13.10 Errors That Cross the Async Boundary

A try/catch only catches what happens while it is running. Anything scheduled for later escapes it:

function broken() {
  try {
    setTimeout(() => { throw new Error('thrown in a later task'); }, 0);
  } catch {
    console.log('this catch can never run');
  }
}
process.on('uncaughtException', (e) => console.log('escaped to the top level:', e.message));
broken();
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 10));

async function fixed() {
  try {
    await new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('rejected later')), 1));
  } catch (e) {
    console.log('await routes it back into the try:', e.message);
  }
}
await fixed();

escaped to the top level: thrown in a later task
await routes it back into the try: rejected later

The try block had finished long before the timer fired, so its catch was no longer on the stack (§12.5). await is what reconnects the two: awaiting a promise turns its rejection into a throw at the await, so ordinary try/catch works again. That is the single biggest practical benefit of async/await over raw callbacks.

The two top-level safety nets, unhandledRejection/unhandledrejection (§12.11) and uncaughtException/window.onerror, are for reporting, not for recovering. After an uncaught exception, the program's state is unknown, so a Node process should log the error and exit rather than carry on.

13.11 From console.log to Structured Logging

Structured logging means writing records rather than sentences: one JSON object per event, with field names that never change, so a log aggregator (a service that collects and searches logs) can filter and group them.

function logEvent(level, message, fields = {}) {
  const record = { level, message, ...fields };
  if (fields.error instanceof Error) {
    record.error = { name: fields.error.name, message: fields.error.message, stack: fields.error.stack };
  }
  return JSON.stringify(record);
}
console.log(logEvent('info', 'user created', { userId: 42, durationMs: 13 }));
console.log(logEvent('error', 'checkout failed', { orderId: 'A7', error: new TypeError('card declined') })
  .slice(0, 118) + '…');

{"level":"info","message":"user created","userId":42,"durationMs":13}
{"level":"error","message":"checkout failed","orderId":"A7","error":{"name":"TypeError","message":"card declined","sta…

The explicit unpacking of the error is the point, and it is the fix for what §13.2 measured: an Error spread into a record serialises as {}, so name, message and stack must be copied out by hand. Every logging library does this internally, which is a good reason to use one.

Error monitoring is the production version: a service that receives uncaught exceptions and unhandled rejections from real users, groups them by where in the code they happened, and tells you how often each occurs and in which release. It is worth setting up for three reasons: you learn about failures you cannot reproduce, you see how many users each one affects instead of guessing, and uploading source maps makes the stacks readable. The hooks are the ones from §13.10 and §12.11, which is why those events exist.

What to carry forward from this subsection: error monitoring.

13.12 What This Section Established

  1. Throw Error objects, never strings — a string loses the name, the stack and every tool's ability to render it.
  2. finally runs before the return completes, and a return inside it silently discards the in-flight value or exception.
  3. JSON.stringify(error) is {}. name, message and stack are non-enumerable, which is why a logger must copy them out explicitly.
  4. The stack is captured at construction, not at throw.
  5. Five built-in types cover diagnosis: TypeError for the wrong kind of value, ReferenceError for a name that does not exist, RangeError for a bad size, SyntaxError for data that does not parse, URIError for the encode/decode family.
  6. cause adds context without losing the original, nests arbitrarily deep, and is forwarded only if a subclass passes options through to super.
  7. Catch narrowly and rethrow the rest — the RangeError was handled and the TypeError was put back.
  8. this.name must be set in a custom error class, or the stack and toString misreport it as Error. Error.isError() is the cross-realm test that an object literal cannot fool.
  9. AggregateError carries .errors; SuppressedError carries .error and .suppressed — the newer failure and the one it displaced, so a throwing disposal cannot hide the original.
  10. Fail fast at the boundary, and put the expected value, the received value and the location in the message.
  11. console.assert prints only when the condition is false, and console.error goes to stderr.
  12. A conditional breakpoint replaces a logging statement in a hot loop, and pause-on-caught-exception finds what a catch is swallowing.
  13. A try cannot catch what a later task throws — it escaped to the top level — while await routes a rejection back into the same try.

Exercises

1. Find every defect in this error handling and rewrite it.

async function saveOrder(order) {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('/api/orders', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(order) });
    const saved = await res.json();
    return saved;
  } catch (e) {
    console.log('error: ' + e);
    return {};
  }
}
Solution

Six defects, and the last is the worst.

No status check. fetch fulfils on a 500 (§17.1), so res.json() runs on an error page and throws an opaque parse error that the catch then reports as though it were a network problem.

No Content-Type. The server receives a JSON body labelled text/plain and will usually reject it — a failure that looks like a validation bug.

The catch is unconditionally broad. A TypeError from a typo inside the try is caught and reported as a save failure.

'error: ' + e stringifies to name: message and throws away the stack and any cause (§13.2).

No cancellation. A user who navigates away leaves the request running.

return {} is the real bug. The function reports success — a falsy-ish but truthy empty object — so the caller renders "order saved" for an order that was not saved. This converts a loud failure into silent data loss, which is the single most expensive mistake in this section.

class SaveFailed extends Error {
  constructor(message, options) { super(message, options); this.name = 'SaveFailed'; }
}

async function saveOrder(order, { signal } = {}) {
  let res;
  try {
    res = await fetch('/api/orders', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify(order),
      signal,
    });
  } catch (cause) {
    if (cause.name === 'AbortError') throw cause;             // cancellation is not a failure
    throw new SaveFailed('the order service is unreachable', { cause });
  }

  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new SaveFailed(`the order service returned ${res.status}`, { cause: res });
  }
  try {
    return await res.json();
  } catch (cause) {
    throw new SaveFailed('the order service returned a malformed body', { cause });
  }
}

Why it is shaped this way. Three narrow try blocks instead of one wide one, so each failure gets a message describing what actually failed — network, status, body — and nothing unrelated is caught. It throws rather than returning a sentinel, so a caller cannot accidentally treat failure as success; the decision of what to show the user belongs to the caller, not here. cause preserves the original at every level (§13.4). AbortError is rethrown unwrapped, because a cancelled request is not an error to report — the same distinction §16's search exercise makes.

On res as a cause: it is not an Error, which is legal — cause accepts any value — and it lets the caller inspect res.status without a second field. If that feels loose, a this.status = res.status on the custom class is the more disciplined alternative.

2. Design an error hierarchy for a payment library, and explain what callers should be able to branch on.

Solution 
class PaymentError extends Error {
  constructor(message, options) {
    super(message, options);
    this.name = new.target.name;              // every subclass names itself, for free
  }
  get retryable() { return false; }           // the default is the safe one
}
class CardDeclined extends PaymentError {
  constructor(code, options) { super(`card declined: ${code}`, options); this.code = code; }
}
class PaymentTimeout extends PaymentError {
  get retryable() { return true; }
}
class RateLimited extends PaymentError {
  constructor(retryAfterMs, options) { super('rate limited', options); this.retryAfterMs = retryAfterMs; }
  get retryable() { return true; }
}
class PaymentConfigError extends PaymentError {}     // our bug, not theirs

const failures = [new CardDeclined('insufficient_funds'), new PaymentTimeout('gateway timed out'),
                  new RateLimited(2000), new PaymentConfigError('missing API key')];
for (const error of failures) {
  console.log(`${error.name.padEnd(18)} retryable=${String(error.retryable).padEnd(5)} ${error.message}`);
}
console.log('one catch-all still works:', failures.every(e => e instanceof PaymentError));
console.log('and the data is on the error:', failures[0].code, '|', failures[2].retryAfterMs);

CardDeclined       retryable=false card declined: insufficient_funds
PaymentTimeout     retryable=true  gateway timed out
RateLimited        retryable=true  rate limited
PaymentConfigError retryable=false missing API key
one catch-all still works: true
and the data is on the error: insufficient_funds | 2000

this.name = new.target.name in the base sets each subclass's name automatically (§7.4), which removes the line every subclass would otherwise have to remember — and which §13.5 showed is not optional.

What callers should be able to branch on, in order of importance.

Retryable or not, as a property rather than a type list. A caller writing if (error.retryable) retry() does not break when the library adds a sixth error type, whereas if (error instanceof PaymentTimeout || error instanceof RateLimited) does. Exposing the decision rather than the taxonomy is the single most useful thing an error hierarchy can do.

Whose fault it is. PaymentConfigError means the integration is wrong and no retry will help; CardDeclined means the user must act; PaymentTimeout means nobody is at fault. Those three lead to three completely different user experiences, and they are the real branches a UI needs.

The machine-readable detail — code, retryAfterMs — as fields rather than parsed out of the message. Message text is for humans and will be reworded; a caller that regexes it will break.

A single base to catch. catch (e) { if (e instanceof PaymentError) … else throw e } lets a caller handle everything the library defines and rethrow everything it does not (§13.4).

What deliberately is not here: an error type per gateway response code. That is what code is for, and a class per code would give callers dozens of names to learn while making the library unable to add a code without a breaking change.

3. A user reports "the page sometimes shows an empty list". No error appears in the console. Describe how you would find it.

Solution

"Sometimes" plus "no error" is a shape, and it narrows the search immediately. Something is failing and being swallowed, or something is racing. Both leave the same trace: a code path that produces an empty result without complaining.

First: make the failure loud rather than hunting for it. Turn on pause on caught exceptions in devtools (§13.9). This is the step people skip, and it is the one that finds a swallowed error in seconds — because a catch that logs nothing still pauses the debugger. If it pauses inside a catch (e) { return [] }, the investigation is over.

Second: check the two async top-level nets. Add addEventListener('unhandledrejection', …) and window.onerror temporarily (§12.11). A rejected promise nobody awaited is invisible in the console in some setups and is exactly the shape that produces an intermittent empty list.

Third: look for the four usual causes, in this order.

A swallowed error — catch { return [] } or .catch(() => []). Search the module for catch and read each one; any that produces a value rather than rethrowing is a suspect (§13.4).

A response that was not checked — fetch fulfilling on a 500 and res.json() yielding an error object whose .items is undefined, which then renders as empty (§17.1). The tell is that the network panel shows a red request while the console is clean.

A race — two requests in flight and the slower, older one landing last, so the list is replaced by a stale or empty result (§12.13). The tell is that it correlates with fast typing or fast navigation, and it reproduces if you throttle the network to Slow 3G.

A cancellation being treated as a failure — an AbortError from an unmounting component caught by a handler that sets the list to [].

Fourth: reproduce it deliberately. Network throttling plus the devtools request-blocking feature turns an intermittent bug into a reliable one, and a bug you can reproduce on demand is already most of the way to fixed.

What I would not do first: add console.log statements. They require a guess about where to look, they need a reload per iteration, and in a race they change the timing enough to hide the problem. A conditional breakpoint on the render function with items.length === 0 gives the whole scope at the exact moment it goes wrong, on the first attempt (§13.9).

And the fix, whatever the cause, includes a test: the reason this reached a user is that an empty list is indistinguishable from a legitimately empty list. Distinguishing "loaded, and empty" from "failed" in the state — rather than representing both as [] — is what stops the whole class of report recurring.

SECTION 14

Modules, Packages and Tooling

A JavaScript file on its own is not much use. This section covers everything between "I wrote a function" and "it runs on someone else's machine, tested, in a browser that never saw my source":

  • the module system, which lets files refer to one another;
  • the package manager, which brings in code you did not write;
  • the bundler, which turns hundreds of files into something a browser can load quickly;
  • the tests and the pipeline that keep it all working.

The module half is part of the language. import and export are syntax with rules: static resolution (imports are worked out before any code runs), live bindings (an import always sees the exporting file's current value) and a defined evaluation order. Knowing those rules is what lets you reason about a circular dependency, where two files import each other, or a mysterious undefined at startup, instead of shuffling lines until it works.

The tooling half is convention. Nothing in it is in the specification, and nearly all of it is universal. That is a different kind of knowledge: less about what is true and more about what everyone agreed to. It is included in full, including writing tests and continuous integration (running the checks automatically on every change), so that finishing this course leaves you able to set up a project rather than only write code inside one.

14.1 A Module Has Its Own Scope

An ES module is a file. Its top-level declarations are private to it, it always runs in strict mode, and its top-level this is undefined (§3.5).

const privateToThisModule = 'not visible anywhere else';
console.log('modules are always strict:', (function () { return this; })() === undefined);
console.log('top-level this is undefined, not globalThis:', typeof globalThis);
console.log('and a top-level const is not a global:', globalThis.privateToThisModule);
console.log('import.meta.url identifies the module:', import.meta.url.startsWith('file:'));

modules are always strict: true
top-level this is undefined, not globalThis: object
and a top-level const is not a global: undefined
import.meta.url identifies the module: true

Four differences from a classic script follow from that, and each removes a kind of bug: no accidental globals, no this pointing at window, deferred running by default, and, the big one, dependencies are declared rather than assumed. A script relies on being loaded in the right order; a module says what it needs.

In a browser, <script type="module"> turns this on. The script is deferred automatically, it is checked under CORS (the browser's rules for loading code from other origins), and it runs only once, however many times it is referenced.

14.2 export

The export keyword has two forms, and choosing between them is one of the few style questions in JavaScript where people genuinely disagree.

const mod = await import('data:text/javascript,' + encodeURIComponent(`
  export const version = '1.0';                 // a named export, inline
  const helper = (n) => n * 2;
  function main() { return 'ran'; }
  export { helper, main as run };               // a named export list, with renaming
  export default class Widget {}                // a default export
`));
console.log('named exports:', mod.version, mod.helper(21), mod.run());
console.log('the default is a property called "default":', typeof mod.default, mod.default.name);
console.log('the namespace object lists everything:', Object.keys(mod).sort().join(', '));

named exports: 1.0 42 ran
the default is a property called "default": function Widget
the namespace object lists everything: default, helper, run, version

Note what is not in that list: main. export { main as run } exports the binding under the name run, and under that name only, so importers never see the internal name. That is what makes renaming safe: a module can rearrange its internals freely, as long as the exported names stay the same.

A named export is the default choice. You can search for it by name, it can only be renamed on purpose, it supports tree shaking (§14.13), and a typo in the import is an error when the module loads rather than an undefined later.

A default export is one per module, and the importer chooses its name. That is its whole problem: the same module gets imported as Widget, widget and W in three files, and no tool can tell they are the same thing. Prefer named exports. Keep default for a module whose entire purpose is one thing, and even then consider exporting it by name as well.

Re-export passes another module's exports on without importing them into the current file's scope. That is how a package offers one entry point over many files:

// index.js — the barrel pattern
// export { Button } from './button.js';
// export { Input } from './input.js';
// export * from './types.js';              // everything, except default
// export { default as Modal } from './modal.js';
console.log('a barrel file re-exports without importing into its own scope');

a barrel file re-exports without importing into its own scope

Barrels (files that only re-export others) have a real cost. Importing one name from a barrel can pull the barrel's whole module graph into the build, unless the bundler can prove it is not needed. That is a common reason for a surprisingly large chunk.

The terms above, gathered: the export keyword.

14.3 import

The import statement has four shapes:

const url = 'data:text/javascript,' + encodeURIComponent(`
  export const a = 1, b = 2;
