  export default 'the default';
`);
const ns = await import(url);
console.log('a namespace import gives one object:', Object.keys(ns).sort().join(','));
console.log('named:', ns.a, ns.b, '| default:', ns.default);
console.log('the namespace object is sealed:',
  (() => { try { ns.a = 9; return 'mutable'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());
console.log('and it is a Module, not a plain object:', Object.prototype.toString.call(ns));

a namespace import gives one object: a,b,default
named: 1 2 | default: the default
the namespace object is sealed: TypeError
and it is a Module, not a plain object: [object Module]
import { a, b as c }
Named, optionally renamed. A name that does not exist is an error before anything runs.
import x from
The default export, under whatever name you choose.
import * as ns from
A namespace import — every export as one sealed object.
import './setup.js'
A side-effect import. Evaluates the module for what it does, binding nothing — polyfills, CSS in a bundler, registering a custom element.

Imports are hoisted and static. The whole import graph is worked out before any module body runs. That is why import must be at the top level (inside an if it is a SyntaxError), and why a bundler can analyse the graph without running anything. It is also why a typo in a named import fails immediately, with a clear message, rather than turning up as undefined three files away.

One line each, for reference: the import statement and a side-effect import.

14.4 Live Bindings

An import is not a copy of a value. It is a live binding to the exporting module's variable:

const mod = await import('data:text/javascript,' + encodeURIComponent(`
  export let count = 0;
  export function increment() { count++; }
`));
console.log('initial:', mod.count);
mod.increment();
mod.increment();
console.log('after the exporter mutated it:', mod.count);
console.log('but the importer may not assign to it:',
  (() => { try { mod.count = 99; return 'assigned'; } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());

initial: 0
after the exporter mutated it: 2
but the importer may not assign to it: TypeError

The binding updated without the importer doing anything. That is the "live" part, and it is a real difference from CommonJS, where module.exports.count would have been a snapshot taken at the moment of require.

The one-sidedness is deliberate: the exporting module may reassign; the importer may only read. That makes data flow in one direction, easy to trace. It is also why a module that wants to expose changeable state should export a function that changes it, rather than relying on importers.

14.5 Specifiers and Resolution

A module specifier is the string after from, and its first character decides how it is resolved (turned into an actual file location).

relative
./util.js, ../lib/x.js. Resolved against the importing module's URL. The extension is required in the browser and in Node ESM.
absolute
/lib/x.js or a full URL. In a browser, resolved against the origin.
a bare specifier
lodash, react/jsx-runtime. A package name. The browser cannot resolve these on its own — it needs an import map or a bundler.
node:
node:fs, node:path. An explicit builtin, which cannot be shadowed by a package of the same name.

Module resolution for a bare specifier (a package name, such as 'lodash') in Node walks up through node_modules folders and then reads the package's exports field (§14.10). In a browser it uses an import map, a table in the page that maps names to URLs:

// In HTML, before any module loads:
// <script type="importmap">
// { "imports": { "lodash": "https://esm.sh/lodash@4.17.21", "#app/": "/src/" } }
// </script>
console.log('an import map is how a browser resolves a bare specifier without a bundler');
console.log('import.meta.resolve does the same lookup from code:', typeof import.meta.resolve);
console.log('node: builtins always resolve:', typeof (await import('node:path')).join);

an import map is how a browser resolves a bare specifier without a bundler
import.meta.resolve does the same lookup from code: function
node: builtins always resolve: function

import.meta carries information supplied by the host. import.meta.url is the module's own URL, which is how a module finds a file sitting next to it. import.meta.resolve() runs the resolution algorithm and returns the URL a specifier would load, without loading it.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: import.meta.resolve(), a module specifier and module resolution.

14.6 Dynamic import()

Dynamic import() loads a module while the program runs, and returns a promise for the module's contents. It is an operator, not a function, so you cannot pass it around as a value. Unlike static import, it may appear anywhere, take a computed specifier, and depend on a condition.

async function loadFormatter(kind) {
  const source = kind === 'json'
    ? 'export const format = (v) => JSON.stringify(v, null, 2);'
    : 'export const format = (v) => String(v);';
  const mod = await import('data:text/javascript,' + encodeURIComponent(source));
  return mod.format;
}
console.log((await loadFormatter('json'))({ a: 1 }).replace(/\n/g, '\\n'));
console.log((await loadFormatter('text'))(42));
console.log('a failed import rejects rather than throwing synchronously:',
  await import('data:text/javascript,syntax error here').then(() => 'loaded', (e) => e.constructor.name));

{\n  "a": 1\n}
42
a failed import rejects rather than throwing synchronously: SyntaxError

It has two jobs. The first is code splitting: loading a route or a heavy library only when it is needed (§14.13). The second is conditional loading, such as fetching a polyfill only when a feature test fails. A bundler treats each dynamic import as a point where it can split the output. So the specifier should be a literal, or a template the bundler can obviously analyse; a fully dynamic string defeats the analysis, and the module ends up either bundled up front or not at all.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: code splitting.

14.7 Import Attributes and JSON Modules

Import attributes tell the host how to interpret the imported file, and they exist for a security reason rather than for convenience:

// A JSON module. The attribute is mandatory, not decorative.
// import config from './config.json' with { type: 'json' };
console.log('the syntax is: import data from "./x.json" with { type: "json" }');
console.log('and the default export is the parsed value, frozen');

the syntax is: import data from "./x.json" with { type: "json" }
and the default export is the parsed value, frozen

A JSON module gives the parsed data as its default export, and has no named exports. The with { type: 'json' } attribute is required because, without it, a server could send JavaScript where JSON was expected and the browser would run it. The attribute makes the expected type part of the request, so a mismatch becomes a load error instead of code running.

14.8 Evaluation Order and Cycles

Module evaluation order is depth-first and post-order: a module's dependencies run before the module itself. Each module runs exactly once, however many modules import it:

// entry.js imports a.js then b.js; both import shared.js

shared.js evaluated      <- deepest first
a.js evaluated
b.js evaluated           <- shared.js is NOT re-evaluated
entry.js evaluated

The run-once guarantee is what makes a module a natural singleton. A module that exports a configured client creates it once, and every importer gets the same one.

A cyclic import, where two modules import each other, is legal, because the bindings are hoisted before any module body runs. Whether it works depends on when each value is read:

// a.js
import { b } from './b.js';
export const a = 'A';
console.log('a.js sees b as:', b);        // undefined — b.js has not run yet

// b.js
import { a } from './a.js';
export const b = 'B';
console.log('b.js sees a as:', a);        // ReferenceError if a is a const in the TDZ

// Reading inside a FUNCTION is always safe:
export function getA() { return a; }      // by the time this is called, a.js has finished

The rule is precise: a cycle is fine as long as no module reads another's binding during its own evaluation. Function declarations are hoisted, so calling a function across a cycle later always works. A top-level read may hit the temporal dead zone (§3.3) and throw, or see undefined for a var.

A cycle is usually a sign of a design problem, not a puzzle to solve. The two honest fixes are to move the shared thing into a third module that both depend on, or to reverse the dependency so that one side receives what it needs as an argument.

To have in hand before moving on: module evaluation order and a cyclic import.

14.9 CommonJS and Interop

CommonJS is Node's original module system: require() to load a module and module.exports to expose values.

const { createRequire } = await import('node:module');
const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);
console.log('createRequire brings require into an ES module:', typeof require);
console.log('and it is synchronous, unlike import():', typeof require('node:path').join);

createRequire brings require into an ES module: function
and it is synchronous, unlike import(): function

Four differences matter for ESM/CJS interop:

timing
require is synchronous and runs at the point of the call; import is resolved before anything executes.
bindings
require gives a snapshot of module.exports; import gives a live binding (§14.4).
analysability
require(someVariable) is legal, so a CJS graph cannot be statically analysed — which is why tree shaking (§14.13) needs ESM.
direction
ESM can import CJS (the whole module.exports arrives as the default). CJS can require ESM only in recent Node, and not if it uses top-level await.

One interop quirk is worth naming. A CJS module whose module.exports is an object with a default property looks exactly like an ES module that a tool has converted to CommonJS. That is the origin of the mod.default.default problem, and of the esModuleInterop flag in build tools.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: require() and ESM/CJS interop.

14.10 package.json

package.json is the manifest. Five fields do the work.

const manifest = {
  name: '@acme/widgets',
  version: '2.4.1',
  type: 'module',
  exports: {
    '.': { types: './dist/index.d.ts', import: './dist/index.js', require: './dist/index.cjs' },
    './styles.css': './dist/styles.css',
  },
  scripts: { build: 'vite build', test: 'node --test', lint: 'eslint .' },
  dependencies: { 'date-fns': '^4.1.0' },
  devDependencies: { vite: '^7.0.0', eslint: '^9.0.0' },
};
console.log('the package entry point comes from exports["."], not "main":',
  manifest.exports['.'].import);
console.log('anything not listed in exports is unreachable to importers');
console.log('scripts are run with npm run:', Object.keys(manifest.scripts).join(', '));

the package entry point comes from exports["."], not "main": ./dist/index.js
anything not listed in exports is unreachable to importers
scripts are run with npm run: build, test, lint

The package type field decides how the package's .js files are interpreted: "module" means ESM, and leaving it out means CommonJS. The explicit extensions .mjs and .cjs override it for a single file, which is the reliable way out.

The exports field replaced main, and does two things main could not. It defines conditional exports, a different file for import, require, types or browser. And it encapsulates: a path that is not listed cannot be imported at all, so import 'pkg/src/internal.js' fails, instead of letting users depend on your internals. That makes adding exports to an existing package a breaking change, which is why so many packages still ship main alongside it.

The package entry point is exports['.']. scripts are the project's commands, run with npm run <name>, and npm test and npm start have shorter forms. Scripts run with the package's node_modules/.bin on the PATH, which is why "lint": "eslint ." works without installing ESLint globally.

In summary, the vocabulary here is the package type field and the exports field.

14.11 Versioning, Ranges and the Lockfile

Semantic versioning is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A major bump may break your code, a minor bump adds features without breaking anything, and a patch bump fixes bugs.

const version = '2.4.1';
const [major, minor, patch] = version.split('.').map(Number);
console.log(`major ${major} — breaking | minor ${minor} — additive | patch ${patch} — fixes`);
console.log('a caret range ^2.4.1 accepts:', '>=2.4.1 <3.0.0');
console.log('a tilde range ~2.4.1 accepts:', '>=2.4.1 <2.5.0');
console.log('below 1.0.0 the rules change: ^0.4.1 accepts', '>=0.4.1 <0.5.0');
console.log('an exact pin is just:', version);

major 2 — breaking | minor 4 — additive | patch 1 — fixes
a caret range ^2.4.1 accepts: >=2.4.1 <3.0.0
a tilde range ~2.4.1 accepts: >=2.4.1 <2.5.0
below 1.0.0 the rules change: ^0.4.1 accepts >=0.4.1 <0.5.0
an exact pin is just: 2.4.1

A caret range, which is what npm install writes by default, allows anything up to the next major version. The 0.x special case is the one people miss: below 1.0.0, ^ behaves like ~, because a package before 1.0 is allowed to break things in a minor release.

A lockfile, package-lock.json, records the exact version and integrity hash of every package in the tree, including the dependencies of your dependencies. It is what makes an install repeatable, so commit it. In CI, use npm ci, which installs exactly what the lockfile says and fails if it disagrees with package.json, where npm install would silently update it.

A dev dependency is needed to build or test the project but not to run it: npm install --save-dev. The distinction matters because someone who uses your library installs its dependencies and not its devDependencies, and because a production install can skip them entirely.

A transitive dependency is a dependency of a dependency, and this is where the numbers get alarming: a handful of direct dependencies routinely pulls in hundreds of packages. That is supply-chain risk: every one of them runs with your permissions, both when installing and when your program runs. Four practices reduce it:

  • run npm audit and treat what it reports as work to do;
  • prefer packages that have few dependencies of their own;
  • use npm ci, so a compromised re-published version cannot slip in;
  • consider --ignore-scripts to stop packages running code during install.

What to carry forward from this subsection: semantic versioning, a lockfile, a dev dependency, a transitive dependency and supply-chain risk.

14.12 npm, Monorepos and Workspaces

const commands = [
  ['npm install', 'install everything in package.json, updating the lockfile'],
  ['npm ci', 'install exactly the lockfile — the CI command'],
  ['npm install pkg', 'add a dependency'],
  ['npm run build', 'run a script from the scripts field'],
  ['npm audit', 'report known vulnerabilities in the tree'],
  ['npx tool', 'run a package binary without installing it globally'],
];
for (const [cmd, what] of commands) console.log(`${cmd.padEnd(18)} ${what}`);

npm install        install everything in package.json, updating the lockfile
npm ci             install exactly the lockfile — the CI command
npm install pkg    add a dependency
npm run build      run a script from the scripts field
npm audit          report known vulnerabilities in the tree
npx tool           run a package binary without installing it globally

A monorepo holds several packages in one repository, and an npm workspace is npm's built-in support for one. You list the packages in a workspaces array in the root package.json. There is one node_modules at the root, and packages that depend on each other are linked, so a change in one is immediately visible in the other. The gain is changes that span packages in one step, and a single install. The cost is that tools have to understand the layout, which is why monorepo-aware task runners exist.

The terms above, gathered: a monorepo and an npm workspace.

14.13 Bundlers

A bundler works out the module graph and produces files a browser can load efficiently. Modern browsers support modules natively, so it is fair to ask whether you still need one. The answer is yes, for three reasons: bare specifiers need resolving, hundreds of small requests are slower than a few large ones even over HTTP/2, and files that are not JavaScript (styles, images) need to be part of the graph.

the Vite build tool
The default choice today. Serves native ESM in development so there is no bundle step while you work, and bundles for production.
esbuild
Extremely fast, written in Go. Often used inside other tools rather than directly.
webpack
The incumbent. The most configurable and the slowest; still correct for a large existing project.

Tree shaking removes exports that nothing imports. It relies on the static structure of ESM, which is why §14.9 noted that CommonJS cannot be shaken. It is defeated by side effects, code that runs just because a module was loaded, so a package declares "sideEffects": false to tell the bundler it is safe to drop an unused module.

Code splitting breaks the output into chunks that load when needed, driven by dynamic import() (§14.6). The usual split is one chunk per route, plus a shared chunk for third-party code.

Minification shortens names and removes whitespace, and a source map links the result back to your source so a stack trace is readable (§13.9). Upload source maps to your error monitor, and do not serve them publicly unless you mean to publish your source.

One line each, for reference: the vite build tool, webpack and a source map.

14.14 Linting, Formatting and Types

ESLint finds problems; Prettier formats. Keeping the two jobs separate is the modern consensus: a formatter has no opinions worth arguing about, and a linter should not spend its time on whitespace.

// eslint.config.js — flat config, the current format
const config = [
  { ignores: ['dist/**'] },
  {
    files: ['**/*.js'],
    languageOptions: { ecmaVersion: 'latest', sourceType: 'module' },
    rules: {
      'no-unused-vars': 'error',
      'no-undef': 'error',
      eqeqeq: ['error', 'smart'],
      'no-console': 'warn',
    },
  },
];
console.log('rules configured:', Object.keys(config[1].rules).join(', '));

rules configured: no-unused-vars, no-undef, eqeqeq, no-console

Run both in CI and in a pre-commit hook (a check that runs automatically before each commit), so a formatting difference never shows up in a review. --fix and --write fix most findings automatically.

JSDoc types give you type checking without TypeScript syntax. You write the types in comments and run tsc --checkJs --noEmit, and an editor gives full completion and error checking on plain .js files.

/**
 * @param {string} name
 * @param {{ retries?: number }} [options]
 * @returns {Promise<string>}
 */
async function greet(name, options = {}) {
  return `hello ${name} (${options.retries ?? 0} retries)`;
}
console.log(await greet('Ada', { retries: 2 }));

hello Ada (2 retries)

This is the right trade for a library that must ship plain JavaScript, or a codebase not ready to switch: the checking uses the same engine, and there is no build step.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: jsdoc types and a pre-commit hook.

14.15 Testing: the Runner and the Vocabulary

A test runner finds test files, runs them and reports the results. node:test is built into Node, needs no dependencies, and is enough for most projects:

// A test file, run with `node --test`.
const source = `
  import test from 'node:test';
  import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

  test('adds numbers', () => {
    assert.equal(1 + 1, 2);
  });

  test('a suite groups related cases', async (t) => {
    await t.test('rejects a negative', () => {
      assert.throws(() => { throw new RangeError('negative'); }, RangeError);
    });
  });
`;
console.log('test file lines:', source.trim().split('\n').length);
console.log('the built-in runner needs no dependencies at all');

test file lines: 12
the built-in runner needs no dependencies at all

describe() and it() are the other common way to write tests: the BDD style that Mocha made popular and that Vitest and Jest use. node:test supports both. describe/it and test are interchangeable in practice, and which you use is a matter of house style.

An assertion is a statement that must be true. Two rules make assertions useful rather than decorative. Prefer the strict forms (assert.strictEqual, or the whole node:assert/strict module), so '1' never passes for 1. And test one behaviour per test, so a failure names that behaviour rather than "something in the checkout flow".

Vitest is the usual choice when a project already uses Vite, because it shares the same code-processing pipeline. Your test files and your source then resolve imports identically, which otherwise is a constant source of configuration drift.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: an assertion and describe() and it().

To have in hand before moving on: a test runner.

14.16 Test Doubles, Coverage and End-to-End

A test double stands in for a real collaborator in a test, the way a stunt double stands in for an actor. The words for the different kinds are worth knowing precisely, because people use them loosely to mean different things:

a stub
Returns canned answers. Used to drive the code under test down a path.
a spy function
Records how it was called, and otherwise behaves normally. Used to observe.
a mock
A double with an expectation built in — it fails the test if it was not called as specified.
a fake
A working implementation unsuitable for production — an in-memory store standing in for a database.
function spy(implementation = () => {}) {
  const calls = [];
  const fn = (...args) => { calls.push(args); return implementation(...args); };
  fn.calls = calls;
  return fn;
}
const onSave = spy(() => 'saved');
onSave('a', 1);
onSave('b', 2);
console.log('result passed through:', onSave('c', 3));
console.log('called', onSave.calls.length, 'times | first call args:', JSON.stringify(onSave.calls[0]));

result passed through: saved
called 3 times | first call args: ["a",1]

Fake timers replace setTimeout, setInterval and the clock with a version the test controls. A test for a debounce (§5.10) or a retry backoff (§12.14) can then move time forward by 30 seconds instantly, instead of waiting. Both node:test and Vitest provide them, and they are the difference between a fast test suite and one nobody runs.

Code coverage measures which lines ran during the tests: node --test --experimental-test-coverage, or Vitest's built-in report. Read it as a finder of untested code, not as a target. 100% coverage with no assertions proves nothing, and chasing a coverage number produces tests written to touch lines rather than to check behaviour. Watch mode re-runs the affected tests whenever you save, and it is what makes tests part of writing code rather than a step afterwards.

Snapshot testing records the output on the first run and compares against it afterwards. It is genuinely useful for large structured output, and genuinely dangerous as a habit, because updating a failing snapshot takes one keystroke. So a real regression gets accepted along with the change you meant. Keep snapshots small, and review their diffs like any other code.

End-to-end testing drives the real application in a real browser. Playwright is the current standard. It runs Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, waits for elements automatically instead of sleeping for a fixed time, and produces a trace you can step through after a CI failure. The usual proportion applies: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a handful of end-to-end tests covering the paths that must never break.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: a mock, a spy function, fake timers, code coverage, watch mode, snapshot testing and end-to-end testing.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: playwright.

14.17 Continuous Integration

Continuous integration means every push is built and tested automatically, so a break is found within minutes by the person who caused it. A CI workflow is a file in the repository that describes those steps, and GitHub Actions is the most common place to run them.

// .github/workflows/ci.yml
const workflow = `
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm            # dependency caching in CI
      - run: npm ci             # exactly the lockfile, never npm install
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
`;
console.log('steps:', workflow.match(/- (uses|run):/g).length);
console.log('the ordering is deliberate: lint, test, build — cheapest failure first');

steps: 6
the ordering is deliberate: lint, test, build — cheapest failure first

Four details make the difference between a pipeline people trust and one they ignore.

npm ci, never npm install. The CI job must install exactly what the lockfile says, or it is testing a different set of dependencies from the one you will ship (§14.11).

Dependency caching in CI (cache: npm above) keeps npm's download cache between runs (the downloaded packages, not the node_modules folder itself), and it is usually the biggest single saving in total time.

Order the steps cheapest-first. Linting takes seconds and catches the most common mistakes; a build takes minutes. Failing fast (§13.7) applies to pipelines too.

Keep it fast and keep it green. A pipeline that takes half an hour gets bypassed. One that fails at random teaches everyone to re-run it rather than investigate, and at that point it has negative value: it costs time and no longer catches anything.

A pre-commit hook runs a fast subset of the checks, such as formatting and linting the changed files, before a commit is created, so trivial failures never reach CI. It must stay fast: a hook that takes ten seconds gets switched off with --no-verify.

In summary, the vocabulary here is github actions and a CI workflow.

14.18 What This Section Established

  1. A module has its own scope, is always strict, and its top-level this is undefined — a top-level const is not on globalThis.
  2. Named exports over default exports: greppable, statically checkable, tree-shakeable. A default export is renamed freely by every importer, so no tool can relate them.
  3. A namespace object is a sealed [object Module] — assigning to one of its properties threw.
  4. An import is a live binding, and it is read-only to the importer. The measured count went 0 → 2 without the importer touching it, and assigning to it threw.
  5. Imports are static and hoisted, which is why import must be top-level and why a bad name fails before anything runs.
  6. A bare specifier needs an import map or a bundler; a relative one needs its extension.
  7. Dynamic import() returns a promise and rejects on failure — the drive for code splitting and conditional loading.
  8. with { type: 'json' } is mandatory for a JSON module, and the reason is security rather than syntax.
  9. Modules evaluate depth-first, once each, which makes a module a natural singleton. A cycle is legal and breaks only when a body reads another module's binding during evaluation; reading inside a function is always safe.
  10. CJS gives a snapshot and cannot be statically analysed; ESM gives a live binding and can be tree-shaken.
  11. The exports field both routes and encapsulates — an unlisted path is unreachable — so adding it is a breaking change.
  12. ^0.4.1 behaves like ~, because a pre-1.0 package may break on a minor bump.
  13. Commit the lockfile and use npm ci. Transitive dependencies are the supply-chain surface, and every one runs with your privileges.
  14. Tree shaking needs ESM and is defeated by side effects; source maps are what make a minified stack trace readable.
  15. Stub to drive, spy to observe, mock to expect, fake to substitute — and fake timers are what keep a suite fast.
  16. Coverage finds untested code; it is not a target. A snapshot accepted without reading its diff is a regression accepted.
  17. CI runs npm ci, caches dependencies, and orders steps cheapest-first. A slow or flaky pipeline has negative value.

Exercises

1. Explain what each of these does and which are errors.

// a
if (condition) { import { x } from './x.js'; }
// b
const name = './' + kind + '.js';
const mod = await import(name);
// c
import { helper } from './util';
// d
import data from './config.json';
// e
export default function () {}
export default 42;
Solution

(a) is a SyntaxError. A static import must be at the top level of a module — it is not a statement that executes, it is a declaration resolved before any code runs (§14.3). The fix is dynamic import(), which is (b).

(b) is legal and works, with a caveat. A computed specifier is fine at runtime, but a bundler cannot see which modules the expression can produce, so it either bundles nothing (and the import fails in production) or, with a partially analysable template like `./${kind}.js`, bundles every file matching the pattern. Prefer a literal specifier inside a switch, or an explicit map of () => import('./json.js') thunks, so the split points are visible to the build (§14.6).

(c) fails in the browser and in Node ESM. Extensionless specifiers are a bundler convenience, not part of module resolution — './util' must be './util.js' (§14.5). Code that relies on extension guessing is not portable to a native-module environment, which is a common surprise when a project moves off a bundler.

(d) fails without an import attribute. It must be import data from './config.json' with { type: 'json' } (§14.7). Without the attribute the host has no assurance the response is JSON, and the load is rejected rather than risking executing a JavaScript response.

(e) is a SyntaxError. A module may have at most one default export. Two named exports of different things are fine; two defaults are a contradiction, and the parser rejects it before evaluation.

2. A teammate reports that importing one component from your UI package pulls in 400KB. Diagnose and fix.

Solution

The likely cause is a barrel file plus something that defeats tree shaking, and the diagnosis is mechanical.

First, confirm it. Build with a bundle analyser (rollup-plugin-visualizer, webpack-bundle-analyzer, or vite build --mode production with the analyser plugin) and look at what is actually in the chunk. Guessing at this stage is how people spend a day removing the wrong dependency.

Then check the four usual causes, in order.

A barrel file. import { Button } from '@acme/ui' goes through index.js, which re-exports every component (§14.2). Tree shaking should remove the rest — but only if it can prove doing so is safe.

A missing sideEffects declaration. Without "sideEffects": false in package.json, a bundler must assume that evaluating any module in the graph might do something observable, so it cannot drop it. This one line is frequently the entire fix:

const manifest = { name: '@acme/ui', sideEffects: ['*.css'] };   // CSS does have side effects
console.log('declaring side effects precisely is what unlocks tree shaking:',
  JSON.stringify(manifest.sideEffects));

declaring side effects precisely is what unlocks tree shaking: ["*.css"]

A CommonJS build being selected. If exports routes the import condition to a .cjs file, the consumer gets CommonJS, which cannot be statically analysed and therefore cannot be shaken at all (§14.9). Check that exports['.'].import points at genuine ESM.

Module-level side effects in the components themselves — a customElements.define(...) or a global registration at the top level of a module — are genuinely unshakeable, because removing them would change behaviour. The fix is to move registration into an explicitly imported entry point.

The structural fix, if the causes above are addressed and it is still large: offer subpath exports so a consumer can bypass the barrel entirely.

const exportsField = {
  '.': './dist/index.js',
  './button': './dist/button.js',
  './input': './dist/input.js',
  './styles.css': './dist/styles.css',
};
console.log('subpaths a consumer may import:', Object.keys(exportsField).join(' '));

subpaths a consumer may import: . ./button ./input ./styles.css

import { Button } from '@acme/ui/button' then loads one module regardless of the bundler's analysis. Note this is a complement to tree shaking, not a replacement: the barrel stays for convenience, and the subpath is there for consumers who need the guarantee.

And measure again after each change. The reason to do these one at a time is that "we did five things and it got smaller" teaches nobody which one mattered, and the next package repeats the mistake.

3. Set up testing and CI for a small library from nothing. Say what you would do first and what you would deliberately leave out.

Solution

First, the smallest thing that gives a signal, because a setup nobody finishes gives none.

const manifest = {
  name: 'my-lib',
  version: '0.1.0',
  type: 'module',
  exports: { '.': './src/index.js' },
  scripts: {
    test: 'node --test',
    'test:watch': 'node --test --watch',
    lint: 'eslint .',
    format: 'prettier --write .',
  },
  devDependencies: { eslint: '^9.0.0', prettier: '^3.0.0' },
};
console.log('runtime dependencies:', Object.keys(manifest.dependencies ?? {}).length);
console.log('scripts:', Object.keys(manifest.scripts).join(', '));

runtime dependencies: 0
scripts: test, test:watch, lint, format

node:test before any test framework. It is built in, so there is no dependency, no configuration file and no transform pipeline to get wrong (§14.15). For a library that is plain ESM this is genuinely sufficient, and moving to Vitest later is a small change if the need arises — whereas starting with a framework means configuring one before writing a single test.

Then the tests themselves, written against the public API only. Import from ./src/index.js — the same entry point a consumer uses — so the tests exercise what is actually exported (§14.10). Tests that reach into internals lock in the implementation and have to be rewritten during every refactor.

Then CI, as four lines that already exist as scripts:

const steps = ['actions/checkout@v4', 'actions/setup-node@v4 (with cache: npm)',
               'npm ci', 'npm run lint', 'npm test'];
console.log(steps.map((s, i) => `${i + 1}. ${s}`).join('\n'));

1. actions/checkout@v4
2. actions/setup-node@v4 (with cache: npm)
3. npm ci
4. npm run lint
5. npm test

Every CI step is a script that already runs locally, which is the property to preserve: a pipeline that can only be reproduced by pushing is one nobody can debug (§14.17).

What I would deliberately leave out at the start, and why each is a later decision rather than a wrong one.

A coverage threshold. Coverage is worth reporting from the beginning and worth gating only once the suite is meaningful; a threshold on day one produces tests written to touch lines (§14.16).

A bundler. A library shipping ESM does not need one. Adding a build step means shipping something different from what you tested, and it is only justified once you must support CommonJS consumers or ship types.

End-to-end tests. There is no application yet. Playwright is right for the consuming app, not for a library.

A matrix of Node versions and operating systems. It multiplies CI time from the first day for a risk that has not materialised. Add a version to the matrix when a bug proves you need it.

Snapshot tests. They are seductive for a new project because they are fast to write, and they are the hardest to remove later once they have accumulated (§14.16).

The principle behind all five: every piece of tooling has a running cost in time and attention, and the ones that pay for themselves immediately are a test runner, a linter and a green pipeline. Everything else should be added in response to a specific problem you can name.

SECTION 15

The DOM and the Rendering Path

The document object model (DOM) is the browser's in-memory tree of the page: every element, every piece of text, as an object JavaScript can read and change. It is where JavaScript stops being a language and starts being a way to change what someone is looking at.

It is also where most of the folklore lives:

  • that innerHTML is slow;
  • that getElementsByClassName and querySelectorAll are interchangeable;
  • that cloneNode copies "just the markup";
  • that reading an element's width costs nothing.

Each of those is wrong in a way you can measure, and this section measures them.

The section follows the shape of the work:

  1. What the tree is, and how to find things in it.
  2. How to change it. There are two genuinely different ways, and one of them is the single largest source of cross-site scripting on the web (an attack where someone else's script runs inside your page).
  3. The part almost nobody is taught. Reading a layout value is not a simple read at all: it can force the browser to recalculate the layout first, and cost a hundred times what the equivalent write costs. The fix is to reorder your code, not to optimise it.

Every number below came from headless Chromium (a browser running without a window), run before the prose around it was written. Where a block prints its results directly, you can run it yourself. Where the browser had to be asked, the measured transcript is shown separately and labelled.

15.1 What the DOM Actually Is

The DOM is not your HTML. It is the document tree: a tree of objects that the browser builds from your HTML. Once it is built, the source text is gone. The DOM is the only thing that exists, and it is what gets drawn. Two consequences follow immediately. The document tree can differ from the markup you wrote, because the parser fixes what it must (§15.5). And changing the tree changes the page, without any reference to the original file.

The tree is made of nodes. Only a handful of node types matter in practice, and nodeType gives each one a number:

document.body.innerHTML = '<p id="intro">Hello <b>world</b><!-- a note --></p>';
const p = document.getElementById('intro');
const kinds = { 1: 'ELEMENT_NODE', 3: 'TEXT_NODE', 8: 'COMMENT_NODE', 9: 'DOCUMENT_NODE', 11: 'FRAGMENT' };
for (const n of p.childNodes) console.log(`${kinds[n.nodeType]} (${n.nodeType})  ${JSON.stringify(n.nodeValue ?? n.nodeName)}`);
console.log(`document itself: ${kinds[document.nodeType]}`);
console.log(`documentElement: <${document.documentElement.tagName.toLowerCase()}>, body: <${document.body.tagName.toLowerCase()}>`);

TEXT_NODE (3)  "Hello "
ELEMENT_NODE (1)  "B"
COMMENT_NODE (8)  " a note "
document itself: DOCUMENT_NODE
documentElement: <html>, body: <body>

Three things to take from that. Whitespace is a text node. That is why firstChild so often is not the element you meant, and why .children exists alongside .childNodes. An element node is a Node and much more: the DOM is a hierarchy of classes, Node → Element → HTMLElement → HTMLInputElement, and each level adds more API. And document is itself a node, of type 9, sitting above document.documentElement (the <html> element), which in turn contains document.body.

A text node holds characters and nothing else: no attributes, no children, no style. That is why setting text is a different operation from setting markup, and why the difference is a security boundary (§15.6).

What to carry forward from this subsection: an element node, document.documentelement, document.body, .children and .childnodes.

15.2 Finding Elements, and the Two Kinds of Collection

Five query methods matter. They fall into two families that behave differently, in a way that has caused real bugs.

document.body.innerHTML = '<ul id="l"><li class="x">a</li><li class="x">b</li></ul>';
const live = document.getElementsByClassName('x');   // an HTMLCollection
const stat = document.querySelectorAll('.x');        // a NodeList
const li = document.createElement('li');
li.className = 'x';
document.getElementById('l').append(li);
console.log(`live collection now: ${live.length}`);
console.log(`static NodeList still: ${stat.length}`);
console.log(`live is a ${live.constructor.name}, static is a ${stat.constructor.name}`);

live collection now: 3
static NodeList still: 2
live is a HTMLCollection, static is a NodeList

The two kinds of result also differ in how you loop over them, measured in Chromium:

HTMLCollection has forEach: false
NodeList has forEach:       true

getElementById() takes an id and returns one element, or null. It is the only query the browser keeps a dedicated index for, and it is by far the fastest thing here.

getElementsByClassName() and its relatives return a live collection: an HTMLCollection that keeps matching the document as the document changes. It is a view, not a snapshot. Occasionally that is exactly what you want, and much more often it causes the classic infinite loop:

document.body.innerHTML = '<div><span class="tag">a</span><span class="tag">b</span></div>';
const tags = document.getElementsByClassName('tag');
let guard = 0;
// for (let i = 0; i < tags.length; i++) tags[i].remove();   // removes only half
while (tags.length && guard++ < 10) tags[0].remove();        // correct with a live list
console.log(`removed everything: ${tags.length === 0}, iterations: ${guard}`);

removed everything: true, iterations: 2

The commented-out loop removes element 0. At that point every element shifts down one place while i moves up one, so the loop skips every second element. With a live collection you must either loop backwards, take a copy ([...tags]), or, as here, keep taking the first one.

querySelector() and querySelectorAll() take any CSS selector, and return the first match or a static NodeList: a snapshot, taken once, that never updates. A NodeList has forEach, entries, keys and values, but not map or filter, so [...nodes] or Array.from(nodes) is the usual first step. They are the general-purpose tools. They accept the full selector language, including :has() and :is(), and their cost grows with the size of the part of the tree searched. That is why container.querySelectorAll('.row') beats document.querySelectorAll('#container .row') when you already have container.

The terms above, gathered: getelementbyid(), queryselector(), queryselectorall(), getelementsbyclassname() and a static nodelist.

15.3 Walking the Tree

Every traversal property comes in two versions: one that sees all nodes, and one that sees only elements. Prefer the element versions, unless you specifically want text and comments too.

.childNodes
Every child, whitespace text nodes and comments included. A live NodeList.
.children
Element children only. A live HTMLCollection. This is almost always the one you want.
.parentNode
The parent — which for a top-level element is document itself, where .parentElement gives null.
.nextElementSibling
The next sibling that is an element, skipping the whitespace between tags. Paired with .previousElementSibling.

Walking the tree by hand is fragile: insert one element and every .nextElementSibling chain is off by one. So the selector-based navigation methods are usually better:

document.body.innerHTML = '<section id="wrap"><div id="mid" class="card"><p id="p">text</p></div></section>';
const p = document.getElementById('p');
console.log(`closest('.card')      -> #${p.closest('.card').id}`);
console.log(`closest('#p')         -> #${p.closest('#p').id}   (it checks the element itself first)`);
console.log(`matches('#wrap p')    -> ${p.matches('#wrap p')}`);
const mid = document.getElementById('mid');
console.log(`mid.contains(p)       -> ${mid.contains(p)}`);
console.log(`mid.contains(mid)     -> ${mid.contains(mid)}  (a node contains itself)`);

closest('.card')      -> #mid
closest('#p')         -> #p   (it checks the element itself first)
matches('#wrap p')    -> true
mid.contains(p)       -> true
mid.contains(mid)     -> true  (a node contains itself)

.closest() walks up from the element, starting with the element itself, to the first ancestor that matches a selector. It is the single most useful method in event delegation (§16.7). .matches() tests an element against a selector without searching anything. .contains() asks whether one node is inside another, and returns true for the node itself, which is a deliberate convenience and an occasional surprise.

One line each, for reference: .parentnode, .closest(), .matches() and .contains().

15.4 Creating, Moving and Cloning Nodes

document.createElement() makes a detached element: it is not on the page until you insert it. .append() adds children at the end and .prepend() adds them at the start; .replaceWith() swaps an element for something else, and .remove() deletes it. All four accept any number of nodes or strings, where a string becomes a text node, safely. They read the way the operation sounds:

document.body.innerHTML = '<ul id="list"><li>middle</li></ul>';
const list = document.getElementById('list');
const first = document.createElement('li'); first.textContent = 'first';
const last  = document.createElement('li'); last.textContent  = 'last';
list.prepend(first);
list.append(last, ' trailing text is escaped, not parsed');
list.querySelector('li:nth-child(2)').replaceWith(Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { textContent: 'replaced' }));
console.log(list.innerHTML);
last.remove();
console.log(`after .remove(): ${list.children.length} children`);

<li>first</li><li>replaced</li><li>last</li> trailing text is escaped, not parsed
after .remove(): 2 children

.prepend() and .replaceWith() share the convenience of the whole family: a string argument becomes a text node, not markup, so neither can inject anything.

Insertion moves rather than copies. A node has exactly one parent, so appending an element that is already in the document removes it from where it was. That is how you reorder a list without touching any markup, and a surprise if you expected two copies.

A DocumentFragment is a container with no parent, used to group insertions together. Building ten elements into a fragment and then appending the fragment once costs one insertion into the live tree instead of ten. When you append it, the fragment's children move into the document, and the fragment itself does not appear there:

const frag = document.createDocumentFragment();
for (const t of ['a', 'b', 'c']) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = t;
  frag.append(li);
}
console.log(`fragment children before append: ${frag.childNodes.length}`);
const ul = document.createElement('ul');
document.body.append(ul);
ul.append(frag);
console.log(`fragment children after append:  ${frag.childNodes.length}`);
console.log(`ul now has ${ul.children.length} children, the first being <${ul.firstChild.nodeName.toLowerCase()}>`);

fragment children before append: 3
fragment children after append:  0
ul now has 3 children, the first being <li>

The <template> element is the declarative version, and the template element is the right home for any markup you stamp out more than once. Its content is parsed but inert: no images load, no scripts run, nothing is drawn. The content lives in a fragment on .content, so cloning it is the standard way to stamp out repeated markup without building it in JavaScript:

document.body.innerHTML = `
  <template id="row"><li class="row"><span class="name"></span></li></template>
  <ul id="out"></ul>`;
const tpl = document.getElementById('row');
const out = document.getElementById('out');
for (const name of ['Ada', 'Grace']) {
  const node = tpl.content.cloneNode(true);
  node.querySelector('.name').textContent = name;
  out.append(node);
}
console.log(out.innerHTML.replace(/\s+</g, '<'));

<li class="row"><span class="name">Ada</span></li><li class="row"><span class="name">Grace</span></li>

.cloneNode() copies an element: only the element itself by default, and all its descendants too when you call .cloneNode(true), which is the form the template stamping above uses. What it copies is more subtle than the usual summary, and this was measured in Chromium rather than assumed:

deep clone input.value            : "user typed"
deep clone getAttribute('value')  : "markup value"
deep clone checkbox.checked       : true
deep clone textarea.value         : "user typed too"
deep clone select.selectedIndex   : 0        <- NOT copied
deep clone dataset.note           : "set via dataset"
clone is in the document          : false
event listeners on the clone      : none

So "cloneNode copies the markup, not the state", the usual summary, is wrong for form controls. HTML defines cloning steps for <input> and <textarea> that carry over the current value and checked state, including the flags that record whether the user has edited it. That is why the clone's .value is "user typed" while its value attribute is still "markup value" (§15.7 is about exactly that gap). <select> has no such steps, so its selection resets. Event listeners are never copied, because they are not part of the element's state at all: they live in a separate registry, looked up by node.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: createelement(), the template element, .clonenode(), .append() and input.value.

15.5 Markup In, Markup Out

Four properties read and write content, and choosing between them is a decision about whether a parser should run.

innerHTML
Get: the element's children serialised as markup. Set: parse the string as HTML and replace all children. Parsing is the hazard.
outerHTML
The same, including the element's own tags. Setting it replaces the element, so your reference now points at a node no longer in the document.
textContent
All descendant text, markup ignored on the way in and on the way out. No parser is involved, so nothing can be injected.
innerText
The text as rendered: hidden elements omitted, whitespace collapsed. Reading it can force layout (§15.12).

The difference between the last two is not stylistic. Measured in Chromium on <div> Hello <span style="display:none">HIDDEN</span> <b>world</b> </div>:

textContent: "  Hello   HIDDEN world  "
innerText:   "Hello world"

textContent returns what is in the tree; innerText returns what a user could copy off the screen. If you want the text of a node, textContent is correct and cheap. If you want what the user sees, innerText is correct and expensive.

.insertAdjacentHTML() parses a string and inserts it at one of four positions relative to an element, without touching the element's existing children. So it does not destroy and rebuild nodes the way innerHTML += does:

document.body.innerHTML = '<section id="wrap"><div id="mid">middle</div></section>';
const mid = document.getElementById('mid');
mid.insertAdjacentHTML('beforebegin', '<b>BB</b>');
mid.insertAdjacentHTML('afterbegin',  '<b>AB</b>');
mid.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend',   '<b>BE</b>');
mid.insertAdjacentHTML('afterend',    '<b>AE</b>');
console.log(document.getElementById('wrap').innerHTML);

<b>BB</b><div id="mid"><b>AB</b>middle<b>BE</b></div><b>AE</b>

innerHTML += deserves to be called out as an anti-pattern of its own. It turns every existing child back into a string, joins the new text on, and parses the whole thing again. So it gets quadratically slower in a loop, it destroys and recreates nodes that had not changed, and any event listener, form state or scroll position on those nodes is silently lost.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: .insertadjacenthtml().

15.6 The XSS Sink, and the Two Safe Replacements

Assigning a string to innerHTML parses it as HTML. If any part of that string came from a user, you have handed the user a parser. This is an XSS sink, a place where cross-site scripting (an attacker's script running in your page) gets in, and it is the mechanism behind a large share of cross-site scripting on the web.

The usual reassurance, "but <script> doesn't run from innerHTML", is true and irrelevant, as the measurement shows precisely:

s.innerHTML  = '<script>window.__ran.push("script")</script>';
s.innerHTML += '<img src=x onerror="window.__ran.push(\'img onerror\')">';

script tag present in DOM : true
handlers that actually ran: ["img onerror"]

The <script> element is inserted and inert: HTML says a script inserted this way does not run. But the <img> with a broken src fires onerror immediately, and its handler runs with the page's full permissions. onerror is one of dozens of routes; <svg onload>, <iframe srcdoc>, <body onpageshow> and javascript: URLs are others. There is no list of "safe" tags you could filter for, which is why home-made sanitising with a regular expression always fails in the end.

Two correct answers, in order of preference.

Use textContent when the value is text. This is the answer nine times out of ten, and it costs nothing: no parser runs, so there is nothing to exploit:

document.body.innerHTML = '<div id="out"></div>';
const hostile = '<img src=x onerror="steal()">';
const out = document.getElementById('out');
out.textContent = hostile;
console.log(`children: ${out.children.length}, text: ${out.textContent.slice(0, 12)}…`);
console.log(`the browser escaped it: ${out.innerHTML.startsWith('&lt;img')}`);

children: 0, text: <img src=x o…
the browser escaped it: true

Use Element.setHTML() when you genuinely need markup. Element.setHTML() is the sanitising counterpart to innerHTML, and it is right when you really need markup, such as a comment body with <em> and links. It parses the string and removes everything unsafe as part of the parse, so there is no moment when a hostile node exists:

// setHTML parses and sanitises in one step, so no hostile node ever exists.
function renderRichText(el, untrustedHtml) {
  el.setHTML(untrustedHtml);
}
console.log(typeof renderRichText);

function

Given '<p onclick="x()">ok <script>bad()</script><img src=x onerror=bad()></p>', that leaves:

typeof Element.prototype.setHTML       = function
typeof Element.prototype.setHTMLUnsafe = function
typeof window.trustedTypes             = object

el.innerHTML after setHTML: <p>ok </p>

The event handler attribute, the <script> and the <img onerror> are all gone, and the text and the safe structure survive. Note the deliberately alarming name of its sibling: setHTMLUnsafe() does not sanitise. It exists only for inserting markup you generated yourself, when you need declarative shadow roots to be honoured.

Trusted Types is the enforcement layer above both. With a require-trusted-types-for 'script' Content Security Policy, the browser refuses to accept a plain string for innerHTML at all. It accepts only a TrustedHTML object created by a policy you registered. That turns "someone will eventually write the unsafe line" from something code review must catch into an error at runtime. It is the only mechanism here that works in a large codebase, because it does not depend on every developer remembering.

To have in hand before moving on: an xss sink and trusted types.

15.7 Attributes Are Not Properties

An attribute versus a property is the distinction this subsection exists for. They are two different things that usually agree, and the cases where an attribute versus a property disagree are where the bugs are. The attribute is the initial, declared value from the markup. The property is the current state of the object.

document.body.innerHTML = '<input id="i" value="initial"><div id="d" class="a b"></div>';
const i = document.getElementById('i');
i.value = 'typed by the user';
console.log(`i.value               = ${JSON.stringify(i.value)}`);
console.log(`i.getAttribute('value') = ${JSON.stringify(i.getAttribute('value'))}`);
console.log(`i.defaultValue        = ${JSON.stringify(i.defaultValue)}`);
i.setAttribute('value', 'changed in markup');
console.log(`after setAttribute, i.value is still ${JSON.stringify(i.value)}`);

i.value               = "typed by the user"
i.getAttribute('value') = "initial"
i.defaultValue        = "initial"
after setAttribute, i.value is still "typed by the user"

The value attribute is the default. Once the user (or your code) has set the property, the attribute no longer follows it, and writing the attribute no longer changes what is shown. That is why form.reset() restores the attribute's value, and why reading getAttribute('value') to find out what someone typed is a bug that survives every test written with pre-filled markup.

A reflected attribute is one where the two are kept in sync in both directions, such as id, className, href and disabled. Even then, the property can be a different type or hold a different value:

a.getAttribute('href') = ../cart?x=1
a.href    (property)   = https://shop.example.com/cart?x=1
m.getAttribute('src')  = thumb.png
m.src     (property)   = https://shop.example.com/catalog/thumb.png

The href and src properties are absolutised against the document's base URL: turned into full URLs. The attributes are the raw strings. If you need the string the author wrote, getAttribute() is the only thing that gives it to you. Boolean attributes add one more twist: disabled as a property is true/false, while as an attribute it is either present or absent. So setAttribute('disabled', 'false') disables the control, because the value does not matter, only its presence.

Three methods make up the attribute API. getAttribute() returns the string, or null. setAttribute() takes a string, converting whatever you give it. toggleAttribute() adds or removes a boolean attribute, and accepts an optional second argument that forces the direction, which makes el.toggleAttribute('hidden', shouldHide) the clean way to write a conditional boolean.

The rule of thumb: use the property when there is one, and the attribute when you mean the markup. Write el.id, el.disabled and el.value rather than setAttribute, and keep setAttribute for aria-*, data-* and custom attributes that have no property.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: setattribute(), toggleattribute() and a reflected attribute.

15.8 dataset and classList

Two conveniences exist because the raw attribute API is painful for the two most common cases.

The dataset property exposes every data-* attribute as an object, converting the attribute's kebab-case name to camelCase. A data attribute is the approved way to attach your own information to an element without inventing attributes that an HTML validator would reject:

document.body.innerHTML = '<article id="post" data-post-id="42" data-author-name="Ada"></article>';
const post = document.getElementById('post');
console.log(`dataset.postId     = ${JSON.stringify(post.dataset.postId)}   (${typeof post.dataset.postId})`);
console.log(`dataset.authorName = ${JSON.stringify(post.dataset.authorName)}`);
post.dataset.readTime = '4 min';
console.log(`writing back adds the attribute: ${post.getAttribute('data-read-time')}`);
console.log(`outerHTML: ${post.outerHTML}`);

dataset.postId     = "42"   (string)
dataset.authorName = "Ada"
writing back adds the attribute: 4 min
outerHTML: <article id="post" data-post-id="42" data-author-name="Ada" data-read-time="4 min"></article>

Note the type. Everything in dataset is a string, always: data-post-id="42" gives you "42", and dataset.count++ produces NaN. Convert explicitly (§2.4). Note also that a data attribute is visible in the DOM, in devtools and to CSS attribute selectors. That makes it excellent for state a stylesheet needs to see, and unsuitable for anything private.

classList is a live list of the class names in the class attribute, and it replaces the string manipulation that className otherwise requires:

document.body.innerHTML = '<div id="d" class="card"></div>';
const d = document.getElementById('d');
d.classList.add('is-open', 'is-tall');
d.classList.remove('is-tall');
console.log(`after add/remove: ${JSON.stringify(d.className)}`);
console.log(`toggle returns ${d.classList.toggle('is-open')} -> ${JSON.stringify(d.className)}`);
console.log(`toggle with force: ${d.classList.toggle('is-open', true)} -> ${JSON.stringify(d.className)}`);
console.log(`contains('card'): ${d.classList.contains('card')}, length: ${d.classList.length}`);
d.classList.replace('card', 'panel');
console.log(`after replace: ${JSON.stringify(d.className)}`);

after add/remove: "card is-open"
toggle returns false -> "card"
toggle with force: true -> "card is-open"
contains('card'): true, length: 2
after replace: "panel is-open"

classList.toggle() returns whether the class is present after the call, and its second argument forces the direction. el.classList.toggle('active', isActive) is the right way to say "make this class match this boolean", and it is not the same as calling classList.toggle() with one argument inside an if.

In summary, the vocabulary here is the dataset property.

15.9 Styles from JavaScript

The style property is the element's inline style: the style attribute, and nothing else. Reading it tells you only what you or someone else set inline, which is almost never what the element actually looks like:

document.body.innerHTML = '<style>#b { width: 50%; color: rebeccapurple }</style><div id="b">x</div>';
const b = document.getElementById('b');
console.log(`b.style.width from a stylesheet rule: ${JSON.stringify(b.style.width)}`);
b.style.width = '10rem';
b.style.setProperty('--gap', '8px');
console.log(`after writing inline: ${JSON.stringify(b.style.width)}, custom prop ${b.style.getPropertyValue('--gap')}`);
console.log(`the attribute now reads: ${b.getAttribute('style')}`);

b.style.width from a stylesheet rule: ""
after writing inline: "10rem", custom prop 8px
the attribute now reads: width: 10rem; --gap: 8px;

A custom property must go through setProperty/getPropertyValue, because --gap is not a valid JavaScript identifier, and there is no camelCase form of it.

getComputedStyle() goes the other way: it asks the browser what the element's style turned out to be after the whole cascade. What comes back is not what you wrote. It is a used value, converted to absolute units:

declared width: 50%      ->  getComputedStyle().width           = 442px
declared padding: 1em    ->  getComputedStyle().padding         = 20px
declared margin-block: 2rem -> getComputedStyle().marginBlockStart = 32px
declared color: rgb(0,128,0) -> getComputedStyle().color        = rgb(0, 128, 0)

Percentages are resolved against the containing block, em and rem against the relevant font sizes, and colours are written out in one standard form. So a test asserting getComputedStyle(el).color === 'green' fails, and one asserting 'rgb(0, 128, 0)' passes. The returned object is live: if you keep it across a change, it shows the new values. That is convenient, and a common source of confusion when a value seems to change by itself.

The critical cost: getComputedStyle() must produce an accurate answer, so it flushes any pending style and layout work first. It is a read that can trigger a full recalculation, and that is what §15.12 is about.

What to carry forward from this subsection: the style property and a used value.

15.10 The CSS Object Model

Beyond individual elements, the CSSOM exposes stylesheets themselves.

CSS.supports() performs a real feature test using the browser's own CSS parser, the same machinery as @supports. It is the honest alternative to guessing from the user agent string:

// In a browser. jsdom has no CSS object, so the measured results are shown below.
if (CSS.supports('display', 'grid')) document.documentElement.classList.add('has-grid');
const canHas = CSS.supports('selector(:has(a))');

Measured in Chromium:

CSS.supports('display','grid')    = true
CSS.supports('display','flexbox') = false
CSS.supports('selector(:has(a))') = true

The middle line is the important one. display: flexbox was never a real value, and a browser asked to apply it drops the declaration silently, which is how CSS is specified to handle errors. CSS.supports() is the only way to ask about that silence from JavaScript, and its two-argument form tests a value, not just whether the property name exists.

CSS.registerProperty() gives a custom property a type, an initial value and a choice about inheritance. That is what makes it animatable, and what makes an invalid value fall back to the initial value, instead of making the whole declaration unset:

CSS.registerProperty({ name: '--brand-pad', syntax: '<length>', inherits: false, initialValue: '4px' });

Registering the same name twice throws an InvalidModificationError, so guard it in code that may run more than once, such as a module that is hot-reloaded or a component that registers when it mounts.

adoptedStyleSheets takes an array of constructable stylesheets and applies them to a document or a shadow root. A constructable stylesheet is a CSSStyleSheet object built in JavaScript, instead of being parsed from a <style> element. Because one sheet object can be adopted by many roots, a hundred instances of a component share one parsed stylesheet, instead of a hundred copies of the same <style>:

// The sheet is parsed once and shared by every root that adopts it.
function adoptSharedSheet(root, cssText) {
  const sheet = new CSSStyleSheet();
  sheet.replaceSync(cssText);
  root.adoptedStyleSheets = [...root.adoptedStyleSheets, sheet];
  return sheet;
}
console.log(typeof adoptSharedSheet);

function

replaceSync() takes the whole sheet's text; replace() is its async version, which you must use if the text contains @import. Adopted sheets take part in the cascade in the same order as any other author stylesheet. And, crucially for §17.16, they are the standard way to style a shadow root without copying CSS into it.

The terms above, gathered: css.registerproperty() and a constructable stylesheet.

15.11 Measuring the Box

There are four families of geometry properties, and they measure different boxes. Mixing them up produces bugs that are off by a border's width and look like rounding errors.

getBoundingClientRect()
The element's rendered rectangle in viewport coordinates, as a fractional number, after transforms. top, left, width, height, x, y.
offsetWidth / offsetHeight
Border box, rounded to an integer, ignoring transforms. Includes padding, border and any scrollbar.
clientWidth / clientHeight
Padding box, integer — content plus padding, excluding border and scrollbar. The one that answers "how much room is there inside".
scrollWidth / scrollHeight
The full extent of the content, including what is scrolled out of view.

Measured on a 50%-wide <div> with 1em padding and a 1px border, in a 900px viewport:

getComputedStyle().width      = 442px      (the content box)
getBoundingClientRect().width = 484        (content 442 + padding 40 + border 2)
offsetWidth                   = 484        (a number, not a string)

Two practical notes. getBoundingClientRect() returns fractional values and offsetWidth does not, so comparing them for equality fails on an element with a fractional size. Use the rect when you need precision. And remember that getComputedStyle().width is a string with units, while all the geometry properties are numbers.

scrollTop is both a read and a write. Setting it scrolls the element, and it is silently limited to the range that can actually scroll. That is why setting scrollTop = 50 on an element that cannot scroll leaves it at 0, and it is the fastest way to test whether something is a scroll container at all. scrollTo() and scrollIntoView() are the friendlier forms, and both accept { behavior: 'smooth' }.

One line each, for reference: clientheight.

15.12 Layout Thrashing

This is the most valuable thing in the section, and you cannot see it in code review unless you know what shape to look for.

The browser is lazy. When you change a style, it does not recalculate anything straight away. It marks the layout as out of date ("dirty") and carries on, intending to do all the work once, before the next paint. That batching is why a hundred style changes cost about the same as one.

Reading a geometry value breaks the batching. offsetWidth, getBoundingClientRect(), getComputedStyle(), innerText, scrollTop and their relatives must return a correct answer now. So the browser applies every pending change and recalculates layout before returning. That is a forced synchronous layout, and one of them is cheap. Alternating reads with writes in a loop is not. Each write makes the layout dirty, each read forces it to be recalculated, and a loop over n elements does n full layouts. That pattern is layout thrashing.

The two versions differ only in the order of their lines. Measured over 500 elements in headless Chromium:

interleaved read/write   : 1086.4ms
batched reads then writes:   61.7ms
ratio                    :    17.6x

Seventeen times slower, for code that does exactly the same work with exactly the same number of operations. The bad version and the good version:

// BAD — read, write, read, write: every read forces a layout the previous write dirtied.
function thrash(rows) {
  for (const r of rows) r.style.width = r.offsetWidth + 'px';
}

// GOOD — all reads, then all writes: one layout for the whole loop.
function batched(rows) {
  const widths = rows.map(r => r.offsetWidth);          // read phase
  rows.forEach((r, i) => { r.style.width = widths[i] + 'px'; });  // write phase
}
console.log(typeof thrash, typeof batched);

function function

Reflow is recalculating geometry, and repaint is redrawing pixels without moving anything. Reflow implies repaint, and reflow is the expensive one. That is why animating transform and opacity costs neither (the compositor, a separate part of the browser, handles them), while animating width or top causes a reflow on every frame.

Three habits follow. Batching reads and writes is the first: do every read first, then every write. That is what libraries mean by a "read phase" and a "write phase", and batching reads and writes is the entire fix. The second: Do the writes in a requestAnimationFrame callback (§12.4), which runs them just before the browser's own layout pass, so there is nothing extra to apply. Third, when you must restructure a large subtree, take it out of the document first: changes to a detached node cost no layout at all, and putting it back once pays for all of them.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: a forced synchronous layout.

15.13 Watching the Document: the Three Observers

Checking the DOM over and over in a loop (polling) is the pattern all three of these replace. Each is asynchronous by design, so none of them can cause the thrashing §15.12 describes.

MutationObserver reports changes to the tree. It batches them: many changes in one turn produce a single callback holding many records, delivered as a microtask (§12.2):

document.body.innerHTML = '<ul id="m"></ul>';
const m = document.getElementById('m');
const calls = [];
new MutationObserver(records => calls.push(records.length)).observe(m, { childList: true, subtree: true });
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) m.append(document.createElement('li'));
console.log(`callbacks during the loop: ${calls.length}`);
await Promise.resolve();
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 5));
console.log(`after the microtask checkpoint: ${JSON.stringify(calls)} — one call, five records`);

callbacks during the loop: 0
after the microtask checkpoint: [5] — one call, five records

You get nothing unless you switch options on: childList for added and removed children, attributes for attribute changes, characterData for text, subtree to extend any of those to descendants, and attributeOldValue/characterDataOldValue to include the previous value in each record.

IntersectionObserver reports when an element enters or leaves the viewport, or another element, without a single scroll handler. It is the correct way to implement lazy loading, infinite scroll, sticky-header state, and "has this ad been seen?":

// In a browser. rootMargin grows the trigger area, so images start loading before they are visible.
const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries, obs) => {
  for (const e of entries) {
    if (!e.isIntersecting) continue;
    e.target.src = e.target.dataset.src;
    obs.unobserve(e.target);              // one-shot: stop watching what has loaded
  }
}, { rootMargin: '200px', threshold: 0 });

ResizeObserver reports when an element's size changes, including changes caused by neighbouring content rather than by the window, which a resize listener on window cannot see at all. It is what lets a component respond to its own box instead of to the viewport.

Both fire once straight away when you call observe(), with the element's current state, which saves you writing a separate first measurement. Measured in Chromium, observing a 100×100 box and then making it wider:

RO 100x100                       <- fired on observe(), before any change
IO isIntersecting=true ratio=1   <- likewise
RO 250x100                       <- after the width change

ResizeObserver callbacks run after layout and before paint. That makes them the one safe place to read a size and write a style in the same turn without thrashing. But writing a style that changes the observed element's own size from inside the callback is how you get the console warning ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications: the browser detected a feedback loop and had to break it.

15.14 Animating, and the Rendering Path

element.animate() is the way into the Web Animations API from code: the same engine CSS animations use, controlled from JavaScript. So it runs on the compositor when it can, and does not fight with your stylesheet.

// Returns an Animation: .finished is a promise, and .pause(), .reverse() and
// .playbackRate let you drive it after it has started.
function fadeIn(el) {
  const anim = el.animate(
    [{ opacity: 0, transform: 'translateY(8px)' }, { opacity: 1, transform: 'none' }],
    { duration: 200, easing: 'ease-out', fill: 'both' });
  return anim.finished;
}
console.log(typeof fadeIn);

function

Its advantages over setting .style in a requestAnimationFrame loop are concrete. The browser controls the timing, so frames are not dropped when JavaScript is busy. anim.finished is a promise you can await. And animating transform and opacity this way stays off the main thread entirely.

document.startViewTransition() is the higher-level tool. Hand it a callback that changes the DOM, and the browser takes a picture of the old state, applies your change, takes a picture of the new state, and fades between them. So a list reordering or a page swap animates without you writing a single keyframe:

// The callback does the DOM update; the browser does the animation around it.
function swapRows(newRows) {
  return document.startViewTransition(() => {
    document.getElementById('list').replaceChildren(...newRows);
  });
}
console.log(typeof swapRows);

function

Feature-detect it rather than assume it, because the fallback is not a broken page, just an update without animation:

function update(mutate) {
  if (!document.startViewTransition) return mutate();
  return document.startViewTransition(mutate).finished;
}
console.log(typeof update);

function

That two-line check is the whole progressive-enhancement story for this API, and the pattern is worth making a habit: a visual enhancement should be a branch around the plain version, never a requirement.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: document.startviewtransition(), element.animate() and the Web Animations API.

15.15 Asking About the Environment

matchMedia() evaluates a media query from JavaScript. And, the part people miss, it gives you an object that fires an event when the answer changes:

// In a browser. The listener is the point; `.matches` alone is a snapshot that goes stale.
const reduced = matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)');
function apply(e) { document.documentElement.dataset.motion = e.matches ? 'reduced' : 'full'; }
apply(reduced);
reduced.addEventListener('change', apply);

Reading .matches once at startup is the common mistake. The user can change the system setting, rotate the device, or drag the window to another display, and a one-time read never notices. The same object handles (prefers-color-scheme: dark), (min-width: 60rem) and (hover: hover). That is how a component can honestly choose between a hover effect and a tap target, rather than guessing from whether a touch API exists.

To have in hand before moving on: matchmedia().

15.16 What This Section Established

  1. The DOM is a tree of objects, not your HTML. Whitespace between tags is a text node, which is why .children exists beside .childNodes, and document is itself a node with documentElement and body beneath it.
  2. Two kinds of collection. getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection that grew from 2 to 3 while a static NodeList from querySelectorAll stayed at 2. A forward loop over a live collection while removing skips every second element.
  3. .closest() includes the element itself, .matches() tests without searching, and .contains() returns true for the node itself.
  4. Insertion moves, it does not copy, and appending a DocumentFragment empties it — 3 children before, 0 after, with the fragment itself absent from the document.
  5. cloneNode copies more than markup for form controls. The clone's .value was "user typed" while its value attribute stayed "markup value"; checked came across, select.selectedIndex did not, and listeners never do.
  6. textContent is the tree's text and innerText is the screen's — " Hello HIDDEN world " against "Hello world" on the same element.
  7. innerHTML is an XSS sink and "script doesn't run" is no defence. The inserted <script> was inert and the <img onerror> executed. textContent for text, setHTML() for markup — which reduced a hostile string to <p>ok </p> — and Trusted Types to enforce it.
  8. An attribute is the declared value and a property is the current state. After typing, .value was "typed by the user" and getAttribute('value') was still "initial"; href and src properties are absolutised against the base URL while the attributes stay raw.
  9. Everything in dataset is a string, and classList.toggle() returns the resulting state and takes a force argument.
  10. getComputedStyle() returns used values — 50% came back as 442px, 1em as 20px, 2rem as 32px — and it flushes pending layout to do so.
  11. CSS.supports('display','flexbox') is false, which is the only way to see CSS's silent error handling from JavaScript.
  12. Layout thrashing measured 17.6× — 1086ms interleaved against 62ms batched, for identical work over 500 elements. Read phase, then write phase, ideally inside requestAnimationFrame.
  13. Observers batch and fire immediately on observe(). Five mutations produced one callback with five records, delivered as a microtask; ResizeObserver reported 100×100 before anything changed.
  14. startViewTransition degrades to nothing. A two-line guard around it is the complete progressive-enhancement story, and matchMedia must be listened to rather than read once.

Exercises

1. This renders a list of user-supplied comments. Name every defect and rewrite it.

function render(comments) {
  const list = document.getElementById('comments');
  list.innerHTML = '';
  for (const c of comments) {
    list.innerHTML += `<li class="comment" data-id=${c.id}>
      <b>${c.author}</b>: ${c.body}
      <button onclick="del(${c.id})">delete</button></li>`;
  }
}
Solution

Defect 1 — c.author and c.body are interpolated into parsed HTML. This is the XSS sink of §15.6, twice.
