An author named <img src=x onerror=fetch('/steal?c='+document.cookie)> runs code in every reader's session. "But <script> doesn't run" is no defence — the measurement in §15.6 showed the <img onerror> firing while the <script> sat inert.

Defect 2 — innerHTML += in a loop. Each iteration serialises every existing <li> to a string, concatenates, and re-parses the entire list. It is quadratic, and it destroys and rebuilds nodes that had not changed — losing focus, scroll position, any listener attached to them, and any CSS transition in flight.

Defect 3 — the unquoted attribute. data-id=${c.id} has no quotes, so an id of 1 onmouseover=alert(1) becomes a second attribute. Even with a numeric id today, this is one schema change away from an injection.

Defect 4 — the inline onclick handler. It requires del to be a global, it is a string evaluated in the global scope (so a hostile c.id is code), and it is exactly what a Content Security Policy blocks. Event delegation (§16.7) replaces every one of these with a single listener.

The rewrite builds nodes, sets text as text, and inserts once:

function render(comments) {
  const list = document.getElementById('comments');
  const frag = document.createDocumentFragment();
  for (const c of comments) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.className = 'comment';
    li.dataset.id = c.id;                       // escaped by construction

    const who = document.createElement('b');
    who.textContent = c.author;                 // text, never markup

    const del = document.createElement('button');
    del.type = 'button';
    del.textContent = 'delete';
    del.dataset.action = 'delete';              // the delegated handler reads this

    li.append(who, `: ${c.body}`, del);         // a string argument becomes a text node
    frag.append(li);
  }
  list.replaceChildren(frag);                   // one insertion, one layout
}

Why each choice. dataset.id escapes the value for you, so the quoting defect cannot recur. textContent and the string form of .append() both create text nodes, so no parser ever sees user data. The fragment means one insertion into the live tree rather than n (§15.4), and replaceChildren clears and fills in a single operation rather than innerHTML = '' followed by appends.

If the comment body must support markup — italics and links, say — then textContent is too strict, and the answer is li.setHTML(c.body) rather than innerHTML, which parses and sanitises in one step. Escaping by hand with a regular expression is the option that always eventually fails.

2. A colleague reports that this "responsive columns" helper makes the page freeze for about a second with 500 cards, and asks you to optimise the loop. Explain why the loop is not the problem, and fix it.

function fitColumns(cards) {
  for (const card of cards) {
    const w = card.offsetWidth;
    card.style.height = (w * 0.75) + 'px';
    card.style.fontSize = (w / 20) + 'px';
  }
}
Solution

The loop is fine; the interleaving is the problem. Each iteration writes two styles, which marks layout dirty, then the next iteration reads offsetWidth, which forces the browser to recompute layout for the whole document before it can answer. Five hundred cards therefore cost five hundred full layouts — the pattern §15.12 measured at 17.6× against the batched equivalent, 1086ms against 62ms. Nothing about the loop body is slow; the cost is entirely in the read-after-write ordering.

Note that the read looks free and the writes look expensive, which is exactly backwards. Writes are cheap because they are deferred. Reads are expensive because they cannot be.

The fix is a rearrangement into two phases:

function fitColumns(cards) {
  const widths = cards.map(c => c.offsetWidth);          // read phase — one layout total
  for (const [i, card] of cards.entries()) {             // write phase — nothing forces layout
    card.style.height = (widths[i] * 0.75) + 'px';
    card.style.fontSize = (widths[i] / 20) + 'px';
  }
}

Better still, put the write phase in a frame callback, so the writes land immediately before the browser's own layout pass and there is nothing extra to flush:

function fitColumns(cards) {
  const widths = cards.map(c => c.offsetWidth);
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    for (const [i, card] of cards.entries()) {
      card.style.height = (widths[i] * 0.75) + 'px';
      card.style.fontSize = (widths[i] / 20) + 'px';
    }
  });
}

Best of all, do not measure in JavaScript. Everything here is "size relative to my own width", which is what aspect-ratio: 4 / 3 and a container query unit express directly — and CSS computes them during the layout pass that was going to happen anyway, at zero JavaScript cost and with no chance of thrashing:

.card { aspect-ratio: 4 / 3; font-size: 5cqw; container-type: inline-size; }

The general lesson is worth more than the fix: when JavaScript measures the DOM in order to write a style back into it, the first question is whether CSS can express the relationship instead. The cases where it genuinely cannot — measuring text to decide where to truncate, positioning against an element in a different subtree — are the cases where the read/write phase discipline earns its keep.

3. Write onVisible(el, fn), which calls fn once when el first becomes visible in the viewport and never again. Then explain why the scroll-listener implementation is worse, and what rootMargin and threshold change.

Solution 
function onVisible(el, fn, { rootMargin = '0px', threshold = 0 } = {}) {
  if (!('IntersectionObserver' in window)) { fn(el); return () => {}; }   // no observer: just run it
  const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries, obs) => {
    for (const e of entries) {
      if (!e.isIntersecting) continue;
      obs.unobserve(e.target);          // one-shot, before fn runs
      fn(e.target);
    }
  }, { rootMargin, threshold });
  io.observe(el);
  return () => io.disconnect();         // let the caller cancel
}
console.log(typeof onVisible);

function

unobserve comes before fn, not after, so a callback that throws still cannot fire twice. Returning a teardown function matters because an observer holds a reference to its target — a component that unmounts without disconnecting leaks the element and everything the callback closes over (§3.9).

Why the scroll listener is worse, in four distinct ways.

It runs on the main thread on every scroll event, which is many times per second, and each run typically reads getBoundingClientRect() — a forced synchronous layout (§15.12) in the hottest path on the page. IntersectionObserver does its work off the main thread and delivers a callback only when the answer changes.

It cannot see anything but the viewport. Intersection with a scrollable panel, or with an arbitrary ancestor, requires re-implementing the geometry by hand. The observer takes a root option.

It misses changes that are not scrolls. An element can enter the viewport because a sibling collapsed, an image loaded, the window resized, or a display toggled — none of which fire scroll.

It fires before it can be useful, or not at all. A scroll listener does not run on load, so an element already visible when the page opens is never noticed until the user scrolls; every implementation ends up calling the handler once manually. The observer fires immediately on observe() with the current state — measured in §15.13 — so that path does not exist.

What the two options do. rootMargin grows or shrinks the trigger rectangle in CSS-length units: '200px' fires 200px before the element reaches the viewport, which is what makes lazy-loaded images appear already loaded rather than popping in. Negative values shrink it, so '-50% 0px' fires only once the element passes the middle of the screen — the usual way to drive a "current section" indicator.

threshold is how much of the element must be inside before the callback fires: 0 (the default) means one pixel, 1 means all of it, and an array like [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1] fires at each crossing so you can drive a progress readout from e.intersectionRatio. For lazy loading, 0 with a generous rootMargin is right; for "was this ad actually seen", the standard is 0.5 held for a duration, which needs a timer on top because the observer reports crossings rather than dwell time.

SECTION 16

Events, Forms and Input

An event is how the platform tells you something happened: a click, a key press, a form being submitted. That sounds simple enough that it is usually taught in a paragraph: attach a function, and it runs. The paragraph is where the trouble starts, because almost every hard bug in interactive JavaScript is an event bug:

  • a listener that fires twice;
  • a handler that cannot be removed;
  • a click that works everywhere except on the icon inside the button;
  • a form that reloads the page when you meant it to send JSON;
  • a modal dialog that a keyboard user can leave but cannot get into.

All of those come from three things this section makes precise.

Events travel. An event moves along a path through the target's ancestors, down and then back up. That is what lets one listener on a parent serve a thousand rows.

Listeners are identified by function identity. Removing a listener needs the very same function object that was added. That is why a fresh arrow function passed to removeEventListener removes nothing.

Third, the browser has default behaviours. A link navigates and a form submits, and your handler either suppresses that or does not. For forms and links, the default is usually better than what you would write yourself.

Forms get the second half of the section, because the platform already solves most of the problem. It has a validation engine, a format for collecting the form's data, built-in accessibility, and a way to show error messages. Code that rewrites them in JavaScript is almost always worse than code that configures them.

Every measured transcript below came from headless Chromium.

16.1 EventTarget, and What an Event Object Is

EventTarget is the interface that provides addEventListener, removeEventListener and dispatchEvent. Every DOM node implements it, and so do window, XMLHttpRequest, AbortSignal, WebSocket and Worker. That is why the same three methods work everywhere on the platform.

An event object carries the facts about what happened. Two of its properties matter more than all the rest, and mixing them up is the single most common event bug:

document.body.innerHTML = '<div id="card"><button id="go"><span id="icon">*</span> Go</button></div>';
const card = document.getElementById('card');
card.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  console.log(`target        = #${e.target.id}      (what was actually clicked)`);
  console.log(`currentTarget = #${e.currentTarget.id}     (where this listener is attached)`);
  console.log(`type = ${e.type}, bubbles = ${e.bubbles}, cancelable = ${e.cancelable}`);
});
document.getElementById('icon').click();

target        = #icon      (what was actually clicked)
currentTarget = #card     (where this listener is attached)
type = click, bubbles = true, cancelable = true

event.target is the deepest element the event happened on: here the <span>, not the <button>. That is exactly the "works everywhere except on the icon" bug. event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running right now, and it is only valid while the event is being delivered. Read it inside a setTimeout and it is null.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: event.currentTarget.

16.2 addEventListener(), and Why removeEventListener() So Often Does Nothing

addEventListener() takes an event type, a handler and an options object. removeEventListener() takes the same three, and removes a listener only when all three match: the type, the same function by identity (the very same function object), and the same capture flag.

document.body.innerHTML = '<button id="b">x</button>';
const b = document.getElementById('b');
let sameFn = 0;
const fn = () => sameFn++;
b.addEventListener('click', fn);
b.addEventListener('click', fn);              // ignored: identical type, function and capture
b.click();
console.log(`the same function added twice fires ${sameFn} time(s) per click`);

let arrow = 0;
b.addEventListener('click', () => arrow++);
b.removeEventListener('click', () => arrow++);   // a DIFFERENT function object
b.click();
console.log(`removing a freshly written arrow removes nothing: ${arrow} call(s)`);

the same function added twice fires 1 time(s) per click
removing a freshly written arrow removes nothing: 1 call(s)

Two rules come out of that. Duplicate registration is silently ignored when the type, function and capture flag are all identical. That is a useful safety net, and also why "I added the listener twice and it still fires only once" is not the bug you are looking for. And you must keep a reference to the function to remove the listener later. Two arrow functions with identical code are different objects, and .bind(this) returns a new function on every call. So el.removeEventListener('click', this.onClick.bind(this)) is guaranteed to remove nothing.

Listener options are the third argument. The modern way to write them is an object, rather than the older boolean; when you meet the boolean in older code, it was the capture option:

capture
Run during the capture phase instead of the bubble phase (§16.3). Part of the listener's identity for removal.
once
Remove the listener automatically after it runs once.
passive
A promise that this handler will not call preventDefault(), which lets the browser scroll without waiting for it.
signal
An AbortSignal; aborting it removes the listener. The cleanest teardown there is.

The capture option and the passive option change when and how a handler runs, and §16.3 and §16.9 cover them in turn. The once option and an AbortSignal for listeners both solve the reference problem by removing the need for a reference at all:

document.body.innerHTML = '<button id="c">x</button>';
const c = document.getElementById('c');
let n = 0;
c.addEventListener('click', () => n++, { once: true });
c.click(); c.click(); c.click();
console.log(`once: ${n} call(s) for three clicks`);

let k = 0;
const ac = new AbortController();
c.addEventListener('click', () => k++, { signal: ac.signal });
c.click();
ac.abort();
c.click();
console.log(`signal: ${k} call(s) across two clicks, the second after abort()`);

once: 1 call(s) for three clicks
signal: 1 call(s) across two clicks, the second after abort()

The once option is the right choice for something that should happen once, such as the end of an animation or a first interaction. It is exactly the same as removing the listener in the first line of the handler. One controller can own every listener a component adds, so tearing them down is a single abort(), however many there are. And it is the same AbortController that cancels a fetch (§12.12), which is why a component can get rid of all its pending work in one line.

In summary, the vocabulary here is listener options, the passive option and an abortsignal for listeners.

16.3 The Three Phases

An event does not fire only on the element it happened to. It travels a path from window down to the target and back up again, and every ancestor gets two chances to see it: on the way down (the capture phase) and on the way up (the bubble phase).

the capture phase
Downwards, from window to the target's parent. Only listeners registered with capture: true run.
the target phase
At the target itself. Both capturing and bubbling listeners run here, in registration order.
bubbling
Upwards, from the target's parent back to window. The default, and where nearly every listener lives.

Measured with one capturing and one bubbling listener on each of three nested elements, clicking the innermost:

outer  capture   phase=CAPTURING  target=btn  currentTarget=outer
mid    capture   phase=CAPTURING  target=btn  currentTarget=mid
button capture   phase=AT_TARGET  target=btn  currentTarget=btn
button bubble    phase=AT_TARGET  target=btn  currentTarget=btn
mid    bubble    phase=BUBBLING   target=btn  currentTarget=btn's ancestor mid
outer  bubble    phase=BUBBLING   target=btn  currentTarget=btn's ancestor outer

Three things are worth taking from this. event.target is the same for all six: the path does not change what happened, only who is being told. At the target itself, eventPhase is AT_TARGET for both listeners, and the capture flag decides only their order. And the whole path is worked out before delivery starts, so moving an element in the middle does not reroute the event.

Not every event bubbles. focus, blur, load, error and mouseenter do not; focusin, focusout, mouseover and almost everything else do. event.bubbles tells you which. For the ones that do not bubble, the capture phase is the only way an ancestor can observe them, which is exactly why the focusin versions were added.

What to carry forward from this subsection: the target phase.

16.4 Stopping Propagation, and Preventing the Default

Three methods, three genuinely different jobs, routinely confused for one another.

stopPropagation() stops the event travelling any further along the path. It does not stop other listeners on the same element. stopImmediatePropagation() does both. preventDefault() stops the browser's own behaviour, and has nothing to do with the path at all.

document.body.innerHTML = '<div id="par"><a id="a1" href="/next">link</a><a id="a2" href="/next">link</a></div>';
const log = [];
const par = document.getElementById('par'), a1 = document.getElementById('a1'), a2 = document.getElementById('a2');
par.addEventListener('click', (e) => log.push(`parent saw #${e.target.id}`));

a1.addEventListener('click', (e) => { e.preventDefault(); e.stopPropagation(); log.push('a1 first'); });
a1.addEventListener('click', () => log.push('a1 second — stopPropagation did NOT stop me'));
a1.click();

a2.addEventListener('click', (e) => { e.preventDefault(); e.stopImmediatePropagation(); log.push('a2 first'); });
a2.addEventListener('click', () => log.push('a2 second — never reached'));
a2.click();
console.log(log.join('\n'));

a1 first
a1 second — stopPropagation did NOT stop me
a2 first

Neither click navigated, because preventDefault() suppressed the default action: the browser's built-in behaviour for that event. Following a link, submitting a form, ticking a checkbox, showing a context menu, scrolling on space: all of them are default actions. event.cancelable says whether one can be suppressed, and event.defaultPrevented tells you afterwards whether an earlier listener already did.

stopPropagation() is almost always the wrong tool, and it is worth saying plainly because it is so widely used. It works by breaking every other listener further along the path. That includes the analytics handler on document, the "click outside to close" handler on body, and any delegated handler (§16.7) that was going to handle this element. If the goal is "the parent should not treat this as a click on itself", the parent should check event.target instead. Keep stopPropagation for nested interactive widgets where the outer one really must not react, and use stopImmediatePropagation almost never.

The terms above, gathered: stopimmediatepropagation() and the default action.

16.5 this Inside a Handler, and Inline Handlers

this inside a handler is the currentTarget, for a normal function. An arrow function has no this of its own (§5.14), so it keeps the surrounding this. That is usually what you want inside a class, and never what you want if you were relying on getting the element:

document.body.innerHTML = '<button id="d" data-role="save">x</button>';
const d = document.getElementById('d');
d.addEventListener('click', function () { console.log(`normal function: this is #${this.id}`); });
d.addEventListener('click', () => console.log(`arrow: this is ${typeof this}`));

class Panel {
  name = 'panel';
  attach(el) { el.addEventListener('click', () => console.log(`arrow in a class: this.name = ${this.name}`)); }
  attachBroken(el) { el.addEventListener('click', function () { console.log(`normal in a class: this.name = ${this?.name}`); }); }
}
new Panel().attach(d);
new Panel().attachBroken(d);
d.click();

normal function: this is #d
arrow: this is undefined
arrow in a class: this.name = panel
normal in a class: this.name =

The last line is worth staring at. It is not undefined, and it is not an error. It is the empty string, because this is the <button>, and a button has a name property of its own that defaults to "". So the broken handler reads a real property from the wrong object and returns a believable value. That is the failure to fear: a this bug that throws is found in a minute, and one that silently reads the element's own property of the same name can survive a review.

The class case is the practical one. A method passed directly as a handler loses its instance. The three fixes are: wrap it in an arrow function; store an arrow function in a class field (onClick = () => …); or call .bind(this) once in the constructor and store the result, so the same reference is available for removing it later.

An inline event handler, such as onclick="save()" in the markup, is worth understanding only so you can recognise it and remove it. Its content is a string compiled as code in the global scope, so the function it calls must be a global. Any decent Content Security Policy blocks it outright (§17.16). Only one can exist per element per event. And if any part of the attribute is built from user data, it is a hole for injecting code. The DOM property form (el.onclick = fn) is better, but still allows only one handler, which is why addEventListener() exists.

One line each, for reference: an inline event handler.

16.6 Event Delegation

Because events bubble, one listener on a container can handle any number of elements inside it, including ones that do not exist yet. That is event delegation, and it is the default technique for lists, tables and any repeated piece of interface.

document.body.innerHTML = `<ul id="todos">
  <li data-id="1"><button data-action="done">done</button><button data-action="delete">delete</button></li>
</ul>`;
const todos = document.getElementById('todos');
todos.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
  const button = e.target.closest('[data-action]');     // handles clicks on an icon inside the button
  if (!button || !todos.contains(button)) return;       // ignore clicks on the padding
  const id = button.closest('[data-id]').dataset.id;
  console.log(`${button.dataset.action} on item ${id}`);
});
document.querySelector('[data-action="delete"]').click();
todos.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', '<li data-id="2"><button data-action="done">done</button></li>');
document.querySelector('[data-id="2"] button').click();       // works with no new listener
todos.click();                                                 // ignored

delete on item 1
done on item 2

The closest() call is what makes this robust rather than fragile. Testing e.target.matches('button') fails as soon as someone puts an icon <span> inside the button, because the target is then the span: the bug §16.1 opened with. closest() walks up from the target and finds the button, whatever was actually clicked.

Three reasons to prefer it over a listener on every element:

  • Elements added later are handled automatically, with no step to attach listeners again.
  • Memory is one listener rather than n, which matters at a thousand rows.
  • And removal is one call, so a component that replaces its contents cannot leak listeners attached to nodes that are gone.

Its limits are worth knowing too. It only works for events that bubble, so focus needs focusin. And it is the wrong choice when the handler must run before something lower down in the tree.

16.7 Custom Events

CustomEvent lets your own components speak the platform's language, instead of inventing their own callback convention. dispatchEvent() sends it, and the detail property carries the data:

document.body.innerHTML = '<div id="host"><div id="widget"></div></div>';
const host = document.getElementById('host'), widget = document.getElementById('widget');
host.addEventListener('item-selected', (e) => {
  console.log(`host heard item-selected: ${JSON.stringify(e.detail)}`);
  console.log(`it bubbled from #${e.target.id}`);
});
const event = new CustomEvent('item-selected', {
  detail: { id: 7, label: 'Widget' },
  bubbles: true,        // false by default — the commonest reason a custom event is not heard
  cancelable: true,
});
const notCancelled = widget.dispatchEvent(event);
console.log(`dispatchEvent returned ${notCancelled} (false would mean a listener cancelled it)`);

host heard item-selected: {"id":7,"label":"Widget"}
it bubbled from #widget
dispatchEvent returned true (false would mean a listener cancelled it)

bubbles defaults to false, unlike almost every built-in event, and that one default is behind most "my custom event never fires" reports. dispatchEvent returns false when a listener called preventDefault(). That is how you offer an action that can be cancelled: dispatch a before-close event, and close only if nobody cancelled it.

Dispatch is synchronous: dispatchEvent runs every listener before it returns, unlike a real user event, which arrives as a task (§12.2).

Any object can be a source of events, because you can construct and extend EventTarget:

class Store extends EventTarget {
  #items = [];
  add(item) {
    this.#items.push(item);
    this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('change', { detail: { size: this.#items.length } }));
  }
}
const store = new Store();
store.addEventListener('change', (e) => console.log(`store changed, now ${e.detail.size} item(s)`));
store.add('a');
store.add('b');

store changed, now 1 item(s)
store changed, now 2 item(s)

That is a complete observable store (an object others can subscribe to for changes) in nine lines, with no library, and its users work with the addEventListener/AbortSignal vocabulary they already know.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: dispatchevent() and the detail property.

16.8 The Input Events, and When Each Fires

Four events cover almost all form interaction, and the differences between them are exact.

The click event fires on activation, not only on a mouse click — pressing Enter on a focused button fires it too, which is why a click handler on a real <button> is keyboard-accessible for free and a click handler on a <div> is not.

The input event fires on every change to a value, as it happens. The change event fires when the value is committed: for a text field, when it loses focus; for a checkbox, radio button or select, immediately.

document.body.innerHTML = '<input id="t"><input id="c" type="checkbox">';
const t = document.getElementById('t'), c = document.getElementById('c');
const log = [];
for (const el of [t, c]) {
  el.addEventListener('input',  () => log.push(`${el.id}: input`));
  el.addEventListener('change', () => log.push(`${el.id}: change`));
}
t.value = 'set from script';
console.log(`after setting .value from script, events fired: ${log.length}`);
t.dispatchEvent(new Event('input', { bubbles: true }));
c.click();
console.log(log.join(' | '));

after setting .value from script, events fired: 0
t: input | c: input | c: change

Setting .value from script fires nothing. These events describe what the user did, and the platform will not pretend the user did something. Code that fills in a field and expects a framework's listener to notice must dispatch the event itself, which is exactly what the dispatchEvent line does. It is also why autofill and password managers dispatch artificial input events.

The submit event fires on the <form>, not on the button, and form handling belongs there. It is fired by the button, by pressing Enter in a text field, and by form.requestSubmit(), and a click handler on the button would miss two of those three. Its default action is loading a whole new page, so a JavaScript form always starts by preventing it (§16.10).

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: the click event, the change event and the submit event.

16.9 Keyboard, Pointer and Scroll

keydown fires when a key goes down, repeats while the key is held, and is the one to use: keypress is deprecated, and keyup misses the repeats. The event carries two different identifiers, and picking the wrong one produces a keyboard shortcut that fails on other keyboard layouts:

const ctrlA = new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'a', code: 'KeyA', ctrlKey: true });
const shiftA = new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'A', code: 'KeyA', shiftKey: true });
console.log(`plain:   key=${JSON.stringify(ctrlA.key)}  code=${JSON.stringify(ctrlA.code)}  ctrlKey=${ctrlA.ctrlKey}`);
console.log(`shifted: key=${JSON.stringify(shiftA.key)}  code=${JSON.stringify(shiftA.code)}`);

plain:   key="a"  code="KeyA"  ctrlKey=true
shifted: key="A"  code="KeyA"

That is key versus code in one line. key is the character produced, after modifier keys and the keyboard layout are applied: 'a', 'A', 'Escape', 'ArrowDown'. code is the physical position of the key, regardless of layout and of Shift: 'KeyA' in both rows above. Use key for text and for named keys (if (e.key === 'Escape')). Use code only for controls based on position, such as WASD movement in a game, where a French AZERTY user should press the same physical key rather than the same letter.

Pointer events (pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup, pointercancel) handle mouse, touch and pen through one API, with pointerType telling you which one it was. They save you writing a mouse version and a touch version separately. And setPointerCapture() solves dragging properly: the element keeps receiving the pointer even after it leaves the element's area, so a slider keeps tracking when the cursor overshoots.

The scroll event fires many times per second, and does not bubble from an element (though document's scroll event does reach window). Never read layout directly inside it (§15.12). The modern answer is usually IntersectionObserver (§15.13) instead of a scroll handler at all. When you do need one, a passive scroll listener is required, not merely polite:

addEventListener('scroll', onScroll, { passive: true });

The passive option is a promise, not a request. Without passive: true, the browser must run your handler before it can scroll, in case you call preventDefault(), so a slow handler makes scrolling itself stutter. With it, the browser scrolls immediately and calls you afterwards, and a preventDefault() inside the handler is ignored with a console warning. For touchstart, touchmove and wheel on the document, browsers now make listeners passive by default for exactly this reason.

To have in hand before moving on: key versus code, pointer events, the scroll event and a passive scroll listener.

16.10 Forms Without a Page Reload

The correct shape for a JavaScript form is short, and every part of it has a job:

document.body.innerHTML = `<form id="signup">
  <input name="email" type="email" required value="a@b.co">
  <input name="tags" value="x"><input name="tags" value="y">
  <button>Sign up</button>
</form>`;
const form = document.getElementById('signup');

form.addEventListener('submit', async (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();                                  // stop the navigation
  const data = new FormData(form);
  console.log(`entries: ${JSON.stringify([...data.entries()])}`);
  console.log(`as a query string: ${new URLSearchParams(data)}`);
  // await fetch('/api/signup', { method: 'POST', body: data });
});
form.requestSubmit();

entries: [["email","a@b.co"],["tags","x"],["tags","y"]]
as a query string: email=a%40b.co&tags=x&tags=y

FormData reads a form exactly the way the browser would submit it, so it already knows every rule you would otherwise have to rewrite. Measured in Chromium on a form with repeated names, an empty field, a ticked and an unticked checkbox, a select and a submit button:

entries: [["q","red shoes"],["size","9"],["size","10"],["skip",""],["gift","yes"],["colour","r"]]
get('size')    = "9"
getAll('size') = ["9","10"]
Object.fromEntries loses repeats: {"q":"red shoes","size":"10","skip":"","gift":"yes","colour":"r"}

Four rules are visible in that one line of output:

  • A control with no name is not submitted.
  • An unchecked checkbox is absent entirely: not false, absent. That is why a server must treat "missing" as unchecked.
  • An empty field is present with an empty string.
  • And repeated names are kept. That is why get() returns the first value and getAll() returns all of them, and why Object.fromEntries(formData) is a lossy shortcut that silently kept only "10".

Submitting a form with fetch can pass the FormData directly as the body, for a file upload (§17.2); or go through URLSearchParams for a URL-encoded body; or through Object.fromEntries and JSON.stringify for a JSON API, with the caveat about repeated names above.

Use form.requestSubmit() rather than form.submit(). The first fires the submit event and runs validation, the second skips both, which makes submit() almost always a mistake.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: submitting a form with fetch.

16.11 Constraint Validation

The constraint validation API is a validation engine the browser already ships. Declarative attributes (required, type="email", min, max, pattern, minlength, step) do the checking, and JavaScript reads the results instead of reimplementing them.

function validate(form, showErrors) {
  for (const field of form.elements) {
    if (!field.name) continue;
    field.setCustomValidity('');                       // clear before re-checking, always
    if (field.name === 'username' && /\s/.test(field.value)) {
      field.setCustomValidity('Usernames cannot contain spaces.');
    }
    showErrors(field, field.validationMessage);
  }
  return form.checkValidity();                         // silent; reportValidity() also shows the UI
}
console.log(typeof validate);

function

The validity object on every control reports which rule failed, as a set of booleans. Measured in Chromium:

empty required email  -> ["valueMissing"]   message: "Please fill out this field."
value "not-an-email"  -> ["typeMismatch"]
value "a@b.co"        -> valid = true
number 99 with max=10 -> ["rangeOverflow"]
pattern [a-z]+ vs ABC -> ["patternMismatch"]
after setCustomValidity -> ["patternMismatch","customError"]
form.checkValidity()  -> false

checkValidity() returns a boolean and fires an invalid event on each failing control, without showing anything. reportValidity() does the same, and also shows the browser's own error bubble and moves focus to the first invalid field. setCustomValidity() adds your own rule: a non-empty string makes the control invalid with that message, and an empty string clears it. Note in the transcript that customError sits alongside patternMismatch instead of replacing it. So you must clear the custom message before checking again, or an old message stays forever.

The reason to prefer this to a hand-made validator is not that it is shorter. The messages are translated into the user's language, they are announced by screen readers through the platform's own mechanism, they work before your JavaScript has loaded, and :invalid/:user-invalid let CSS style the state without a class. Reimplementing all that correctly is a large job; configuring it takes an afternoon.

input.value is always a string, even for type="number". Use valueAsNumber, or +field.value, and remember that an empty number field gives "" and NaN respectively. The checked property is the true/false state of a checkbox or radio button, and indeterminate is a third visual state that can only be set from JavaScript. A file input exposes input.files, a FileList of File objects, and FileReader (or the newer file.text() and file.arrayBuffer() promises) reads their contents:

function readFirstFile(input, onText) {
  const file = input.files?.[0];
  if (!file) return;
  if (file.size > 5_000_000) throw new Error('too large');   // check before reading
  file.text().then(onText);                                  // FileReader is the older callback form
}
console.log(typeof readFirstFile);

function

In summary, the vocabulary here is the constraint validation API, setcustomvalidity(), the validity object, the checked property and a file input.

16.12 Focus

The focus event and the blur event do not bubble. That is why an ancestor cannot hear them directly, and why focusin/focusout exist as the bubbling pair. document.activeElement always names the element that has focus, and it is the first thing to log when focus behaves oddly.

You cannot simply declare an element focusable; the platform decides. Measured, calling .focus() on five elements in turn:

at load, activeElement       = BODY
after plain div .focus()     -> BODY        (a plain div cannot take focus)
after tabindex="0" .focus()  -> tabbable
after tabindex="-1" .focus() -> prog        (programmatic only, not in the Tab order)
after button .focus()        -> btn
after disabled button.focus()-> btn         (unchanged: disabled is not focusable)
after btn.blur()             -> BODY

tabindex="0" puts an element into the Tab order at its position in the document. tabindex="-1" makes it focusable from script only, which is what you want for a heading you move focus to after a route change. A positive tabindex reorders the whole page, and is essentially always a bug. Note that focus falls back to <body> rather than to nothing.

A focus trap, keeping keyboard focus inside a dialog while it is open, is the one piece of focus management every modal needs. Getting it wrong either locks a keyboard user out of the dialog or lets them wander into the page behind it:

function trapFocus(container, { signal } = {}) {
  const SELECTOR = 'a[href], button:not([disabled]), input:not([disabled]), select, textarea, [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])';
  const previouslyFocused = document.activeElement;
  container.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
    if (e.key !== 'Tab') return;
    const items = [...container.querySelectorAll(SELECTOR)].filter(el => el.offsetParent !== null);
    if (!items.length) return;
    const first = items[0], last = items.at(-1);
    if (e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === first) { e.preventDefault(); last.focus(); }
    else if (!e.shiftKey && document.activeElement === last) { e.preventDefault(); first.focus(); }
  }, { signal });
  return () => previouslyFocused?.focus();               // restore on close — not optional
}
console.log(typeof trapFocus);

function

The list is rebuilt on every Tab press, because the dialog's contents can change, and the offsetParent filter drops hidden items. The returned function puts focus back on whatever opened the dialog, the step most implementations forget, and the one a keyboard user notices immediately. A native <dialog> element opened with showModal() does all of this for you, and should be the first thing you try.

What to carry forward from this subsection: the focus event, the blur event, document.activeelement and a focus trap.

16.13 Clipboard, Drag and Drop, and the Page Lifecycle

The Clipboard API is promise-based and needs permission. Writing is allowed in response to a user action such as a click; reading usually asks the user:

async function copy(text, button) {
  try {
    await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text);
    button.textContent = 'Copied';
  } catch {
    button.textContent = 'Press Ctrl+C';                 // denied, or not a secure context
  }
}
console.log(typeof copy);

function

It requires a secure context (§17.16), so it is undefined over plain HTTP. That is one of the most common "works on my machine, broken in staging" reports.

Drag and drop has an API whose defaults are backwards: a drop target must call preventDefault() on both dragover and drop, because the default action of each is to reject the drop. That single fact is most of what makes the API feel broken.

function acceptDrops(zone, onFiles) {
  zone.addEventListener('dragover', (e) => { e.preventDefault(); });   // required, or drop never fires
  zone.addEventListener('drop', (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    onFiles([...e.dataTransfer.files]);
  });
}
console.log(typeof acceptDrops);

function

The page lifecycle matters for saving state. beforeunload can ask the browser to show a "leave site?" confirmation, but only if the user has interacted with the page, only with the browser's own wording, and it turns off the back/forward cache (which makes the back button instant). So use it only for genuinely unsaved work. visibilitychange is the reliable one. It fires when a tab is hidden, including when a phone is locked or the user switches apps, and that is the last moment your code is guaranteed to run:

document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => {
  if (document.visibilityState === 'hidden') {
    navigator.sendBeacon('/api/save', JSON.stringify({ draft: 'text' }));   // fetch would be cancelled
  }
});
console.log(`visibilityState is currently: ${document.visibilityState}`);

visibilityState is currently: visible

Use sendBeacon rather than fetch, for the reason §17.11 gave: a fetch started as the page goes away is routinely cancelled, and a beacon is not.

The terms above, gathered: the clipboard api and beforeunload.

16.14 What This Section Established

  1. event.target is what was clicked and event.currentTarget is where the listener lives — clicking an icon inside a button made the span the target, which is the bug behind most "works except on the icon" reports.
  2. A listener is identified by type, function identity and capture flag. The same function added twice fired once; removing a freshly written arrow removed nothing; .bind(this) returns a new object every call.
  3. once and signal remove the need to keep a reference, and one AbortController tears down every listener a component owns — the same object that cancels a fetch.
  4. Three phases, and both listeners run AT_TARGET. Capture goes outer to inner, bubble inner to outer, and focus, blur and load do not bubble at all.
  5. stopPropagation does not stop other listeners on the same element — the second handler still ran — while stopImmediatePropagation does. Both are usually the wrong tool; check event.target instead.
  6. preventDefault() is unrelated to propagation. It suppresses the browser's behaviour, and cancelable says whether that is possible.
  7. this in a normal handler is currentTarget, and an arrow keeps the enclosing this — measured as #d against undefined, and this.name = panel against undefined inside a class.
  8. Delegation needs closest(), not matches(), and it serves elements that did not exist when the listener was attached.
  9. A CustomEvent does not bubble unless you say so, and dispatchEvent is synchronous and returns false when cancelled. EventTarget is extendable, so any object can be an event source.
  10. Setting .value from script fires no events — zero, measured — because the events describe user interaction.
  11. key is the character and code is the physical key. 'a' versus 'A' for the same 'KeyA'.
  12. A scroll listener must be passive, or the browser waits for it before scrolling.
  13. FormData already knows the submission rules: no name means not submitted, an unchecked checkbox is absent rather than false, an empty field is "", and repeats are preserved — which Object.fromEntries silently discards.
  14. The browser has a validation engine. validity reports which constraint failed, customError sits alongside the built-in flags rather than replacing them, and setCustomValidity('') must clear before every re-check.
  15. A plain div cannot take focus and a disabled button cannot either; focus falls back to <body>; and a focus trap that does not restore focus on close is incomplete.
  16. visibilitychange plus sendBeacon is the reliable save-on-exit, and beforeunload costs you the back/forward cache.

Exercises

1. Predict the exact output, then explain each line.

document.body.innerHTML = '<div id="a"><div id="b"><button id="c">go</button></div></div>';
const [a, b, c] = ['a', 'b', 'c'].map(id => document.getElementById(id));
a.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('a bubble'));
a.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('a capture'), true);
b.addEventListener('click', (e) => { console.log('b capture'); e.stopPropagation(); }, true);
b.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('b bubble'));
c.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('c'));
c.click();
Solution 
a capture
b capture

a capture is first, even though it was registered second. Registration order only decides ties within one element and one phase; the phase itself is decided by the path, and capture runs from the outside in before anything bubbles.

b capture runs next as the path continues inward — and calls stopPropagation().

Everything else is cancelled. stopPropagation() stops the event travelling further along the path, and at the moment it was called the path had not yet reached c at all. So the target's own listener never runs, and neither does either bubbling listener. This is the case that makes stopPropagation in a capturing listener so destructive: it can prevent an element from ever learning it was clicked.

Note what would have changed the answer. Had b's capturing listener called stopImmediatePropagation(), the output would be identical — there is only one capturing listener on b, so there is nothing extra to stop. Had it called preventDefault() instead, all five listeners would have run and only the browser's default action would have been suppressed; the two operations are unrelated (§16.4).

And had the click come from a real user rather than c.click(), the output would be the same. HTMLElement.click() dispatches a full synthetic click that travels the entire path exactly as a trusted one does — the only difference is event.isTrusted, which is false for synthetic events and is what stops a script from faking a user gesture for permission-gated APIs such as the clipboard.

2. This search form works, but it fires a request on every keystroke, breaks when the user presses Enter, and occasionally shows results for a query the user has already replaced. Fix all three.

function setUpSearch({ input, results }) {
  input.addEventListener('keyup', async () => {
    const res = await fetch('/search?q=' + input.value);
    results.innerHTML = await res.text();
  });
}
Solution

Four defects, and the third is the interesting one.

A request per keystroke. keyup fires on every key, including arrows, Shift and Tab, none of which change the value. The event should be input, which fires only on an actual value change and also catches paste, autofill and speech input — three routes keyup misses entirely.

Enter submits the form and reloads the page. There is no submit handler, so the browser's default action runs. Handling submit on the form and preventing it is the fix, and it is also what makes the form work for someone who never triggers input at all.

Stale results overwrite fresh ones. This is the race condition of §12.13: two requests are in flight, the earlier one is slower, and it lands last. Nothing about await prevents this — the responses arrive in whatever order the network delivers them.

And innerHTML with server-returned text is an XSS sink (§15.6) unless that endpoint is guaranteed to return sanitised markup.

function setUpSearch({ form, input, results, render }) {
  let inFlight = null;                                // the controller for the current request

  async function search(term) {
    inFlight?.abort();                                // cancel the superseded request outright
    if (!term.trim()) { results.replaceChildren(); return; }
    const controller = new AbortController();
    inFlight = controller;
    try {
      const res = await fetch(`/search?${new URLSearchParams({ q: term })}`, { signal: controller.signal });
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
      const items = await res.json();
      if (controller !== inFlight) return;            // belt and braces: ignore a stale response
      render(items);
    } catch (err) {
      if (err.name !== 'AbortError') results.textContent = 'Search is unavailable.';
    }
  }

  const debounced = debounce(search, 250);
  input.addEventListener('input', () => debounced(input.value));
  form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => { e.preventDefault(); search(input.value); });
  return search;
}
console.log(typeof setUpSearch);

function

Why each piece. debounce (§5.10) collapses a burst of typing into one request after 250ms of quiet — the difference between ten requests and one for the word "shoes". AbortController cancels the superseded request rather than merely ignoring its answer, which frees the connection and, on the server side, can stop the work (§12.12). The controller !== inFlight check covers the window where a response was already decoding when the abort was issued. URLSearchParams encodes the term, so a query containing & or # does not corrupt the URL (§17.5). AbortError is filtered out of the error path, because a cancelled request is not a failure and showing an error for it would flash a message on every keystroke.

The rendering fix. render(items) builds nodes and sets text (§15.6) rather than assigning markup. Submitting on Enter calls search directly rather than through the debounce, because the user has explicitly asked for it now.

Why not keydown with a check for Enter? Because the form's submit event already covers Enter in any field, the button, and requestSubmit() — and it is the only one of the four that also works for a user pressing Enter on a virtual keyboard's "Go" key (§16.8).

3. Write openDialog(el) for a modal that must be usable by keyboard and screen-reader users. List what it has to do beyond showing the element, and say why <dialog> is a better starting point.

Solution

The obligations, none of which are visual:

Move focus into the dialog when it opens — to the dialog itself or its first control — because a keyboard user's focus is otherwise still behind it, on a page they can no longer see.

Trap Tab inside it (§16.12) so focus cannot wander into the inert page behind.

Restore focus to the element that opened it on close. Skipping this drops the user at the top of the document with no idea where they were.

Close on Escape, which users expect and which costs one listener.

Hide the rest of the page from assistive technology, or a screen-reader user can read content they cannot reach. inert on the background is the modern way to do this.

Announce it as a dialog — role="dialog", aria-modal="true" and an accessible name via aria-labelledby — or it is announced as an anonymous group.

function openDialog(el, { onClose } = {}) {
  const opener = document.activeElement;
  const ac = new AbortController();
  const { signal } = ac;

  el.hidden = false;
  el.setAttribute('role', 'dialog');
  el.setAttribute('aria-modal', 'true');
  for (const sibling of document.body.children) if (sibling !== el) sibling.inert = true;

  const untrap = trapFocus(el, { signal });
  (el.querySelector('[autofocus]') ?? el).focus();

  addEventListener('keydown', (e) => { if (e.key === 'Escape') close(); }, { signal });
  el.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
    if (e.target === el) close();                       // a click on the backdrop, not inside the panel
  }, { signal });

  function close() {
    ac.abort();                                          // every listener above, in one call
    for (const sibling of document.body.children) sibling.inert = false;
    el.hidden = true;
    untrap();                                            // restores focus to `opener`
    onClose?.();
  }
  return close;
}
console.log(typeof openDialog);

function

The AbortController is doing real work here. Three listeners on three different targets — window, the dialog, and whatever trapFocus attached — are all removed by a single abort(), so there is no way to close the dialog and leave one behind. That is the pattern §16.2 introduced, and a modal is where it pays best, because a leaked Escape handler on window silently closes the next dialog too.

Why <dialog> is the better starting point. dialog.showModal() gives you, natively: the focus trap, the initial focus, focus restoration on close, Escape handling, the ::backdrop pseudo-element, promotion to the top layer so no z-index can cover it, and inertness of everything behind it — the entire list above, correctly, in every browser. The remaining work is one close event listener and an aria-labelledby.

When the manual version is still needed: a non-modal panel that must not make the page inert, or a design that must animate the dialog out (which needs @starting-style and allow-discrete, and used to fight display: none). Even then, starting from <dialog> without showModal() and adding only what is missing beats building the whole thing.

The mistake worth naming explicitly: el.style.display = 'none' as the close mechanism, with focus left inside. The element is gone visually, focus falls back to <body> (§16.12), and the user's next Tab starts from the top of the document. Restoring focus deliberately is what makes a dialog feel native.

SECTION 17

Network, Storage, Workers and Components

Everything so far has been JavaScript talking to itself and to the page. This section is JavaScript talking to everything else: a server, the disk, another thread, another tab, and the browser's own security rules. These are not language features. They are APIs the host environment (the browser or Node) provides. But a JavaScript developer who cannot use them cannot do the everyday work, and several have sharp edges that no amount of language knowledge protects you from.

The organising idea is that the platform gives you a small number of building blocks and expects you to combine them:

  • One object, AbortSignal, cancels a fetch, a listener and a stream.
  • One algorithm, structured clone, copies data between a worker, a tab and IndexedDB (the browser's built-in database).
  • One pair of concepts, origin (the scheme, host and port a page came from) and secure context (a page served over HTTPS or from your own machine), decides what is allowed at all.

Learn the building blocks, and the twenty APIs stop being twenty things to memorise.

Where a block prints results, it was run and checked. Where the browser had to be asked directly, the transcript is labelled as measured. Network calls are written as functions rather than executed, because a course whose examples depend on someone else's server is a course that breaks.

17.1 fetch(), and the Two Failure Modes

fetch() returns a promise for the Response object. It takes a URL, or the Request object, plus an object of options, and it is the only HTTP API worth learning.

async function getJSON(url, { signal } = {}) {
  const res = await fetch(url, {
    headers: { 'Accept': 'application/json' },
    signal,
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${res.status} ${res.statusText} for ${url}`);
  return res.json();
}
console.log(typeof getJSON);

function

The if (!res.ok) line is the whole lesson, and leaving it out is the most common fetch bug there is. fetch() rejects only when the request could not be made: a DNS failure, a refused connection, a CORS denial, an abort. A server that answers 404 Not Found or 500 Internal Server Error has answered, so the promise fulfils, and res.json() then throws a confusing parse error on the error page's HTML. response.ok is true exactly when response.status is between 200 and 299, and checking it is not optional.

The Request object, the Response object and the Headers object are ordinary objects you can construct yourself, which is what lets you test fetch code without a server. The Headers object in particular is a real multi-map (one name can hold several values) with case-insensitive lookup, not a plain object:

const req = new Request('https://api.example.com/items?page=2', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: new Headers({ 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }),
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: 'widget' }),
});
console.log(`${req.method} ${new URL(req.url).pathname}${new URL(req.url).search}`);
console.log(`content-type: ${req.headers.get('content-type')}`);
console.log(`headers are case-insensitive: ${req.headers.get('CONTENT-TYPE') === req.headers.get('content-type')}`);
const res = new Response(JSON.stringify({ ok: true }), { status: 201, headers: { 'X-Trace': 'abc' } });
console.log(`status ${res.status}, ok ${res.ok}, body used ${res.bodyUsed}`);
console.log(`parsed: ${JSON.stringify(await res.json())}, body used now ${res.bodyUsed}`);

POST /items?page=2
content-type: application/json
headers are case-insensitive: true
status 201, ok true, body used false
parsed: {"ok":true}, body used now true

Note bodyUsed. A response body can be read once. Calling .json() after .text() throws, because the underlying stream has been used up. Calling res.clone() before the first read is the fix when you really need two passes, for instance to log the raw text and also parse it.

One line each, for reference: response.ok and response.status.

17.2 Bodies, and Streaming a Response

Five methods read a body, and each one uses it up: response.json(), .text(), .blob(), .arrayBuffer() and .formData(). response.json() is the one you reach for nine times out of ten, and it parses the text rather than merely decoding it. Each returns a promise, because the body may still be arriving.

A request body may be a string, FormData, URLSearchParams, a Blob, an ArrayBuffer or a stream. In most cases your choice sets the Content-Type for you. That is why setting Content-Type: multipart/form-data by hand on a FormData body breaks the request: the browser must add a boundary parameter to that header, and cannot if you have overwritten it:

function uploadForm(url, formElement) {
  return fetch(url, { method: 'POST', body: new FormData(formElement) });  // no Content-Type header
}
function postJSON(url, data) {
  return fetch(url, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(data),
  });
}
console.log(typeof uploadForm, typeof postJSON);

function function

Streaming a response means handling the bytes as they arrive, instead of waiting for the whole body. res.body is a ReadableStream, and it is what makes a progress bar, or a model's answer appearing word by word, possible:

async function* streamLines(res) {
  const reader = res.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader();
  let buffer = '';
  try {
    for (;;) {
      const { value, done } = await reader.read();
      if (done) break;
      buffer += value;
      const lines = buffer.split('\n');
      buffer = lines.pop();                 // the last piece may be incomplete
      yield* lines;
    }
    if (buffer) yield buffer;
  } finally {
    reader.releaseLock();
  }
}
console.log(typeof streamLines);

function

Two details make that correct rather than nearly correct. The buffer/lines.pop() routine exists because a chunk boundary is not a line boundary: a chunk can end in the middle of a line, and splitting each chunk separately silently corrupts the data. And the finally releases the reader's lock even if the consumer abandons the loop. That is the difference between a cancelled download and a leaked connection.

Because a ReadableStream is async-iterable in modern runtimes, for await (const chunk of res.body) (§11.9) is often all you need.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: a request body.

17.3 The Same-Origin Policy, CORS, and Credentials

The same-origin policy is the foundation of browser security: a script from one origin cannot read data from another. An origin is the combination scheme + host + port. https://example.com and https://api.example.com are different origins, and so are the http:// and https:// versions of the same host.

CORS, cross-origin resource sharing, is how a server lifts that restriction for particular callers. The critical thing to understand: CORS is enforced by the browser and granted by the server. Your JavaScript cannot switch it on, your fetch options cannot get around it, and a request that works in curl but fails in the browser is almost always this.

The flow has two shapes. A simple request (a GET, a HEAD, or a POST with a form-like content type and no custom headers) is sent straight away. The browser then checks the response for Access-Control-Allow-Origin before letting your code see it. Note what that means: the request already happened, side effects and all. CORS hid the answer, not the call.

Anything else triggers a preflight request: an OPTIONS call the browser sends first, announcing the method and headers it intends to use, which the server must approve.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin
The origin permitted to read the response, or *. Required on every cross-origin response.
Access-Control-Allow-Methods
Answered to a preflight. PUT, PATCH and DELETE always need one.
Access-Control-Allow-Headers
Which custom request headers are allowed. One Authorization header is enough to require a preflight.
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
Must be true for cookies to be sent — and then Allow-Origin may not be *. This pairing is deliberate and catches everyone once.

The credentials mode decides whether cookies and HTTP authentication are sent with the request:

function callApi(url) {
  return fetch(url, {
    credentials: 'include',   // 'same-origin' is the default; 'omit' sends nothing
    mode: 'cors',
    headers: { 'Authorization': 'Bearer ' + getToken() },
  });
}
console.log(typeof callApi);

function

credentials: 'include' on a cross-origin call requires the server to send both Allow-Credentials: true and a specific Allow-Origin. And mode: 'no-cors' is not a way around any of this: it produces an opaque response, whose status reads as 0 and whose body you cannot read at all.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: a preflight request and the credentials mode.

17.4 Cookies

document.cookie is one of the worst APIs on the platform. Reading it gives one semicolon-separated string of every cookie you are allowed to read. Writing it adds or replaces one cookie, rather than replacing them all.

document.cookie = 'theme=dark; Max-Age=31536000; Path=/; SameSite=Lax';
document.cookie = 'lang=en; Path=/';
const jar = Object.fromEntries(document.cookie.split('; ').map(c => {
  const i = c.indexOf('=');
  return [decodeURIComponent(c.slice(0, i)), decodeURIComponent(c.slice(i + 1))];
}));
console.log(JSON.stringify(jar));
console.log(`deleting is setting an expiry in the past`);
document.cookie = 'lang=; Path=/; Max-Age=0';
console.log(`lang still present: ${document.cookie.includes('lang=en')}`);

{"theme":"dark","lang":"en"}
deleting is setting an expiry in the past
lang still present: false

Four attributes matter, and you cannot read any of them back: document.cookie returns names and values only.

  • HttpOnly makes a cookie completely invisible to JavaScript. That is where a session token belongs, precisely so that an XSS bug (§15.6) cannot steal it.
  • Secure restricts it to HTTPS.
  • Path and Domain limit which URLs it is sent to.
  • And SameSite decides whether it is sent on requests from other sites: Strict never, Lax only when the user navigates to your site at the top level (the modern default), None always, and None requires Secure.

SameSite is the platform's built-in defence against cross-site request forgery (another site making requests as your logged-in user), and understanding it is worth more than any token scheme added on top.

17.5 URLs Are Objects, Not Strings

The URL object parses, resolves and rebuilds URLs, and manipulating URLs as strings is a bug waiting to happen.

const u = new URL('/catalog/item?q=red shoes&size=9&size=10#reviews', 'https://shop.example.com');
console.log(`href     = ${u.href}`);
console.log(`origin   = ${u.origin}, pathname = ${u.pathname}, hash = ${u.hash}`);
console.log(`get('q')       = ${JSON.stringify(u.searchParams.get('q'))}`);
console.log(`getAll('size') = ${JSON.stringify(u.searchParams.getAll('size'))}`);
u.searchParams.set('size', '11');
u.searchParams.append('tag', 'a&b=c');
console.log(`after set + append: ${u.search}`);

href     = https://shop.example.com/catalog/item?q=red%20shoes&size=9&size=10#reviews
origin   = https://shop.example.com, pathname = /catalog/item, hash = #reviews
get('q')       = "red shoes"
getAll('size') = ["9","10"]
after set + append: ?q=red+shoes&size=11&tag=a%26b%3Dc

Three measured details. The second argument is a base, so relative URLs resolve exactly as they do in markup. URL.searchParams decodes for you (get('q') returned red shoes with a real space), and a repeated key is not an error, which is why getAll() exists alongside get(). And note that the space changed spelling: the parsed href kept %20, while rebuilding it through searchParams produced +, because URLSearchParams uses form encoding. Both decode to the same string; a server that treats + literally will disagree, and that is the server's bug.

encodeURIComponent() escapes everything that has meaning inside one part of a URL, including &, =, ? and /. encodeURI() deliberately does not, because it is meant for encoding a whole URL. Measured: encodeURIComponent('a&b=c') gives a%26b%3Dc, and encodeURI('a&b=c') gives a&b=c unchanged. Building a query string by hand is where injection bugs live; searchParams encodes correctly by design, so use it.

To have in hand before moving on: the url object, url.searchparams and encodeuricomponent().

17.6 localStorage, sessionStorage and the Storage Event

localStorage is a synchronous map from strings to strings, separate for each origin, that survives browser restarts. sessionStorage is identical, but belongs to one tab and is cleared when the tab closes.

localStorage.clear();
localStorage.setItem('count', 42);
localStorage.setItem('user', { name: 'Ada' });
localStorage.setItem('userJson', JSON.stringify({ name: 'Ada' }));
console.log(`getItem('count') is a ${typeof localStorage.getItem('count')}: ${JSON.stringify(localStorage.getItem('count'))}`);
console.log(`an object stored directly: ${JSON.stringify(localStorage.getItem('user'))}`);
console.log(`through JSON.stringify:    ${JSON.stringify(localStorage.getItem('userJson'))}`);
console.log(`a missing key returns:     ${JSON.stringify(localStorage.getItem('nope'))}`);

getItem('count') is a string: "42"
an object stored directly: "[object Object]"
through JSON.stringify:    "{\"name\":\"Ada\"}"
a missing key returns:     null

Everything is a string. The number 42 came back as "42", and an object stored directly became the literal text [object Object]: silently, with no error, and impossible to recover. Convert with JSON.stringify on the way in and parse on the way out, and wrap the parse in a try, because the stored string may have been written by an older version of your code.

Three more constraints:

  • It is synchronous, so it blocks the main thread. That is fine for a handful of small keys, and wrong for anything large or used constantly.
  • A storage quota applies, typically around 5MB per origin. Going over it throws a QuotaExceededError, which you must catch, because it is the one failure that only shows up for your heaviest users.
  • And the storage event fires in other tabs of the same origin when a key changes, never in the tab that made the change. That makes it a free way to keep tabs in sync:
// Fires in every OTHER tab of this origin. e.key is null when clear() was called.
addEventListener('storage', (e) => {
  if (e.key === 'theme') document.documentElement.dataset.theme = e.newValue;
});
console.log('a storage listener keeps tabs in step for free');

a storage listener keeps tabs in step for free

Named once more, since each is referred to later: a storage quota.

17.7 IndexedDB

IndexedDB is the real database: asynchronous, transactional, indexed, and able to hold hundreds of megabytes. It stores values using structured clone rather than strings, so objects, Maps, Dates, Blobs and typed arrays all go in without being converted.

Its API is old and based on events rather than promises, so in practice a small wrapper is not optional:

function openDb(name, version, upgrade) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const req = indexedDB.open(name, version);
    req.onupgradeneeded = (e) => upgrade(req.result, e.oldVersion);
    req.onsuccess = () => resolve(req.result);
    req.onerror = () => reject(req.error);
    req.onblocked = () => reject(new Error('another tab holds an older version open'));
  });
}
function putAll(db, storeName, records) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const tx = db.transaction(storeName, 'readwrite');
    const store = tx.objectStore(storeName);
    for (const r of records) store.put(r);
    tx.oncomplete = resolve;
    tx.onerror = () => reject(tx.error);
  });
}
console.log(typeof openDb, typeof putAll);

function function

Four concepts carry the whole model:

  • An object store is a table. It can be created only inside an upgradeneeded handler, because the structure can change nowhere else, and that is why the version number exists.
  • An IndexedDB transaction is the unit of all-or-nothing work, and it has a lifetime trap that catches everyone. It auto-commits when the event loop yields without any pending request against it, so an await on anything unrelated in the middle of a transaction ends it. Keep transactions synchronous in shape.
  • An index lets you query by a field other than the key.
  • An IndexedDB cursor walks through a store or an index in key order without loading everything at once, which is how you page through a large store.

The onblocked handler is not optional either. If another tab has the database open at an older version, the upgrade waits forever unless that tab closes its connection.

In summary, the vocabulary here is an indexeddb transaction and an indexeddb cursor.

17.8 Talking Between Contexts

Three mechanisms move data across a boundary, and all three use the structured clone algorithm instead of JSON. So Date, Map, Set, RegExp, ArrayBuffer and cyclic references survive, while functions, DOM nodes and class identity do not.

structuredClone() gives you that algorithm directly, and it is the correct way to make a deep copy (§2.14):

const original = { when: new Date(0), tags: new Set(['a']), nested: { n: 1 } };
original.self = original;                       // a cycle
const copy = structuredClone(original);
console.log(`cycle preserved: ${copy.self === copy}`);
console.log(`Date survived as a Date: ${copy.when instanceof Date}, Set as a Set: ${copy.tags instanceof Set}`);
console.log(`deep, not shallow: ${copy.nested !== original.nested}`);
try { structuredClone({ fn: () => 1 }); } catch (e) { console.log(`functions cannot cross: ${e.constructor.name}`); }

cycle preserved: true
Date survived as a Date: true, Set as a Set: true
deep, not shallow: true
functions cannot cross: DOMException

postMessage() sends a structured clone to another window, iframe or worker. Across origins it takes a target origin, and the receiving side must check event.origin. Leaving out that check is how a page ends up accepting commands from any site that can get a reference to it:

function listenForMessages(trusted, handle) {
  addEventListener('message', (event) => {
    if (event.origin !== trusted) return;        // the check that is always omitted
    handle(event.data);
  });
}
console.log(typeof listenForMessages);

function

BroadcastChannel is the simple case. Every page or worker of the same origin that subscribes to the same channel name receives whatever any of them posts, with no references to pass around. It is the right tool for "the user logged out in another tab":

const bus = new BroadcastChannel('auth');
bus.onmessage = (e) => console.log(`received: ${JSON.stringify(e.data)}`);
bus.postMessage({ type: 'logout' });
await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 5));
console.log('the sending context does not receive its own message');
bus.close();

the sending context does not receive its own message

A transferable object is the way out of copying: an ArrayBuffer listed for transfer is moved rather than cloned. It becomes detached in the sender, and the move costs nothing whatever the size.

What to carry forward from this subsection: postmessage().

17.9 Workers

A Web Worker runs JavaScript on a worker thread, in parallel with the main thread, and with no access to the DOM. That last restriction is what makes it safe: there is no shared changeable state to fight over, only messages.

function startWorker(url, onResult) {
  const worker = new Worker(url, { type: 'module' });
  worker.addEventListener('message', (e) => onResult(e.data));
  worker.addEventListener('error', (e) => console.error('worker failed:', e.message));
  return {
    run: (payload, transfer = []) => worker.postMessage(payload, transfer),
    stop: () => worker.terminate(),
  };
}
console.log(typeof startWorker);

function

Inside the worker, self is the global object, postMessage sends results back, and importScripts (classic workers) or import (module workers) loads code. What belongs there is anything that keeps the processor busy and would otherwise block a frame: parsing a large JSON or CSV file, image processing, cryptography, building a search index, comparing large texts. What does not belong there is anything that needs the DOM. A worker has fetch, WebSocket, IndexedDB, crypto and timers, but no document.

The cost to weigh is crossing the message boundary. Structured-cloning a large object has a real price, so a worker that receives 50MB, does 2ms of work and sends 50MB back is slower than doing the work in place. Transferables remove that cost for binary data. For everything else, move enough work into the worker to make the crossing worthwhile.

The terms above, gathered: a web worker and a worker thread.

17.10 Service Workers, the Cache API and Offline

A service worker is a worker that sits between the page and the network, as a proxy you can program. It has no DOM, the browser can start and stop it at any time, and it keeps running after the page closes, which is what makes push notifications and background sync possible.

The service worker lifecycle is the part that causes confusion, and it is deliberately cautious:

install
Fires once for a byte-different script. The place to pre-cache. skipWaiting() overrides the wait.
waiting
A new worker waits until every tab controlled by the old one is gone. Reloading is not enough — the old page overlaps the new one.
activate
Now in charge. The place to delete old caches. clients.claim() takes over existing pages.
fetch
Every request from a controlled page, yours to answer. Not calling respondWith lets it go to the network normally.
// sw.js — cache-first for static assets, network-first for everything else.
function installServiceWorkerHandlers(self, CACHE, ASSETS) {
  self.addEventListener('install', (e) =>
    e.waitUntil(caches.open(CACHE).then(c => c.addAll(ASSETS))));

  self.addEventListener('activate', (e) => e.waitUntil((async () => {
    for (const key of await caches.keys()) if (key !== CACHE) await caches.delete(key);
    await self.clients.claim();
  })()));

  self.addEventListener('fetch', (e) => {
    if (e.request.method !== 'GET') return;              // never cache a mutation
    e.respondWith((async () => {
      const hit = await caches.match(e.request);
      if (hit) return hit;
      const res = await fetch(e.request);
      if (res.ok) (await caches.open(CACHE)).put(e.request, res.clone());
      return res;
    })());
  });
}
console.log(typeof installServiceWorkerHandlers);

function

The Cache API is a separate store of Request/Response pairs. Calling res.clone() before caching is mandatory, for the reason §17.1 gave: a body can be read once, and you must both return it and store it. Offline support follows directly from this. With the app's shell in a cache and a fetch handler that falls back to it, the app opens with no network at all. navigator.onLine reports connectivity, but treat it as a hint: it says a network interface exists, not that anything can be reached.

Two rules that save real pain. Never cache a non-GET. And never cache your service worker script or your HTML entry point with a cache-first strategy, or you can ship a version that can never update itself.

One line each, for reference: the service worker lifecycle.

17.11 Live Connections

There are three ways to receive data that the server sends without being asked, and choosing between them is mostly about direction.

WebSocket is two-way (full-duplex) over a single long-lived connection, and it is the right answer for chat, collaborative editing and games:

function connect(url, onMessage) {
  const ws = new WebSocket(url);
  ws.addEventListener('message', (e) => onMessage(JSON.parse(e.data)));
  ws.addEventListener('close', (e) => {
    if (!e.wasClean) setTimeout(() => connect(url, onMessage), 1000);  // reconnect with backoff
  });
  return ws;
}
console.log(typeof connect);

function

There is no automatic reconnection and no guarantee of delivery. So a real client needs the reconnect-with-backoff of §12.14, a heartbeat to notice a dead connection that was never properly closed, and acknowledgement of each message if delivery matters.

Server-sent events are the one-way alternative: an EventSource over plain HTTP that the browser reconnects automatically, with event ids so the server can resume where it stopped. For notifications, live scores or a progress feed, anything the client never replies on, it is simpler than a WebSocket and gets through proxies better.

navigator.sendBeacon() solves the case both of those handle badly: sending a small amount of data as the page goes away. A fetch started in a visibilitychange or pagehide handler is routinely cancelled when the page unloads. A beacon is queued by the browser and delivered anyway, and it is the only correct way to send analytics or save final state on exit.

Collected, because the rest of the course leans on them: server-sent events and navigator.sendbeacon().

17.12 Navigation and Client-Side Routing

history.pushState() changes the URL without loading a new page, and it is the foundation of every single-page router (the code that decides what to show for each URL).

function navigate(path, state = {}) {
  history.pushState(state, '', path);          // replaceState to avoid a new entry
  render(path);
}
addEventListener('popstate', (e) => render(location.pathname, e.state));
console.log(typeof navigate);

function

Two facts about it are easy to get wrong. pushState does not fire popstate: it changes the URL and nothing else, so you must call your own render function, which is why the pattern above pairs them explicitly. And the popstate event fires only when the user moves through history (back, forward, history.go()), carrying the state object you pushed.

Client-side routing built on that has three duties beyond keeping the URL right, and skipping them is what makes a single-page app feel broken to some users:

  • The server must serve the app's shell for every route, or refreshing on a deep link gives a 404.
  • Focus must move to the new content and the change must be announced, or a screen-reader user is told nothing happened (§16.13).
  • And the scroll position must be restored when the user goes back, which history.scrollRestoration = 'manual' deliberately hands to you.

The Navigation API is the modern replacement, and it is much better designed.
