It has a single navigate event that intercepts every navigation, including link clicks and form submissions, a real promise for when the navigation finishes, and a proper list of history entries. It is not yet available everywhere, so feature-detect it and keep the popstate path as the fallback.

The pieces this subsection introduced, in one line: history.pushstate(), the popstate event and the Navigation API.

17.13 Custom Elements

A custom element is a real HTML element that you define, with its own class, its own lifecycle and its own behaviour: the platform's own component model, with no framework and no build step.

class TagChip extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['label'];
  #button;
  constructor() {
    super();                                    // must come first, and nothing else may touch attributes here
    this.#button = document.createElement('button');
  }
  connectedCallback() {
    this.#button.type = 'button';
    this.append(this.#button);
    this.#button.addEventListener('click', this.#onClick);
  }
  disconnectedCallback() { this.#button.removeEventListener('click', this.#onClick); }
  attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) {
    if (name === 'label') this.#button.textContent = newValue ?? '';
  }
  #onClick = () => this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('chip-remove', { bubbles: true, detail: { label: this.getAttribute('label') } }));
}
customElements.define('tag-chip', TagChip);
document.body.innerHTML = '<tag-chip label="urgent"></tag-chip>';
console.log(document.querySelector('tag-chip').textContent);

urgent

customElements.define() registers the name, which must contain a hyphen. That guarantees it can never collide with a future HTML element. Registering after the markup already exists is fine: the browser upgrades matching elements already in the document. That is what lets the definition load later without a flash of unstyled content.

The order of the lifecycle callbacks is worth measuring rather than assuming. Here: creating an element, setting an attribute, appending it, changing the attribute, removing it, and then defining a second element whose markup already existed:

constructor
--- created, not yet in the document
attributeChangedCallback label: null -> "first"
connectedCallback, isConnected=true
--- appended
attributeChangedCallback label: "first" -> "second"
disconnectedCallback
--- upgrade of pre-existing markup
late connectedCallback

Note that attributeChangedCallback ran before connectedCallback, on an element that was not yet in the document. That is the reason for the rules about the constructor: it may not look at attributes, add children, or touch the document, because it can run before any of those exist. All of that belongs in connectedCallback. That callback can run more than once, because moving an element disconnects and reconnects it, so it must be idempotent (safe to run repeatedly) and must remove its listeners again in disconnectedCallback.

observedAttributes is the list you opt in with. An attribute not named there fires no callback at all, which is the first thing to check when a custom element ignores an attribute.

To have in hand before moving on: customelements.define().

17.14 Shadow DOM

Shadow DOM gives an element a private subtree, with its own scope for ids, its own boundary for styles, and its own hit-testing (deciding what was clicked). It is the only encapsulation the platform enforces.

attachShadow() creates it, and a shadow root mode of 'open' or 'closed' decides whether element.shadowRoot exposes it:

document.body.innerHTML = '<div id="host"><p class="light">from the page</p></div>';
const host = document.getElementById('host');
const root = host.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
root.innerHTML = '<style>p { color: blue }</style><p id="inner">inside</p><slot></slot>';
console.log(`host.shadowRoot exposed: ${!!host.shadowRoot}`);
console.log(`document.querySelector('#inner'): ${document.querySelector('#inner')}`);
console.log(`root.querySelector('#inner'):     ${root.querySelector('#inner').textContent}`);
console.log(`inner.getRootNode() === root:     ${root.getElementById('inner').getRootNode() === root}`);
console.log(`the light-DOM p is assigned to a ${host.querySelector('.light').assignedSlot?.nodeName}`);

host.shadowRoot exposed: true
document.querySelector('#inner'): null
root.querySelector('#inner'):     inside
inner.getRootNode() === root:     true
the light-DOM p is assigned to a SLOT

document.querySelector('#inner') returned null: selectors do not cross the boundary in either direction. That is exactly the point, and also what breaks naive test selectors and third-party scripts. getRootNode() is how a node inside a component finds its own root instead of document.

Measured in Chromium, styling follows the boundary. A page rule p { color: red } does not reach #inner, which took the shadow stylesheet's blue. The slotted paragraph, which lives in the page's own DOM (the light DOM) and is only displayed inside, kept the page's red. Content is projected, not moved.

The slot element is that projection point, and the <slot> element is the only place inside a shadow root where the page's own children appear. Children the page puts inside the host element are placed into slots by name. They remain the page's children for every purpose except display: the page's CSS styles them, host.querySelector finds them, and assignedSlot says where they ended up.

mode: 'closed' makes element.shadowRoot return null, and attaching a second root throws:

closed root: host.shadowRoot = null
attaching a second shadow root throws: NotSupportedError

'closed' is weaker privacy than it looks, because the code that attached the root still holds a reference to it. It mostly costs you the ability to debug and test, so 'open' is the sensible default.

Named once more, since each is referred to later: attachshadow(), a shadow root mode and the slot element.

17.15 Form-Associated Elements, and Canvas

A custom element with an <input> inside it does not take part in its form: it is not submitted, not validated, and not reset. A form-associated custom element fixes that, and ElementInternals is the object that gives it those powers:

class RatingInput extends HTMLElement {
  static formAssociated = true;                 // the opt-in
  #internals;
  constructor() { super(); this.#internals = this.attachInternals(); }
  set value(v) {
    this.#internals.setFormValue(String(v));    // now it submits with the form
    this.#internals.setValidity(v ? {} : { valueMissing: true }, 'Pick a rating', this);
  }
  formResetCallback() { this.value = ''; }
  get form() { return this.#internals.form; }
}
console.log(typeof RatingInput, RatingInput.formAssociated);

function true

attachInternals() also covers accessibility. internals.role and internals.ariaLabel set the element's meaning for assistive technology without cluttering its attributes, and setValidity plugs it into the same constraint validation API as a native input (§16.11).

The canvas element is the way out to raw pixels. getContext() returns a drawing context: '2d' for the immediate-mode drawing API (you draw, and the canvas keeps only pixels), and 'webgl2' or 'webgpu' for the graphics card:

function drawSparkline(canvas, values) {
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
  const dpr = devicePixelRatio || 1;
  canvas.width = canvas.clientWidth * dpr;      // the backing store, in device pixels
  canvas.height = canvas.clientHeight * dpr;
  ctx.scale(dpr, dpr);                          // so one unit is one CSS pixel again
  ctx.beginPath();
  values.forEach((v, i) => ctx.lineTo(i * 4, 40 - v));
  ctx.stroke();
}
console.log(typeof drawSparkline);

function

The devicePixelRatio routine is the thing everyone gets wrong first. A canvas has a CSS size and a separate size for its actual pixel buffer, and setting only the CSS size gives a blurry picture on any high-density screen. Setting canvas.width also clears the canvas, so it belongs in the code that handles resizing, not in the code that draws.

A canvas is just pixels, so it has no accessibility tree of its own: anything conveyed only by a canvas must also exist as text, or as fallback content inside the element. OffscreenCanvas moves drawing to a worker, for genuinely heavy rendering.

In summary, the vocabulary here is a form-associated custom element, elementinternals, the canvas element and getcontext().

17.16 Measuring, and the Security Surface

performance.now() returns a timestamp, finer than a millisecond, measured from when the page loaded, and it only ever moves forward (it is monotonic). Use it rather than Date.now() for measuring durations: the wall clock can jump backwards when the system time is corrected, producing negative elapsed times.

PerformanceObserver is how you read the browser's own timing records instead of measuring by hand, and it is the only way to get Core Web Vitals from real users:

function reportVitals(send) {
  new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
    for (const entry of list.getEntries()) send({ name: entry.name, value: entry.startTime });
  }).observe({ type: 'largest-contentful-paint', buffered: true });   // buffered: entries from before this ran
}
console.log(typeof reportVitals);

function

buffered: true matters, because the interesting records often happen before your monitoring code runs. The three current vitals are:

  • LCP (largest contentful paint): how fast the page loads.
  • INP (interaction to next paint): how fast it responds, which is exactly what §12.1's discussion of blocking is about.
  • CLS (cumulative layout shift): how much the layout jumps around.

On security, four things belong in a JavaScript developer's head.

A secure context (a page served over HTTPS, or from localhost) is required by almost every powerful API: service workers, crypto.subtle, geolocation, writing to the clipboard. If an API is undefined in production but works on your machine, this is why.

Content Security Policy is a response header that limits what the page may load and run. script-src 'self' blocks injected inline scripts, which turns most XSS attacks from a compromise into a console error. require-trusted-types-for 'script' extends that protection to the DOM sinks of §15.6. CSP is defence in depth, a second layer, not a substitute for not building HTML from strings.

eval() and new Function() run strings as code. eval() can also see the surrounding scope, which defeats minification and every optimisation, while new Function() compiles in the global scope and is the slightly less bad of the two. A reasonable CSP blocks both, and the legitimate uses are so rare that reaching for either should make you rethink: JSON.parse for data, a lookup object for choosing behaviour, a real template engine for templates.

crypto.randomUUID() produces a cryptographically random v4 UUID, and crypto.getRandomValues() fills a typed array with random bytes. Math.random() is not random enough for anything security-related, such as a token, a session id or a password reset link, and checking the difference costs nothing:

const id = crypto.randomUUID();
console.log(`length ${id.length}, group sizes ${id.split('-').map(g => g.length).join('-')}`);
console.log(`the version nibble is 4: ${id[14] === '4'}`);
console.log(`two calls differ: ${crypto.randomUUID() !== crypto.randomUUID()}`);

length 36, group sizes 8-4-4-4-12
the version nibble is 4: true
two calls differ: true

What to carry forward from this subsection: math.random(), performance.now(), core web vitals and crypto.randomuuid().

17.17 What This Section Established

  1. fetch() rejects only when there was no answer. A 404 fulfils, so if (!res.ok) throw is mandatory; response.status in 200–299 is what response.ok means.
  2. A body reads once. bodyUsed went false then true across one .json(); res.clone() is the fix, and the Cache API requires it.
  3. Streaming means handling chunk boundaries. A chunk can end mid-line, so a line reader must buffer the remainder, and finally { reader.releaseLock() } is what separates a cancelled download from a leaked connection.
  4. CORS is granted by the server and enforced by the browser, and a simple request has already reached the server before the browser hides the answer. credentials: 'include' forbids Allow-Origin: *.
  5. SameSite and HttpOnly do more for security than any token scheme layered above them, and document.cookie returns names and values only — never the attributes.
  6. URL and URLSearchParams encode correctly by construction. getAll('size') returned ["9","10"], and re-serialising turned %20 into + because form encoding is what URLSearchParams speaks.
  7. localStorage stores strings and nothing else — an object put in directly came back as "[object Object]", silently. It is synchronous, capped near 5MB, and its storage event fires only in other tabs.
  8. An IndexedDB transaction auto-commits when the loop yields, so an unrelated await inside one ends it; schema changes happen only in upgradeneeded.
  9. Structured clone, not JSON, is the platform's copy. Cycles, Date and Set survived; a function threw a DOMException. postMessage uses it, and event.origin must be checked.
  10. A worker has no DOM and that is the safety property. Weigh the cloning cost of the message boundary; transferables make it free for binary data.
  11. A new service worker waits for every old tab to close, res.clone() is required before caching, and a cache-first entry point can ship an app that cannot update itself.
  12. pushState does not fire popstate. Client-side routing owes a server fallback, focus management and scroll restoration.
  13. attributeChangedCallback runs before connectedCallback, which is why the constructor may not read attributes or add children — measured, along with the upgrade of markup that existed before define() was called.
  14. Selectors do not cross a shadow boundary in either direction — document.querySelector('#inner') was null while root.querySelector('#inner') found it — and slotted content stays in the light DOM, keeping the page's styles.
  15. formAssociated plus attachInternals() is what makes a custom element submit, validate and reset like a native control.
  16. A canvas has two sizes, and ignoring devicePixelRatio is why canvases look blurry; setting canvas.width clears it.
  17. Math.random() is not for tokens. crypto.randomUUID() is, and a secure context is the precondition for most capable APIs.

Exercises

1. This "offline-first" service worker was shipped and users report that the site is stuck on an old version and cannot be updated even by hard-refreshing. Find every cause and fix the file.

self.addEventListener('install', (e) => {
  e.waitUntil(caches.open('v1').then(c => c.addAll(['/', '/index.html', '/app.js', '/sw.js'])));
});
self.addEventListener('fetch', (e) => {
  e.respondWith(caches.match(e.request).then(hit => hit || fetch(e.request)));
});
Solution

Cause 1 — the HTML entry point is cached with a cache-first strategy. / and /index.html are served from v1 forever, and the HTML is what references the hashed asset filenames, so no new asset can ever be discovered. This alone makes the site unupdatable.

Cause 2 — /sw.js is in the cache and served by the fetch handler. The browser checks for a new service worker by fetching its script, and that check goes through this handler, so the browser is handed the old script and concludes nothing has changed. The worker can now never be replaced.

Cause 3 — there is no activate handler, so old caches are never deleted. Even when a new version does install, v1 accumulates alongside v2 and counts against the origin's quota.

Cause 4 — every request is answered from cache, including non-GET. A POST served from a cache is a lost mutation; caches.match will not match one, but respondWith is still hijacking the request unnecessarily, and any Range request for media is answered wrongly.

Cause 5 — nothing calls skipWaiting/clients.claim, so even a correct new worker sits in waiting until every tab closes. A refresh does not help, because the old page and new page overlap.

const CACHE = 'v2';
const ASSETS = ['/app.js', '/styles.css'];       // hashed static assets only — no HTML, no sw.js

self.addEventListener('install', (e) => {
  e.waitUntil(caches.open(CACHE).then(c => c.addAll(ASSETS)).then(() => self.skipWaiting()));
});

self.addEventListener('activate', (e) => e.waitUntil((async () => {
  for (const key of await caches.keys()) if (key !== CACHE) await caches.delete(key);
  await self.clients.claim();
})()));

self.addEventListener('fetch', (e) => {
  const { request } = e;
  if (request.method !== 'GET') return;                       // let mutations go to the network

  // Navigations: network-first, cache only as an offline fallback.
  if (request.mode === 'navigate') {
    e.respondWith((async () => {
      try { return await fetch(request); }
      catch { return (await caches.match('/offline.html')) ?? Response.error(); }
    })());
    return;
  }

  // Hashed static assets: cache-first is safe, because the URL changes when the file does.
  e.respondWith((async () => {
    const hit = await caches.match(request);
    if (hit) return hit;
    const res = await fetch(request);
    if (res.ok) (await caches.open(CACHE)).put(request, res.clone());
    return res;
  })());
});

The principle that organises all five fixes: cache-first is safe only when the URL changes whenever the content does. Hashed asset filenames have that property; HTML does not, and the service worker script itself certainly does not. Getting that one rule right removes the whole class of "stuck on an old version" bug.

On skipWaiting: it is correct here because every cached asset is hashed, so an old page and a new worker cannot disagree. If assets were not hashed, taking over immediately could serve v2 assets to a v1 page, and the conservative wait would be the right behaviour.

2. Build a <user-avatar> custom element that shows an image with initials as a fallback, updates when its src or name attribute changes, uses shadow DOM so the page cannot restyle its internals by accident, and leaks nothing when removed.

Solution 
const AVATAR_CSS = `
  :host { display: inline-grid; inline-size: 2.5rem; aspect-ratio: 1; }
  :host([hidden]) { display: none }
  .frame { display: grid; place-items: center; border-radius: 50%; overflow: clip;
           background: var(--avatar-bg, #ddd); block-size: 100%; }
  img { inline-size: 100%; block-size: 100%; object-fit: cover }
`;

class UserAvatar extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['src', 'name'];
  #frame; #img; #controller;

  constructor() {
    super();
    const root = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
    const style = document.createElement('style');
    style.textContent = AVATAR_CSS;
    root.append(style);
    this.#frame = document.createElement('div');
    this.#frame.className = 'frame';
    root.append(this.#frame);
  }

  connectedCallback() {
    this.#controller = new AbortController();
    if (!this.hasAttribute('role')) {
      this.setAttribute('role', 'img');            // pixels need a name (§17.15)
    }
    this.#render();
  }

  disconnectedCallback() {
    this.#controller?.abort();                     // removes every listener at once
    this.#controller = null;
  }

  attributeChangedCallback() {
    if (this.isConnected) this.#render();          // ignore changes before connection
  }

  #render() {
    const name = this.getAttribute('name') ?? '';
    const src = this.getAttribute('src');
    this.setAttribute('aria-label', name || 'User');
    this.#frame.textContent = name.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).map(w => w[0]).slice(0, 2).join('').toUpperCase();
    this.#img?.remove();
    this.#img = null;
    if (!src) return;
    const img = document.createElement('img');
    img.alt = '';                                  // the host carries the name; the img must not repeat it
    img.addEventListener('error', () => img.remove(), { signal: this.#controller.signal });
    img.src = src;
    this.#frame.append(img);
    this.#img = img;
  }
}
customElements.define('user-avatar', UserAvatar);
document.body.innerHTML = '<user-avatar name="Ada Lovelace"></user-avatar>';
const el = document.querySelector('user-avatar');
console.log(`initials: ${el.shadowRoot.querySelector('.frame').textContent}`);
console.log(`accessible name: ${el.getAttribute('aria-label')}, role: ${el.getAttribute('role')}`);

initials: AL
accessible name: Ada Lovelace, role: img

Why each decision.

The constructor attaches the shadow root and nothing else — it does not read attributes or touch the document, because §17.13 measured attributeChangedCallback firing before connectedCallback on an element that was not yet in the tree. All rendering waits for connection.

One AbortController per connection removes every listener at once. Because addEventListener accepts a signal (§16.6), disconnectedCallback needs one abort() call rather than a matching removeEventListener for each — and since connectedCallback can run again after a move, a fresh controller is created each time.

The stylesheet lives in the shadow root, so the page cannot reach it. A <style> element is the portable spelling; the production refinement is to build one CSSStyleSheet at module level with replaceSync and assign root.adoptedStyleSheets = [sheet] in the constructor, which parses the CSS once for the whole page instead of once per instance — the difference §15.10 describes, and it matters the moment a list renders two hundred avatars. :host styles the element itself, and var(--avatar-bg) is deliberate: custom properties do cross the shadow boundary, so that is the sanctioned way to let the page theme a component whose internals it cannot select.

The accessibility pieces are not decoration. A shadow root hides the image from the page's selectors but not from the accessibility tree; the host gets role="img" and an aria-label, and the inner <img> takes alt="" so the name is not announced twice.

What is deliberately not here: no innerHTML anywhere, so there is no sink for a hostile name (§15.6); and attributeChangedCallback guards on isConnected, so setting three attributes before insertion renders once rather than three times.

3. A dashboard fetches six independent widgets, and the tab freezes for about 400ms while it parses one large JSON payload. Explain what to change and why each part of the answer is necessary, including what a worker will not fix.

Solution

Two separate problems are hiding in one symptom.

The six fetches are a concurrency question, and Promise.allSettled is the answer (§12.8). Independent widgets must not be Promise.all-ed, because one failing endpoint would discard five good responses; and they must not be awaited in a loop, which turns six round trips into a sum rather than a maximum.

The 400ms freeze is JSON.parse, and no amount of async will help. This is the point people miss about asynchrony: await does not make anything parallel, it only lets other tasks run while something else is pending. JSON.parse is synchronous CPU work on the main thread, so it blocks layout, paint and input for its whole duration regardless of how many awaits surround it (§12.1). It is a 400ms INP failure.

A worker fixes it, with a caveat:

// main thread
const parser = new Worker(new URL('./parse-worker.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' });

function parseInWorker(text) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const id = crypto.randomUUID();
    parser.addEventListener('message', function onMsg(e) {
      if (e.data.id !== id) return;                 // one worker, many outstanding jobs
      parser.removeEventListener('message', onMsg);
      e.data.error ? reject(new Error(e.data.error)) : resolve(e.data.value);
    });
    parser.postMessage({ id, text });
  });
}

async function loadWidgets(urls, { signal } = {}) {
  return Promise.allSettled(urls.map(async (url) => {
    const res = await fetch(url, { signal });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${url} -> ${res.status}`);
    return parseInWorker(await res.text());
  }));
}

// parse-worker.js
self.addEventListener('message', (e) => {
  const { id, text } = e.data;
  try { self.postMessage({ id, value: JSON.parse(text) }); }
  catch (err) { self.postMessage({ id, error: err.message }); }
});

The caveat is the message boundary. The worker parses off the main thread, but the resulting object must be structured-cloned back, and cloning a large object is itself main-thread work — so a worker that parses 20MB and returns the whole object may save less than it costs. It wins when the worker returns something smaller than what it received: the aggregate the widget actually renders, not the raw payload. Moving the reduction into the worker is what makes the pattern pay.

What is necessary and why, in one list. allSettled so one dead endpoint does not blank the dashboard. .map before await so the six requests overlap. A correlation id per message because one worker serves many concurrent jobs and message events carry no reply channel. removeEventListener in the handler, or the listeners accumulate one per parse — a real leak in a dashboard that refreshes. And a signal threaded through so navigating away cancels the fetches (§12.12).

The alternative worth knowing: if the server can be changed, streaming newline-delimited JSON (§17.2) removes the problem entirely rather than relocating it — each line is parsed as it arrives, so no single parse is ever long enough to block a frame, and the first widget renders before the last byte has been received.

SECTION 18

Capstone: Build a Real Application, Then Harden It

Seventeen sections of mechanism are worth nothing until they meet an application that has to work. This section is a single build, carried from an empty directory to something you would ship: a task manager that runs in the browser and

  • loads its data from a network API;
  • keeps working while offline;
  • renders a list without leaking memory;
  • validates a form using the platform's own engine;
  • can be used entirely from a keyboard.

Build it as you read. Every stage names the sections it draws on, so when a stage misbehaves you have a place to go back to rather than a search. The code here is real and runs. The parts that need a browser are marked, and the parts that need a server are replaced with stand-ins, so the logic can still be tested.

The final three stages are the ones that matter most, and the ones usually skipped:

  1. an audit against what the earlier sections measured;
  2. a set of tests;
  3. a list of the things that would still be wrong.

18.1 The Brief

Data
Tasks come from a JSON API. A failed request must not blank the list. Two overlapping loads must not render out of order.
Rendering
A list of any length, filterable, with no XSS sink and no layout thrashing. Adding a task must not rebuild the world.
Input
One delegated listener for the whole list. A form using constraint validation. Search that debounces and cancels.
Lifetime
Every listener, timer and request removable in one call. Nothing retained after teardown.
Delivery
ES modules, a lockfile, a test suite, a CI pipeline, and a feature-detected enhancement that degrades cleanly.

18.2 The Model

Start with the data, with no DOM and no network: a pure module that can be tested in milliseconds (§5.5).

export class Task {
  #done = false;
  constructor({ id, title, due = null }) {
    if (!Number.isInteger(id)) throw new TypeError(`id must be an integer, got ${JSON.stringify(id)}`);
    if (typeof title !== 'string' || !title.trim()) throw new TypeError('title is required');
    this.id = id;
    this.title = title.trim();
    this.due = due;                                   // an ISO date string, never a Date (§10.5)
  }
  get done() { return this.#done; }
  toggle() { this.#done = !this.#done; return this; }
  static isTask(value) { return typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && #done in value; }
  toJSON() { return { id: this.id, title: this.title, due: this.due, done: this.#done }; }
}

const t = new Task({ id: 1, title: '  Write the capstone  ' });
console.log('trimmed:', JSON.stringify(t));
console.log('toggled:', t.toggle().done);
console.log('brand check beats duck typing:', Task.isTask(t), Task.isTask({ id: 1, done: false }));
console.log('validation fails fast:',
  (() => { try { new Task({ id: '1', title: 'x' }); } catch (e) { return e.constructor.name; } })());

trimmed: {"id":1,"title":"Write the capstone","due":null,"done":false}
toggled: true
brand check beats duck typing: true false
validation fails fast: TypeError

Four decisions, each taken from an earlier section:

  • A private field with a getter (§7.6) means code outside the class can read done but not change it; only toggle() can.
  • A brand check with #done in value (§7.4) cannot be faked by a plain object. instanceof would also reject a plain object, but duck typing would accept one.
  • toJSON (§2.13) keeps serialisation together with the type, so a private field can still be saved.
  • And validation in the constructor (§13.7) means an invalid Task cannot exist at all.

18.3 The Store

export class TaskStore extends EventTarget {
  #byId = new Map();                                  // keys are data, so a Map (§8.11)
  add(task) {
    this.#byId.set(task.id, task);
    this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('change', { detail: { size: this.#byId.size } }));
    return this;
  }
  remove(id) {
    const existed = this.#byId.delete(id);
    if (existed) this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('change', { detail: { size: this.#byId.size } }));
    return existed;
  }
  get(id) { return this.#byId.get(id); }
  get size() { return this.#byId.size; }
  *[Symbol.iterator]() { yield* this.#byId.values(); }
  filter(predicate) { return [...this].filter(predicate); }
}

const store = new TaskStore();
const changes = [];
store.addEventListener('change', (e) => changes.push(e.detail.size));
store.add({ id: 1, title: 'a', done: false }).add({ id: 2, title: 'b', done: true });
console.log('iterable because of Symbol.iterator:', [...store].map(t => t.title).join(','));
console.log('change events fired with sizes:', changes.join(','));
console.log('remove returns whether it existed:', store.remove(1), store.remove(99));
console.log('final size:', store.size);

iterable because of Symbol.iterator: a,b
change events fired with sizes: 1,2
remove returns whether it existed: true false
final size: 1

Extending EventTarget (§16.7) gives the store the platform's own vocabulary for observers, so code that uses it calls addEventListener with an AbortSignal, instead of a home-made subscribe. Symbol.iterator as a generator method (§11.2) makes the store spreadable and loopable in three lines. And a Map rather than an object (§8.11), because ids are data: an object would reorder integer keys, and an id could collide with constructor.

18.4 Loading, With Failure and Races Handled

export async function loadTasks(url, { signal, fetchImpl = fetch } = {}) {
  const res = await fetchImpl(url, { headers: { Accept: 'application/json' }, signal });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${url} -> HTTP ${res.status}`);      // fetch does not reject (§17.1)
  const raw = await res.json();
  if (!Array.isArray(raw)) throw new TypeError('expected an array of tasks');
  return raw;
}

export function createLoader(store, { onError = () => {} } = {}) {
  let inFlight = null;
  return async function load(url, options = {}) {
    inFlight?.abort();                                 // cancel the superseded request (§12.12)
    const controller = new AbortController();
    inFlight = controller;
    try {
      const tasks = await loadTasks(url, { ...options, signal: controller.signal });
      if (controller !== inFlight) return null;        // a stale response (§12.13)
      for (const t of tasks) store.add(t);
      return tasks.length;
    } catch (error) {
      if (error.name === 'AbortError') return null;    // cancellation is not a failure
      onError(error);                                  // the list is NOT blanked
      return null;
    }
  };
}

// A minimal stand-in for §18.3's store, so this block runs on its own.
const makeStore = () => ({ items: [], add(t) { this.items.push(t); }, get size() { return this.items.length; } });

const fakeFetch = async (url) => url.includes('bad')
  ? new Response('nope', { status: 500 })
  : new Response(JSON.stringify([{ id: 1, title: 'from the api' }]), { status: 200 });

const apiStore = makeStore();
const errors = [];
const load = createLoader(apiStore, { onError: (e) => errors.push(e.message) });
console.log('loaded:', await load('/api/tasks', { fetchImpl: fakeFetch }), '| store size:', apiStore.size);
console.log('a 500 is reported, not thrown at the caller:', await load('/api/bad', { fetchImpl: fakeFetch }));
console.log('and the store is untouched:', apiStore.size, '| errors:', errors);

loaded: 1 | store size: 1
a 500 is reported, not thrown at the caller: null
and the store is untouched: 1 | errors: [ '/api/bad -> HTTP 500' ]

fetchImpl as an injected parameter (passed in, rather than used directly) is what makes this testable with no network and no mocking library (§14.16). The fake is a stub that returns ready-made Response objects, which are ordinary values you can construct (§17.1).

All three failure behaviours from the brief are here. First, a 500 is an error, because res.ok is checked. Second, the list is not blanked, because the catch reports the error instead of returning []. Third, a stale response is discarded by comparing tokens, while the request it replaced is actually aborted, not merely ignored.

18.5 Rendering

export function renderTasks(container, tasks) {
  const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();   // one insertion, one layout (§15.4)
  for (const task of tasks) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.className = 'task';
    li.dataset.id = task.id;                            // escaped by construction (§15.8)
    li.dataset.done = String(task.done);

    const label = document.createElement('label');
    const box = document.createElement('input');
    box.type = 'checkbox';
    box.checked = task.done;
    box.dataset.action = 'toggle';

    const text = document.createElement('span');
    text.textContent = task.title;                      // text, never markup (§15.6)

    const remove = document.createElement('button');
    remove.type = 'button';
    remove.dataset.action = 'remove';
    remove.textContent = 'Delete';
    remove.setAttribute('aria-label', `Delete ${task.title}`);

    label.append(box, text);
    li.append(label, remove);
    fragment.append(li);
  }
  container.replaceChildren(fragment);                  // clear and fill in one operation
  return container.children.length;
}

document.body.innerHTML = '<ul id="list"></ul>';
const list = document.getElementById('list');
const hostile = { id: 7, title: '<img src=x onerror="steal()">', done: false };
console.log('rendered rows:', renderTasks(list, [{ id: 1, title: 'Real task', done: true }, hostile]));
console.log('the hostile title is TEXT, not markup:', list.querySelectorAll('img').length, 'img elements');
console.log('it round-trips intact:', list.lastElementChild.querySelector('span').textContent);
console.log('and the id is on the row for delegation:', list.firstElementChild.dataset.id);

rendered rows: 2
the hostile title is TEXT, not markup: 0 img elements
it round-trips intact: <img src=x onerror="steal()">
and the id is on the row for delegation: 1

Zero <img> elements, from a title designed to create one. That is §15.6's measurement put to use: textContent runs no parser, so there is nothing to inject into. And the title is kept exactly as written, where a sanitiser would have stripped it.

No innerHTML += anywhere. A DocumentFragment groups the insertions and replaceChildren swaps the contents in one step (§15.4), so n rows cost one layout rather than n.

18.6 One Listener for the Whole List

export function wireList(container, store, { signal, onChange = () => {} } = {}) {
  container.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
    const control = event.target.closest('[data-action]');       // not .matches (§16.6)
    if (!control || !container.contains(control)) return;
    const row = control.closest('[data-id]');
    if (!row) return;
    const id = Number(row.dataset.id);                            // dataset is always a string (§15.8)
    if (control.dataset.action === 'remove') store.remove(id);
    if (control.dataset.action === 'toggle') store.get(id)?.toggle();
    onChange(control.dataset.action, id);
  }, { signal });
}

document.body.innerHTML = `<ul id="l">
  <li data-id="3"><button data-action="remove"><span id="icon">x</span></button></li>
</ul>`;
const container = document.getElementById('l');
// A stand-in with just the two methods wireList calls.
const listStore = {
  rows: new Map([[3, { toggle() { return this; } }]]),
  get size() { return this.rows.size; },
  get(id) { return this.rows.get(id); },
  remove(id) { return this.rows.delete(id); },
};
const seen = [];
const ac = new AbortController();
wireList(container, listStore, { signal: ac.signal, onChange: (a, id) => seen.push(`${a}:${id}`) });

document.getElementById('icon').click();                          // click the ICON, not the button
console.log('a click on the inner span still resolved to the action:', seen.join(','));
console.log('the store was updated:', listStore.size);
ac.abort();
document.querySelector('[data-action]')?.click();
console.log('after abort, no further handling:', seen.join(','));

a click on the inner span still resolved to the action: remove:3
the store was updated: 0
after abort, no further handling: remove:3

The click landed on the <span>, and closest() walked up to the button: the exact bug §16.1 opened with, avoided by using closest instead of matches. One listener serves every row, including rows that do not exist yet (§16.6), and abort() removes it without needing a reference to the handler (§16.2).

18.7 The Form

// A stand-in for §18.2's Task and §18.3's store, so this block runs on its own.
const makeTask = ({ id, title }) => ({ id, title: title.trim() });
const makeFormStore = () => ({
  items: [],
  add(t) { this.items.push(t); },
  get size() { return this.items.length; },
  [Symbol.iterator]() { return this.items[Symbol.iterator](); },
});

export function wireForm(form, store, { signal, nextId = () => Date.now(), Task = makeTask } = {}) {
  form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
    event.preventDefault();                                       // stop the navigation (§16.10)
    const data = new FormData(form);
    const title = String(data.get('title') ?? '');
    const field = form.elements.title;
    field.setCustomValidity('');                                  // clear before re-checking (§16.11)
    if (title.trim().length < 3) {
      field.setCustomValidity('A task needs at least three characters.');
      return;
    }
    store.add(Task({ id: nextId(), title }));
    form.reset();
  }, { signal });
}

document.body.innerHTML = `<form id="f">
  <input name="title" required minlength="3" value="Ship it">
  <button>Add</button>
</form>`;
const form = document.getElementById('f');
const formStore = makeFormStore();
let counter = 100;
wireForm(form, formStore, { nextId: () => counter++ });
form.requestSubmit();                                             // fires submit and validates (§16.10)
console.log('added:', formStore.size, '| title:', [...formStore][0].title);
console.log('the form was reset:', JSON.stringify(form.elements.title.value));

added: 1 | title: Ship it
the form was reset: "Ship it"

Look at the last line. form.reset() did not empty the field; it put it back to "Ship it", the value of the value attribute in the markup. That is §15.7's attribute-versus-property distinction with a practical consequence: reset() restores defaults, and the default is whatever the markup declared. A form rendered with pre-filled values resets to those values, not to empty, which is correct and regularly surprising.

requestSubmit() rather than submit(), so that the submit event fires and constraint validation runs. FormData rather than reading .value, so the browser's own submission rules apply (§16.10). And setCustomValidity('') before every check, because otherwise customError stays set and the field stays invalid forever (§16.11).

The declarative required and minlength="3" do the ordinary work, and the JavaScript adds only the rule that HTML cannot express.

18.8 Search, Debounced and Cancelled

export function wireSearch(input, { signal, onResults, search }) {
  let inFlight = null;
  const run = async (term) => {
    inFlight?.abort();
    if (!term.trim()) { onResults([]); return; }
    const controller = new AbortController();
    inFlight = controller;
    try {
      const results = await search(term, controller.signal);
      if (controller === inFlight) onResults(results);
    } catch (error) {
      if (error.name !== 'AbortError') onResults([], error);
    }
  };
  const debounced = debounce(run, 30);
  input.addEventListener('input', () => debounced(input.value), { signal });
  return run;
}

function debounce(fn, ms) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => { clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms); };
}

document.body.innerHTML = '<input id="q">';
const input = document.getElementById('q');
let calls = 0;
const rendered = [];
// Wait for the render rather than for a fixed number of milliseconds, so the
// demonstration cannot race the timers (§12.13).
const { promise: firstRender, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers();
const search = async (term) => { calls++; await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 5)); return [term]; };
wireSearch(input, {
  search,
  onResults: (r) => { rendered.push(r.join('')); resolve(); },
});

for (const value of ['s', 'sh', 'shi', 'ship']) { input.value = value; input.dispatchEvent(new Event('input')); }
await firstRender;
console.log('four keystrokes produced', calls, 'request(s)');
console.log('and rendered:', JSON.stringify(rendered));

four keystrokes produced 1 request(s)
and rendered: ["ship"]

Four keystrokes, one request, and the value shown is the last search term. Debounce collapses the burst of keystrokes into one call (§5.10), the token check discards a stale response, and the abort stops the superseded request instead of merely ignoring it (§12.12).

Note that input.value = value fires nothing by itself. The explicit dispatchEvent is required, as §16.8 measured, and it is exactly what a test for this code must do.

18.9 Composing It, With One Teardown

// Compact local versions of §18.3, §18.5, §18.6 and §18.7, so this block runs on its own.
class MiniStore extends EventTarget {
  #byId = new Map();
  add(t) { this.#byId.set(t.id, t); this.dispatchEvent(new Event('change')); return this; }
  get size() { return this.#byId.size; }
  *[Symbol.iterator]() { yield* this.#byId.values(); }
}
const render = (list, tasks) => list.replaceChildren(
  ...tasks.map((t) => Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { textContent: t.title })));
const wireAdd = (form, store, signal, nextId) => form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  const title = String(new FormData(form).get('title') ?? '').trim();
  if (title.length >= 3) { store.add({ id: nextId(), title }); form.reset(); }
}, { signal });

export function createApp(root, { store = new MiniStore() } = {}) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const { signal } = controller;

  const list = root.querySelector('[data-list]');
  const form = root.querySelector('[data-form]');

  wireAdd(form, store, signal, (() => { let n = 1; return () => n++; })());
  store.addEventListener('change', () => render(list, [...store]), { signal });

  return {
    store,
    destroy() {
      controller.abort();          // every listener on three different targets, in one call
      list.replaceChildren();
    },
  };
}

document.body.innerHTML = `<div id="app">
  <form data-form><input name="title" required minlength="3" value="First task"><button>Add</button></form>
  <ul data-list></ul>
</div>`;
const app = createApp(document.getElementById('app'));
document.querySelector('[data-form]').requestSubmit();
console.log('rendered rows after submit:', document.querySelector('[data-list]').children.length);
app.destroy();
document.querySelector('[data-form]').requestSubmit();
console.log('after destroy — store size:', app.store.size,
            '| rendered rows:', document.querySelector('[data-list]').children.length);

rendered rows after submit: 1
after destroy — store size: 1 | rendered rows: 0

One AbortController owns everything: a listener on the list, one on the form, and one on the store. The store is itself an EventTarget, so it accepts the same signal. destroy() is a single abort(), and it cannot leave a listener behind, because there is no per-listener cleanup to forget (§3.11).

18.10 A Feature-Detected Enhancement

function renderRows(list, tasks) {
  list.replaceChildren(...tasks.map((t) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = t.title;
    return li;
  }));
}
export function update(list, tasks) {
  const apply = () => renderRows(list, tasks);
  if (typeof document.startViewTransition !== 'function') return apply();   // the plain path
  return document.startViewTransition(apply).finished;
}
document.body.innerHTML = '<ul id="vt"></ul>';
const target = document.getElementById('vt');
update(target, [{ id: 1, title: 'a', done: false }, { id: 2, title: 'b', done: true }]);
console.log('rows rendered whether or not the API exists:', target.children.length);
console.log('the guard is the entire progressive-enhancement story:', typeof document.startViewTransition);

rows rendered whether or not the API exists: 2
the guard is the entire progressive-enhancement story: undefined

The verifier's DOM has no startViewTransition, so the fallback ran and the list was drawn anyway, which is exactly the property being shown (§15.14). An enhancement must be a branch around the working version, never something it depends on.

18.11 The Audit

Go through the application against what the earlier sections measured. Each line is a question with an answer you can check.

1
Is there an XSS sink? Search for innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML and eval. Every one must take a literal, never a value (§15.6).
2
Does every fetch check res.ok? A 404 fulfils (§17.1).
3
Can two loads render out of order? Every async render path needs a token check or an abort (§12.13).
4
Is every listener removable? One AbortController per component, aborted on teardown (§16.2).
5
Is anything retained after teardown? Detached nodes in a Map, an uncleared interval, a listener on window (§3.11).
6
Does any loop read a layout value? offsetWidth or getBoundingClientRect after a write is 17× slower (§15.12).
7
Is any await sequential that should be parallel? Start everything, then await (§12.10).
8
Is every promise chain terminated? An unhandled rejection is reported once and then invisible (§12.11).
9
Does || appear where ?? was meant? A legitimate 0 or '' is silently replaced (§4.2).
10
Is money a float, or a date a Date? Integer minor units, and ISO strings for calendar dates (§2.15, §10.5).
11
Can it be used from a keyboard? Real <button> elements, focus moved on route change, focus restored on close (§16.12).
12
Does every enhancement degrade? A feature test with a working fallback, not a requirement (§1.11).

Run the audit against the application above and it passes eleven of the twelve points. The twelfth is deliberately failed, and finding it is the exercise. renderTasks is called on every change event, so adding one task redraws the entire list. That is correct but wasteful, and §18.13 says what to do about it.

18.12 Testing It

// tasks.test.js — run with `node --test`
const testFile = `
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { Task, TaskStore, createLoader } from './tasks.js';

test('a Task validates its input', () => {
  assert.throws(() => new Task({ id: '1', title: 'x' }), TypeError);
  assert.equal(new Task({ id: 1, title: '  a  ' }).title, 'a');
});

test('the store emits change events', () => {
  const store = new TaskStore();
  const sizes = [];
  store.addEventListener('change', (e) => sizes.push(e.detail.size));
  store.add({ id: 1 }).add({ id: 2 });
  assert.deepEqual(sizes, [1, 2]);
});

test('a failed load does not blank the store', async () => {
  const store = new TaskStore();
  store.add({ id: 1, title: 'existing' });
  const errors = [];
  const load = createLoader(store, { onError: (e) => errors.push(e) });
  await load('/bad', { fetchImpl: async () => new Response('', { status: 500 }) });
  assert.equal(store.size, 1);
  assert.equal(errors.length, 1);
});
`;
console.log('test cases:', testFile.match(/^test\(/gm).length);
console.log('no test framework, no mocking library, no DOM required');

test cases: 3
no test framework, no mocking library, no DOM required

Every one of those tests runs without a browser, because the model, the store and the loader were written with no dependency on the DOM, and the loader receives its fetch as a parameter (§18.4). That is the reward for the layering: the parts with the most logic are the easiest to test, and the parts that depend on the DOM are thin enough to cover with a handful of Playwright tests (§14.16).

The pipeline is the one from §14.17: npm ci, npm run lint, npm test, npm run build, cheapest first.

18.13 What Is Still Wrong

Being able to name a system's remaining weaknesses is the difference between finishing something and abandoning it.

It re-renders the whole list on every change. That is correct, and costs O(n) per keystroke on a long list (the work grows with the length). The honest fixes, in order: batch the changes into one render per frame with requestAnimationFrame (§12.4); or compare old and new and update only the rows that changed; or use a rendering library, which is what they exist for.

There is no offline story. The brief asked for one, and §17.10 has the mechanism: a service worker, cache-first for assets whose file names contain a content hash, and network-first for page loads. But adding it changes how the app is deployed, so it is a deliberate second milestone, not an oversight.

Nothing is persisted. localStorage (§17.6) is one line, and the wrong answer for anything large or used constantly, because it is synchronous. IndexedDB (§17.7) is the right answer, and enough work to be a stage of its own.

Errors go to a callback and no further. A real application reports them (§13.11): an unhandledrejection listener, a window.onerror listener, and an error monitor with the source maps uploaded.

There is no virtualisation. Virtualisation means drawing only the rows currently visible. Ten thousand rows means ten thousand DOM nodes. IntersectionObserver (§15.13) with a render limited to a window of rows is the fix, and it is only worth doing once the list really is long.

Accessibility is checked but not tested. The buttons are real buttons with accessible names, but nothing verifies that automatically. An axe-core check in the Playwright suite is what turns it from an intention into a guarantee.

That list is the honest state of the build, and every item on it names the section that solves it. The measure of this course is not that the application is finished — it is that you can read that list, understand every entry, and know what you would do about each one.

18.14 What This Section Established

  1. Layering by dependency is what makes an application testable. The model, the store and the loader have no DOM and no network, so three tests run in milliseconds with no framework and no mocks.
  2. A private field plus a getter makes state one-way, and #field in value is a brand check no plain object can forge.
  3. Injecting fetch as a parameter removes the need for a mocking library entirely.
  4. The three loading failures each need their own fix: res.ok for a 500, reporting rather than returning [] so the list is not blanked, and a token plus an abort for the race.
  5. textContent produced zero <img> elements from a title designed to create one, and preserved it exactly.
  6. A DocumentFragment plus replaceChildren makes n rows cost one layout.
  7. closest() resolved a click on an inner <span> to its button — one delegated listener for a list of any length, including rows not yet created.
  8. requestSubmit() fires validation where submit() bypasses it, and setCustomValidity('') must clear before every check.
  9. Four keystrokes produced one request, with the stale response discarded and the superseded request aborted.
  10. One AbortController tore down listeners on three different targets — including the store, because it extends EventTarget.
  11. A feature-detected enhancement rendered correctly with the API absent, which is the whole progressive-enhancement story.
  12. A twelve-point audit turns "does it work" into twelve questions with checkable answers, and the ability to name what is still wrong is the point of the exercise.

Exercises

1. The audit in §18.11 says the application fails point 6 in one place if you are not careful. Find where a layout read could creep into renderTasks, and write the version that would be wrong.

Solution

The trap is any per-row measurement. renderTasks as written never reads geometry, but the natural next requirement — "truncate the title to fit", "set each row's height to match its content", "highlight rows below the fold" — introduces one, and the naive implementation interleaves reads and writes:

// WRONG — a forced synchronous layout per row (§15.12).
function renderAndFitWrong(container, tasks) {
  renderTasks(container, tasks);
  for (const row of container.children) {
    row.style.setProperty('--w', row.offsetWidth + 'px');   // read after the previous write
  }
}

// RIGHT — one read phase, then one write phase.
function renderAndFit(container, tasks) {
  renderTasks(container, tasks);
  const rows = [...container.children];
  const widths = rows.map(r => r.offsetWidth);              // all reads
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {                             // writes, just before the frame
    rows.forEach((r, i) => r.style.setProperty('--w', widths[i] + 'px'));
  });
}
document.body.innerHTML = '<ul id="fit"></ul>';
const c = document.getElementById('fit');
renderAndFit(c, [{ id: 1, title: 'a', done: false }, { id: 2, title: 'b', done: false }]);
console.log('both versions produce the same DOM:', c.children.length, 'rows');
console.log('the difference is entirely in the ordering of reads and writes');

both versions produce the same DOM: 2 rows
the difference is entirely in the ordering of reads and writes

Why the wrong one is wrong. Each style.setProperty marks layout dirty; each offsetWidth on the next iteration forces the browser to recompute the whole document to answer. §15.12 measured that pattern at 1086ms against 62ms for 500 elements — 17.6× — and the code does exactly the same work either way.

Why the right one is right, in two steps. Separating the phases means one layout for the whole loop instead of n. Putting the writes in requestAnimationFrame (§12.4) lands them immediately before the browser's own layout pass, so there is nothing extra to flush.

And the better answer is not to measure at all. Every requirement in the list above — fit to content, match height, respond to width — is something CSS expresses directly with aspect-ratio, container queries and text-overflow, computed during a layout that was going to happen anyway. When JavaScript measures the DOM in order to write a style back into it, the first question is whether CSS can state the relationship instead (§15.12's exercise). The cases where it genuinely cannot — measuring text to decide a truncation point, positioning against an element in a different subtree — are where the read/write discipline earns its keep.

2. Add offline support to the application. Say what changes, what breaks, and what you would test.

Solution

Three changes, and the third is the one people forget.

A service worker with two strategies (§17.10). Cache-first for hashed static assets, because the URL changes when the content does; network-first with a cached fallback for navigations and for the API, because stale data is better than nothing and a cache-first HTML entry point can ship an app that cannot update itself.

A local write queue. Offline support that only reads is half a feature: a user who adds a task offline expects it to survive. That means writes go to IndexedDB (§17.7) with a pending flag and are replayed when connectivity returns — which is a real design change, not a configuration.

An honest UI state. The application now has three states rather than two — fresh, stale, and offline-with-pending-writes — and hiding that from the user is how a task appears to save and then vanishes. navigator.onLine plus the online/offline events drive it, treated as a hint rather than a guarantee (§17.10).

What breaks.

Deployment becomes stateful. A user can be running last week's service worker against this week's API, so the API needs versioning and the worker needs skipWaiting reasoned about rather than copied.

Debugging gets harder. Requests you never see in the network panel are being answered from a cache, and a hard reload does not necessarily bypass a service worker. "Update on reload" and "Bypass for network" in devtools become part of the daily loop.

Every cached response is a decision with an expiry, and there is no correct default. An unbounded cache grows until the origin's quota is exceeded, which surfaces as a QuotaExceededError for your heaviest users only.

Tests must handle the ordering. A test that asserts on a network response now races the cache.

What I would test.

Unit — the queue logic with a fake IndexedDB and a fake clock: a write while offline is queued; a replay after reconnection is idempotent, so a retried write does not create two tasks (§12.14).

Integration — the service worker's fetch handler directly, with constructed Request objects (§17.1), asserting that a POST is never served from cache and that a navigation falls back to the offline page.

End-to-end, and this is the one that catches the real bugs — Playwright with context.setOffline(true): load the app, go offline, add a task, reload, assert the task is still there, go online, assert it reaches the server exactly once.

And a deliberate update test: deploy version 2 while a tab is open on version 1, and assert the tab converges rather than getting stuck. That is the failure §14's exercise describes, and it is only ever found by testing the transition rather than either version.

3. Someone reviewing this application says "you should have used a framework". Give the honest answer.

Solution

They are probably right, and the reason matters more than the conclusion.

What a framework would have replaced here is §18.5 and §18.9 — the rendering and the composition — and nothing else. The model, the store, the loader, the race handling, the debounce, the validation and the teardown discipline are all still needed, all still written by hand, and all still exactly what §18.2–§18.8 built. A framework is not a substitute for knowing any of it; that is the honest core of the answer.

What it genuinely buys, in order of value:

Declarative rendering. §18.13's first admission is that the application re-renders everything on every change. A framework's whole purpose is to make "describe the output for this state" cheap and correct, and doing that well by hand is a large project.

A component boundary. createApp composes three wirings by hand; at thirty components that is a build system of your own invention, worse-documented than an existing one.

Ecosystem and hiring. Routing, forms, data fetching and testing utilities exist and are maintained, and a new colleague already knows the conventions.

What it costs, which is a real list and not a rhetorical one: a build step, a dependency tree (§14.11), a runtime, a version treadmill, and an abstraction that eventually leaks — at which point you need exactly the material in this course to see through it.

When not to reach for one: a widget embedded in someone else's page, a page where startup cost dominates, a library other people will consume, or an interface simple enough that the framework is most of the bundle. Custom elements plus shadow DOM (§17.13–§17.14) cover several of those honestly.

The reason to have built it this way at all, and the real answer to the reviewer: every bug this application avoids is a bug a framework does not avoid for you. A framework will not check res.ok, will not discard a stale response, will not stop you putting user text through innerHTML, will not clean up a listener on window, and will not tell you that || overwrote a legitimate 0. Those failures appear in production applications built with every framework there is, and the reason is that they are language- and platform-level, not rendering-level.

So the mature answer is: yes, use a framework — and understand that it solves the second-hardest part of this list. Choosing it deliberately, knowing what it does and does not cover, is a different act from reaching for it because you would not know how to proceed otherwise. That difference is what the last seventeen sections were for.

You started this course able to write JavaScript. You now know what the runtime, the engine that executes your code, actually does with it. That is the difference between code that works on your machine and code you can be trusted with in production.

What you can now do

  1. Predict what a value will do before running it. Eight types, eight falsy values, and a coercion algorithm (the rules for converting between types) you can apply by hand. [] == false is true after three conversions. 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 because IEEE 754, the standard for storing numbers in binary, says so. An id above 2⁵³ arrives from JSON.parse already corrupted.
  2. Read a scope chain and see what it keeps alive. The scope chain is the list of places a function looks for a variable. var gives one binding (one variable slot) per loop, and let gives one per iteration. The TDZ, the temporal dead zone before a let line runs, turns a silent undefined into a loud ReferenceError. The four leak shapes are a listener never removed, a detached node, a cache that is never pruned, and a timer that is never cleared, and all four are one reference someone forgot they held.
  3. Answer any this question in five seconds. Check the five rules in this order: lexical (an arrow function takes this from the code around it), new, explicit, implicit, default. A bound function cannot be rebound, and every .bind() returns a new object. A normal event handler's this is the element, which is why this.name reads the button's own empty name instead of throwing.
  4. Choose the right collection. A plain object for a record, a Map when keys are data, a Set when the question is "is this in it?", a WeakMap when the entry should disappear with its key, a typed array when you hold bytes. set.has is O(1), meaning it takes the same time however big the set is, and array.includes is O(n), meaning it gets slower as the array grows. Inside a loop, that choice is the difference between linear time and quadratic time (time that grows with the square of the size).
  5. See through the class syntax to the link underneath. One prototype link, one lookup rule, and everything else (extends, super, instanceof, mixins) is an arrangement of it. A private field is not a property. That makes #field in obj the only brand check, a test of "was this object made by my class?", that nothing can forge.
  6. Reason about text as the platform actually stores it. One string can have three different lengths. .charCodeAt can return half a surrogate pair, one of the two slots used for a character such as an emoji. There are two encodings of é that are not equal until normalised (converted to one standard form). btoa of héllo produces valid base64 of the wrong bytes, silently.
  7. Write a regular expression that finishes. /g makes a regex stateful: it remembers where it stopped. .match with /g discards capture groups. A negative lookahead after a quantifier can backtrack (go back and try a shorter match) into a false positive. Catastrophic backtracking, where the attempts multiply out of control, went from imperceptible to 50ms with twelve more characters.
  8. Run the event loop in your head. One task, then every microtask (small follow-up jobs, such as the code after an await), then perhaps a frame. await on a resolved promise costs one tick and not two. Sequential awaits took three time units where Promise.all took one. .forEach with an async callback returns before anything has finished.
  9. Cancel work rather than ignoring it. One AbortController stops a fetch, removes a listener and closes a component. The difference from Promise.race is whether the underlying work actually stops.
  10. Change the DOM without breaking it. Use textContent for text and setHTML() for markup, because an inserted <script> does not run while an <img onerror> does. getComputedStyle returns used values (the final numbers after layout) and forces the browser to recalculate layout first. Interleaving reads with writes measured 17.6× slower than batching them.
  11. Handle input the way the platform expects. One delegated listener, a single listener on a parent that handles events from all its children, combined with closest(). FormData for the submission rules you would otherwise rewrite yourself. And the browser's own validation engine, which is localised, announced to screen readers and styleable, instead of a hand-rolled one.
  12. Use the platform's own building blocks rather than a library's. Structured clone, the browser's built-in way of copying data, moves data between a worker, a tab and IndexedDB (the browser's database). Custom elements and shadow DOM give you components with no framework. Intl formats numbers, dates, lists and plurals correctly in languages you do not speak.
  13. Fail loudly and diagnose quickly. cause keeps the original error. JSON.stringify(error) is {}, so a logger must unpack the error itself. A conditional breakpoint, which pauses only when a condition is true, replaces a logging statement in a hot loop with no edit and no reload.
  14. Ship it. Modules with live bindings (an import always sees the exporter's current value) and a defined evaluation order. A lockfile and npm ci, so every install gets the same versions. Tree shaking, which removes unused code and needs ESM. A test suite, with the vocabulary to describe what each test double replaces. And a pipeline that runs the cheapest checks first, so it fails early.

Where to go next

Some of this is still changing, and those parts are worth watching rather than learning once:

  • Temporal, the new date and time API, is in two engines and not yet the third. Today it needs a polyfill (a library that adds the missing feature); tomorrow it replaces all of §10.
  • Iterator helpers and Math.sumPrecise have only just reached Baseline, meaning every major current browser supports them.
  • The Navigation API is replacing pushState.
  • The Sanitizer API is replacing every hand-rolled escape function.

The two habits that keep this knowledge current are smaller than they sound.

When you reach for a workaround you learned more than a year ago, check whether it is still needed. || for defaults, a library for deep equality, a polyfill for fetch, a bundler for a bare specifier (an import of a package by name, such as 'lodash'), a date library for a date: each was correct once, and several are not any more. The check costs a minute on MDN, and Baseline turns "is this safe?" from an opinion into a lookup.

And read what the runtime actually did. Every number in this course was measured rather than recalled, and a surprising number of them contradicted what is widely repeated:

  • process.nextTick does not always win.
  • cloneNode does copy a typed input's value.
  • RegExp.escape escapes a leading a.
  • form.reset() restores the markup's value rather than emptying the field.

The console, the debugger and a five-line probe are the whole method, and they will keep being right long after any particular fact here has changed.
